title: The Great ADHD Myth? review – the most controversial show of the year is here | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Dr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend many
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Dr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend many
Content: Having his ‘fun-ness’ taken away? … Mason on The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsView image in fullscreenHaving his ‘fun-ness’ taken away? … Mason on The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Great ADHD Myth? review – the most controversial show of the year is hereDr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend manyLucy ManganTue 18 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePresenter Max Pemberton, a psychiatrist in the NHS, Daily Mail columnist and author, and the experts he has assembled, waste no time in setting out their stall in The Great ADHD Myth?. This is a documentary that will incense and offend some of its viewers, and its scepticism regarding ADHD is clear from the outset. “It’s certainly not a medical condition as far as I’m concerned,” says the former president of the Royal College of General Practitioners, Dr Iona Heath. “We’re going to look back and think: did we actually put a chemical cosh on an entire developing generation of brains?” says a neurophysiological psychologist. “The industry around ADHD is about making money at the cost of the misery of others,” says a former president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists.These represent the three main questions raised by Pemberton. The first is whether ADHD is a neuro-developmental disorder – ie do those diagnosed with the condition have different brains from those without – or whether it is a way of suppressing natural tendencies (especially those of children) and inducing behaviours that society deems acceptable. The second is how doctors should approach treatment, which most often involves amphetamines. “These are controlled drugs,” says consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Sami Timimi. “There’s good reason why we warn the rest of the population [about them].” The third question is – who benefits from the increase in diagnoses we have seen in the past decade or so? How has ADHD moved from a relatively unknown condition 10 years ago to affecting about 2.5 million people in the UK today (including a 200% increase in people being referred for diagnosis in the past five years)?Pemberton interviews cognitive neuroscientist Prof Katya Rubia, who has 30 years of experience working with brain imaging. She says that there is no convincing data that “ADHD brains” are any different from “normal” brains. Others go through the list of diagnostic criteria, which include things such as finding it difficult to wait your turn, squirming in your seat and being unable to play quietly. The broadness with which the criteria are drawn means that, according to Dr Heath: “If you want the diagnosis, you will be able to get it.”View image in fullscreen‘Wastes no time in setting out his stall’ … Max Pemberton in The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsPemberton himself undergoes a £1,200 private assessment and comes away with a diagnosis of “combined” ADHD (impulsivity, hyperactivity, inattentiveness) and a prescription for medication. He takes a dose to see what it’s like and reports feeling blunted, not wanting to chat as he usually does (“The fact you’re here is quite irritating actually,” he tells the crew) and feeling as if he could happily sit quietly alone. It’s a stunt, but, I suppose – much as I would love him to stick with the science and do a deeper dive on the data – an inevitable one.The main stunt, however, is following 10-year-old Mason as he comes off the ADHD meds he has been on for two years (“They take my fun-ness away”) for a six-week period to see if a programme of yoga, outdoor activities, no screen time and less processed food and sugar can help instead. It can. Mason, says his mother, Shauna, is funnier, happier, more of a character, more himself. But he is more trouble at school. His teacher says that seeing “his true, honest self” is more important than him being easier to teach. His mother decides to keep him off the drugs.We live in a time when to question any prevailing orthodoxy will, in many cases, be met with an emotional outpouring. Casting any form of doubt on ADHD will absolutely not be the exception. But Pemberton answers his questions convincingly. And the redresses proposed – try changing diet, screen and activity levels first, making school curricula more flexible, and making drugs the last resort – seem neither radical nor uncompassionate. They seem, if primum non nocere (“first do no harm”) is your goal rather than profit (there is little money to be made in encouraging parents to take their children to the park), to be quite the opposite.The Great ADHD Myth? is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Things get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awareness | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Telling the country to enjoy the heat while it burns, you have to wonder if Tice has lost all sense of reality
Author: John Crace
Headline: Telling the country to enjoy the heat while it burns, you have to wonder if Tice has lost all sense of reality
Content: Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, mulls his next idiotic statement.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenReform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, mulls his next idiotic statement.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe politics sketchRichard TiceThings get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awarenessJohn CraceTelling the country to enjoy the heat while it burns, you have to wonder if Tice has lost all sense of realityTue 18 Aug 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThese are the doggiest of dog days. Times when hours turn into days and almost nothing happens in between. Days of precious R&R, when only a few politicians venture out, and then only to fend off accusations they are doing next to nothing and prove they are still alive. Much like the rest of us. The silliest days of the silly season. Days that are made for men likeRichard Tice.There are some politicians who have the gift of sounding as if they know what they are talking about. There are those who you suspect are bullshitting but still give the benefit of the doubt. Then there are the ones you only have to look at to know they are completely clueless in every way. Never within the same postcode as plausibility. A walking miracle because somehow they have managed to persuade their party association and constituency voters that what they really need is someone who is visibly dim and incompetent. August gives us space to celebrate these men and women. None more so than Dicky. The apex male of stupidity. The idiot’s idiot.It’s not clear if there has ever been much point to Dicky. Other than to encourage other halfwits that they can make half a name for themselves in public life providing they are blessed with plenty of cash and a total absence of self-awareness. Dicky likes to moan about diversity, equality and inclusion policies while remaining totally oblivious to the fact that were life to be a genuine meritocracy, he wouldn’t even make it to the starting line.But that’s not to say Dicky doesn’t have his uses. A man with no idea of his own limitations could be just what Nigel Farage was looking for. The perfect beta supplicant who could be relied upon to do whatever he was told. Just as long as the instructions were crystal clear. There were no complaints from Dicky when just before the 2024 general election, Nige decided he was going to be Reform party leader after all.Dicky knew his place. He smiled like the Mr Congeniality he hoped to be. Life was going quite well up untilthe Guardian revealed the £5m gift to Nigefrom Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Then the Sunday Times got in on the act with its reporting that if Farage became leader, Reform would repay or write off loans it received from Tice’s company in a deal presented by Farage andconvicted fraudster George Cottrell. Things really began to fall apart.The last few months haven’t been kind either to Reform or Dicky. One misstep after another. The party has been sliding in the polls, has called a byelection in Clacton which achieved little more than delaying aninvestigation by the parliamentary watchdogand handing 9,500 votes to a man with a bin on his head. As for Nige, he’s chosen to keep a much lower profile ever since he failed to come up with a plausible explanation for why he needed so much money. He didn’t even bother to attend the Clacton count, instead spending the night dancing with Dicky at Farage Fest.All of which has made life tricky for Dicky. Reform have needed someone to step up and fill the vacuum left by Nige and the only one who has been consistently available has been Tice. And replacing one vacuum with another doesn’t really cut it. Their combative home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf has been sidelined, Lee Anderson has kept a low profile and the others don’t really count. Nige had high hopes for Robert Jenrick but Reform’s ratings plummet every time Honest Bob makes an appearance.Which may be why Dicky was sent out with Honest Bob on Monday to try and dilute the animosity. Only it didn’t quite work out as Dicky rather stole Jenrick’s thunder. Because what people took away from Reform’s press conference wasn’t that Dicky would quite like benefits claimants to clean the high streets, it was thatDicky was thoroughly enjoying the extreme hot weather.1:29Not all 'doom and gloom': Reform's deputy leader downplays climate crisis – videoWhile the rest of the country was worried about drought and wildfires, and farmers were predicting armageddon, Dicky was having the time of his life. Forget the pint of beer that he has to drink when photographed with the riff-raff, Dicky was thrilled he would soon be able to neck vintage English fizzy wines that were better than champagne. When all things were considered, climate change was really just a state of mind. You could either get all doom and gloom about it. Or you could pretend it wasn’t really an issue, that attempts to combat it were a complete waste of time and try to make the most of it. We should all go out and have a barbecue. What was one more fire among so many?Now try to imagine just how half-witted you have to be to actually say that. It’s bad enough thinking it. After all, we know that Kemi Badenoch appears to have much the same attitude as she plans to throw any Tories who believe in net zero targets out of the party. But even she knows better than to say any of this while there is a national emergency in place: however much it goes against her better judgment. But Dicky has no such qualms. Just says it as he sees it. Why worry about the state of the planet in 25 years time? As far as he is concerned all we have is today. Make hay while the sun shines. Only we can’t because the fields are burned.So we are left with a conundrum. Were silly seasons always quite this silly? Does Dicky actually believe a word of what he says? Or has he infantilised himself so much by talking nonsense that he no longer knows what’s true. Or maybe he’s a secret agent, playing the long game to bring down Reform. The more you see of Dicky, the less there is.Explore more on these topicsRichard TiceThe politics sketchReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Brain-breaking sex, bad boys in leather and queer glory: why TV vampires are so intoxicating | Television | The Guardian
description: The Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced blood
Author: Kayleigh Dray
Headline: The Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced blood
Content: Sam Reid as the eponymous glam rocker in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudView image in fullscreenSam Reid as the eponymous glam rocker in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudTelevisionBrain-breaking sex, bad boys in leather and queer glory: why TV vampires are so intoxicatingThe Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced bloodKayleigh DrayTue 18 Aug 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want TV audiences to forgive a fictional man for absolutely anything, just sharpen his fangs and stick him in velvet. Case in point? The horny musical drama The Vampire Lestat, which became a cult hit in the US earlier this year. The show has now arrived in the UK and Sam Reid’s searing performance as Lestat has fans on their knees.The Vampire Lestat review – a mega-fun glam-rock musical … with bloodsuckingRead moreThe first two seasons, which went by the title Interview With the Vampire, were about the “interview” in which Louis (Jacob Anderson) tells a journalist about his toxic relationship with Lestat. Now, the focus has shifted to Lestat – hence the new title and new narrator – as the golden-locked prince of darkness swaps centuries of secrecy for glam-rock stardom.View image in fullscreenToxic love … Jacob Anderson as Louis de Pointe du Lac in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC All Rights Reserved/Sophie GiraudReid turned to bootlegs of David Bowie’s 1974 Cracked Actor tour for inspiration on the “showmanship, magic and mystery” needed to hypnotise an arena, with the result that Lestat now embodies a magnificent “dandy of the underworld” energy. He writhes, growls and grinds on stage as he plays the fiddle and belts out ridiculously campy songs. He wears glittery eyeshadow, his hair is in ribboned pigtails. He appears to have lost his shirt permanently and bares his scarred chest to adoring fans, while singing “Don’t wanna learn another TikTok dance/Wanna stay in bed, eating black liquorice” and “You can’t fuck away the loneliness / It’ll wait til you’re done / Til you come / Like a vampire”. Off-stage he is in a sexual relationship with his mother, gets high off LSD-laced blood and comes out with phrases such as: “I carry with me an immortal erection.”View image in fullscreenBreakthrough role … Alexander Skarsgård in True Blood.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIt’s not the first time a vampire has sucked in audiences. Eric Northman’s full-frontal glory as he lounges on an ice peak reading a book in True Blood was Alexander Skarsgård’s breakthrough role, while Lady Gaga’s The Countess in season five of American Horror Story proved that bloodlust is the ultimate couture accessory. Endlessly seductive vamps show up, too, in The Vampire Diaries, Supernatural and the entire cast ofWhat We Do in the Shadows, who are somehow ridiculously hot despite being total buffoons (Matt Berry has ruined normal men for me). Claes Bang in the BBC’s otherwise chaotic Dracula wasundeniably easy on the eye, and even Jeff’s fleeting stint as a vampire in Community’s Horror Fiction in Seven Spooky Steps episode sees Annie swoon over her tame bloodsucker, breathlessly sighing, “Look how much I’ve changed you!” when he begins quoting literature at her.View image in fullscreenHigh vamp … Lady Gaga as the Countess in American Horror Story: Hotel.Photograph: Suzanne Tenner/APWhy we are so hooked? Vampires embody absolute freedom, power, immortality, beauty and often forbidden love. They can also tap directly into our shadow selves, serving as the ultimate canvas for the toxic romantic tropes we secretly indulge in on screen. (Think about it: pop culture has long conditioned us to desire the romcom hero who relentlessly pursues a female lead despite being told no until he wears her down, such as Joe Fox (Tom Hanks) in You’ve Got Mail orJoe Goldberg (Penn Badgeley) in You.) When it comes to vampires as romantic figures, we’re leaning heavily into the ultimate “I can fix him” trope. What is more intoxicating than a dangerous immortal who wipes out entire towns, yet kneels at your feet?Just look at Spike inBuffy the Vampire Slayer– the ultimate leather-bound bad boy who is quite literally “changed” by the love of a good slayer. On the flipside, you have Angel, whose curse dictates that one night of mindblowing sex with Buffy literally breaks his brain, shatters his morality and turns him back into a psychopathic monster.View image in fullscreenMindblowing … Sarah Michelle Gellar as Buffy and David Boreanaz as Angel in Buffy the Vampire Slayer.Photograph: 1997 Twentieth Century Fox Film CorporationAnd there’s even more beneath the surface level of camp leather jackets, bad-boy redemptions and jawlines that could cut glass. In her 2024 book, Vampires: A Handbook of History & Lore of the Undead, Agnes Hollyhock explores how gothic fiction used the vampire to subvert Victorian moral panic. In a society that strictly forbade non-normative intimacy, the vampiric bite symbolised forbidden desire in the form of a total surrender of control, an exchange of bodily fluid and a rejection of polite society.Disrupting heteronormative expectations, vampires exist entirely outside the linear mortal timeline. They don’t participate in conventional family units or rigid gendered expectations. Their power relies on aura and seduction rather than traditional gender roles.Lestat embodies all of this in his flamboyant, powerful and unapologetically queer glory, which is why we can’t stop thinking about his unhinged romance with Louis (that passionate kiss-turned-skull-smashing-murder in season two lives rent-free in fans’ heads). It’s why he’s become a poster-vamp for sexual freedom. And why we can apparently all get on board with his sordid affair with Gabriella (Jennifer Ehle), the lover he turned into a vampire, who also happens to be his mother.View image in fullscreenSexy buffoon … Matt Berry as Laszlo in What We Do in the Shadows.Photograph: Russ MartinIs it the danger? The immortal good looks? The need to be set free from societal constraints? The TV vampire is irresistible. No wonder so many of us are queueing up for a bite from Lestat.The Vampire Lestat is on iPlayer now in the UK, on SBS and SBS on Demand in Australia and on AMC+ in the US.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionHorror (TV)Anne RicefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringe | Theatre | The Guardian
description: How do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to Edinburgh
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: How do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to Edinburgh
Content: About-to-fall-apart energy … Megan Tomei in SpinQueen™.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAbout-to-fall-apart energy … Megan Tomei in SpinQueen™.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianTheatre‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringeHow do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to EdinburghKate WyverTue 18 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlood and sweat drip to the floor. Tears are on their way. In a small room in Edinburgh, Megan Tomei is cleat-clipped into a stationary bike, yelling above the music as she leads a high-intensity spin class gone wrong. “We take the thing you’re running from,” Tomei shouts, pink lights bouncing off her gleaming shoulders, “and turn it into fuel!” This is SpinQueen™, one of a handful of shows at this year’s fringe demanding epic endurance from their performers through the use of jazzed-up gym equipment. Employing various bikes and a treadmill to authentically illustrate the struggle for success, the pain of failure, and the escape from reality, a profoundly fit group of actors are pushing themselves to their physical limits.Across the city, Connor Delves’s calves are worth watching. The workout from his cycling-obsessed play,Cadel: Lungs on Legs, is so powerful that people have come up to him after, wanting to touch them. “To make sure they’re real,” says Delves, who cycles a whopping 27km per show. Does he mind this attention? He shrugs. “If they’re OK with getting their hands sweaty, go for it.”double quotation markYou’re watching it cost me something. You’re watching this body really workDelves grew up in his parents’ bike shop in Perth, Western Australia. His mum was a triathlete, his dad an international mountain-biker. “It’s always been acting and sport for me,” he says. When he was replaced by a bigger name in a transferring show, he decided to make a production in which he was irreplaceable. “I’d never seen a play that showed endurance sport at its best,” he says, “where the sport is an actual effort.”In 2016, Baby Reindeer’s Richard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award forMonkey See Monkey Do, an exposing show about toxic masculinity and sexual assault, performed on a treadmill. Two decades before, performance artist Kim Noble pounded away on a treadmill while the other half of theirdouble act, Stuart Silver, played chess against the audience. Over lockdown, Katie Mitchell created eco-theatre showA Play for the Living in a Time of Extinction, with cyclists generating the show’s lights and sound. But few shows that involve this kind of equipment are about sport, where the exercise is in the story as well as in the doing.View image in fullscreenHero’s arc … Connor Delves in Cadel: Lungs on Legs.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianWith Cadel, this is what Delves set out to do. The result is a sincere, leg-burning ode toCadel Evans, the first Aussie to win the Tour de France. Delves performs on a series of the real bikes that Evans used to win the 2011 race, clamped in place. The operation is a family affair: Delves’s father is the show’s mechanic. Head down, Delves’s teardrop-shaped helmet is steady as his legs whir round for the sprint stages. Remarkably riding the same mountain gradients as they do in the Tour, Delves is adept at explaining clearly to the uninitiated how the race works. It’s evident just how tough it is: every stage, every day, every kilometre. “It means you’ve got to think about nutrition,” Delves says of his show. “About sleep.” He quit drinking to train for it. “It means treating acting like being an athlete.”While Evans’s story is the hero’s arc, The Distance is about the also-rans. “I’m interested in what happens to the legions of sportspeople who are very, very good, but not good enough to make a living from it,” says Ben Norris, the show’s writer and performer, and vocally recognisable as farmer’s son Ben in The Archers. “For every one who wins the Olympics,” he says, “there are at least eight who lose the final. Then 100 or 200 who were in the heats. Then tens of thousands who are very good but don’t get there.” So, he asks, what happens then? “Who are you when the thing to which your identity has been shackled is no longer viable?”double quotation markI’ve had to start behaving like I’m an elite athlete againNorris plays Chris, a young boy realising his potential as a cross-country runner and dreaming of competing in the Olympics. The Distance is inspired by Norris’s time as a teenage international long-distance runner, but he worked hard to extricate it from himself. When he was mentored by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, she told him: “Be less concerned with being likable.” During each show, he runs roughly 8km on a “geriatric, old, foldable treadmill” that he’s wheeled all over the country. “One time, a local MP helped me on to the train with it,” he says. In Edinburgh, on Summerhall’s main stage, the treadmill is surrounded by a scaffolding pole, which Norris nimbly clambers over as Chris’s success rises and rises – and then begins to fall.Norris starts running as the audience file into the room. Soon, his clothes are drenched. As he strips down, we see the effort this is taking; his chest heaving, his body glistening. The sweat and ragged breath are important, he explains. “You’re watching it cost something. You’re watching this body really work.” That cost is already making itself evident. Norris pulled his calf in March, then again in April. “I’ve had to start behaving like I’m an elite athlete again, in terms of the rigour of my training and recovery,” he says. “I’m not 18 any more. Everything takes longer on an older body.”To be fit enough for the show, he has been cross-training, doing strength and conditioning, and phoning friends while on the treadmill to practise speaking at the same time as running at a furious speed. Throughout the fringe, he’s forcing himself to rest. “I’ve done a musical at the fringe and that requires a different kind of discipline. This will be like that, but on steroids.” He frowns. “Although crucially,” he says, “not on steroids.” His one request for accommodation: could he please have a bath?View image in fullscreen‘I’m not 18 any more!’ … Ben Norris in The Distance.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicI want to get a sense of the effort demanded by these shows, so when I talk to Tomei, the creator and performer of SpinQueen™, before the fringe, I suggest we do it on exercise bikes. My thighs soon regret it. “Oh God,” says Tomei, halfway through our chat. “I’m sweating so much.” She is in New York, calling from the spin studio at which she works. I quickly realise how hard it is to speak and ride at the same time.In SpinQueen™, Tomei plays a heightened, emotionally cracked version of herself as our manic spin instructor, spewing out “toxic positivity” as Tomei calls it, her character obsessed with thinness, optimisation and escape from the quiet that lets thoughts seep in. “Keep pushing, keep starving!” she calls in the show with a too-wide grin. In real life, Tomei is similarly peppy, but without the desperate about-to-fall-apart energy of her character. But that version of herself isn’t a world away, she says; the story’s climax borrows from a traumatic experience she had with an ex. When our narrator won’t allow herself to stop cycling, Tomei says: “It’s a physical representation of her emotional state.”View image in fullscreenRunning to survive … Richard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award for Monkey See Monkey Do in 2016.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSweat is blurring my vision now. “Oh God, no, same,” Tomei tries to reassure me. Every show, she cycles 16km, wanting people to feel the pain her character goes through, emotionally and physically. Tomei started taking spin classes with her dad in high school, and began teaching it as a way to earn money alongside acting. But after running the New York marathon, she got injured. “I had to slow down for the first time in my life,” she says. “I struggled with it, and it made me think of all the standards we hold ourselves to, because of what we think makes us better or successful. It made me think: ‘Why are we killing ourselves trying to reach this standard that can’t be met?’”What happens if these performers fall or twist an ankle during the fringe? “The same thing as in the Tour de France,” Delves says frankly. “I think that’s part of the allure of this. There’s no understudy.” With her massage gun packed, Tomei is more conscious of the emotional health she needs to maintain across the festival. “Every performance, I’m reliving what happened to me,” she says. “It’s a high-intensity emotional workout too.”Even when their characters near the dreamed-of success in these shows, failure is only a breath away. One fall, one second behind in a race, one last chance. These plays capture the itch of pushing just that tiny bit harder, as well as the dangers of running on empty. “There’s a little ambition monster within you,” Norris says, “that will wonder if you should just quit everything else and give this one last big go.” You can keep batting it down, he says, but the monster is persistent. “LA Olympics 2028?” Norris muses, only just joking. “Is it too late?”SpinQueen™is atJade StudioatGreenside @ George Street, until 29 August.The Distance,Main Hall at Summerhall, until 31 August.Cadel: Lungs on Legs,Auditorium at Gilded Balloon at the Museum, until 30 August; thenRiverside Studios, London, 13 October-15 NovemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsTheatreEdinburgh festival 2026FitnessEdinburgh festivalTraining programmesFringe theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I’m 50 years old. Why do I still struggle with the need to be liked? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: An over-investment in people-pleasing can be emotionally costly. Here’s how I’m training myself to be OK with letting people down
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An over-investment in people-pleasing can be emotionally costly. Here’s how I’m training myself to be OK with letting people down
Content: ‘I’ve spent most of my life people-pleasing. It wasn’t until the last few years of my 40s that I started resisting that urge.’Illustration: Vanessa Saba/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve spent most of my life people-pleasing. It wasn’t until the last few years of my 40s that I started resisting that urge.’Illustration: Vanessa Saba/The GuardianWell actuallyI’m 50 years old. Why do I still struggle with the need to be liked?An over-investment in people-pleasing can be emotionally costly. Here’s how I’m training myself to be OK with letting people downStephanie FairyingtonTue 18 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew months ago, my 10-year-old daughter and I went to our neighborhood cafe. At the counter, the owner greeted us with her typical effusion of warmth and welcome. Instead of greeting her in kind, my daughter looked on with a stony expression and ungiving eyes.My face flushed. I was embarrassed and incensed by what I perceived as blatant rudeness. You could at least smile, I thought.When we left, I pulled my daughter aside and gave her a firm talk about respect and manners, but her face dropped and she looked like she might cry. I quickly realized that she was in a bad mood, and totally unaware of her external affect. I felt bad for not approaching the conversation differently – I had assumed she recognized her impoliteness, that she was taking a stab at playing “sulky irreverent teen”.That’s when it hit me: by dictating that she should comport herself contrary to how she was actually feeling, I was reinforcing society’s attempts to mold girls and women into automatons who reflexively try to please everyone but themselves. It’s ironic, because I had written an entire book to warn her about doing just that:Ugly: A Letter to My Daughter. I knew these types of messages often lead to what psychologist Mary Pipher writes about in Reviving Ophelia: a “split self” that often results in the creation of a “false self” in line with gendered expectations.Psychologistsandstudiesindicate that an over-investment in people-pleasing and the quest to appear “nice” are emotionally costly. They amplifystress, impede individual fulfillment and self-actualization, and can lead toself-alienation.I had to ask myself: isn’t my daughter entitled to be in a bad mood? To not mirror someone else’s happy disposition? Why shouldshe fake a smile or express enthusiasm she doesn’t feel? Surely being raised to participate in these gendered theatrics is where the “split” Pipher talks about begins.Don’t get me wrong – I don’t think manners are trivial. Smiling, holding the door, greeting people and expressing gratitude nurture mutual respect and affection between friends and strangers alike. But a lesson in politeness can so easily tip into encouraging servility in girls.I’ve spent most of my life people-pleasing. It wasn’t until the last few years of my 40s that I started resisting that urge.But before then, how often had I violated my own feelings, boundaries and wishes to ensure I was likable? How often had I said “yes” to plans I didn’t really want to partake in or echoed a sentiment I didn’t entirely agree with?My deep – nearly existential – desire to be likable came, in part, from feeling abnormal and believing I could hide my queerness with 24/7 agreeability. Concealing my lesbianism in situations that felt unwelcome – or worse, unsafe – I’d adopted the affectations of femininity in various ways. As long as I remained feminine in my extreme likability, I could offset the internal and external cultural messaging that lesbians are angry, ugly freaks. But nothing made me realize the extent to which I wanted to be liked as when I started substitute teaching at public schools in New York City at the age of 48.The first time I stood in front of a classroom buzzing with unimpressed kids, I desperately, stupidly, pathetically wanted them to like me. I felt like an awkward teenage girl again, trying to adapt to 10-year-old notions of cool. I softened my voice and overworked the muscles in my face to evince a perma-smile, even when students were being loud, disruptive and disrespectful.I felt angry, but knew better than to yield to a displeasing scowl or a voice tinged with fury.Is it true that I ‘don’t get angry’? Or am I actually dangerously suppressing it?Read moreAs feminist journalist Rebecca Traister put it in her brilliant book,Good and Mad: The Revolutionary Power of Women’s Anger: “Women’s anger will be – as it has long been – cast as ugly, unappealing, dangerous, something to be shut down or jeered. Nothing, we have long been assured, is more unattractive in a woman than anger.”Think of all the language used to describe – or rather, dismiss – an irritated or furious woman. She’s difficult, aggressive, challenging, crazy, a witch, a bitch, a Medusa, a hellcat. Her “upset” is pathologized – and it’s enough to make any woman reach for the social ease of likability.For me, as a queer person whose gender isn’t fully aligned with traditional femininity, I felt that expressing my anger would only amplify my aesthetic inadequacies. Being cheerful was a way to soften my less conventional presentation and manner – to sidestep the “angry lesbian” trope and the ugliness other people ascribe to it.Furious outbursts and chronic expressions of anger are never acceptable in a classroom, but neither is quietly enduring inappropriate behavior. The days of stiff smiles and a voice dripping with syrup began grating on me. I didn’t want to tacitly teach children that misbehavior and disrespect would be greeted with a silent, acquiescent smile. I needed to get comfortable with my authority and their displeasure, fast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI started watching seasoned teachers manage their classrooms and I noticed the most effective educators followed four core practices: they give clear directives about what behavior is and is not acceptable at the outset and throughout the school year. They address transgressors immediately after they have defied a classroom rule, every single time. They balance discipline with affection and encouragement. Finally, they are not punitive.In return, they earned more than likability – they earned students’ respect and trust. I adopted these practices and even started applying them to my life outside the classroom.As I’ve gained more experience, turned 50 and experienced the many daily assaults ofperimenopause, I’ve grown less patient and less concerned with popular opinion. These days, I raise my voice, clarify my boundaries and express discontent with insolence.Now, instead of going along with what other people say, I’m more assertive. “Thanks for inviting me, but I feel like nesting today,” I might respond during an exhausting week. Or, to friends who pick restaurants closer to their neighborhood than mine, I might redirect: “Hey, can we meet somewhere in the middle?”After being dumped at 58, I realized I was not equipped for the griefRead moreThe likability norm still has its hold on me. But what’s really helped me get comfortable with the discomfort of not people-pleasing is wanting to model for my daughter the OK-nessof disappointing others or setting them straight. And I’ve started to see her do the same: she told a boy who liked her that she only wanted to be friends. At a slumber party, she took out a book while her friends played Roblox. On a family vacation, her cousin wanted to play inside, but she wanted to go to the beach – so she went by herself.It’s not easy to disappoint people or go it alone, especially in the face of resistance; women often face gaslighting, retaliation, even violence when they refuse to accept mistreatment. In those moments, do I feel like the strands of my hair have transformed into snakes and that I’ve just sprouted a face full of warts? Yes. Do I care? Less and less, especially when I see my male colleagues, with their broad shoulders and deep voices, command attention and respect to a degree I’m denied. This is, of course, a symptom of a sexist culture – one we have no hope of changing until we stop over-prioritizing everyone else’s pleasure and comfort above our own.And ultimately, I don’t care how people respond to my assertiveness. What matters to me is that I’m demarcating my limits, which is critical to my own dignity and self-respect. But dropping the mask of accommodation and self-denial doesn’t just affect the individual. The more we all do it, the more it feels OK to express our full humanity – our likability and our disagreeability, our beauty and our ugliness.Stephanie Fairyington is a writer in New York City who just published her first book,Ugly: A Letter to My DaughterExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyParents and parentingFriendshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality | Reparations and reparative justice | The Guardian
description: Right for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisers
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Right for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisers
Content: Author Barbara Blake Hannah said the drive to return to Africa was ‘the most powerful and continuous demand made by Rastafari’.View image in fullscreenAuthor Barbara Blake Hannah said the drive to return to Africa was ‘the most powerful and continuous demand made by Rastafari’.Cotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceHow slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a realityRight for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisersNatricia Duncanin KingstonTue 18 Aug 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTShareSupporting the right for people of African descent to return to the continent has become a key pillar of the growing global push for reparatory justice from Britain and other colonisers.When Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, visitedJamaicathis month he addressed the issue of repatriation for Jamaicans and others whose ancestors were kidnapped from Africa and sold into transatlantic chattel slavery.His visit coincided with a month-long series of emancipation celebrations and came as Jamaican officials prepare to travel to the UK toformally lodge an unprecedented petitionwith King Charles to seek legal guidance on their slavery reparations claim from Britain.Speaking in Jamaica’s parliament, Mahama describedrepatriationas “a right of all persons of African descent”.View image in fullscreenJohn Dramani Mahama said Ghana was considering a homeland return bill to ‘codify residence and citizenship pathways for all members of the global African family’.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesHe said this was whyGhanahad in 2000 passed the Right of Abode Act, which allows eligible people of African descent to apply for the right to live and work in Ghana without a visa.His country was also “considering a new homeland return bill that will codify residence and citizenship pathways for all members of the global African family”.This was welcomed by the Caribbean reparations movement. Repatriation and resettlement is one of 10 points outlined in the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission’svision for reparatory justice.For the Jamaican author and cultural activist Barbara Blake Hannah, Mahama’s visit was a signal that Africa was beginning to open its doors, and “an achievement in the struggle for repatriation”.Like many Rastafarians across theCaribbean, she yearns to be repatriated to the continent from which her ancestors were kidnapped and transported across the Atlantic in the most inhumane conditions to become the property of Europeans.“When you become a Rastafarian, there are certain things you get taught as principles … one of them is to return home,” said Blake Hannah, who started becoming a Rastafarian in the early 1970s.In her new book,The Jamaica Reparations Handbook, Blake Hannah, a cultural liaison for Jamaica’s ministry of culture, describes this drive to return to Africa, as “the most powerful and continuous demand made by Rastafari”.View image in fullscreenBarbara Blake Hannah (left) with Jamaica’s minister of culture, Olivia ‘Babsy’ Grange, and the president of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama.“Every Rasta wants to return. So, Rastafari said we need reparations to finance our repatriation … so, reparations was to be the payment for our return to Africa,” she said.Aaron “Ras Iron” Alexander, the president of the Iyanola Council for the Advancement of Rastafari and Pan African People in St Lucia, agreed.“We’ve been the vanguard of these issues, which we have been championing for many decades. And because of it, we were vilified and branded insane. And now we see that these issues are fast becoming part of one of the most important movements of the 21st century: the fight for reparations,” he said.For Dr June Soomer, a founding member of the Saint Lucia National Reparations Committee, repatriation is inseparable from identity. Returning to Africa either physically or by connecting with the history and culture that was ruptured by transatlantic enslavement was important for all people of African descent.“In every attempt at rebellion … those who jumped over the ships in chains, the aim was to go back to Africa,” Soomer said.Describing her first visit to Johannesburg, she added: “My heart started to beat differently. You felt like you were coming home. So, I understand how Rastafarians feel disconnected from their origin. And if you’re looking at origin and identity, it is very important to go back to Africa.”In her book, Blake Hannah argues that “the cruelty of slavery was not erased by emancipation” and there was no attempt to restore the heritage, land rights, language and customs that had been ripped away from African people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Rather, it was expected that all citizens should aspire to copy the colonial behaviour, create versions of their own, and conform to the rules that kept ‘The System’ operating in a continuous repetition,” she writes.She sees repatriation as a spiritual homecoming, but also a right of those who lost their true identity through the trauma of slavery.Steven Golding, of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations, stressed that repatriation was not solely about physical relocation. It was about rebuilding the economic, cultural and psychological ties severed by slavery.“It doesn’t necessarily mean all of us are going to physically move to Africa … but by recognising your citizenship, the continent recognising you as a citizen … that is what repatriation means,” he said.Repatriation was also about undoing the mental damage of slavery and colonialism, he said.“We lost our language, we lost our culture, we lost our religion … it was systematically done,” he said. “Repatriation reflects the reclaiming of those things.”But Golding, who is the president of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League, which was founded by the Jamaican pan-Africanist Marcus Garvey, stressed that there was precedent for physical repatriation.“Because the issue is the trafficking of the people, a fundamental part of the remedy has to be the return of the people,” he said. Golding points to Ayuba Diallo and Abdul Rahman, two African princes who were kidnapped in the 1700s and trafficked by Europeans, but were later repatriated.He also refers to the 18th and 19th centuries, when Britain and the US established Sierra Leone and Liberia specifically to repatriate freed Africans. Then in the 20th century, the Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie gifted land to African people in the diaspora.Following this, Garvey’s movement placed African redemption and repatriation at the centre of its political philosophy.“It’s not some highfalutin ‘smoke ganja and we want to go home’ concept,” Golding said. “It really comes from a sound socio‑economic political theory”.The Rastafari movement, he added, emerged directly from Garvey’s Black nationalist project, which envisioned Africans in the diaspora returning to help develop the continent.The idea of people returning to Africa, Golding said, was becoming a policy conversation, with Ghana and several other countries offering forms of citizenship or right-of-return programmes for people of African descent.Explore more on these topicsReparations and reparative justiceCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaicaGhanaAfricaAmericasCaribbeanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham launches ‘national drive’ to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Prime minister urges local leaders to act as homelessness campaigners welcome move but say more needs to be done
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Prime minister urges local leaders to act as homelessness campaigners welcome move but say more needs to be done
Content: Burnham says local leaders must offer people a route out of homelessness if they want one.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham says local leaders must offer people a route out of homelessness if they want one.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesHomelessnessBurnham launches ‘national drive’ to get rough sleepers off streets by ChristmasPrime minister urges local leaders to act as homelessness campaigners welcome move but say more needs to be doneI won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promiseKiran StaceyPolicy editorTue 18 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has urged local leaders to offer all rough sleepers in England a route off the streets by Christmas, as he pledges another £100m to end street homelessness.Arguing in the Guardian that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, Burnham promised he would mount a Covid-style campaign to get everyone off the streets this winter.The announcement solidifies tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success – although without a concrete target for ministers to hit.Homelessness campaigners welcomed the move, but warned more will need to be done to tackle the longer-term temporary accommodation crisis, which has given the UK theworst homelessness problemin the western world.In his article for the Guardian, the prime minister writes: “We see people bedded down in doorways and sat outside stations, carrying their lives in rucksacks and sleeping bags on their backs. And I think most people have the same reaction: this isn’t right.“It shouldn’t be happening here. But we’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.”He adds: “We did it in the pandemic. We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again.“That’s why the first thing I announced when I became prime minister was a commitment to end rough sleeping. Not to manage it, not to reduce it – but to end it. And today, we’re taking the first step in getting it done.“We’re putting £442m behind a national drive to get everyone in for Christmas.”Burnhamannounced his driveto end rough sleeping outside No 10 immediately after becoming prime minister, pledging £340m over the next three years to provide more accommodation for rough sleepers.Officials say that money will pay for 1,200 new homes and help support 3,000 people over five years.On Wednesday, he will tell local leaders they must offer a route off the streets to anyone who wants one by Christmas, announcing an additional £102m for additional services such as medical care and addiction support to help them do so.Of that, £8.4m will go to charities and other community organisations as part of theEnding Homelessness in Communities Fund.graphicBurnham said he would not instruct local authorities and mayors how to use the money, saying they would know best which services were most needed in their areas.Officials said the prime minister was not considering changing the law to force local authorities to provide accommodation for any rough sleeper who asked for it. At the moment they are only required to do so for people deemed a “priority need”, such as families with children.Burnham’s aides acknowledge that some people are likely to still be on the streets at Christmas, given authorities cannot force people into accommodation if they do not want it.But the prime minister is not setting a target for how much rough sleeping will have fallen by Christmas, with officials saying only that “real progress” should have been made.Burnham is not the first prime minister to make such a pledge. Boris Johnson also promised to end rough sleeping, while Keir Starmer said he would cut it in half during his time in office.The numbers fell sharply during the Covid pandemic as the government mobilised student accommodation, B&Bs and holiday rentals to provide a bed to anyone who wanted one under the “Everyone In” scheme.They haverisen againsince the funding for that scheme was withdrawn, however, and a record 4,793 people were found to be sleeping rough in England as of the government’slast snapshotin autumn 2025.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham on a visit to a charity that deals with homelessness and rough sleepers last month.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetBurnham himself promised to end rough sleeping as mayor of Greater Manchester. He had some success with his plans, largely by forcing greater collaboration between different organisations.For example, he made the 10 councils under his jurisdiction share data so that someone who was rough sleeping in one area could be tracked if they travelled to another during the day. He also made sure landlords did not evict tenants because of relatively minor misdemeanours, which experts say is a major cause of street homelessness.After several years of falling numbers, however, the level of street homelessness in the city region has risen again in each of the last four years.Homelessness campaigners welcomed the prime minister’s announcement on Tuesday night, though said that more long-term solutions would have to be put in place to deal with the country’s far bigger temporary accommodation problem.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “The prime minister’s pledge to get everyone sleeping rough off the streets by Christmas is a game-changing move and exactly the kind of bold leadership needed to end the housing emergency.But she added: “Tackling the most visible form of homelessness is a strong start, but the almost 178,000 children hidden away in grim temporary accommodation also need somewhere to call home. The prime minister must apply the same unwavering ambition to delivering the council housing revolution he promised.”John Bird, the crossbench peer and co-founder of the Big Issue, said: “Covid proved that when we decide rough sleeping is unacceptable, we can act and get people in off the streets. This Christmas commitment is a welcome return to that spirit.”Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessAndy BurnhamLocal governmentPovertyHousingEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ulez led to better lung size and function among London children, study finds | Low emission zones | The Guardian
description: Researchers find capacity stunted by pollution restored after introduction of ultra-low emission zone
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Researchers find capacity stunted by pollution restored after introduction of ultra-low emission zone
Content: Londoners’ health was explicitly cited by the city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, to justify the introduction of the Ulez in 2019.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLondoners’ health was explicitly cited by the city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, to justify the introduction of the Ulez in 2019.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesLow emission zonesUlez led to better lung size and function among London children, study findsResearchers find capacity stunted by pollution was restored after introduction of ultra-low emission zoneDamien GayleEnvironment correspondentTue 18 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren’s lungs grew bigger and stronger after the most polluting vehicles were restricted from entering London, a study has found.Examinations ofLondonschoolchildren before and after the introduction of the city’s ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) found a restoration of lung capacity that had been stunted by exposure to pollution.The researchers said the findings were a vindication of the low-emission zone policy, which had been criticised as a burden on motorists.“Traffic pollution in cities damages children’s health and development,” said Chris Griffiths, a professor of primary care at the University of Oxford and Queen Mary University of London (QMUL), and the study’s joint senior author.“We provide the strongest evidence yet on how these harms can be prevented. Ambitious clean-air zones should be considered a priority for cities globally with traffic-related air pollution.”Air pollution from traffic has stunted the development of children’s lungs in London for decades.Previous researchfound that by the age of eight or nine, children from the most polluted areas had 5-10% less lung capacity than their peers elsewhere.That impairment, which scientists said was the result of exposure to nitrogen dioxide, put them at increased risk as adults of developing respiratory diseases, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular and metabolic disease, and premature death.Londoners’ health was explicitly cited by the mayor, Sadiq Khan, to justify the introduction of Ulez – the world’s largest and most ambitious low-emission zone – in 2019. At the time, the policy, while intuitively sensible, lacked evidence, but researchers at QMUL saw an opportunity.Before Ulez came into force, they recruited 1,664 children aged six to nine in London and 1,750 in Luton, which, as a town with a similar mix of traffic pollutants but no clean air zone, was used as a control.The team measured and monitored the children’s size and health at annual school visits from 2018 to 2022 to assess how air quality changes after the introduction of Ulez had affected their lung development.Initial measurements showed children in London had significantly smaller lungs compared with those in Luton. But after Ulez came into force, the size and health of the London children’s lungs improved until they were comparable with those of the children in Luton.The children’s lung function improvements correlated strongly with air quality improvements. The researchers found that within five years of Ulez coming into force, the London children’s exposure to nitrogen dioxide fell twice as fast and twice as much as that of the Luton children.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWritingin the Guardian on Tuesday, Khan said: “Introducing and expanding the Ulez involved some incredibly difficult decisions. I never took them lightly, but I knew that – as mayor – I could not stand by while Londoners young and old lost their lives to a problem it was within my power to solve.“For years, politicians and pundits opposed to the Ulez have cynically sought to turn questions of public health into a crude culture war. Today, though, it’s clear that we’re winning the battle against toxic air in the capital – and it’s London’s children who are reaping the rewards,” he added.The health minister Karin Smyth said the study was “a powerful reminder of the impact that air quality has on children’s lung health. “[It] will help to improve our understanding of how reductions in air pollution can restore normal lung growth among children, reduce the risk of respiratory illnesses in adulthood, and support our goal to give every child the best start in life.”Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge who was not involved in the research, said it was not clear that the changes observed were truly attributable to Ulez, as opposed to other factors such as the impact of the Covid pandemic on pollution levels.“Nevertheless, the finding is important because lung function in childhood is an important measure of health, and the study provides encouraging evidence that changes in the urban environment may benefit children’s lung development,” he said.Explore more on these topicsLow emission zonesAir pollutionPollutionLondonChildrenChildren's healthEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Do not cut benefits for disabled young people, dozens of UK charities urge ministers | Universal credit | The Guardian
description: More than 40 charities write to Pat McFadden and review head Alan Milburn over fears of stricter eligibility rules
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: More than 40 charities write to Pat McFadden and review head Alan Milburn over fears of stricter eligibility rules
Content: Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training).Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training).Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesUniversal creditDo not cut benefits for disabled young people, dozens of UK charities urge ministersMore than 40 charities write to Pat McFadden and review head Alan Milburn over fears of stricter eligibility rulesRowena MasonandPatrick ButlerTue 18 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 40 of the UK’s leading charities have warned ministers against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people, as the government considers how to encourage more young people into work.The charities raised concerns that an imminent review of young people and work by Alan Milburn could bring in stricter eligibility rules for keeping disability benefits – or remove them altogether – as part of a wider plan to boost flagging youth job rates.Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-oldsin the UK are classed as Neet (not in employment, education or training). Milburn has warned this is economically unsustainable and disastrous for a generation of young people.In their joint letter to Milburn and Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, charity leaders warn cutting support or bringing in sanctions risks pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.The charities fear that a previous Labour government proposal for thehealth element of universal creditto be removed for under-22s with a disability or long-term sickness, saving around £300m a year, may be resurrected.Milburn – a former minister in the Tony Blair government – has made it clear England’s welfare, education and skills infrastructure needs to be overhauled but has so far refused to be drawn on whether he will recommend specific cuts to benefits.However, hisinterim report, published in May, argued that state support was too focused on benefit support at the expense of practical programmes to help young people into work, inadvertently “trapping” them on benefits.The report estimated that for every £1 spent on youth job support last year, £25 was spent on benefits for young people. This “clearly stacked” financial incentives “in favour of inactivity, not participation [in the job market]”, it said, with some young people able to achieve total benefit income of more than £2,000 a month.It said failure to reform the benefits system alongside education and skills would result in “far too many young people spending far too long out of work or learning, poorer [job] prospects over time and a rising benefits bill”.However, an analysis by the charity Scope suggests about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.About 184,000 young people aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. Charities say this is a cohort with multiple complex physical and mental health needs, not “mild” conditions.The letter, whose signatories include Action for Children, Save the Children, Barnardo’s, Scope, Sense, Mind and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, says: “Change is needed. But this must be built around the principles of support and opportunity, rather than the failed punitive approaches of the past.“Evidence shows that cutting benefits worsens health and deepens poverty, while strict conditionality and sanctions is particularly counterproductive and harmful for disabled people.”The charities challenge claims,notably from Reform UKand the Conservatives, that social security budgets are out of control, pointing out that spending on working-age benefits will remain flat as a percentage of GDP over the remainder of the parliament.Lucy Schonegevel, director of influencing at Action for Children, said: “Cutting benefits or ramping up sanctions will simply drive up poverty and push young people further away from work.“If ministers want better outcomes for disabled young people, the evidence points to earlier intervention, tailored support and meaningful job and volunteering opportunities, not sanctions or cuts.”Milburntold the Guardianearlier this week that specialist internships designed to secure work for young people with special educational needs should be put on “turbocharge” to help tackle the growing youth jobs crisis. He is also likely to callfor primary schools to identify childrenat risk of becoming Neet aged 16.Whitehall sources said no decision had been made on the proposal put forward in a 2025 green paper on removing the universal health element for those under 22. They said the issue was being looked at as part of the review.A DWP spokesperson said: “We want to see the potential of young people up and down this country fully realised, whether that be through education, training or work.“We are pushing ahead with the biggest youth employment reforms in a generation to create almost a million opportunities for young people and our wider £2.5bn youth employment support package includes a new apprenticeship bursary for families on universal credit.“We have also commissioned Alan Milburn to investigate the barriers stopping young people from getting into work and look forward to receiving his final report in the autumn.”Any attempts to restrict disability benefits further could be met with resistance from Labour MPs who stopped the bulk of cuts proposed under Starmer, although the government has consulted more widely and worked with charities more since then. On Monday, Andy Burnham unveiled a policyof 24-hour free bus passes for disabled people, removing the previous time restrictions and enabling more people to have free travel to work.Rachael Maskell, theLabourMP who helped lead the campaign against previous cuts to disability benefits, said: “It is vital that disabled young people are given the support they need in order to access work.“We have to not only change the culture of employment to ensure that adjustments are made so disabled people can access work, but also recognise the challenges that are experienced by disabled young people and co-produce solutions and support to open up opportunities with them.”Explore more on these topicsUniversal creditDisabilityYoung peopleBenefitsLabourWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Migration minister asked how he intends to stop deportations of people ‘who had lived in Sweden for decades’
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Migration minister asked how he intends to stop deportations of people ‘who had lived in Sweden for decades’
Content: ‘An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell.’ Joyce Thomas, 78, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years but must now leave.Photograph: Helena Karlsson/Helena Karlsson/NWTView image in fullscreen‘An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell.’ Joyce Thomas, 78, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years but must now leave.Photograph: Helena Karlsson/Helena Karlsson/NWTBrexitSwedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leaveMigration minister asked how he intends to stop deportations of people ‘who had lived in Sweden for decades’Lisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentTue 18 Aug 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe deportation and removal of British citizens fromSwedenover Brexit residency rights is damaging relations with the UK amid efforts to improve links with London, a Swedish MP has said.Häkan Svenneling, representative for Vârmland, where a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, has been given four weeks to leave Sweden after 21 years of residency, has written to the migration minister, Johan Forssell, asking what he “intends to do to stop the deportations”.Sevenneling, who is an opposition MP for the left, is to meet Thomas on Wednesday, exactly a week after she wastold her appeal had failed over the removal order.Thomas told the Guardian: “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong.”The retired nurse moved to Sweden with her financier husband, to be closer to one of their sons and their grandchildren, when she was 57.Her husband, who died of cancer in 2023, did all the administrative work in the household, but both Thomas and her friends have said repeatedly they checked if they had to complete any forms to remain in the country afterBrexit, and were told they did not.Thomas made a late application to remain in Sweden in 2023, just weeks after they returned from the UK, but missing the deadline of 31 December 2021. She and her friends testify that her husband checked whether Brexit was going to affect their residency and they were told they did not need to do anything.Thomas, who is self sufficient and is not drawing benefit from the Swedish state, hasspoken of the “hell”she is now in with the threat of imminent removal, separating her from her family, strong network of friends, and her husband’s grave.Svenneling says in his letter to Forssell that Britons lawfully in Sweden before the UK’s exit from the EU would see their “existing residency rights continue to apply” under the withdrawal agreement (W/A).“It was not intended to result in elderly people who had lived in Sweden for decades losing their rights to remain because of a missed deadline or deficiencies in their application [to stay],” he said.Svenneling’s written parliamentary question adds to growing pressure on the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson’s, centre-right minority coalition to address increasing concerns over the way Sweden is implementing the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, an international, legally binding, treaty.“The United Kingdom has long been an important partner for Sweden in a wide range of areas. It is clear that the deportations now taking place are damaging bilateral relations between Sweden and the United Kingdom,” Svenneling said.View image in fullscreenHorace (George) Mason and his daughter Michelle. Despite his dementia he was given four weeks to leave.Photograph: Mason family photographHe raised the case of Thomas, but also ofanother elderly Briton, Horace (George) Mason, 74, who has dementia and Parkinson’s and is in full-time care. Thomas moved to Sweden 25 years ago to be closer to his son Carl and his grandchildren.He, too, was given four weeks to leave.His family tried a second legal route for him to remain in Sweden, arguing he had rights, under the European conventionon human rights, to stay close to family on whom he relied. But the migration court of appeal ruled that “the state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden.Writing in the Guardian,David Milstead, who heads the campaign group Brits in Sweden, said the group raised the alarm over Sweden’s approach as far back as 2020 and the safeguards put in place were “untested”.“Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late,” he said.The UK Foreign Office said it has repeatedly raised concerns with the European Commission “that Sweden is taking a considerably stricter approach” to late applications than any other EU member state, with a disproportionate number of refusals.It said it appeared that “in practice, individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds [for a late application] accepted”.Milstead is concerned that Sweden’s wider migration policy could be affecting decisions made under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, and has called on the European Commission and Sweden to urgently address the issues.“Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically,” he said.The migration agency in Sweden said it was unable to discuss individual cases, but that not knowing a Brexit application had to be made to remain in the country was not a “reasonable ground” to stay.Explore more on these topicsBrexitSwedenMigrationEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: GPs’ advice service is causing cancer diagnoses to be missed, inquiry finds | Cancer | The Guardian
description: Advice and guidance services for doctors in England found to be creating risk of missed or late detection of illness
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Advice and guidance services for doctors in England found to be creating risk of missed or late detection of illness
Content: The advice and guidance services had been used even when a general practitioner had requested a specialist assessment of a patient who was suspected of having cancer.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe advice and guidance services had been used even when a general practitioner had requested a specialist assessment of a patient who was suspected of having cancer.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyCancerGPs’ advice service is causing cancer diagnoses to be missed, inquiry findsAdvice and guidance services for doctors in England found to be creating risk of missed or late detection of illnessPA MediaTue 18 Aug 2026 18.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCancer diagnoses have been missed or delayed because of a system designed for GPs to seek specialist advice before referring patients to hospital, according to an investigation.The Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) identified patient risks linked to how advice and guidance (A+G) services have been implemented acrossEngland.A+G was brought in to slash unnecessary hospital visits and reduce waiting times, allowing family doctors to seek specialist input before making referrals.The service has “positively influenced patient care” by improving communication betweenGPsand consultants, and “enabled efficient specialist input into care”, the HSSIB said.However, the investigation found evidence that A+G had “contributed to near misses and incidents of patient harm, both physical and psychological” where it had been poorly implemented or monitored.NHS to use AI on its app to direct patients to appropriate servicesRead moreThe report said “harm had arisen as a result of delayed or missed diagnoses, and delays to care and treatment”.It added: “Evidence demonstrated that A+G services were being used in some pathways where general practice had requested specialist assessment for suspected cancer.“Incidents demonstrated that this had contributed to delays in diagnosis.”Gaps in how systems were being implemented were also found.For example, some local pathways required GPs to use A+G instead of making direct referrals, or referrals were rejected despite persistent concerns from family doctors.The HSSIB recommended that NHS England and the Department ofHealthand Social Care rapidly evaluate A+G services to address resource and capacity gaps, training needs and weaknesses in reporting patient safety incidents.Dr Nick Woodier, a senior safety investigator at the HSSIB, said: “A+G services are making a real difference for patients in many parts of theNHS, and we heard genuine enthusiasm for what they can achieve.“But we also heard serious concerns, and found evidence of harm where implementation has not been adequately designed or monitored.“Our recommendations are about ensuring that expansion happens safely with the right support, standardisation and oversight in place to ensure patient safety is a priority.”A spokesperson for NHS England said: “As HSSIB acknowledges, advice and guidance has positively influenced patient care by reducing waiting times and giving people quicker access to specialist advice, but we know more needs to be done to make it work even more effectively.“That is why we’re giving GPs and hospitals clear guidance and practical tools to help deliver the service safely, consistently and effectively across the NHS, and have already commissioned an evaluation of its impact which will be published this year.”The HSSIB report followed a survey of 712 GPs by Pulse that found about a quarter of patient referrals are being rejected and returned as unsolicited A+G.Family doctors also estimated that 36% of the A+G they received asked them to do work considered outside their remit, and others raised concerns that the process is creating waits for people with suspected cancer.Dr Clare Bannon, the GPs’ committee chair at the British Medical Association, said: “Since its introduction, GPs have expressed deep concern with the advice and guidance system – we know our patients and know when a referral needs to be made. So this report is tragic vindication for these concerns, now showing that patients have come to harm as a result of this rushed-out and inconsistently applied process.“Just this week we had GPs telling a survey that a quarter of referrals were being sent back as advice and guidance, while genuine advice and guidance requests were taking 10 days or more for a response.“We know the pressures our colleagues in secondary care are facing and it’s clear that this process is not working for either of us, nor our patients.“The HSSIB is right to recommend an urgent evaluation of the advice and guidance system to address these clear patient safety risks.”Explore more on these topicsCancerGPsNHSHealthEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister calls for wartime presidential election | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mykhailo Fedorov’s appeal is most direct challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russian invasion in 2022
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Mykhailo Fedorov’s appeal is most direct challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russian invasion in 2022
Content: The sacking of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister triggered a wave of protests in Ukraine.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe sacking of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister triggered a wave of protests in Ukraine.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersUkraineUkraine’s dismissed defence minister calls for wartime presidential electionMykhailo Fedorov’s appeal is most direct challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russian invasion in 2022Dan Sabbaghin KyivTue 18 Aug 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s recentlydismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorovhas called for a wartime presidential election in the most direct political challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.The politician, whoseabrupt sacking last month triggered a wave of protests, said that Ukraine had to “restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war” in a video address released online late on Tuesday evening.“Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state,” Fedorov said in his nine-minute speech.Though he did not mention Zelenskyy by name, Fedorov implied the current president presided over a poorly functioning state that was struggling to tackle corruption despite the national emergency.“People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made.
