Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked,” Fedorov said, arguing thatUkrainecould fight a war and hold a national poll.“It is particularly dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” he said.Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there has been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while war continues.The US president, Donald Trump, has previously demanded that Ukraine hold an election, though his once-fraught relationship with Zelenskyy has gradually improved over the past year as Kyiv has shown it can hold its own on the battlefield.Fedorov, 35, was Ukraine’s digital minister from 2019 until January, fronting the country’s wartime adoption of drones, before briefly serving in what was considered to be a successful stint as defence minister until July.Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv could hit Russia with domestic ballistic missiles in months, former defence minister saysRead moreBut he was suddenly dropped by Zelenskyy in a government reshuffle after a falling out with military commander Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi. Street protests followed, leading to thesacking of Syrskyi, but there was no sign Fedorov would be reinstated.On Tuesday Zelenskyy formally nominated Yevhen Khmara, the acting defence minister, to take the post permanently. Khmara’s nomination has to be confirmed by Ukraine’s parliament, and a vote is expected to take place on Wednesday.Artem Bronzhukov, a Ukrainian political analyst, questioned whether it would be practical to hold elections given that Russian bombing was continuing. “Today there is no clear understanding of how to ensure people’s safety in the context of a full-scale war,” he said.There was, he added, “a fairly deep-rooted view within Ukrainian society” that elections are necessary but only after the hot phase of the war ends – and that the country remained “a warring democracy – confirmed precisely by the protests taking place after Fedorov’s resignation from the government”.Protests had been taking place nightly in a square below the presidential office in the heart of Kyiv, but the numbers attending had been dwindling. However, the campaign was relaunched in a special rally on Sunday night that attracted about 2,000 people with regular chants of “Fedorov, Fedorov, Fedorov …”Polling conducted at the turn of the month reported the ex-minister would come third in the first round of a presidential election with 13.1%, behind Zelenskyy on 22.3% and the former head of the armed forces, who is now Ukraine’s ambassador to the UK, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, on 21.4%.The same polling, conducted by the Socis Centre for Social Research, also concluded that Zelenskyy would then be defeated in the run-off election by both Fedorov and Zaluzhnyi. Ukraine uses a two-stage voting system.If Ukraine were to hold an election, it would have to contend with the fact that millions have been exiled and displaced since the start of the war, and that more than 1 million are serving in the armed forces, many on the frontline. About a fifth of the country’s territory is also under Russian occupation.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Shrews may grow bigger snouts in winter to cope with cold air, scientists say | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Study of long-clawed shrew skulls from Japan shows that, while skulls get smaller in winter, snouts elongate
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Study of long-clawed shrew skulls from Japan shows that, while skulls get smaller in winter, snouts elongate
Content: The common shrew (pictured) has previously been shown to shrink its body mass and skull size in winter.Photograph: blickwinkel/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe common shrew (pictured) has previously been shown to shrink its body mass and skull size in winter.Photograph: blickwinkel/AlamyWildlifeShrews may grow bigger snouts in winter to cope with cold air, scientists sayStudy of long-clawed shrew skulls from Japan shows that while skulls get smaller in winter, snouts elongateNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 18 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumans turn to heated blankets and fluffy socks to cope with winter, but long-clawed shrews have a very different adaptation: they increase the size of their snouts.Researchers have previously discovered that certain small mammals, including thecommon shrewandEuropean mole, reversibly shrink their body mass, skull size and brain mass in winter, with regrowth seen in the spring – a strategy that has been named Dehnel’s phenomenon.Scientists now say they have documented similar changes in the long-clawed shrew, but have discovered the opposite trend occurs for the snout.“This is precisely why we termed it the ‘reverse Dehnel’s phenomenon’,” said Dr Yugo Ikeda, first author of the research from Toyo University inJapan.Writingin the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Ikeda and colleagues describe how they examined 136 skulls from long-clawed shrews, collected in Hokkaido between 1948 and 1988 and now housed at the Botanical Garden of Hokkaido University in Japan.“Measuring skull structures in live, wild shrews repeatedly without harming them is practically impossible,” said Ikeda.The researchers note that wild, long-clawed shrews are born between spring and autumn and typically die before they reach their second winter. The specimens available covered each month of this lifespan, and were classed as belonging to either a sexually immature or sexually mature shrew.Tracking 16 measurements by month, they found several changed by month or season – and not in a uniform way.Among other findings, shrews collected over the winter season, between January and April, were found to have a brain case height (vertical skull measurement) 12% smaller than that of younger shrews collected from August to September in their first year of life. However, the height of the snout, also known as the rostrum, was 7% larger and its width was 6% greater in shrews collected in winter.“This is a ‘true change’ where the bone structure of the rostrum itself physically alters its size,” said Ikeda. “What makes this particularly unique is that the rostrum expands while other parts of the skull shrink during winter.”The team said these changes were reversible, with measurements including brain case height found to be larger in shrews that survived winter and were collected between August and November in their second year. By contrast, snout width – although not snout height – was smaller.The researchers suggest a number of explanations for the seasonal change in snout size, including regulating body temperature.“Expanding the nasal cavity creates more room for a rich vascular network,” said Ikeda. “When the shrew inhales freezing air, this network efficiently warms it before it reaches the delicate, winter-shrunken brain – helping maintain core cognitive functions.” The expansion of the nasal cavity, he noted, may also boost shrews’ ability to sniff out prey such as earthworms.The researchers said a third possible explanation was mechanical reinforcement of the snout, allowing the shrew to process tougher prey when food is scarce – although they found little evidence to support this.Ikeda said it was possible seasonal changes in snout size could occur in other shrews, adding that Hokkaido was home to three further species.“We are very excited about investigating the presence, absence, and degree of both Dehnel’s and reverse Dehnel’s phenomena among these species in future research,” he said.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAnimal behaviourBiologyJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: Social media on trial as $200bn case against Facebook and Instagram begins | Meta | The Guardian
description: Twenty-nine US states are seeking huge damages, claiming Meta’s platforms were addictive by design
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Twenty-nine US states are seeking huge damages, claiming Meta’s platforms were addictive by design
Content: Online safety campaigners in Oakland, California on Tuesday.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersView image in fullscreenOnline safety campaigners in Oakland, California on Tuesday.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersMetaSocial media on trial as $200bn case against Facebook and Instagram beginsTwenty-nine US states are seeking huge damages, claiming Meta’s platforms were addictive by designAisha DownTue 18 Aug 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1994, more than 40 US states came together to sue one of the most powerful industries on Earth: big tobacco.The suits brought together diverse claims centred on tobacco companies’ misleading advertising and contribution to a mounting public health crisis. They ended in a negotiated settlement with the US government, in which the companies agreed to pay more than any industry ever, and the states agreed to drop a large portion of their claims.Thirty years later,smoking is on the risein the developing world, the companies involved remain profitable and the global tobacco market is worth nearly $1tn.On Tuesday a majortrialagainst Meta began, in which 29 states have brought the claim that the parent of Facebook and Instagram designed a deliberately addictive product and targeted it at children.View image in fullscreenBoxes are brought into the Ronald V Dellums courthouse in Oakland, California, on 18 August, as opening arguments begin in the Meta trial.Photograph: Godofredo A Vasquez/AFP/Getty ImagesThat trial follows abellwether caseearlier this year, in which a Los Angeles jury found the social media company – and YouTube, its co-defendant – liable for deliberately designing an addictive product that had deleterious effects on the mental health of a single young claimant.That case, which awarded the claimant $6m, opened the door for this and other litigation. At about the same time, Meta was forced to pay a total of $942m in a separatetrialin New Mexico. The New Mexico case focused on whether the company was aware of – and took measures to prevent –child sexual exploitationon its platforms.This next wave of litigation will focus less on child exploitation, and more on the fundamental design of Meta’s platform: the algorithm that underlies which content it shows to users and how. So, how far could the litigation go?Kate Winick, an analyst at Forrester, said the trial was “potentially the end of social media as we know it” and, while a ruling against Meta would not permanently kill the industry, it could “significantly reduce usage over the long term”.The figures that Meta and other social media companies could stand to pay are immense. The attorneys general are seeking $200bn in damages, the amount of revenue the company takes in a year. Meta has said in a court filing that they could amount to $1.4tn, which is just short of the company’s market capitalisation. The judge in the case has called the company’s estimation “unreasonable”.Perhaps a more realistic risk for the company is the potential for permanent changes to the way its social networks operate, which are the engine for its entire business. Meta is essentially a digital advertising company. Its recommender algorithm ranks posts in users’ feeds and fuels engagement in part by showing people posts that are likely to inflame emotion and keep them hooked.It is this algorithm that American attorneys general seem interested in changing, because it is this “dopamine-manipulating” feature – in the words of the AGs’ lawsuit – that makes social media addictive. Changes to this algorithm may not alter howFacebookadvertises, said Steven Murdoch, a professor at University College London. But it could reduce engagement, which could gravely reduce its opportunity to advertise to users.But all this depends on how big of a swing a US jury – and US regulators – are willing to take at the platform. Discontent is brewing worldwide about Meta and its business; the EUalso wantsthe company to modify its “addictive design”.“There’s a plausible path” for global changes to the algorithm, said Murdoch. “But whether it’s devastating or not – I’m not convinced the things that are plausibly going to be asked for are going to be devastating for the company.”Take the recent case of Google. US regulators sued the search company in 2023 in a landmark antitrust case – which could have ended with authorities breaking up the company, perhaps forcing it to sell Chrome, the most popular web browser in the world. Google lost the case but that extreme penaltywasn’t imposed. Despite finding that the company had engaged in monopolistic practices, it got away with what critics called a “slap on the wrist” and remains a juggernaut.“I don’t think anyone really wants to destroy Facebook. It’s a valuable company and there would be so many bad outcomes,” said Murdoch.A Meta spokesperson said: “The state AGs may call this a landmark case but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate.“Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. We stand by our record of creating strong protections for teens, and look forward to making our case in court.”Or take the case of big tobacco. The US government sought $289bn from major tobacco companies – including Philip Morris – in one of its landmark cases, which was prosecuted under a US anti-racketeering statute. Philip Morris and its co-defendants lost the case.But in the course of proceedings, the government’s original monetary demand was modified to less than 5% of the original amount – $14bn, to be paid over 10 years. Philip Morris continued doing business, although it and other tobacco companies were forced to put out statements about the harms of smoking, and change how they marketed their products in the US.Thirty years later, although smoking continues its long-term decline in the developed world, Philip Morris’s revenues are at roughly $40bn a year – less than they were 20 years ago, but not by much. They have been steadily increasing for the past four years.Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookSocial mediaDigital mediaGoogleAlphabetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Can’t enjoy your pint’: Wetherspoons customers welcome ban on loud phones | JD Wetherspoon | The Guardian
description: Patrons at two of the chain’s London pubs were all for Tim Martin’s ban on playing music or taking calls on speaker
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Patrons at two of the chain’s London pubs were all for Tim Martin’s ban on playing music or taking calls on speaker
Content: ‘In a world dominated by other people’s music and amplified sound, Wetherspoon pubs are an oasis of tranquillity,’ the chain’s owner said.Photograph: Gavin Rodgers/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘In a world dominated by other people’s music and amplified sound, Wetherspoon pubs are an oasis of tranquillity,’ the chain’s owner said.Photograph: Gavin Rodgers/AlamyJD Wetherspoon‘Can’t enjoy your pint’: Wetherspoons customers welcome ban on loud phonesPatrons at two of the chain’s London pubs were all for Tim Martin’s ban on playing music or taking calls on speakerHelena HortonTue 18 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe terrace of the Moon Under Water Wetherspoons pub in Leicester Square was full of people enjoying the warm weather and chatting between tables – without a TikTok video or speakerphone call in earshot.At Wetherspoons, the convivial atmosphere can no longer be punctuated by rude customers taking phone calls on blast, or playing videos without headphones after Tim Martin, the owner of the pub chain,banned both on his premises.Gary and Mark, brothers who were catching up over pints, both thought anyone playing loud sounds in the pub should be barred.View image in fullscreenGary: ‘External noise is becoming part of the pub.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“There is no way anyone should be allowed to be obnoxious enough to have their phone on loud. Why should people choose to play music that I don’t like and that other people around them don’t like?” asked Mark. “I listen to music with headphones on, in a private way.”But Gary pointed out: “First they didn’t used to allow televisions in Wetherspoons but now they have TVs with the sound on. External noise is becoming part of the pub.”Abdslam Elidrisi, 65, who was puffing on a cigar with a glass of white wine while people-watching, also welcomed the move.View image in fullscreenAbdslam Elidrisi.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“I come here because I am a member of a film club nearby and they don’t let me smoke my cigar, so I visit here to smoke it and watch the world go by,” he said, “Music is a personal thing, so I agree with Mr Martin. You can’t impose it on other people. Loud phone calls are the same thing. I don’t want to hear about your personal life – unless you are having a conversation with me about it!”The company announced on Tuesday it had introduced the ban across its 792 pubs, saying sound from smartphones and tablets had become an “increasing problem in recent years”.“In a world dominated by other people’s music and amplified sound, Wetherspoons pubs are an oasis of tranquillity and contemplation,” Martin said. “We are kindly asking phone users to pipe down.”The pub company has recently been clamping down on some modern behaviours – includingbanning the use of Meta’s “spy glasses”to record inside pubs. The glasses contain very small cameras that enable the wearer to discreetly film.Lily, 21, and Avril, 22, both students, agreed it was antisocial and inconsiderate to play video and phone calls out loud in the pub, but said they weren’t regularly troubled by it when visiting Wetherspoons for chicken burgers and spritzes. “I’ve seen it on the train,” Avril said.View image in fullscreenLily (left) and Avril.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianTrev and John, who work laying cables for telecoms, were enjoying a quiet after-work pint. “I think it’s a great idea,” said Trev. “People have loud speakerphone conversations right next to you and you can’t enjoy your pint. In a pub, you don’t want that. I take my phone calls outside.”Over at the Montagu Pyke Wetherspoons near Tottenham Court Road in central London, not everyone had got the memo.“Someone was doing it just now, taking a loud call on speakerphone; it annoys me and it is inconsiderate,” said Mel Burton, 41, who works in the packaging industry and had just finished a late pub lunch.View image in fullscreenMel (left) and Sam.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianHer colleague Sam Reid, 48, was supportive of the ban. “It does piss me off when people play music out of their phones,” he said. “I don’t want to hear someone else’s music.”The manager of the Montagu Pyke said she had had to tell people to turn off the sound on their phones on a number of occasions. “It annoys me, it annoys other customers. I have to ask them to stop,” she said. “If it’s been banned by the whole company, it means it must be an issue across the different Wetherspoons. Some people understand when we ask them to turn off the noise – others are looking for a fight.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s loud and annoying’: Holly and Eleanor.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianHolly and Eleanor, both 18, were enjoying a meal after a day of shopping in central London, having come down from Darlington on the train. “We actually saw this happening on the train this morning, someone was on their phone playing music out loud,” said Holly.“I agree with banning it in pubs, it’s loud and annoying, it should be banned on the train as well,” Eleanor added.The London mayor, Sadiq Khan,started a campaign last yearencouraging people to use headphones when playing music on the city’s transport network.Explore more on these topicsJD WetherspoonPubsSmartphonesMobile phonesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Little Bird review – no wonder this masterly drama has already cleaned up awards | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s impossible not be be enraged by this story of Indigenous children who were taken from their families. This heartbreaking show has been a hit in Canada – and it would be a crime for the rest of the world to miss it
Author: Patrick Smith
Headline: It’s impossible not be be enraged by this story of Indigenous children who were taken from their families. This heartbreaking show has been a hit in Canada – and it would be a crime for the rest of the world to miss it
Content: Bezhig (Keris Hope Hill) and her mother Patti (Ellyn Jade) try to evade the police in Litte Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.View image in fullscreenBezhig (Keris Hope Hill) and her mother Patti (Ellyn Jade) try to evade the police in Litte Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.TV reviewTelevisionReviewLittle Bird review – no wonder this masterly drama has already cleaned up awardsIt’s impossible not be be enraged by this story of Indigenous children who were taken from their families. This heartbreaking show has been a hit in Canada – and it would be a crime for the rest of the world to miss itPatrick SmithTue 18 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew dramas will enrage you as much as Little Bird. Not because it’s in any way hokey or problematic. On the contrary. Based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – a period in Canada from the mid-1950s to the 1980s, when an estimated 20,000 First Nations children were forcibly removed from their families and adopted by non-Indigenous families – this heartbreaking tale is restrained and carefully measured. Melodrama is swerved, letting the injustice at this story’s core slowly metastasise.Spread across six episodes, the series juggles two timelines – 1968 in Saskatchewan; 1985 in Montreal – tracking one family’s rupture; and the decades-long reckoning that follows. We meet Esther Rosenblum (Darla Contois), a first-year law student, at her engagement party, where her fiance David (Rowen Kahn), a doctor, mingles with his wealthy Jewish family. When his mother describes her as “exotic”, the word lodges like shrapnel. She was transplanted when she was five from the (fictional) and raised in the Jewish faith by a Canadian family.She flees to Saskatchewan without warning, clutching a newspaper clipping – a classified ad from the Adopt Indian and Métis programme placing First Nations children up for adoption, displaying each with a photograph and a brief description. On this scrap of paper, she discovers her real name is Bezhig Little Bird. From there she begins an odyssey that takes her across the reserves to find the family she barely knew. When she returns to Montreal, to David’s world, she realises just how isolated she feels. “There’s a reason why your mum tries so hard to let me know that I don’t fit in,” she sobs. “It’s because I don’t.”Meanwhile, in flashbacks to 1968, we see how we got here. Triggered by a rock hurled by a young girl at a passing police car, officers arrive at the Little Bird family home. There, they walk through rooms with no electricity or clean water, deciding, there and then, that Bezhig’s mother is unfit for parenting. They set about “apprehending” her children – “apprehending” being the verb used by these child welfare agencies to mask their atrocities. Later on, we cut to the father coming home to find his wife handcuffed to the wall, their children gone. When, grief-stricken and apoplectic, he squares up to the cops outside, they beat him to death.Little Bird, co-created by Jennifer Podemski, a writer of First Nations descent, arrives as proof of a larger reckoning: that Indigenous voices are ready to tell their own stories, their own way. Plaudits must go to both Podemski and to Contois, who carries the series so masterfully.View image in fullscreenAn odyssey … Darla Contois as Esther (Bezhig) Rosenblum in Little Bird.Photograph: © Original Pictures Inc.Her performance conveys the fractures at the heart of this story, slipping between steeliness and vulnerability, between lawyer and lost child. Contois shows Bezhig’s spiralling internal angst with her face often completely still and silences allowed to linger, which only amplifies the moments when the pain really comes to the surface.While the series is keen to teach – at the beginning and end of each episode, an epigraph reminds us that more Indigenous children are in the care system than ever before – it doesn’t have the fusty feel of a history lecture. As Podemski and her co-writer Hannah Moscovitch understand, tragedy and hope are real-life bedfellows. There’s a suggestion, too, that Bezhig, her adoptive mother Golda (Lisa Edelstein) and her birth mother Patti (Ellyn Jade) are different sides of a singular shared experience. Throughout the series, right up to the unpredictable and cathartic final episode, the writers work overtime to humanise their experiences.Yes, there is the odd caricature – most notably a welfare officer whose stock villainy is a rare lapse into cliche – and the show’s score feels at times overwrought. But giving voice to characters who have previously been sidelined, Little Bird is an impressive and heartfelt work, tender and moving. It cleaned up at the Canadian Screen Awards, winning 13 gongs, including for Contois. For it to be ignored globally would be a crime.Little Bird aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now in the UK and on Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Even its loos are on the outside’: hi-tech, inside-out marvel the Lloyd’s building is partying with the public | Architecture | The Guardian
description: It has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the inside
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: It has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the inside
Content: ‘There was whooping in the office’ … the Lloyd's building, designed by Richard Rogers.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘There was whooping in the office’ … the Lloyd's building, designed by Richard Rogers.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Rex/ShutterstockArchitecture‘Even its loos are on the outside’: hi-tech, inside-out marvel the Lloyd’s building is partying with the publicIt has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the insideAlice FisherTue 18 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his 2012 book A New Kind of Bleak, the criticOwen Hatherleycalled it “monstrous, compelling” and utterly messed-up. Back in the 1980s, a then Prince Charles suggested it had been inspired by a North Sea oil rig. But none of this stopped it from becoming, in 2011, the youngest ever building to be given Grade I-listed status in the UK.And now, as part of its 40th anniversary celebrations, the Lloyd’s building will open to the public for the first time since 2014 for one day only during London’s Open House festival. The iconic building in the heart of the financial district was designed by architectRichard Rogersto house the global insurance marketplace. Its futuristic facade has been a celebrated part of the City of London skyline since it opened in 1986, but the interior is rarely seen by the public. Visitor galleries with a view of the trading floor have long been shut for security reasons.double quotation markThe Adam Room was sliced into 1,500 pieces and moved to Lloyd’s HQOpen House festival is organised by the charity Open City, which aims to make architecture more accessible by inviting government offices, private properties and heritage buildings to let the public in. Free tickets for the Lloyd’s building are released tomorrow for the one day the building is open, on 19 September. The tour will include the underwriting room and the Adam Room as well as examining how the building was designed. “There was whooping in the office when the Lloyd’s building came in,” says festival director Celia Mead, “because we know our visitors really, really want to get inside this landmark institution.”View image in fullscreenCompared with the Parthenon … Lloyd’s main trading floor, with its mahogany ‘temple’ holding the Lutine Bell, rung at moments of disaster.Photograph: Jason Alden/LloydsLloyd’s is a key example of British hi-tech architecture. This late modernist style evolved in the 1970s and celebrates industrial engineering and prefabricated materials. Lloyd’s is famous for its exposed concrete frame and the six external steel towers that house its staircases, lifts, pipes and ducts. The building’s 12 glass lifts were the first of their kind in the UK, and each tower is permanently topped with steel cranes - partly for maintenance but also to make the building look like a gothic cathedral.“It’s a masterpiece of radical, inside-out architecture,” says Mead, “representing London’s confidence and swagger.” From the street, she says, “it catches the attention and you wonder, ‘What could it be like inside?’” Mead has experienced the building first-hand: “My mum was an economics teacher and I joined one of her school trips to Lloyd’s 38 years ago. I remember then thinking it was huge.”With all the infrastructure removed from the inside, the Lloyd’s building has capacity for a double-height space for the trading floor and a galleried atrium that reaches to the steel and glass barrel-vaulted roof, 14 floors above. Historian Reyner Banham compared the atrium to the Parthenon when he presented Rogers with the Royal Institute of British Architects’ gold medal in 1985.The building also includes historical artefacts from Lloyd’s of London’s 338-year history. The Adam Room, originally designed in 1763 for Bowood House in Wiltshire by neoclassical architect Robert Adam, was sliced into 1,500 pieces in 1958 and moved to Lloyd’s HQ. The old library from Lloyds’ former home in the Cooper building on Leadenhall Street – designed by Sir Edwin Cooper in 1928 – was similarly salvaged. There is also a 1958 war memorial stained glass by artist Hugh Easton while, on the main trading floor, the Lutine Bell sits, hung within a mahogany, pillared temple. The bell, rescued from the wreck of HMS Lutine, has been used since 1858 to alert insurance underwriters to a maritime disaster. It’s still used to acknowledge ceremonial occasions such as Remembrance Sunday.View image in fullscreenPieced together …the 18th-century Adam Room within the Lloyds building at One Lime Street.Photograph: Northern Exposure/AlamyThe Lloyd’s building’s place in British culture is nuanced. It appeared in 1986,the same year the City was deregulated, and came to symbolise that gear change to a voracious capitalist financial market shaped by international powers. The design’s references to industrialism and religion married to futurism invite ruminations about ideas of power in British history.Architecturally, though, its reputation has endured. Not everyone is as damning as King Charles. Historian Geraint Franklin, of Historic England, who last year featured the building on the cover of his book High-Tech Britain, says it was designed to adapt and evolve. “Lloyd’s is flexible. Its services, lifts and even loos are mounted on the outside, freeing up the workplace inside. In recent years, the glazing has been renovated, carefully recutting the original ‘sparkle glass’.” This refers to textured glass panes that refract light so the building glitters in the sun.“The main trading areas have been recently refurbished,” adds Franklin. “On paper, the plan is rational and diagrammatic, but it’s a dynamic, romantic exterior. Lloyd’s was never intended to be taken in at a single glance but to be encountered in snatched views from the streets. It’s obsessively detailed – with stainless steel, glass and white concrete making up a sharp City palette, highlighted by careful lighting.”Mead is just pleased that more people will get to experience this. “In our programme of over 730 buildings, Lloyd’s is perhaps the greatest statement building. It’s heavyweight, look-at-me and counterintuitive. We’re all about the social impact that access brings – it gives people a sense of belonging to the city. Can’t wait to hear what they say about Lloyd’s.”Tickets to Lloyd’s are free but must be booked in advance atopenhouse.org.uk. Booking opens at noontomorrow. London Open House festival runs 12-20 September.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureCity of LondonOpen HouseHeritageDesignLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The ‘big-ass bag’ – do you really need a tote you can carry a small human in? | Accessories | The Guardian
description: Lululemon’s absurdly capacious 80-litre bag will set you back a small fortune – and it’s one of the cheapest giant holdalls on the market
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lululemon’s absurdly capacious 80-litre bag will set you back a small fortune – and it’s one of the cheapest giant holdalls on the market
Content: Lululemon’s giant tote.Photograph: LululemonView image in fullscreenLululemon’s giant tote.Photograph: LululemonPass notesAccessoriesThe ‘big-ass bag’ – do you really need a tote you can carry a small human in?Lululemon’s absurdly capacious 80-litre bag will set you back a small fortune – and it’s one of the cheapest giant holdalls on the marketTue 18 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Big-Ass Bags.Age:The titular “Big-Ass Bag” launched this month (but large carrying receptacles have been available for centuries).Appearance:Big ass.Hey, who are you calling big ass?Anabsurdly capaciousLuluemon tote.How big is it really?Oh, it’s enormous-ass: 80 litres.I don’t understand why bags are measured in litres – what am I going to do, fill it with milk?People on TikTokare managing tofill it with themselves.View image in fullscreenBalenciaga’s £975 shopping bag.Photograph: Matches FashionOK, that is pretty big-ass.People are loving mockingits ludicrous dimensions online: “I know a studio apartment when I see one,”an Instagram commenter said. Product reviews include: “I took it with me to my summer backpacking trip. I was able to bring back the Eiffel Tower, coliseum [sic] and many other monuments.” Others have joked that it “runs small”: “I can only fit two of my five kids in this bag,”someone complained.Does it have anygenuine fans?Refinery 29claims it’s a “brilliant solution for lugging everything at once”.Are other big-ass bags available?Yes, they’re extremely on trend. There’s Loewe’s Puzzle Fold XL, The Row’s Marlo 14, or the cavernous Chanel beach bag Dua Lipawas recently seen carrying. That’s the one Women’s Wear Daily said back in April signalled “a return to dramatically oversized bags”.Dramatically oversized is right.Bet it’s dramatically pricey too.The Chanel one will cost about £6,000 ($8,000).That’s the price of a car!But what price a bag you could actually put a carinto? Lululemon’s bag is a more reasonable £228.Alternatively, I could plump forone of those zip-up plastic laundry bags – six for a tenner atTesco.Alsotrès chic! Balenciaga dida high-fashion versionin 2016 (for £975).Wasn’t “high fashion” trying to get us excited about absurdly tiny handbags five minutes ago? It needs to make its mind up.Yes,nano-bagshave had their moments – you might recall seeingLizzo carrying a Valentino onebig enough for a single piece of chewing gum at the American Music Awards in 2019. And now you mention it, US Vogue actuallysaid in Aprilwe “need a Teeny-Tiny Tote this Summer”.View image in fullscreenThe other extreme … Lizzo with a nano-bag at the American Music Awards in 2019.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Variety/Rex/ShutterstockWhat? Fashion can’t have it both ways! Argh, I’m ditching bags altogether.Sorry, I can’t let you do that – abandoning handbags and holding all your stuffin a claw gripwas briefly a thing last year, but that’s ancient history.Do say:“I like big bags and I cannot lie.”Don’t say:“That was no solar eclipse, it was a Lululemon Big-Ass Bag.”Explore more on these topicsAccessoriesPass notesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best packing cubes in the UK to save space and travel smarter – tested on real trips | Travel | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re trying to squeeze more into a carry-on or simply want a tidier suitcase, our expert rounds up the top cubes, from compression to lightweight
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Whether you’re trying to squeeze more into a carry-on or simply want a tidier suitcase, our expert rounds up the top cubes, from compression to lightweight
Content: View image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterTravelReviewThe best packing cubes in the UK to save space and travel smarter – tested on real tripsWhether you’re trying to squeeze more into a carry-on or simply want a tidier suitcase, our expert rounds up the top cubes, from compression to lightweightThe best suitcases for your next holidayPete WiseTue 18 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNightmarish scenes reminiscent of a Hieronymus Bosch painting used to erupt whenever I travelled with a case. Skirts and shirt sleeves slithered out from under compression straps, worn clothes frolicked with unworn clothes in the lid compartment, and even thebest suitcaseswould sometimes leave my clothing creased and jumbled.Packing cubes have changed all that. Boxy, zippable and small to varying degrees, these organisation accessories are designed to keep items neat and separate inside a suitcase or bag.Luggage organisation accessories have been around for decades, but only in recent years has interest in packing cubes boomed. Formerly the preserve of travel aficionados, they’re now part of mainstream travel, borne on a wave of social media recommendations and celebrity endorsements.You’ll often find packing cubes sold as a set, with assorted sizes to suit different types of luggage (such as larger cubes for shirts, dresses or trousers, and smaller ones for socks and underwear). Most are a soft-sided cuboid shape, so packingcubeis a misnomer. Some brands call them “packing cells”.As products go, packing cubes are not especially varied, but you may still notice meaningful differences between them. Some are slightly more rigid; some are made from smarter-looking or softer materials; and some have special features, such as double-zippered compression packing cubes, which squeeze air out to save space.I tested 14 of the best packing cube sets (and related products such as shoe bags) to help you solve your own particular packing puzzles. The best 11 are reviewed below.At a glanceBest packing cubes overallJulyPacking cells, four pack£40 at JulyBest budget packing cubesM&SPacking cubes, five pack£15 at M&SBest packing cubes with sectionsStubble & CoPacking cubes, three pack£60 at Stubble & CoBest compression packing cubesAntlerStripe packing cubes, four pack£55 at AntlerBest shoe storageTroubadourElemental shoe bag£39 at TroubadourWhy you should trust meThere are few travel essentials I’ve yet to review for the Filter. Mytravel pillow testingtook me aboard trains, buses and arcade machines; I reviewedcabin bagsby hauling them over an assault course; and I’ve applied a similar spirit of adventurous rigour to assessing the packing cubes featured here.I’ve been testing products for this publication and others for the past decade, as well as writing articles on travel and other topics. On the rare and serene occasions when product samples aren’t whizzing in and out of my home, I like to explore this country and – when I’m lucky enough – others. The reviews below are all grounded in real travel experiences.How I testedView image in fullscreenCase closed? Testing exposed the packing cubes’ ability to keep clothes neat.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianI tested the packing cubes during a period in which I had staycations and work trips around England planned, so that I’d have the opportunity to field-test everything while travelling. I packed the cubes with appropriately sized items and assessed their ability to keep clothing neat and crease-free.For a sterner test, I made sure to jostle each set of packing cubes inside my suitcase or bag, then noted how well the items inside had retained their stored shape. There’s no doubt that subjective factors such as feel and aesthetic also play into the appeal of a packing cube, so I’ve referenced these considerations where noteworthy.Most of the brands didn’t need their packing cubes back after testing. These review units have been donated for fundraising toCat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.The best packing cubes in 2026View image in fullscreenPack attack: writer Pete has travel cubes covered (or vice versa).Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianBest packing cubes overall:July packing cells, four packJulyPacking cells, four packfrom£40£40 at July£40 at ReversibleWhat we loveExcellent at keeping clothes neatWhat we don’t loveLack rigidity when part-filledView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£40 at July£40 at ReversibleBetween the four cubes in this set – two large, one medium and one small – there’s ample scope to store different types of clothing separately. The large cubes are best for shirts, while smaller items can roll or fold up neatly into the medium and small ones.Why we lovethemI put some smart shirts and trousers into these packing cubes, slung them into a duffel bag and travelled well over 200 miles by bus, train and ferry, stopping to add a secondhand cat ornament to my luggage along the way. At the end of all this, I was impressed to find that the cubes had kept the clothes crease-free and neatly folded, just as they were when I packed them.The cubes themselves are simple and nicely finished. On the sides and base, the material is shiny and smooth, with a fine texture providing some grip for stored items. A mesh top layer provides breathability and easy identification of which clothes are in which cube, while the double zipper feels decent quality.It’s a shame that …you may find that these are a little too soft to keep some items straight and orderly, especially when you don’t have enough suitable clothing to fill a cube – or if your luggage will have to go through the ordeal of an aeroplane’s hold.Type:standard packing cube setOther options:yes,this eight-packSizes included (WDH):small (26 x 17 x 8cm), medium (37 x 17 x 13cm), large (37 x 26 x 10cm)Colours available:fourMaterials:polyesterJulyPacking cells, four packfrom£40£40 at July£40 at ReversibleWhat we loveExcellent at keeping clothes neatWhat we don’t loveLack rigidity when part-filledBest budget packing cubes:M&S packing cubes, five packM&SPacking cubes, five pack£15£15 at M&SWhat we loveFunctional and affordableWhat we don’t loveToo small for folding certain clothesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£15 at M&SThis eclectic polyester packing set covers a lot of bases, with three packing cubes of different sizes, plus a shoe bag and a laundry pouch for worn items. It is by far the lowest-priced set I’ve tested.Why we lovethemI slung this packing cube set into my holdall for a camping trip to Wensleydale, and although it’s not flashy, it made it blissfully simple to keep my things (and therefore mytent) organised. The three pouches are perfect for items such as T-shirts, underwear and socks, and I appreciated being able to quarantine worn hiking socks and other garments inside the drawstring laundry bag.The design of the cubes is plain and practical. A mesh section on the front of each affords visibility and breathability, and a single zipper provides access. I couldn’t fit my size 11hiking bootsinside the shoe bag, but it proved large enough for smart shoes or low-cut walking shoes.It’s a shame that …none of the three packing cubes are particularly large. If you like to fold larger items such as dresses, trousers or shirts flat, rather than rolling them, then you may struggle for space.Type:standard packing cube set (plus shoe bag and laundry pouch)Other options:yes,this three-packSizes included (WDH):small (24 x 10 x 10cm); medium (24 x 22 x 10cm); large (31 x 23 x 10cm); shoe bag (26 x 45cm WH); laundry bag (36 x 45cm WH)Colours available:oneMaterials:polyesterM&SPacking cubes, five pack£15£15 at M&SWhat we loveFunctional and affordableWhat we don’t loveToo small for folding certain clothesBest packing cubes with sections:Stubble & Co packing cubes, three packStubble & CoPacking cubes, three pack£60£60 at Stubble & CoWhat we loveExtra compartments for fastidious packersWhat we don’t loveNot always space-efficientView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£60 at Stubble & CoDo you require internal organisation for your internal organisation? This Stubble & Co set has storage options galore, with useful compartments inside each cube. The smallest cube divides in two, with a transparent zippered pocket occupying one half; the medium one has two zippered pockets (including a transparent wipe-clean pocket that’s ideal for toiletries); and the largest cube has a large mesh zippered pocket on one side.Why we lovethemI suspect some people will find the added sections more useful than others. For me, having dedicated spaces within each cube proved handy, as I was able to store items of a certain kind (such as socks or underwear) inside each cube, then move worn items into the zippered compartment to keep them separate and organised. My hotel room looked much neater for not having worn clothes piled up on a chair, and I was able to return clothes that I didn’t wear on holiday to my wardrobe at home.Made mostly from recycled nylon ripstop material, these cubes are pleasant to handle. You can choose from two colours for each cube in the set: black or off-white.It’s a shame that …the abundance of internal storage means that the cubes’ capacity is slightly lower than you might expect at first glance.Type:standard packing cube setOther options:available individually,packing cube 2.5l,packing cube 8l,packing cube 11lSizes included (WDH):small (21 x 6 x 14.5cm); medium (31 x 9 x 24cm); large (29 x 10 x 33cm)Colours available:twoMaterials:nylon ripstop, recycled polyester mesh, semi-transparent thermoplastic polyurethaneStubble & CoPacking cubes, three pack£60£60 at Stubble & CoWhat we loveExtra compartments for fastidious packersWhat we don’t loveNot always space-efficientBest compression packing cubes:Antler Stripe packing cubes, four packAntlerStripe packing cubes, four pack£55£55 at AntlerWhat we loveBrilliant compressionWhat we don’t loveTwo cubes are very smallView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£55 at AntlerThese compression cubes from Antler make efficient use of space, with a second zipper that can be used to squash down the cube after you’ve filled it. The set includes two small cubes, one medium and one (fairly) large, so you’ll have options to store different types of items.Why we love themIf you haven’t used compression packing cubes before, you’re in for a treat. The second zipper does a great job of squishing the cubes, making a meaningful difference to their size and the luggage space they take up.Among Antler’s many packing cube designs, I particularly liked this stripy green colourway, which features the brand’s Icon Stripe motif on the expandable sides and base of each cube. While I enjoy stripes as much as the next person, the key benefit here is that the contrasting pattern will help you identify when and how the cube is expanded or compressed. The cubes are beautifully finished with pleasing plastic zip pulls and mesh windows on the upper sides.It’s a shame that …while the two smallest cubes are cute and boxy, I found it difficult to identify items of clothing that could be stored inside (beyond a few pairs of socks in each). For me, a single larger cube would have been more useful.Type:compression packing cube setOther options:yes,this six-pack (solid colour)Sizes included (WDH):small x 2 (17.5 x 10 x 16.5cm), medium (33 x 10 x 17.5cm), large (33 x 10 x 24.5cm)Colours available:twoMaterials:recycled polyesterAntlerStripe packing cubes, four pack£55£55 at AntlerWhat we loveBrilliant compressionWhat we don’t loveTwo cubes are very smallBest shoe storage:Troubadour Elemental shoe bagTroubadourElemental shoe bag£39£39 at TroubadourWhat we loveWell made and effectiveWhat we don’t loveHigh price for an individual pouchView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£39 at TroubadourFor adventures that will feature a few dressier moments along the way, this could be the ideal packing accessory to keep shoes smart, safe and fresh. In fact, it’s a suitable choice for packing just about anything inside a backpack, where the Elemental shoe bag’s soft, lightweight construction works well.Why we love itThe pouch was long enough for my UK size 11 shoes with a little wriggle room. It is closed by rolling and then buckling the stiffened material at the open end, much like a messenger bag or wet-or-dry bag.I was pleased with how my leather shoes looked after a long journey in this bag, with the ripstop material protecting them from marks and scratches. I also made use of the airlock sewn into the bag, choosing to leave it open so the shoes could “breathe”. This would be good for preventing the buildup of odours or mildew during long, sweaty journeys – or for sealing in smells whenever fellow travellers are nearby.A woven handle at the closed end of the bag provides a handy way to yank it out of your rucksack or duffel in a hurry.It’s a shame that …I couldn’t fit my bulkiest hiking boots inside the bag.Type:shoe bagOther options:yes,large packing dome,small packing domeSize (WH):32.5 x 49cmColours available:oneMaterials:ripstop nylonTroubadourElemental shoe bag£39£39 at TroubadourWhat we loveWell made and effectiveWhat we don’t loveHigh price for an individual pouchThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Offers added protection to valuables or items vulnerable to water damage’: the Thule Chasm small gear cube.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianThule Chasm small gear cube 3lThuleChasm small gear cube 3lfrom£27£27 at Blacks£29.99 at AmazonWhat we loveBrilliant quality and designWhat we don’t loveLimited storage capacityView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£27 at Blacks£29.99 at AmazonBest for:a weather-resistantoptionEven the most dependable rucksack or suitcase might let in water occasionally – especially if the material is damaged or its waterproof layer is depleted. The Thule Chasm small gear cube offers added protection to valuables or items vulnerable to water damage, with a weather-resistant tarp fabric and polyurethane-coated zippers to limit water ingress.I used this cube to keep my travel documents and smartphone safe while travelling in poor weather. It kept its contents perfectly dry, and I found that I could make the Chasm slightly more cavernous by manipulating the material at the bottom, which naturally tends to pucker inwards. The clippable handle attaches to rucksacks and other items that have a loop or bar.It didn’t make the final cut because …while it performed well during testing in rainy weather, I expect some would prefer a fully waterproof or a larger option.Type:weather-resistant packing cube;other options:yes,this 11l packing cube;size (WDH):21.5 x 11.5 x 14cm;colours available:two;materials:100% recycled 900D polyester, phthalate-free laminateThuleChasm small gear cube 3lfrom£27£27 at Blacks£29.99 at AmazonWhat we loveBrilliant quality and designWhat we don’t loveLimited storage capacityAway Insider packing cubes, four packAwayInsider packing cubes, four packfrom£48£48 at Away£48 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy on the eye – and on fabricsWhat we don’t loveWork best with suitcase compression strapsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£48 at Away£48 at AmazonBest for:a vibrant selection of coloursOf all the packing cubes I’ve used, these are perhaps the most pleasing to look at and handle. There’s an eye-popping range of colours to choose from, including the cherry red shown and a lovely limited-edition pink sand. The nylon body is soft and water-repellent, but a mesh upper means they can’t be fully relied on for protecting items vulnerable to water damage. There’s a good range of sizes, with the largest cube providing ample space for most larger items of clothing, and because each cube is a different size, there’s plenty of versatility relative to the number of cubes in the set.It didn’t make the final cut because …these cubes are a little floppy-sided for my taste. However, they work very well under compression straps in a suitcase.Type:standard packing cube set;other options:yes,this set of six, andthis set of four compression packing cubes;sizes included (WDH):small wide (25.5 x 10.5 x 21cm); medium slim (25.5 x 10.5 x 11cm); medium wide (33 x 10.5 x 25.5cm); large slim (33 x 10.5 x 17.5cm) ;colours available:14;materials:nylonAwayInsider packing cubes, four packfrom£48£48 at Away£48 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy on the eye – and on fabricsWhat we don’t loveWork best with suitcase compression strapsBriggs & Riley Check-In packing cube setBriggs & RileyCheck-In packing cube setfrom£99£99 at Briggs & Riley£99 at SelfridgesWhat we loveGenerous sizes and excellent constructionWhat we don’t loveJet-set pricingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£99 at Briggs & Riley£99 at SelfridgesBest for:storing larger itemsOne of the downsides to many of the packing cube sets I’ve reviewed is that they’re missing a cube that’s wide or long enough for storing larger clothes folded flat. This bougie Briggs & Riley set is the perfect fix for travellers who share my finickiness in this matter, with check-in-luggage-appropriate cubes that can easily house a smartly folded shirt or a pair of trousers.Using the compression zipper makes a decent difference to the cubes’ storage capability, albeit not as drastically as certain competitors. The materials look lavish, and the construction is impeccable.It didn’t make the final cut because …while these are undoubtedly excellent packing cubes, the set’s price will be a no-go for many travellers.Type:compression packing cube set;other options:yes,this smaller set of three packing cubes;sizes included (WDH):small (21.6 x 7.6 x 16.5cm); medium (33 x 7.6 x 21.6cm); large (43.2 x 7.6 x 21.6cm);colours available:six;materials:recycled polyesterBriggs & RileyCheck-In packing cube setfrom£99£99 at Briggs & Riley£99 at SelfridgesWhat we loveGenerous sizes and excellent constructionWhat we don’t loveJet-set pricingLifeventure Storm Cube large boot bagLifeventureStorm Cube large boot bagfrom£19.95£19.95 at Outdoor Action£21.99 at LifeventureWhat we loveIdeal for storing large bootsWhat we don’t loveRelatively limited appealView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£19.95 at Outdoor ActionBest for:storing hiking bootsIf there’s one item of apparel that ought to be kept separate from other luggage, it’s surely your hiking boots. This boot bag from outdoor brand Lifeventure fulfilled this requirement perfectly during my Yorkshire Dales camping trip, generously housing footwear up to a UK size 11.Boots tend to be tougher than the average garment, and this pouch felt suitably hardy, holding up well to my boots as they jostled around inside its ripstop nylon fabric.It didn’t make the final cut because …this type of packing accessory has more of a niche audience than the average packing cube set – but that’s no slight on its performance.Type:boot bag;other options:yes,this shoe bag;size (WDH):28 x 11 x 42cm;colours available:one;materials:ripstop nylonLifeventureStorm Cube large boot bagfrom£19.95£19.95 at Outdoor Action£21.99 at LifeventureWhat we loveIdeal for storing large bootsWhat we don’t loveRelatively limited appealCarl Friedrik the packing cubesCarl FriedrikThe packing cubesfrom£75£75 at Carl Friedrik£75 at John LewisWhat we loveGood selection of sizesWhat we don’t loveSurprisingly plain for the priceView image in fullscreen£75 at Carl Friedrik£75 at John LewisBest for:simplicity meets high qualityPerfectly made and variously sized, these packing cubes will suit travellers who value quality over elaborateness. The four sizes included gave me plenty of scope to pack a variety of clothes, whether I was on a work trip to London or camping in the countryside. The standard of the recycled synthetic material and weighty zippers was clearly a cut above the average cube, too. They’re very lightweight and fit perfectly inside acabin bag.It didn’t make the final cut because …considering the price you pay, this packing cube set is surprisingly plain. A little more embellishment would make the expense feel warranted.Type:standard packing cube set;other options:no;sizes included (WDH):small (11 x 10 x 26cm); medium (20.5 x 10 x 26cm); large (32 x 10 x 17.5cm); extra-large (26 x 10 x 32cm);colours available:two;materials:recycled PET plasticCarl FriedrikThe packing cubesfrom£75£75 at Carl Friedrik£75 at John LewisWhat we loveGood selection of sizesWhat we don’t loveSurprisingly plain for the priceLittleLife Otter packing cube setLittleLifeOtter packing cube set£24.99£24.99 at LittleLifeWhat we loveCute design and wipeable materialWhat we don’t loveKids will grow out of itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£24.99 at LittleLifeBest for:young childrenIt never hurts to have more otter-themed items in your life. This packing cube set from LittleLife is particularly endearing, with a lovely print and materials and dimensions designed to suit very young children.I’m contentedly babyless, but two of my friends are parents to a cherubic infant and took this set for a spin. They found it useful for carrying baby care items day to day, as well as for bigger adventures. Importantly, the materials are wipe-clean.It didn’t make the final cut because …some parents may prefer to buy a generic packing cube set for their child to use for longer.Type:children’s packing cube set;other options:no;sizes included (WH):2 x small pouches (23 x 17cm); large pouch (25 x 22cm); small case (20 x 15cm); large case (30 x 20cm);colours available:one;materials:polyesterLittleLifeOtter packing cube set£24.99£24.99 at LittleLifeWhat we loveCute design and wipeable materialWhat we don’t loveKids will grow out of itWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenNeat trick: packing cubes can help clothes stay folded in transit.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianWhat’s the best way to pack a packing cube?Testing for this article taught me that the most important consideration is to make sure your packing cube is filled close to capacity. This prevents items from moving around and getting creased inside the cube, which would limit its usefulness. If you’re using a compression packing cube, this is somewhat less relevant, as you can shrink the cube down to suit its contents.Packing cubes are ideal for travellers who like to fold smart clothes flat, as they can help them stay folded. Of course, you can roll clothes up inside them if you prefer. There’s more than one way to pack a cube.How do compression packing cubes work?If you want to pack as much as possible into your suitcase, then a set of compression cubes could save you a little space (relative to ordinary ones).Typically, compression packing cubes have two zippers – one to seal your items inside, and another that allows you to squeeze the cube into a tighter form. Close the first zipper, squish the packing cube down until you’re satisfied, then do up the second zipper.A more extreme option, generally reserved for lengthy trips or moving home, is a vacuum bag, which uses a vacuum cleaner to remove air and compress your belongings. Unlike a compression packing cube, however, you can’t open and reseal whenever you need something during your journey.Are packing cubes suitable for backpacks?Packing cubes are perhaps at their most useful inside a backpack, where solutions for organising clothes are often limited. I use a packing cube inside my day-to-day backpack to keep my five-a-side football kit separate from non-sweaty things. I’ve also started taking a few of them on multiday hikes and camping trips – one or two for fresh clothes, and one or two for grubby ones.Some packing accessories are pouch-shaped, which are arguably more convenient for a backpack than blocky packing cubes, especially if you want something to store flip-flops or casual shoes for your downtime.Particularly large packing cubes may not be suitable for backpacks, as it may be difficult to fit them inside the bag or through its opening.For more ways to travel smarter with the Filter:The best suitcases for your next holidayThe best carry-on luggage – testedBased in the US?
