title: Why is Sweden deporting Britons faster than any other EU country post-Brexit?  | David Milstead | The Guardian
description: The official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another story, says David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner
Author: David Milstead
Headline: The official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another story, says David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner
Content: Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years, has been told to leave the country.Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardianView image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, a retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years, has been told to leave the country.Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardianOpinionSwedenWhy is Sweden deporting Britons faster than any other EU country post-Brexit?David MilsteadThe official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another storyTue 18 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTShareThere is anger about the case ofJoyce Thomas, a 78-year-old retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years. Her husband died there; her son, grandchildren and home are there. Yet she has been told to leave because her post-Brexit residence application was late. Her case is appalling and predictable – but far from isolated.The Guardian has also reported on the plight ofHorace Mason, 74, who faces being deported after a court ruling, despite having lived in Sweden for 25 years. This is sad but not surprising.When Sweden set out its plans in 2020, we at theBrits in Swedencampaign warned in an official submission that the application scheme could strip vulnerable people of their rights if they missed the deadline. We urged a flexible and generous approach, and later raised concerns about outreach and refusals with the UK government and European Commission. We have watched Britons fall off that cliff edge since 2021; only occasionally does a case reach the media.The new scheme gave British residents safeguards under free-movement law – including assistance, reasonable grounds for lateness and proportionality – that were untested.View image in fullscreenKenny Solomons with his wife, Tess. Solomons’ application to remain in Sweden was rejected.Photograph: Kenny SolomonsWe were not alone. The Swedish Bar Association said the new rules must be applied generously to both evidence and deadlines, to which the government insisted that the authorities already had sufficient flexibility.The truth of the situationis now clear, for the statistics only point in one direction. Almost4,000 of 14,200 applications in Sweden have been refused. The UK Foreign Office calculates a 27.5% refusal rate – three times that of any other member state and far above the EU average of 3–4%. Eurostat records 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave Sweden since 2021, about a third of the EU total.Reporting differences complicate detailed comparisons, but the statistics show a red flag consistent with lived experience.Kathleen Poolehad advanced Alzheimer’s when Sweden tried to remove her in 2023.Nichola Stanlickarrived aged seven, 40 years ago, and applied on time, yet was refused withdrawal agreement protection and given a national permit expiring in 2027.Kenny Solomons, the husband of a Swedish singer, was forced to leave and would have to qualify under national law to return as a resident.Data on genuine missed-deadline applications remains opaque. Earlier figures mixed them with legitimate later applicants, including people joining family members and those seeking permanent status. After we raised this with Whitehall, the UK challenged the data andSwedenno longer show it in EU reports. Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late.TheBrexittreaty called for an awareness campaign, but unlike Denmark and the Netherlands, the Swedish government chose not to contact registered Britons individually. Some people who enquired to Swedish authorities were told they need do nothing; official information did not always say that this meant “not yet”. Older people and those without computers were easily missed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSweden also tried to deport Kathleen Poole, seen here in a dementia care home with her son Wayne and daughter-in-law Angelica.Photograph: Angelica PooleThe then director general of the SwedishMigrationAgency stated that he believed contacting registered Britons individually would not have made a difference. This is difficult to reconcile with the evidence base.The problem is not confined to those who submitted late applications. Sweden sometimes refused withdrawal agreement status but granted temporary national permits. That merely kicks the can down the road. As those permits expire, some people cannot meet newer permanent-residence requirements, or no longer have the family circumstances on which their permits depended.So why Sweden, and why now? The answer is that Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically. A Swedish faith in neutral rules and independent agencies can also mistake procedural uniformity for justice when radically different human circumstances are reduced to data points.Britons in the EU are caught in a political perfect storm. EU citizens in Britain have a constituency and dedicated monitoring authority, whereas Britons are divided among 27 systems. Brexit created the problem, but did not require Sweden to conduct inadequate outreach, obscure statistics or stretch proportionality.We are stuck in a very difficult middle: Brexiters resist admitting that Brexit created these problems, while some remainers resist criticising an EU member state. Both, in their relative positions, abandon the people the agreement protects.In the Whitehall satire Yes, Prime Minister, the official response to a foreign problem progresses from “nothing is going to happen”, to “maybe we should do something about it, but there’s nothing wecando”, and finally to “maybe there was something we could have done, but it’s too late now”. The UK government and commission must intervene before reaching that final stage. Sweden should pause disputed removals, publish reliable cohort statistics and submit the scheme to independent review before more lives are irreversibly uprooted.David Milstead is a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner, working through theBrits in SwedengroupExplore more on these topicsSwedenOpinionBrexitMigrationEuropean UnionEuropeForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on global inequality: extreme wealth threatens democracy | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani shows Britain’s Andy Burnham that confronting billionaires need not mean the end of cooperation with Donald Trump
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani shows Britain’s Andy Burnham that confronting billionaires need not mean the end of cooperation with Donald Trump
Content: Zohran Mamdani and Donald Trump at the White House. ‘Despite clashing, the leftwing mayor and the rightwing president continue to talk.’Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenZohran Mamdani and Donald Trump at the White House. ‘Despite clashing, the leftwing mayor and the rightwing president continue to talk.’Photograph: ReutersOpinionInequalityThe Guardian view on global inequality: extreme wealth threatens democracyEditorialNew York mayor Zohran Mamdani shows Britain’s Andy Burnham that confronting billionaires need not mean the end of cooperation with Donald TrumpTue 18 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareIn November,Californianswill vote on a one-off 5% levy on residents worth more than $1bn. The union-backed plan could raise $100bn, more than enough to replace federal healthcare funding stripped away byDonald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. About 200 very rich people would pay. But the referendum is becoming a test of whether extreme wealth can buy the political power todefeata popular redistributive policy. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has already spent $100m backing opposition to the tax – a fraction of the $13bn bill he could face. Otherbillionairesare joining him. Whether voters can impose costs on the super-rich once their fortunes are big enough to shape the political process is now an open question. That alone should trouble any democracy.It’s a long way from Mr Brin’s west coast lair ofMountain Viewto Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency. But the prime minister should heed the call from prominent progressive academics – led by the Nobel prize winnerJoseph Stiglitz– urging Britain to join a new global push to tackle inequality. Prof Stiglitz wants help creating a new UN International Panel on Inequality (IPI). This stems from the G20’sfirst-ever inequality report, which warned that the yawning gap between rich and poor was a human-made crisis corroding democracy and social cohesion while blocking efforts to tackle the climate emergency.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: AFP/GettyThe academics argue that Mr Burnham’s Makerfield test – which aims to be fairer to places neglected by Westminster – should apply abroad as well as at home. By connecting the government’s domestic programme to its foreign policy, a distinct Burnhamism could take shape. Between 2000 and 2024, the richest 1% captured 41% of new global wealth; the poorest half received 1%. Britain mirrors this divide. The economistGabriel Zucmansays the UK’s richest 0.001% – about 200 families – held wealth worth 5% of GDP in 1989. Today, those families command an astonishing 25% of the country’s GDP.When Mr Burnhamtravels to the UNnext month, he should back the IPI and make tackling global inequality a priority of Britain’s 2027 G20 presidency. Prof Stiglitz argues that extreme inequality is a policy choice, turbocharged by financial deregulation, weaker labour protections and privatisation. Highly unequal countries areseven timesmore likely to suffer democratic backsliding or authoritarian drift. Taxing theultra-wealthyshould be part of Britain’s response to a worldwide emergency.After Labour’s aid cuts, Mr Burnham also needs a credible way of saying Britain is back in global development. The IPI gives him an inexpensive initiative around which to build reform ofinternational taxation, debt relief and illicit financial flows. None of this suggests that the UK wants an unproductive relationship with Washington. The White House is threatening the UK over its plans for a digital services tax, with the USwarningthat Mr Trump’s threat of retaliatory 100% tariffs is real. Policy disagreement need not poison the relationship.Mr Trump has denounced Zohran Mamdani’s New York luxury second-home tax as a “dangerous political experiment” and threatened to block it. Yet despite clashing, the leftwing mayor and the rightwing presidentcontinueto talk,cooperatingonhousingandimmigrationcases. Their warm White Housemeetingin February suggests that Mr Trump may respect politicians who openly disagree with him more than those who bend over backwards not to offend him. Perhaps Mr Burnham should take heart: being true to himself may work.Explore more on these topicsInequalityOpinionG20Donald TrumpSergey BrinTax and spendingZohran MamdaniAndy BurnhameditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s own | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Wordsworth Trust has acquired a second home. Cherished authors including George Eliot don’t even have one
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Wordsworth Trust has acquired a second home. Cherished authors including George Eliot don’t even have one
Content: Rydal Mount in the Lake District.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenRydal Mount in the Lake District.Photograph: AlamyOpinionMuseumsThe Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s ownEditorialThe Wordsworth Trust has acquired a second home. Cherished authors including George Eliot don’t even have oneTue 18 Aug 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTShareInterest in all things Jane Austen remains high, following the celebrations of her 250th anniversary. In September, the museum based in her former home in Chawton, Hampshire, will host aPersuasion festival. But a less obvious beneficiary of this spike in interest is a museum dedicated to two writers she never met: William and Dorothy Wordsworth. The success of the BBC television series The Other Bennet Sister – which portrayed Mary, a minor character in Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, as a Wordsworth enthusiast – has led to aninflux of visitorsto Dove Cottage in Cumbria.This has been a big year for the Wordsworth Trust, which owns the cottage, owing to its purchase of another house:Rydal Mount, two miles to the east. When this building is reopened, the poet will become one of a handful of authors, along with Charles Dickens and Thomas Hardy, to have more than one of his homes opened to visitors.These can be extraordinarily evocative places, brought to life by knowledgable guides. The modest cottages occupied by Hardy and Coleridge before they were famous stand in stark contrast to the aristocratic grandeur of other National Trust houses – and are an important reminder of how ordinary people once lived. In homes such as Monk’s House in East Sussex, near where Virginia Woolf drowned in the River Ouse, andKeats Housein Hampstead, where the poet became ill with tuberculosis, death casts unavoidable shadows.View image in fullscreenGeorge Eliot.Photograph: Print Collector/GettyRydal Mount was sold by its previous owners in part due to a drop in numbers, and curators must be adept in capitalising on any new sources of interest. At the Brontë Parsonage in Yorkshire, an exhibition accompanied this year’s release of a new Wuthering Heights film; at Anne Hathaway’s cottage in Stratford-upon-Avon,Hamnet toursare on offer.Turning their homes into museums is, of course, not the only way to commemorate writers in the built environment. Edinburgh’s main railway station, Waverley, is famously the only one in the world named after a novel; Walter Scott, who wrote it, also has a monument across the road. National portrait galleries in Edinburgh and London depict authors alongside artists, scientists, royals, politicians and others. Buildings across the UK are adorned with blue plaques; William Shakespeare has a statue in Leicester Square.No writer of colour has yet had their British home turned into a museum. Since this transformation generally happens years after an author’s death, this is not surprising; immigrants from India, the Caribbean and Africa, and their descendants, mostly made their mark on the world of books from the mid-20th century onwards. Hopefully more houses, or flats, will be opened in future;VS Naipaul’sbook The Enigma of Arrival offers a vivid, semi-fictional account of his years in a borrowed cottage on a Wiltshire estate.George Eliot is a more perplexing absence from the map of homes to visit – all the more so since her novelMiddlemarchrecently topped two Guardian polls. While the London house that she shared with George Henry Lewes was demolished, and the Arbury Estatewhere she was bornis currently closed, efforts to restore abuilding linked to her familynear Nuneaton have so far not succeeded. But a replica of her sitting room is in thetown’s museum, while Coventry’s Herbert Art Gallery has her piano and desk. Fundraisers should be encouraged to try again: the 150th anniversary of her death falls in 2030.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Andy Burnham should resist populist pressure on jail sentences | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Nik Wood says the prime minister must be tough on the causes of crime, Henry Rossi calls for him to resolve the IPP crisis, while Janet Carter considers victims of domestic abuse
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Nik Wood says the prime minister must be tough on the causes of crime, Henry Rossi calls for him to resolve the IPP crisis, while Janet Carter considers victims of domestic abuse
Content: ‘Resolving IPP would end one of the greatest scandals in our criminal justice system.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Resolving IPP would end one of the greatest scandals in our criminal justice system.’Photograph: AlamyPrisons and probationLettersAndy Burnham should resist populist pressure on jail sentencesNik Woodsays the prime minister must be tough on the causes of crime,Henry Rossicalls for him to resolve the IPP crisis, whileJanet Carterconsiders victims of domestic abuseTue 18 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTShareAs you say in your editorial (The Guardian view on early prisoner release: don’t lose sight of systemic reform, 12 August), governments of all stripes have bowed to pressure for ever longer sentencing. For instance, the killers of PC Andrew Harper would now face mandatory life sentences, campaigned for across the board. It was the unlikely figure of Douglas Hurd, the Conservative home secretary, who said thatprison is an expensive way of making bad people worse. That expense is always one that is tempting for governments demonstratively to minimise.The result is a prison service that hasn’t got room for all those the courts convict, nor enough staff or scope to reform and rehabilitate them for the benefit of society. The assault that has been made on Parole Board and probation decision-making and capabilities compounds this.So,Andy Burnhamhas inherited a decision that has nothing to do with judicially assessed sentencing and remission, merely to do with patching a hole in the balance sheet. If he does indeed want to avoid a repeat of this shambles, as you report, then he has to grow a backbone and stand up against the populist pressures to appear “tough on crime”, and find the money to be “tough on the causes of crime”.Nik WoodLondonThe government’s scramble to keep PC Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars while freeing up space in prisons is the latest example of UK policy shortcomings and a subsequent failure to remedy the scandal. None stand out more than the unaddressed injustice of imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences. Abolished over a decade ago and described as “psychological torture” by the UN,over 2,000people remain trapped in prisons on IPP sentences.Andy Burnham has pledged to find an early resolution to the IPP crisis, but too often politicians have decried scandals, only to then kick the can down the road.Resolving IPP would end one of the greatest scandals in our criminal justice system and also ease the burden on our creaking prisons – resentencing IPP prisoners couldfree upthe equivalent of four prisons. The time for acknowledging injustices and promising to conduct a review is over. It’s time to act.Henry RossiBristolWith reference to your article (More women will die if domestic abusers leave prison early, victim’s parents warn, 17 August), there is an effective way for the government to mitigate this sad fact. This is to legislate to ensure that the court must always consider future protection in all cases of domestic abuse, rather than just focus on immediate incarceration.How? To make it a presumption that the relevant “add-on” ancillary order is always considered whenever available, or give reasons why the order is not appropriate. For instance, it may be disproportionate given the facts of the case, or the victim may give freely held views that they genuinely do not want an order to be made.For instance, an add-on restraining order with terms to exclude the perpetrator from the home and work areas of the victim, for life, so that the victim has some security and safety whenever the release date happens to fall. Various protective orders are available, but they are not yet an obligatory consideration in open court. They should be, along with obligatory victim consultation before sentence.Janet CarterRetired barrister, LeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Contemplating death helps us to really value life | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: Letters: Say the thing, mend the relationship, share the story – and then get on with living, says end-of-life doula Rebecca Jo-Rushdy, while Jane Andrew thinks EM Forster said it best
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Say the thing, mend the relationship, share the story – and then get on with living, says end-of-life doula Rebecca Jo-Rushdy, while Jane Andrew thinks EM Forster said it best
Content: ‘Perhaps the most loving response to that uncertainty is not to fear death, but to use its inevitability as an invitation.’Photograph: Posed by model; Rohappy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Perhaps the most loving response to that uncertainty is not to fear death, but to use its inevitability as an invitation.’Photograph: Posed by model; Rohappy/Getty ImagesDeath and dyingLettersContemplating death helps us to really value lifeSay the thing, mend the relationship, share the story – and then get on with living, says end-of-life doulaRebecca Jo-Rushdy, whileJane Andrewthinks EM Forster said it bestTue 18 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTShareWhat struck me most about this article (What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work, 13 August) is the idea that preparing for the end of life can actually help us live more fully now.As an end-of-life doula, I have seen how a terminal diagnosis can suddenly bring clarity. The things that once felt urgent often fall away, while relationships, memories, unfinished conversations and the question of what we leave behind become profoundly important. But I don’t believe that we should have to wait for a diagnosis to begin that work.We often think of “getting our affairs in order” as something practical: writing a will, sorting passwords or deciding what happens to our possessions. Yet there is something much more human underneath all of this. It is about asking: what matters to me? What do I want my family to know? What stories, photographs, objects or values do I want to pass on? And, perhaps most importantly, what can I let go of so that the people I love are not left carrying unnecessary burdens?I have come to see this as creating a joyful legacy. Decluttering, when approached this way, isn’t simply about having a tidier home. It can be a way of making space for the life we are actually living – while making things a little easier for those who may one day have to sort through what we leave behind.The article rightly reminds us that none of us knows how much time we have. Perhaps the most loving response to that uncertainty is not to fear death, but to use its inevitability as an invitation: say the thing, mend the relationship, celebrate the birthday, sort the photographs, share the story – and then get on with living.Rebecca Jo-RushdyEdinburghI recently recovered from major cancer surgery, and Sarah Phillips’ article rang very true. Being forced to embrace my own mortality has helped me find what truly shines in ordinary life. EM Forster put it so well: “Death destroys a man: the idea of Death saves him”.Jane AndrewPerthHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Poverty and weariness in Nigel Farage’s Clacton | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Letters: Vanessa Scanlan says the constituency is desperately in need of a decent MP who would offer genuine support for the problems it faces. Plus letters from Leila Roberts and Richard Ellis
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Vanessa Scanlan says the constituency is desperately in need of a decent MP who would offer genuine support for the problems it faces. Plus letters from Leila Roberts and Richard Ellis
Content: ‘Is there any wonder that a charismatic man offering a simple answer to complex problems is held on to so tightly?’Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Is there any wonder that a charismatic man offering a simple answer to complex problems is held on to so tightly?’Photograph: AFP/GettyNigel FarageLettersPoverty and weariness in Nigel Farage’s ClactonVanessa Scanlansays the constituency is desperately in need of a decent MP who would offer genuine support for the problems it faces. Plus letters fromLeila RobertsandRichard EllisTue 18 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTShareI live in the Clacton constituency, in one of the surrounding villages, some distance from the town, and I agree with Sarah Elizabeth Cox’s characterisation of the town (Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here, 12 August).When I go to Clacton to take my kids to the beach or to the cinema, there is a sudden shift in the character of the area. The deprivation radiates in some streets. It is painful to see the residents so keenly in need of a decent MP to offer genuine support for a town with so many problems being exploited byNigel Farage.I have worked my way through a number of podcasts and news articles during this byelection and the 2024 general election campaigns. Those cherrypicked vox pops and even the broader and more balanced reporting speak of poverty and weariness in the Clacton population. Is it any wonder that a charismatic man offering a simple answer to complex problems is held on to so tightly?Vanessa ScanlanGreat Bentley, EssexSo Nigel Farage couldn’t attend his election results because ofsecurity concerns– despite the £5m he was given forhis security. Blimey, Clacton must be dangerous.Leila RobertsRipon, North YorkshireThe Clacton byelection’s rash of joke candidates has been pretty much passed off by every media outlet as just another example of the “British sense of humour”, originating more or less from the frivolous establishment of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 1982. However, I am sufficiently old enough to recall that amid the laughter, anxious voices warned then that this could also fuel a debasement of the serious importance of politics and government in the UK. A case can be made that the far right’s rise in the UK has been partly fuelled by the way that politics has been reduced to a joke by such allegedly harmless shenanigans, which in fact implicitly or openly rely on reducing mainstream politics to the status of uniformly useless – “they are all the same”.Richard EllisDerbyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Autonomous drones and the future of war in an AI-driven world | Technology | The Guardian
description: Letter: Machines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe, writes military surgeon Dr Darren Mann
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Machines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe, writes military surgeon Dr Darren Mann
Content: An autonomous drone ‘does what it is told, killing whatever is inside, combatant or child’.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenAn autonomous drone ‘does what it is told, killing whatever is inside, combatant or child’.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPATechnologyLettersAutonomous drones and the future of war in an AI-driven worldMachines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe, writes military surgeonDr Darren MannTue 18 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.07 EDTShareStuart Russell is right that AI’s builders fear losing control of it (Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk, 11 August). But it is not only a future superintelligence’s problem; it is already loaded into weapons, where a loss of control kills a civilian today, not humanity tomorrow.An autonomous drone told to clear a “kill box” is the genie your other columnists described (How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement, 18 July): it does what it is told, killing whatever is inside, combatant or child. The gap between a target and a lawful target is the principle of distinction, which no instruction closes, because the instruction was lawful.Russell doubts asking a superintelligence how to control itself. In war the check need not be another opaque mind but a deterministic one: its rulebook the Geneva conventions, its judgments auditable, returned to a human. We need not trust it; we can check it. Some of us are working on it.A further danger is peculiar to war. Autonomy is sold as combat without our own dead, and a bloodless war is easier to start. But that is a fallacy: you can take the human from the targeting loop, not the nation from the war. Ground must be won and held; the dead still come, in attack or defence. Armies no longer go to war; nations do.If we cannot teach a drone to keep the laws of war, we will not teach a greater intelligence to keep faith with all we value. To abandon those laws for survival is the confusion of interests with values that our strategists warn against; here the two are one. Machines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe. Our interests do not merely permit us to hold the line; they demand it.Dr Darren MannMilitary surgeon, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Self-saboteurs England and Pakistan face off in ‘El Dysfunctiono’ series | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: With Pakistan at a low ebb and England at the start of their semi-reset the series at Headingly looks to be an interesting one
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: With Pakistan at a low ebb and England at the start of their semi-reset the series at Headingly looks to be an interesting one
Content: England will be focusing on the next three Tests, which they will be doing without the balance and presence of Ben Stokes.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEngland will be focusing on the next three Tests, which they will be doing without the balance and presence of Ben Stokes.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamSelf-saboteurs England and Pakistan face off in ‘El Dysfunctiono’ seriesWith Pakistan at a low ebb and England at the start of semi-reset, the series at Headingly looks to be an interesting oneAli MartinTue 18 Aug 2026 15.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe history of Test cricket between England and Pakistan stretches back to 1954 and has been a vibrant one over the years. Yet, for all the memorable battles, plus the cultural ties between the two countries and a fair bit of scandal along the way, a trophy that denotes the rivalry is still to be created.England lost the Crowe-Thorpe trophy to New Zealand this summer, will look to retain the Basil D’Oliveira trophy in South Africa this winter, and hope they can win back the Ashes next year. Trophies for encounters with India and West Indies go back so far they have been retired and replaced by new ones in recent times.Pakistan have pedigree but lack wizardry 10 years on from glorious summer | Taha HashimRead moreBut aside from the Benaud‑Qadir trophy, inaugurated when Australia visited in 2022, Test series involving Pakistan simply have whatever cup the sponsor at the time commissions. When England were last in Pakistan, for example, they watched their hosts lift the Bank Alfalah presents Kingdom Valley trophy.Until something more meaningful is devised, perhaps the series should be known as “El Dysfunctiono”. Admittedly it sounds like something Pelé raised awareness about back in the day. But given the two teams involved – both capable of self‑sabotage that drives supporters up the wall – it kind of works. That it gets under way at Headingley, home to English cricket’s most volatile county, is also fitting.Pakistan are at something of a low ebb, frozen out of the top table at the InternationalCricketCouncil and one place off the bottom in the World Test Championship after claiming the wooden spoon last time around. Their past 18 Tests have featured 13 defeats, including a record eight in a row away from home – a run only ended this month when they left the Caribbean with a 1-1 series draw.Underpinning this has been a rolling cast of head coaches and team directors – 11 in the past five years across formats in the men’s game, including interims – and they have recently turned back to Babar Azam as Test captain. This despite a battle for form that has seen him go 36 innings without a century. Babar will miss the series opener, however, with a hand injury, forcing Salman Ali Agha to step in.Things are not much rosier for the hosts. English cricket is comparatively more stable, it must be said, and at the very least, has the ear of Jay Shah, the ICC chair. In contrast to those itchy trigger fingers at the Pakistan Cricket Board, they also tried their best not to rip things up after that dismal Ashes winter.View image in fullscreenEngland have returned to Joe Root as captain, who would rather not have comparisons made with his first stint.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesBut in failing to bring about meaningful change, they ended up soundly beaten by New Zealand in June, fell to seventh in the nine‑team World Test Championship table, and in an even bigger mess than before. Ben Stokes jumped ship, Brendon McCullum lost half of his job as head coach, and now a mere semi-reset is only just under way.Like Pakistan, England have turned back to their princely senior batter to lead, in Joe Root. Hisfirst press conference back in the jobfull-time was much like those that came before: polite, engaging, generous timewise if a touch light on substance. Although Root would sooner comparisons with his first stint were not made, insisting he is a very different person and cricketer to four years ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeyond this, his pride at pulling on the blazer in Yorkshire, and the news that he will swap first slip for mid-off to speak more directly to his bowlers, Root’s overriding message was one of refinement rather than overhaul. He wants to lead a team that is more adaptable and nuanced, not wedded to a one‑size-fits-all approach. The focus, he stressed, is squarely on these next three Tests.Doing so without the balance and presence of Stokes makes this trickier, as does the new Test coach, Stephen Fleming, not starting until the winter; Marcus Trescothick steps up into an interim role. The tight turnaround after a month of playing in the Hundred also represents a significant gear shift for England’s fast bowlers and demands a significant adjustment from their batters. Pakistan have been playing with a red ball for weeks.In Root’s favour this week is the weather. The seemingly relentless heatwave threatened to make England’s intended lack of a frontline spinner look daft, only for clouds to roll in and point to the quicks coming to the fore between showers. That said, this will also make as skilful an operator as Mohammad Abbas a handful.Either way, the lack of a lofty mission statement from Root was probably for the best. Over on the official PCB website it sets out six “priority areas” to be addressed over the next five years. Amusingly there is no publication date, however, making this a rolling deadline that rather sums up the green half of El Dysfunctiono.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 15: Manchester City | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: With the departures of Pep Guardiola and Rodri it looks like the end of an era at City. Will Enzo Maresca be able to sustain their position as a domestic and continental superpower?
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: With the departures of Pep Guardiola and Rodri it looks like the end of an era at City. Will Enzo Maresca be able to sustain their position as a domestic and continental superpower?
Content: Enzo Maresca has big boots to fill. Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAWith the departures of Pep Guardiola and Rodri it looks like the end of an era at City. Will Enzo Maresca be able to sustain their position as a domestic and continental superpower?ByJamie JacksonTue 18 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:2nd (NB: this is not necessarily Jamie Jackson’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:2ndProspectsEnzo Maresca was already in herculean task mode by signing on as the man charged with continuing the dynasty built by Pep Guardiola at Manchester City beforeRodri decided to leave the cluband join Barcelona. The 30-year-old may be headed for a second Ballon d’Or after his displays in Spain’s triumphant World Cup campaign, so the loss of a midfielder capable of moulding games domestically and in the Champions League represents a sizeable blow for Maresca.There are further negatives too, with John Stones, Nathan Aké and Bernardo Silva also no longer at City. On the positive side, Elliot Anderson hasjoined for £116mfrom Nottingham Forest having impressed for England at the World Cup. City’s new manager also has Erling Haaland, who will be favourite to claim a fourth Premier League Golden Boot in five seasons. Less certain is how Phil Foden will perform despite being boosted by a bumper new contract. Can the boy from Stockport dovetail with Rayan Cherki and once more pull the strings for his boyhood side?Manchester City league positions graphicOff-field pictureCity are a best-in-class organisation, who can be used as an exemplar of how to pursue excellence on and off the field. This, of course, would change were they found guilty over the 130 charges brought against them for alleged breaches ofPremier Leaguerules. It has been more than three years since the charges were announced, with City continuing to deny any wrongdoing. The new Pep Guardiola Stand, opened for the great man’s final home game last season, means 61,000 fans can now witness Haaland and co go to work, the Etihad Stadium’s capacity having previously stood at 53,400.Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City opener was startlingly badRead moreOwner-fan relationshipSheikh Mansour is a hero to the City faithful for a glittering period of ownership that has elevated their team to a domestic and continental superpower. Listening to fans, the club have also frozen ticket prices for a third consecutive season. Meanwhile in the Pep Guardiola Stand, 4,000 new flexi season tickets – a pay-as-you-go scheme – have sold out, half of which are for junior fans, with City introducing £10 seats for those who live in the five wards around the ground.The managerIs Maresca courageous for followingThe Manor naive for believing he can? Over to the 46-year-old, who has zero doubt the City job is no chalice laced with poison. “It’s fantastic, nice and exciting, and for me, a privilege,” he said. “First of all, the most important thing has been that Khaldoon [al-Mubarak, the chair], Hugo [Viana, the director of football] and Ferran [Soriano, the chief executive] all speak the same language in terms of this is a club that has to win games, titles and has to compete, but we also talk about how we can continue to make this club better, season after season.” Maresca’s CV shows the Championship crown with Leicester, and the Conference League and Club World Cup glory with Chelsea. How he would love to add thePremier Leaguetitle to that roll of honour at the first time of asking.Star signingView image in fullscreenElliot Anderson of Manchester City holds off Martin Ødegaard and Myles Lewis-Skelly of Arsenal during the 2026 FA Community Shield.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesRodri’s departure offers Anderson an opportunity to run City’s midfield. Can he do so? Maresca and Viana obviously believe this or £116m would not have been splurged on the lad from Whitley Bay who could not nail down a starting berth for Newcastle in five years as a senior professional there. At the World Cup there were flashes of a schemer who can spray passes long range – Rodri-style – as well as the shorter, metronomic stuff. What’s for sure is that Anderson has a career-defining opportunity in front of him.Stat attackManchester City conceded more league goals from set pieces last season than they had in the previous two campaigns combined. They were costly at times too: the winning goals in their losses at Aston Villa and Newcastle both came from corners, for instance. Maresca’s Chelsea conceded from a set play every three league games so his record there was a shade worse than City’s in 2025-26. He has work to do.Manchester City’s set-piece goal concessions 2016-26Set for a breakthroughVitor Reis was signed in January 2025 and made four appearances that season. The defender’s debut was also forgettable as, then 19, he was hooked at half-time with City trailing 1-0at Leyton Orientin the FA Cup fourth round. The Brazilian played all of the 3-1 victory in the following round, and was fielded in the 89th-minute of the 2-0 league victory at Leicester in April before his sole other City appearance: a full outing in the 2-0 Club World Cup win over Wydad Casablanca that June. Last season’s loan at City’s sister club Girona ended in relegation, but Reis is said to have impressed.World Cup impactThe departed Rodri made real the ultimate fantasy of all players by captaining his country to the World Cup and being so vital to that glory that he was named player of the tournament. Cherki fared less well, making six substitute appearances and one start for a France side that fell, to Spain,in the semi-finals. France’s attacking ranks may overflow with quality, but for a player with magic in both boots, that seemed odd.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Manchester CityPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Israel withdraws support for embattled Fifa president Gianni Infantino | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The Israel Football Association blamed an ‘unprecedented crisis of confidence’ and lack of ‘proper vision’ in retracting its backing for Fifa’s Gianni Infantino
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Israel Football Association blamed an ‘unprecedented crisis of confidence’ and lack of ‘proper vision’ in retracting its backing for Fifa’s Gianni Infantino
Content: Gianni Infantino (centre) tried to stage a photo between IFA vice-president Basim Sheikh Suliman (left) and Jibril Rajoub, president of the Palestinian Football Association.Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino (centre) tried to stage a photo between IFA vice-president Basim Sheikh Suliman (left) and Jibril Rajoub, president of the Palestinian Football Association.Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/ReutersGianni InfantinoIsrael withdraws support for embattled Fifa president Gianni InfantinoIFA points to ‘unprecedented crisis of confidence’Premier League chief says Infantino ‘hit self-destruct’Matt HughesandNick AmesTue 18 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s decision to sack his chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, after the Frenchman’s criticism of the World Cup sell-off plan has hardened some opposition to the Fifa president, with the efforts to force him out expected to intensify over the next few days.On TuesdayIsraelbecame the latest Fifa member to officially withdraw their support for Infantino’s re-election in a letter sent by the head of the Israel Football Association (IFA), Moshe Zuares.Infantino ally insists Fifa president still has backing of most football associationsRead moreThe move is not a surprise as the IFA has been a member of Uefa since 1994 and Zuares sits on the European governing body’s executive committee, but it remains another blow to Infantino, who has invested significant political capital in attempting to improve sporting relations with Palestine.At Fifa’s congress in April Infantino tried to stage a photo involving the two delegations in Vancouver, but the Palestinian Football Federation president, Jibril Rajoub, refused to stand alongside IFA ⁠vice-president, Basim Sheikh ⁠Suliman. Undeterred by this setback, Infantino wants Israel and Palestine to compete in the first match of a new under-15 tournament in the United States next month, as reported by the Guardian in June.In his letter, which has been seen by the Guardian, Zuares says recent events have triggered an “unprecedented crisis of confidence” between the visions of Uefa and Fifa when it comes to global governance, adding that the rift is “profound, substantive, and principled, and compelling all stakeholders to reconsider the path forward”.In a decision he described as being taken unanimously after a meeting of the IFA’s board, Zuares confirmed: “We have no choice but to retract our previous letter of support, in the sincere hope that fruitful dialogue among all parties will eventually restore a shared, proper vision and direction for world football.”Israeli’s intervention echoes the withdrawal of support from other Uefa members including England, Wales, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland, and followed confirmation on Monday night that Lamour had left Fifa, having been deeply critical of Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.“If that means I lose my job, then so be it,” he said prophetically in a statement on 31 July. “I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.”Another Uefa executive committee member, the former Wales Women international Laura McAllister, said the decision to sack Lamour “sends a deeply troubling message” and casts serious doubt over any efforts by the global governing body to recalibrate after the FFE scandal.McAllister, who is one of five Uefa vice-presidents and worked there with Lamour before his move to Fifa in 2024, praised her former colleague for standing up to Infantino’s doomed scheme. “During the shabby events of the past weeks, he showed himself to be a courageous advocate for the most important stakeholders in football,” she said in a statement. “Kevin’s sacking seriously weakens Fifa’s administration, while undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at Fifa and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones.“Fifa is not the president, it is the whole football family. As I have said repeatedly, world football needs strong, principled, independent leaders who are prepared to speak up, challenge when necessary, and stand firmly by their values and those of the global game. Instead, the loss of a leader of Kevin’s calibre sends a deeply troubling message to all of us seeking change.”View image in fullscreenRichard Masters, the Premier League chief executive, said: ‘I don’t think Fifa should be ever contemplating selling off a stake in the World Cup.’Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAMeanwhile, Richard Masters, the Premier League chief executive, told the BBC that Infantino pressed the “self-destruct button” over his botched plan to bring private investment into theWorld Cup.“This is a problem of Fifa’s making,” Masters said. “This is a self-inflicted wound. The organisation has pressed the self-destruct button, and the consequences of that flow now into the solutions that need to be found.“I don’t think Fifa should be ever contemplating selling off a stake in the World Cup. They’re a not-for-profit organisation. They should really be holding that competition in trust for the future of football.”Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaWorld CupFootball politicsIsrael (Football)Israel (World news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Tour of Britain Women begins under cloud but with hope of stronger future | Tour of Britain | The Guardian
description: Women’s peloton returns after death of Finlay Tarling, who died during the Volta a Portugal last week
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Women’s peloton returns after death of Finlay Tarling, who died during the Volta a Portugal last week
Content: The women’s peloton from the Tour de France Femmes, including Lorena Wiebes and Lotte Kopecky, returns for the Tour of Britain Women.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe women’s peloton from the Tour de France Femmes, including Lorena Wiebes and Lotte Kopecky, returns for the Tour of Britain Women.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesTour of BritainTour of Britain Women begins under cloud but with hope of stronger futureWomen’s peloton returns after death of Finlay Tarling, who died during the Volta a Portugal last weekJeremy WhittleTue 18 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2026 Tour of Britain Women starts in Cumbria on Wednesday under a cloud after thedeath of the Welsh rider Finlay Tarlingin the Volta a Portugal last Friday.Tarling was in a collision with a non-race vehicle during the race’s eighth stage and, while police investigations into the exact circumstances surrounding the incident continue, the professional cycling community remains in shock.Tour de France Femmes steps out of Pogacar’s shadow to showcase truly compelling racing | Jeremy WhittleRead moreTarling’s death has overshadowed the European racing scene and, 10 days after the Tour de France Femmes finished in Nice, the women’s peloton returns to the road, tributes will be paid to the 19-year-old, who was one of the brightest young stars on the British scene.Less than a year before the Tour de France Femmes stages its 2027 Grand Départ in the UK, large crowds are expected on the roadside to watch racing from a peloton that has greater strength in depth than ever before.Like the Tour de France Femmes, Britain’s only World Tour race is going from strength to strength, increasing in duration from four days to five and further boosting the status of women’s professional racing to unprecedented heights.Although neither Kasia Niewiadoma, runner-up to Demi Vollering in the Tour de France Femmes, nor the Dutch double Tour winner are competing, the starting lineup is of high quality.View image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling, pictured with his parents, died after a collision with a non-race vehicle last Friday.Photograph: Huw Fairclough/Getty ImagesSeveral luminaries from the French race will feature, including stage winners Kim Le Court and Lorena Wiebes, and the former world road race champion Lotte Kopecky.Le Court, whowon stage sixof the Femmes and finished ninth overall in Nice, crashed out of last year’s Tour of Britain after winning the opening stage.“I’m looking forward to racing theTour of BritainWomen again,” she said. “Last year was a mix of emotions for me personally, so I’m looking forward to coming back and making this edition a good one from start to finish.”The defending champion Ally Wollaston, whoheld off the challenge of Yorkshire’s Cat Fergusonin last year’s race and won a silver medal in the team pursuit at the Commonwealth Games, will be on the start line in Cockermouth. The five-day race takes the peloton through Cumbria, the north-west, Wales and the Borders, prior to a final stage next Sunday in Royal Leamington Spa.The route combines rolling roads with flatter stages and some long climbs, particularly in Wales, characteristics that will suit Le Court and Kopecky well.Wednesday’s opening stage is based on a long loop through Cumbria, out from and back to Cockermouth, with narrow lanes and plenty of scope for attacking racing. From Cumbria the peloton heads to what is likely to be a sprint finish in Blackpool, before moving to north Wales for the third stage from Mold to Llandudno which concludes with a tough, and potentially decisive, finish on the Great Orme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWiebes, winner of two stages in the Tour de France Femmes and also of the points classification in the nine-day race, will be the favourite to add to her tally of wins in Blackpool. But she also has the punch to compete in the race’s hillier stages in Wales.Kopecky, winner of the Tour of Britain in 2024, is a past stage winner in Llandudno and may again use the Welsh seaside resort as the platform for her challenge. The Belgian’s epic but fruitless lone pursuit of Sigrid Haugset in stage three of the Tour Femmes was one of the highlights of the race.View image in fullscreenLotte Kopecky, a former Tour of Britain winner, is part of a strong lineup in 2026.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesWhile Ferguson, last year’s runner-up, is still recovering from an ankle fracture, Zoe Backstedt, from Pontyclun, who played a key role in supporting Niewiadoma’s challenge in the Tour de France Femmes, may be active in the Tour’s Welsh stages.The British national road and time trial champion has already won on the World Tour this year, taking the third stage of the Tour of Switzerland and went on to finish 50th overall and 10th in the youth classification in her first Tour de France Femmes.After the finish of the hilly fourth stage, in Hay-on-Wye, the race moves to its finale, based around Royal Leamington Spa, next Sunday. With audiences for women’s racing rapidly growing, TV coverage has become a hotly debated issue and free-to-air highlights packages will be available on ITV with live coverage on YouTube.Explore more on these topicsTour of BritainCyclingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jeff Bezos consortium could be majority Liverpool shareholder within a year | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: 1892 Holdings has first refusal to take over Liverpool if FSG opts to sell in the next 12 months, as part of the £2bn-plus deal for a 38% initial stake
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: 1892 Holdings has first refusal to take over Liverpool if FSG opts to sell in the next 12 months, as part of the £2bn-plus deal for a 38% initial stake
Content: The Anfield club is valued at around £5.5bn after 1892 Holdings bought a 38% stake.Photograph: Aidan Hunter/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Anfield club is valued at around £5.5bn after 1892 Holdings bought a 38% stake.Photograph: Aidan Hunter/Action Plus/ShutterstockLiverpoolJeff Bezos consortium could be majority Liverpool shareholder within a year1892 Holdings has first refusal if FSG opts to sellGroup paid more than £2bn for initial 38% slice of clubAndy HunterTue 18 Aug 2026 14.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1892 Holdings, the new investor in Liverpool, has first refusal to become the majority shareholder in the next 12 months shouldFenway Sports Groupdecide to sell.The consortium led by Amit Bhatia and including the Amazon founderJeff Bezoswas believed to have bought 30% to one-third of Liverpool when the deal was announced on Friday. However, the agreement is for 38% of the Anfield club, meaning 1892 has paid FSG just over £2bn to become a minority shareholder. The increased stake, first reported by the Athletic, still values Liverpool at about £5.5bn.Premier League 2026-27 preview No 14: LiverpoolRead moreFSG also insisted on Friday the deal with 1892 was not part of an exit strategy from a club it bought for £300m in 2010 and it was not compelled to sell more ofLiverpoolto the consortium at a future date. That remains the case but should FSG decide to sell or reduce its shareholding in the next 12 months, then 1892 has an agreement in place that gives it the option to buy a controlling stake.Liverpool’s majority owner has stressed it is an option for 1892 over the next 12 months, one that could lead to further investment, and is not a formal commitment on its part. FSG remains in operational control of Liverpool. But it does raise the possibility of Bezos, Bhatia and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, another billionaire member of the consortium, replacing FSG as Liverpool’s majority shareholders in the near future.Bezos, one of the richest men in the world, is deemed a passive investor in Liverpool at this stage, having bought into 1892 through the K5 Sports fund, of which he is the lead investor. Bryan Baum, the co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will have a seat on an expanded Liverpool board alongside Bhatia as vice-chair and Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo. Bhatia has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust to buy into Liverpool. His father-in-law is the Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, another billionaire. The Mittal family are worth around $17bn and Saverin an estimated $33bn.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolFenway Sports GroupJeff BezosBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lisa Nandy urges deal to keep Rugby League World Cup on free-to-air TV | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has spoken out after it emerged that this year’s Rugby League World Cup will not be shown on the BBC
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has spoken out after it emerged that this year’s Rugby League World Cup will not be shown on the BBC
Content: Australia players celebrate after winning the Rugby League World Cup in 2022.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenAustralia players celebrate after winning the Rugby League World Cup in 2022.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersRugby leagueLisa Nandy urges deal to keep Rugby League World Cup on free-to-air TVPremier Sports secure rights with BBC not biddingNandy: ‘As a fan myself, I share fans’ disappointment’Aaron BowerTue 18 Aug 2026 16.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe culture secretary,Lisa Nandy, has urged administrators to strike a deal to allow this autumn’s Rugby League World Cup to be shown on a free-to-air broadcast after it was announced the event would be shown in the United Kingdom exclusively on subscription TV.The BBC’s longstanding relationship with the sport has led to it consistently showing the Rugby League World Cup irrespective of where and when the tournament has been held. But that tradition will seemingly end this autumn, after it was confirmed the broadcaster would not bid for the rights to show the event, which will be held in Australia.Leigh dent Leeds’ title ambitions as Super League set to reject NRL’s opening £7m offerRead moreInstead, Premier Sports has acquired exclusive rights to stream the event in the UK and Ireland, meaning rugby league supporters will have to pay if they want to watch the biggest event the sport has to offer. The decision has already provoked a strong backlash, including from within parliament.Nandy, a keen rugby league supporter and the MP for Wigan, has pleaded with the International Rugby League (IRL) to do a deal that will at least show some – most likely England’s games – of the tournament on free-to-air television, whether that be the BBC or another terrestrial broadcaster.“Rugby league is a source of pride and identity that brings communities together across the country,” she said. “As a fan myself, I wholeheartedly share fans’ disappointment that the upcoming World Cup will not be on free-to-air television. I urge the International Rugby League to work with UK free-to-air broadcasters, so the millions of fans can follow the tournament.”The 2022 World Cup, which was staged in England, broke TV audience records as the men’s, women’s and wheelchair tournaments were held simultaneously alongside one another, a format which will be repeated this autumn. The BBC showed every match live, with England’s men’s team attracting audiences well in excess of one million and the cumulative audience for the whole tournament over 30 million. But those numbers will be significantly lower this year if a deal cannot be reached for the tournament to be put on free-to-air television.Premier Sports has shown World Cup fixtures before in 2017, but it is now the exclusive home of the tournament. The IRL’s secretary, Danny Kazandjian, said: “Premier Sports has had a strong partnership with international rugby league events for many years and has showcased some of the sport’s elite tournaments – none more so than the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“IRL is really excited about renewing that relationship as we continue to develop our business, increasing the IF’s [International Federation] capacity to invest consistently and in a meaningful way in the global game.”Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueSports rightsLisa NandyShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona steal Rodri away from Real Madrid and plan to make him new Busquets | Barcelona | The Guardian
description: Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has completed his move to Camp Nou where he is a natural successor to club legend
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has completed his move to Camp Nou where he is a natural successor to club legend
Content: ‘I’m happy to be here’: Rodri poses with a Barcelona shirt at his official unveiling.Photograph: Quique García/EPAView image in fullscreen‘I’m happy to be here’: Rodri poses with a Barcelona shirt at his official unveiling.Photograph: Quique García/EPABarcelonaBarcelona steal Rodri away from Real Madrid and plan to make him new BusquetsSpain’s World Cup-winning captain has completed his move to Camp Nou where he is a natural successor to club legendSid LoweTue 18 Aug 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time Flight PTN27B started its descent into El Prat a bit before 8pm on Monday evening, a small crowd had gathered by the terminal doors, waiting for it to land. A few people stood and watched the sky, cameras out to capture its arrival. A lot more watched on their phones. In the two hours it had taken to get there from Manchester, taking off at 5.11pm, 101 minutes behind schedule, the Pilatus PC-24 had become the most tracked plane on the planet. Everyone knew that Rodrigo Hernández was on board. Unless, of course, he had been sneaked away in a catering cart.Five days earlier, Rodri had been seen, and recorded, at Barajas airport waiting to get on a flight back to Manchester from Madrid. He wheeled a small RFEF (Spanish football federation) case with his name on, stood alone in the queue, the World Cup-winning captain just a bloke in shorts and T-shirt, and his stay in the UK was supposed to be brief, just long enough to say goodbye. The plane he was boarding was a Ryanair one: that was the detail everyone homed in on, something extraordinary in the ordinariness. This time, though, he came on a private jet, one way. His family travelled with him. He came to sign for FCBarcelona.Rodri calls it ‘a dream to play for Barcelona’ as he flies in for medicalRead moreRodri was late: an agreement betweenManchester Cityand Barcelona had taken a little longer than expected, long enough for concern to creep in, and his flight landed 70 minutes behind schedule. Maybe he islate-late, too: at 30, and three years after the departure of Sergio Busquets – the man to whom he had always been likened and whose natural successor he has always been … this transfer could perhaps have come sooner. Yet it was rarely even contemplated, virtually up until the moment it happened. In that sense, it had actually been quick. A fortnight ago, few thought of this.Now here he was, heading out in jeans and a white T-shirt. There was expectation, a hint still of disbelief that they had got him. A touch of relief, too, after the delay. They had been “intense days”, Rodri said, but now it was done. Barcelona’s third bid had been accepted: €60m plus a further €15m in add-ons, €11m of which are virtually guaranteed. He will earn around €15m a year, an increase on his salary at City, and has signed a four-year deal.Quick GuideRodri seals Barcelona transferShowThe Spain midfielder Rodri has completed his €60m move from Manchester City to Barcelona, signing a four-year contract after undergoing a medical on Tuesday."Barcelona and Manchester City have reached an agreement for Rodri, who is committing to the Catalan club until 30 June 2030," read a club statement.Barça added that the 30-year-old is "considered one of the best players in the world in his position", and "stands out for his tactical intelligence, composure on the ball, ability to regain possession and precision in his passing".Rodri (pictured) was named the best player of the World Cup after Spain’s triumph this summer. He spent seven seasons at the Etihad Stadium, winning the Premier League four times and scoring the winner in the 2023 Champions League final against Inter. The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner joined from Atlético Madrid in July 2019, and was in the final year of his contract.In a message to City fans on the club’s website, Rodri wrote: "I found that saying goodbye is one of the most difficult things in life but I am going to try. I knew I came into a top team but I never thought we could be able to create the legacy we made – winning trophies, fans around the world, love and respect."We made an example to inspire the next generations not only because the success, also because the way we did it," he added. "And the fans were with us every step of the way. City didn’t just make me grow as a player. They made me grow as a human ... Manchester shaped my whole life. It’s time to say goodbye, thanks to the club, the fans, the staff and my teammates. This journey couldn’t be the same without you, my heart will always be blue."Barcelona saw an initial £40m offer and an increased bid turned down before an agreement was struck on Sunday. Rodri flew to Barcelona’s El Prat airport on Monday and told reporters: "Playing for Barcelona is a dream come true for me."The new City manager, Enzo Maresca, faces a race to rebuild his midfield, with Rodri joining Bernardo Silva in departing the club, Tijjani Reijnders poised to join Saudi Pro League side Al Qadsiah, and Newcastle reportedly interested in Nico González. Elliot Anderson has joined from Nottingham Forest for £116m and City have been linked with Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi and Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández.Photograph: Quality Sport Images/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I’m happy to be here,” Rodri said, and they were happy to have him. The following morning he arrived at the club’s Joan Despí training ground to complete his medical, everything signed off. As he left the terminal building, Rodri had been asked if this was a dream come true. He of course said yes it was, which he had to say. The question had been direct, leading. It had been loaded too.A Ballon d’Or winner and the embodiment of a style, an identity, that is theirs too, Rodri is the perfect fit. The time was right for him too. Voted the best player at the World Cup, the culmination of his recovery from injury, there was just one year left on his contract at City. He had won it all in England and Pep Guardiola had gone. After seven years away, home called. But home didn’t mean Barcelona; in fact, it had seemed more likely to mean Real Madrid.View image in fullscreenRodri lifts the World Cup after Spain’s victory over Argentina.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesRodri grew up to the north-west of the capital and even Real’s refusal to turn up the night he won the Ballon d’Or, an act of grubbiness and disrespect, didn’t mean closing the door. Instead, he was increasingly open about his willingness – his apparent desire – to go. “Obviously, when the best club in history, the most successful with everything that brings, call you it is an honour and you always have to pay attention,” he said not long after the ceremony. In the spring, Rodri admitted he would like to return to Spain and that he would not rule out going to Real, even if he had been in the academy at Atlético. When Real held presidential elections in May, the pretender, Enrique Riquelme, announced that his signing would be Rodri. For his part, Rodri kept his counsel and come the end of the World Cup he had three offers: Paris Saint-Germain, who he ruled out because he wanted a return to Spain, Barcelona and Real.Real, ambivalent before, appeared convinced by his status as the World Cup’s best player, president Florentino Pérez’s reticence seemingly overcome. He wasexactlythe footballer they needed, someone to get them to actually play, and Real were confident that he would come, that theirs was the only real offer. One headline summed it up: “Rodri is next”. This was done, which is when things tend to get undone. Rodri had an offer that was impossible to turn down. Only the terms of the negotiation shifted, doubts growing about Real’s commitment, frustration growing.Barcelona, seeing an opportunity, pushed at an unexpectedly opening door. Rodri might not have been the player they needed most – a forward was their priority – but, well, he’s Rodri. This was undeniably a step up in quality, even for a midfield like theirs. Meanwhile, doubts over Frenkie de Jong’s fitness brought a reframing: maybe he was more necessary than they had believed. Likewise, that slight nagging doubt about his fit with Pedri in theselecciónfeels like a small one, easily overcome, certainly no obstacle to bringing together arguably the best two midfielders in the world. Good luck getting the ball off them.On the day that Real announced ViníciusJúnior had renewed his contract at the club and that they had made Yan Diomande the most expensive signing in their history, they also briefed that Rodri wasn’t coming after all. The excitement among fans at the Santiago Bernabéu turned to disappointment, a kind of lingering doom. That huge hole in the middle of Madrid’s midfield was still not plugged, their issues still not addressed.View image in fullscreenRodri enjoyed seven successful seasons at Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAFor Barcelona this was the signing of the summer. The World Cup winning-captain, perhaps the best player on the planet, was coming to Catalonia. There was a kind of gleeful disbelief, the expectation huge. Rodri thanked Madrid, but he had made his decision. As usual, Jorge Valdano put it best when the €75m deal had been done. “Rodri’s deal is worth €35m for what it gives Barcelona and €40m for what it takes away from Madrid,” he said. “At Real Madrid he would have revolutionised their play and improved everything.”Valdano added he will not have the impact on Barcelona’s style that he would have had on Real’s, but that was because it is already his. “I always try to learn from Busquets,” said Rodri. “I watched him especially closely: he, and others, laid down a model of playing I knew I had to follow.” When Rodri joined City, Guardiola had found his other Busquets, or so it goes. Waiting patiently for his moment, when Busquets finally left the national team, it was always going to be Rodri who stepped in. A “perfect computer”, Luis de la Fuente called him. Doing so with Barcelona would seem natural, maybe even overdue, his signing a no-brainer.Rodri’s World Cup overcame any doubts that it was too late, that his time had gone, and brought an extra dimension too, a shift in his role which he didn’t just embrace but consciously sought. He had the maturity, the leadership, the ascendancy over Spain’s young players – Barcelona’s young players – that they needed. And he needed too: there is something almost paternal about him and they had the youth that hewantedto lead, to guide. And, of course, the talent too. He knows how good it is to play with them: he had done so all summer, winning the ultimate award. And so it was done.Now all that was needed was for City and Barcelona to reach an agreement. Eventually, they did, so Rodrigo Hernández had another plane to catch.Explore more on these topicsBarcelonaManchester CityTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US states accuse Meta of covering up research on teen social media addiction in pivotal trial  | Meta | The Guardian
description: State attorneys general claim tech company intentionally designed addictive products that harm young people
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: State attorneys general claim tech company intentionally designed addictive products that harm young people
Content: The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the social media company.Photograph: Iryna Khabliuk/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the social media company.Photograph: Iryna Khabliuk/AlamyMetaUS states accuse Meta of covering up research on teen social media addiction in pivotal trialState attorneys general claim tech company intentionally designed addictive products that harm young peopleDara KerrTue 18 Aug 2026 16.15 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers representing 29 US states have accusedMetaof covering up internal research showingInstagramwas addictive for teenagers. In a packed courtroom Tuesday, on the opening day of a landmark legal challenge, they said the company knew its products harmed children but hid that information from the public.“I heard from many of you at jury selection that the health and wellbeing of kids is a shared responsibility,” said Megan O’Neill, a deputy attorney general forCalifornia, in her opening statements. “Meta didn’t do its share.”O’Neilltold jurors that she would be giving them a preview of what they could expect to see over the course of the trial, which would include witness testimony and internal documents the attorneys general uncovered while investigating the social media company.She referenced one document that said, “the young ones are the best ones”,along with another whereMeta stated: “Teens are hooked despite how it makes them feel.Instagramis addictive.”“They knew,” O’Neill said. “Time and again, profits won.”The lawsuit againstMetaaccuses the parent company of Instagram and Facebook of deliberately designing addictive products that lure in young people and damage their mental health.The jury trial is taking place in federal court in Oakland,California, and is expected to last six to eight weeks. The jury will hear from Meta CEOMark Zuckerberg, Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri and other company executives. After opening statements on Tuesday, the government called former employee turned whistleblowerArturo Béjaras its first witness.New Mexico’s attorney general pushes new social media safety laws after $900m court victory over MetaRead moreThe 233-page lawsuit, firstfiledin October 2023, alleges that Meta regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. The lawmakers claim in court documents that Meta “refuses to abandon its use of known harmful features” and that its motives are based solely on profit to “maximize its financial gains”.The suit was filed jointly by 29 state attorneys general in what is known as multidistrict litigation, though the trial proceedings will be led by attorneys for California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey.The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the social media company. The attorneys general say that if Meta is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be compelled to change the design of its products to make themsafer for children, which may have longer-term effects than a fine.Metadenies all allegations. In opening statements, Paul Schmidt, a lawyer for Meta, said the internal documents and emails the government lawyers showed the jury were taken out of context and cherry-picked from longer conversations. He said Meta has done several studies on young users with the goal of asking “what can we do to support teens in this space”.Schmidt said thatMetahas disabled more than 1m accounts of children under the age of 13 and that it is “acting in a meaningful way to remove” young users.In a statement, a company spokesperson said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.“The state AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate. The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification.”The attorneys general disagree, saying Meta “developed and refined a set of psychologically manipulative” features designed to maximize people’s time on its apps. Those include an infinite scrolling recommendation algorithm, constant notification alerts, thumbs-up “likes” and visual filters for altering one’s image.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe lawmakers say young people are especially vulnerable to falling prey to such features and that excessive time online can lead to increased depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other mental health issues.Mounting lawsuitsThe federal trial comes just two weeks after a judgeorderedMeta to pay $567m to New Mexico in a similar case brought by the state’s attorney general. This was the second court-ordered financial penalty for Meta in New Mexico, bringing the total it is responsible for paying the state to $942m. Astate trial in Tennesseeis also now under wayMeta faces expensive child safety reckoningRead moreFamilies, school districts and other attorneys general have brought thousands of lawsuits against Meta and other social media companies in recent years. The plaintiffs hope a death-by-a-thousand-cuts legal strategy will induce Meta to change its social networks to be safer for children.In California, thousands of coordinated cases have been filed in state court against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February,beingorderedto pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.)
