Two more lawsuits slated to go to trial this summer,one federalandone in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.The lawsuits have borrowed from the legal approach used against tobacco companies in the 1990s, which focused on cigarettes’ addictive qualities and the makers’ knowledge that their products caused harm. Those thousands of suits resulted in a $200bn payout by the four largest companies in 1998 and enforced changes to their marketing practices.Russell Coleman, the attorney general of Kentucky, said he and his colleagues were using that blueprint and aimed to show the jury that “Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people”.“AGs are in the perfect position to get this done,” he added. “We did it with the tobacco settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We’ll do it again with Meta.”Explore more on these topicsMetaSocial mediaCaliforniaDigital mediaWest CoastMark ZuckerbergInstagramnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heavy rain on dry ground may cause UK floods but will not reverse drought | Drought | The Guardian
description: ‘First meaningful rain for a long time’ is forecast but water firms continue to ask customers to restrict use
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: ‘First meaningful rain for a long time’ is forecast but water firms continue to ask customers to restrict use
Content: Experts say it will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and  rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenExperts say it will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and  rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockDroughtHeavy rain on dry ground may cause UK floods but will not reverse drought‘First meaningful rain for a long time’ is forecast but water firms continue to ask customers to restrict useDamien GayleTue 18 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFloods and drought could hit the UK at the same time this week, with heavy rain forecast to fall on hard, parched soil.While some parts of the UK will have the “first meaningful rain for a long time” in the coming days, it will not reverse widespreaddrought conditionsthat have put pressure on wildlife, farmers, firefighters and water resources.On Tuesday,South East Watertold customers in Kent to use water only for “essential” purposes, after taps ran dry on Monday for around 8,000 customers. Wessex Water imposed the UK’s latest hosepipe ban, covering 1.4m customers in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire.The summer’s fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave will be followed by wetter and cooler weather that is much closer to the usual conditions for the time of the year, according to the Met Office.Its deputy chief forecaster, Mike Silverstone, said showers were expected on Tuesday in the north of the country, particularly in the north-west, and that another area of rain would move into the south-west by the evening.This would then probably spread east across the south, bringing the first spell of widespread rain to areas most in need. “Thursday will be a day of heavy showers across much of the UK. While some of these will be heavy, some areas will miss them altogether,” Silverstone said.“As some of these showers could be intense, there is a chance of some surface water flooding as the rain falls on very dry and hard ground,” he added.The forecast rain may bring some welcome relief to parched land and firefighters tackling wildfires, but water shortages will persist.South EastWatertold customers in Kent on Tuesday that the levels in its storage tanks remained “critically low”, despite having restored supplies to 7,400 homes in Herne Bay, Rough Common and Blean on Tuesday. About 400 homes still had no water, the company’s spokesperson said.A spokesperson from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the situation was “simply not good enough”.“South East Water needs to go further and faster to reduce leaks and follow their drought plans to ensure supplies are not disrupted in even the driest of weather,” the spokesperson said.South East Water was the first water company to issue ahosepipe banthis summer, on 3 July for customers in some parts of Kent. On Tuesday, Wessex Water became the latest, with its first ban since thesummer of 1976.The company blamed increased demand during the dry weather, but also longer-term weather forecasts that mean resources must be protected for customers and the environment.On Friday, Environment Agency datashowedfive of England’s key reservoirs are currently “exceptionally low”, while the the National Hydrological Monitoring Programme warned low supplies were likely to persist into the autumn.Thames Water also urged customers to continue to limit water use. The company said in an update on Tuesday that since it imposed its hosepipe ban on 23 July household demand had fallen by 3% across London and more than 6% across the Thames Valley and home counties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJuly rainfall in the Thames catchment area was less than 1mm, which is 2% of the long-term average. Customers used about 100m litres more water a day than normal, putting pressure on rivers, reservoirs and the water network.London reservoir storage is at 74% as a result, far lower than expected for this time of year.Thames Water’s director of water, Martin Padley, said: “With reservoir levels below where we would expect them to be for this time of year and demand remaining high, we’re asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.Liz Stephens, a professor in climate risk and resilience at the University of Reading, told PA Media it could take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.“Here in the south-east, we’re still a month’s worth of rain below what we would normally expect by this point in the year, despite the heavy rainfall in January and February,” she said.“As a result, while any rain which falls this week may help reduce the immediate wildfire risk, it will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and our rivers and reservoirs to return to normal. This means that we should expect hosepipe bans to be in place for some time.“Floods can still occur during drought conditions and surface water flooding can even become more likely as baked soils are unable to soak up rainwater as quickly.”PA Media contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDroughtUK weatherWaterExtreme weatherSouth East WaterWater industryKentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three dead after family get into difficulty in water off Shoreham-by-Sea | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: A man, woman and teenage girl have died, while a younger girl is in a critical condition, say Sussex police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: A man, woman and teenage girl have died, while a younger girl is in a critical condition, say Sussex police
Content: Two air ambulances at Shoreham-by-Sea after reports of people getting into difficulty in the water.Photograph: David McHugh/Brighton PicturesView image in fullscreenTwo air ambulances at Shoreham-by-Sea after reports of people getting into difficulty in the water.Photograph: David McHugh/Brighton PicturesWest SussexThree dead after family get into difficulty in water off Shoreham-by-SeaA man, woman and teenage girl have died, while a younger girl is in a critical condition, say Sussex policeNadeem BadshahTue 18 Aug 2026 18.23 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA couple and their teenage daughter have died after getting into difficulty in the sea off theWest Sussexcoast, police said on Tuesday.A man, a woman and a teenage girl died after the incident in Shoreham-by-Sea, the chief superintendent of Sussex police, James Collis, said.A younger girl from the same family was taken to hospital in a critical condition, Collis added. The next of kin have been informed.Collis said it is understood that all four got into difficulty in the water after going for a swim.He added: “Our thoughts are with the friends and family. I know this incident will have a profound effect on the community.”Emergency services were called at about 2.40pm to reports of four people in difficulty in the sea. All four were brought to shore. The coastguard is not searching for anyone else.A spokesperson for Air Ambulance Charity Kent Surrey Sussex said both of its helicopters and critical care team had been sent to the scene as part of the response, and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out at 3pm.Tom Rutland, the MP for Shoreham, offered his condolences. “My thoughts are with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives, and I know the whole community here in Shoreham will be hoping and praying for the recovery of the young girl receiving medical treatment in hospital,” he said.A local said the water was “incredibly rough” and the winds were “incredibly strong”, Sky News reported.Rutland thanked the emergency services, which he said “responded swiftly” and “worked tirelessly in exceptionally difficult circumstances”.Speaking at a press conference, Collis added: “At this point we believe all four entered the water from the land to swim and sadly got into difficulty. Our partners in His Majesty’s Coastguard have completed an extensive search of the water and we are not searching for anyone else.“I would like to thank the public for their patience and understanding during the emergency response.The A259 Brighton Road was blocked in both directions from New Road to Kingston Lane because of the incident.There have been a number of water-related deaths in recent months during the extreme heat.On Saturday, a 12-year-old boy drowned in the River Lea, near the Hackney Marshes, in north-east London.In April, a woman and her young child died after getting into difficulty in the water in west London. Both died at the scene in Elthorne Park, Ealing, the Metropolitan police said.Anyone with information or with video footage relating to the incident in Shoreham-by-Sea should contact Sussex police.Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charity campaigner who died after microlight crash was filming Apple TV series, inquest hears  | Apple | The Guardian
description: Claire Lomas was filming content for project promoting tech company’s Vision Pro headset in Jordan, hearing told
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Claire Lomas was filming content for project promoting tech company’s Vision Pro headset in Jordan, hearing told
Content: Claire Lomas raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for disability charities after being paralysed in a riding fall.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenClaire Lomas raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for disability charities after being paralysed in a riding fall.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAAppleCharity campaigner who died after microlight crash was filming Apple TV series, inquest hearsClaire Lomas was filming content for project promoting tech company’s Vision Pro headset in Jordan, hearing toldRaphael BoydTue 18 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA disability campaigner who was paralysed from the chest down died after hermicrolight crashedwhile filming a TV series for Apple, an inquest has heard.Claire Lomas, 44, who was the first person to complete a marathon with the help of a “bionic” suit, died five weeks after the adapted aircraft she was travelling in “veered off the runway” and hit a large rock while landing in Amman,Jordan.The mother of two had become a noted campaigner for disability charities after a horse riding accident in 2007 left her paralysed.Louise Pinder, senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, told the inquest on Tuesday that Lomas suffered multiple severe traumatic injuries during the crash on 15 July and was taken to King Hussein medical centre, where she died on 22 August.The hearing, which took place at County Hall in Glenfield, Leicester, heard that at the time of her accident, Lomas had been wearing anAppleVision Pro headset and was in the process of filming content for the tech company to be used in a series promoting the product.View image in fullscreenClaire Lomas finishing the London Marathon in a bionic ReWalk suit in 2012.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PALina Zilinskaite, a senior producer for Atlantic Productions, told the inquest that Apple had commissioned her company to create the series, and Lomas was one of several athletes selected to perform “some sort of challenge or feat” in different episodes.Zilinskaite told the court that Lomas had been “very enthusiastic and keen and excited about the opportunity” and that she had obtained a licence to fly a microlight, the small aircraft she was piloting at the time of the crash, years before the series was commissioned.This was supported by Ben Ashman, a microlight designer and manufacturer, who said that Lomas had bought her own version of the aircraft between 2022 and 2023, which had been adapted to support her inability to use her feet.Speaking on the events leading up to the crash, Zilinskaite told the hearing that Lomas’ flight had been scheduled for the day before but was cancelled “because of strong winds”. Zilinskaite also said that there had been test flights using the Vision Pro in the UK without Lomas, and that she had flown the microlight herself before the accident, albeit without wearing the headset.On the day of the flight, the inquest was told that Lomas had taken off from the runway in Jordan without issue and remained in the air for roughly 15 minutes before attempting to land, but that upon descending her “approach was not quite straight on” and that she “veered off the runway” before striking a large rock.The inquest heard that Lomas, who had completed the London Marathon over the course of 17 days in 2012 with the assistance of “bionic” legs, had been “excited” to return to the UK after the crash and see her family, but that her health rapidly deteriorated after catching an infection which led to her death.Pinder said Lomas’ family had raised concerns about the quality of care in the Jordanian hospital, but that it was not within her jurisdiction to investigate that formally.The inquest continues.Explore more on these topicsAppleApple TVDisabilityCharitiesJordanLeicesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration to rescind rule protecting old-growth forests  | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Almost 45m acres of national forests could be potentially opened to road construction, drilling and logging
Author: Mark Oliver
Headline: Almost 45m acres of national forests could be potentially opened to road construction, drilling and logging
Content: The entrance to George Washington national forest on 5 June 2023.Photograph: Erin Edgerton/AFP via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe entrance to George Washington national forest on 5 June 2023.Photograph: Erin Edgerton/AFP via Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump administration to rescind rule protecting old-growth forestsAlmost 45m acres of national forests could be potentially opened to road construction, drilling and loggingMark OliverTue 18 Aug 2026 16.13 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationsaid on Tuesday it plans to rescind the “roadless rule” that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years, potentially opening up almost 45m acres of national forests to road construction, drilling and logging.Conservationists had feared the announcement was coming since last summer after Brooke Rollins, Trump’s secretary of agriculture, targeted a rule brought in by Bill Clinton’s administration, describing it as “overly restrictive” and an “absurd obstacle” to development.On Tuesday the US Forest Service, an agency inside the Department of Agriculture, formallyannouncedit had filed the proposal to rescind in its entirety the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.Environmental groups immediately criticized the plan for rollbacks of protections to forests from Alaska to Oregon to North Carolina.“[The rule] is the only thing preventing much of our wildest remaining national forests from industrial development. These forests offer critical habitat for wildlife, provide clean, fresh air and water for millions and contain vast swathes of the last remaining old-growth forests in the country,” said Alex Craven, forest campaign manager for the Sierra Club.The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC)appealedfor submissions for the public comment period to “defend our forests from the administration’s chopping block”.“Their scheme would open up tens of millions of acres of our national forests to destructive logging, drilling and road building – including iconic public lands from California’s Tahoe national forest to Alaska’s Tongass national forest to the Appalachian Trail,” the NRDC said.The Trump administration said the move would remove obstacles to managing forests and fighting wildfires.Rollins said: “For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities.“Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands.”“Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” said Tom Schultz, the forest service chief. “More than 40% of inventoried roadless areas, primarily in the west, have high or very high wildfire hazard potential. And only 5% of those areas have received hazardous fuels reduction treatments since 2014.”But Craven of the Sierra Club said: “The administration’s attempt to blame the roadless rule for worsening wildfire risk ignores both the facts and the rule itself. Roads generally lead to more ignitions and result in more wildfires – not fewer.“And, the roadless rule has always allowed for targeted actions to reduce hazardous fuels. What it does not allow is using wildfire as an excuse to open some of America’s most intact public forests to industrial exploitation and new road construction.”Clinton had championed the roadless rule late in his second term as president after concerns grew around unsustainable logging of national forests.The biggest roadless area isthe Tongass national forest in Alaska, which stores huge amounts of carbon and is home to brown and black bears, wolves and bald eagles.“America’s last great backcountry forests are not bargaining chips,” Emma Powell, government affairs manager at Alaska Wilderness League, said on Tuesday about the plan. “The Tongass and Chugach national forests are global treasures.“From fisheries to tourism and outdoor recreation, these landscapes also support thousands of jobs and generate billions in economic activity each year.”Concerns of environmentalists were especially focussed on logging.“It’s clear the processes required by the National Environmental Policy Act are being treated as merely boxes to check on the path to enacting an entirely political agenda to clear-cut the last remaining intact old-growth forests in America,” added Maggie Rabb, executive director of the Southeast Alaska Conservation Council.The public has until 21 September to comment on the plan.“Trump is pushing for the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history and against what Americans want,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Once you start bulldozing roads for commercial logging and industrial development, there’s no getting them back.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationNational parksBill ClintonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We humans are inept at taking care of baby animals’: why well-fed orphan bears die in the wild | Animals | The Guardian
description: Scientists surprised to find all but two of 12 grizzlies were dead within a year of ‘feelgood’ release, unable to sustain their high-calorie diet and inclined to approach humans
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: Scientists surprised to find all but two of 12 grizzlies were dead within a year of ‘feelgood’ release, unable to sustain their high-calorie diet and inclined to approach humans
Content: A tranquilised grizzly bear is prepared for release into the wild in British Columbia, Canada.Photograph: Alana Paterson/NYT/EyevineView image in fullscreenA tranquilised grizzly bear is prepared for release into the wild in British Columbia, Canada.Photograph: Alana Paterson/NYT/EyevineThe age of extinctionAnimals‘We humans are inept at taking care of baby animals’: why well-fed orphan bears die in the wildScientists surprised to find all but two of 12 grizzlies were dead within a year of ‘feelgood’ release, unable to sustain their high-calorie diet and inclined to approach humansThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeTue 18 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe orphaned grizzly bear cubs were bulked up with a generous diet of roadkill, watermelon, dog food and snacks donated by the public. Their contact with carers was limited to two people. Then, after up to a year in rehabilitation, they returned home to the wilds of British Columbia.“It’s a feelgood thing – people feel good when the cage opens,” says Dr Lana M Ciarniello, a bear specialist who tracked the Canadian yearlings ina recent study. There is a perception that bears will thrive in their natural habitat, she says. “The reality is they’re not followed up on.”When Ciarniello studied their fate, she was surprised by her bleak findings. All but two of 12 bears that could be monitored died within a year. Most were killed before their first winter hibernation. The young bears may have unintentionally been set up for failure, she concluded.Beefed up so much they were 3.5 times the size of typical wild-reared yearlings, they were apparently burdened by their outsize frames and unable to meet their calorie needs after their release. Some bears also appeared to be unafraid of humans, with one female persistently approaching mine workers in search of food.View image in fullscreenArthur, a male bear, explores his new home after being tranquilised and taken to Bella Coola, British Columbia, in January 2021.Photograph: Alana Paterson/NYT/EyevineRescue and release projects often appeal strongly to the public, but the study warns that if such work produces bears that are ill-equipped to navigate the wild then it remains “a form of sympathetic management” rather than an effective conservation tool.Teaching a cub to forage and avoid dangers when they have had little or no maternal care – all while preventing them from growing used to human contact – is highly challenging.Bears have a culture that they learn from their mother over a period of two to three years, says Chris Servheen, co-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN)North American bears expert team. “Their mother teaches them what to eat and where to go to look for foods at different times of the year, what to avoid, what to be afraid of,” he says.“An orphaned animal of any kind, people want to take care of them.” The problem is, he says: “We humans are very inept at taking care of baby animals.”Broad guidelines, which are shaped by research relating to American black bears, suggest that a larger body mass gives rehabilitated bears an advantage against predators. A target release weight of about 1.5 times that of a wild-reared bear is recommended.View image in fullscreenLana Ciarniello, the bear specialist who tracked the Canadian yearlings.Photograph: Taylor GreenCiarniello’s study, which was funded by the Grizzly Bear Foundation, suggests going beyond this could be detrimental. In the bears she observed, which were 3.5 times the weight of wild-reared yearlings, a high calorie intake had increased all metrics: body length, chest girth and neck circumference.“They’re not just fat little roly-poly things. It’s skeletal. Once you’ve got that big frame, now you have to maintain it,” says Ciarniello. This led to what she terms a “metabolic trap”.Two females, released in areas without salmon access, lost on average 0.48kg (1lb) a day. Even in areas with abundant food sources, the bears could not eat enough.Giving the bears a small buffer makes sense, says Ciarniello, who is also co-chair of the IUCN’shuman-bear conflictexpert team. Too much could be counterproductive.Experts had previously hypothesised that cutting off contact for two weeks before release would undo familiarity bears have developed with humans. However, the bears continued to associate humans with food, even after much longer periods in the wild without contact. Siggi, a female, spent 59 days in a remote alpine zone before she encountered workers from a mine, whose food supplies she raided. Undeterred even by a noisy helicopter, Siggi was killed after the incident, one of five bears that died in human-wildlife conflict.View image in fullscreenSiggi, who was killed after she raided food supplies from mine-workers.Photograph: Taylor GreenOf the remaining bears, two were illegally killed and three were killed by wild bears.Ciarniello says rearing must be as hands-off as possible. “We can’t treat them like we are feeding or raising our dogs. We can’t feed them at 8am and 5pm twice a day by going into their enclosure, even if it’s one person.”Rehabilitation projects elsewhere are finding ways to do this. Free the Bears, which has sanctuaries in Laos and Cambodia housing Asiatic black bears and sun bears that are being considered for release, uses catapults to deliver food, while a special system picks up on high-frequency beeps that are emitted from bears’ collars, allowing the staff to track their movements. When the animals are due to be weighed, honey is dripped on to a scale inside the enclosure to encourage them to step on to it.Rewilding orphaned bears is controversial, especially in areas where they are not threatened. Some biologists argue money should be focused elsewhere, on preventing conflict with humans – and bears being orphaned – in the first place.View image in fullscreenIsa (dark) and Arthur (light), who arrived at the Northern Lights sanctuary after their mother was killed in a collision with a truck in 2020.Photograph: Lana Ciarniello/The Grizzly Bear FoundationOthers say we need as much information as possible about how to rehabilitate and release bears. “This is going to be an essential conservation tool that is going to need to be employed, particularly for species like sun bears that are not looking good,” says Dr Zachary David, research programme manager at Free the Bears.The Grizzly Bear Foundation says the findings, which will also form a best practice report, will “ensure that science informs future policy and practice in British Columbia, where rewilding is currently possible, and other jurisdictions considering which options should be available”.Brown bears (of which grizzlies are a subspecies) are not endangered globally, but there are many small, isolated populations that are threatened and Ciarniello hopes her work will inform efforts to protect populations in Europe and Asia. “I’m worried those bears will be wiped out if we can’t figure this out.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldon the app for all the latest news and featuresExplore more on these topicsAnimalsThe age of extinctionWildlifeConservationCanadaAmericasRewildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scientists who turned to OnlyFans to fund marmot research receive crypto boost | US news | The Guardian
description: Funding boost worth $100,000 has recently materialized in form of new marmot-themed cryptocurrency
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Funding boost worth $100,000 has recently materialized in form of new marmot-themed cryptocurrency
Content: 1:12Scientists create OnlyFans account for marmots to fund research – videoUS newsScientists who turned to OnlyFans to fund marmot research receive crypto boostFunding boost worth $100,000 has recently materialized in form of new marmot-themed cryptocurrencyOliver MilmanTue 18 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScientists who turned to OnlyFans to help save long-running research into marmots have raised more than $100,000 after harnessing the support of another, very modern, funding avenue – cryptocurrency.The 60-year project of continuous study of marmots – stout, ground-dwelling rodents that are the largest members of the squirrel family – across the US west was facing termination following science funding cuts imposed by Donald Trump’s administration.In desperation, researchers in Junedecided to put the marmots on OnlyFans, the adult-content website, to raise funds. Since then, posts on the new account, named OnlyMarms, have shown marmots scurrying across rocky landscapes and entering their burrows, rather than anything sexually explicit.“Our goal isn’t really to sexualise the marmots,” said Daniel Blumstein, a professor at UCLA who got the idea after watching Margo’s Got Money Troubles, a TV show based on a novel about a single mother who turns to OnlyFans in order to support herself and her child. “It’s to celebrate the marmots.”This effort has raised a modest $6,000 for the marmots but a further, much larger, funding boost for the project has recently materialized in the form of a new marmot-themed cryptocurrency. A new “meme coin” named $OnlyMarms was created by outside supporters of the project who donated all transaction fees to the study.This marmot memecoin, a type of cryptocurrency based on online culture and memes that fluctuates in price cased on viral trends, has raised more than $88,000 in just two weeks. Along with outside donations from marmot allies who were uncomfortable donating through the OnlyFans platform, the research program has gained more than $100,000 in funding, enabling it to continue for a further year.“It’s been a crazy last two weeks, it’s been incredible to see and it’s a relief that the research can continue for another year,” said Julien Martin, a University of Ottawa researcher who co-leads the project with Blumstein.“I’m completely amazed that this internet culture that I barely know of has raised so much money. It’s fascinating and shocking to me. Of course I dream for more – if we get $300,000 that will fund a PhD student on the project for the next four years – but for now we are talking about how to make this money stretch as long as possible.”The memecoin was created by an unknown online community on the Solana blockchain and Martin initially thought it was a scam before accepting that it could raise funds for the study. He added it was “ironic” that researchers were having to turn to cryptocurrency, an area that has personallynettedTrump about $635m through his own memecoin, to make up for science funding slashed by Trump’s administration.The US president has sought toshrink federal scientific fundingvia the National Science Foundation and has frozen more than $700m in grants in order to reshape the system to suit political and ideological goals, scrapping research that mentionsblacklistedterms such as “climate” or “women”.In April, the administrationfiredthe entire 22-person board that independently oversees the NSF. Michael Kratsios, a Silicon Valley investor and Trump’s science adviser, has since said that the US’s research priorities will focus upon artificial intelligence and robotics rather than life sciences, a dominion that includes the study of wildlife.View image in fullscreenA marmot perches itself on a rock in Yellowstone.Photograph: Nathan Bilow/Getty ImagesThis realignment has strangled funding for the marmot study at theRocky Mountain Biological Laboratory(RMBL), a non-profit field station in the Rocky Mountains near Crested Butte, Colorado.The study of yellow-bellied marmots, one of the 15 recognized species of marmot in the northern hemisphere, was started by Kenneth Armitage, a University of Kansas academic, in 1962 and has grown to be one of the longest-running animal monitoring projects in the world. The project also has public outreach such as an annual vote for “fat marmot week”, whichstarts next week.The documentation of the marmots – researchers are on to their 11th generation of marmot to be spied upon – is important, Martin said, as it has illustrated the warping environment around the creatures as the world heats up due to the burning of fossil fuels.While the marmots are not in any imminent danger of extinction, they are being affected by the climate crisis. “We’ve seen them increase in body mass as the summers get longer and the winters get shorter – they are getting fatter,” said Martin.“But the other aspect is we have had a record lack of snowfall in Colorado and we saw a big die-off of marmots, more than we ever saw before,” he added. “The snow cover arrived so late and the extent was so small this past winter. The marmots need the snow as a layer of insulation as they hibernate in their burrows, so without this many of them just froze to death.”Martin said that continued monitoring was needed to ascertain the impact of the climate crisis on marmots, other wildlife and the broader landscape. While the injection of OnlyFans and crypto cash will keep the marmot project alive for now, he acknowledged it was not an adequate substitute for standard government funding.“Of course we have been lucky and we might get luckier if the memecoin does even better but I understand it’s not for everyone,” he said. “It worked for us because we were the first. But it has been nice to see crypto be used for good.”Martin added that “it is a bit of a dream” to at some point see the creation a broader memecoin that could support all sorts of scientific projects, including those not involving marmots at all.Explore more on these topicsUS newsAnimalsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Waiting for a nightjar is elusive and maddening – then thrilling | Birds | The Guardian
description: Goyt Valley, Derbyshire: My patience into dusk is rewarded with a full display of unlikely calls and aerial prowess
Author: Mark Cocker
Headline: Goyt Valley, Derbyshire: My patience into dusk is rewarded with a full display of unlikely calls and aerial prowess
Content: A male nightjar in flight. ‘As the bird moves so the glittering call shifts through the plantation shadows.’Photograph: David Tipling/AlamyView image in fullscreenA male nightjar in flight. ‘As the bird moves so the glittering call shifts through the plantation shadows.’Photograph: David Tipling/AlamyCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: Waiting for a nightjar is elusive and maddening – then thrillingGoyt Valley, Derbyshire:My patience into dusk is rewarded with a full display of unlikely calls and aerial prowessMark CockerTue 18 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 04.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe setting sun spread a last Iberian glow over the hills opposite before they were drained of colour and sound, and by 9pm, the world was in monochrome.In line withnational increases in their numbers and range, nightjars have prospered here recently. It seems especially so with the clearance of conifers, which has left a mix of old Scots pine and open space perfectly suited to this crepuscular ground-nesting migrant.You hear nightjars much more than see them. Churring is the name given to their vocalisation – a continuousunfurling throat songthat is one-part stridulation, one-part deep earth rumble. It feels subterranean, but also flows weightlessly like mist. Intermittently the unseen bird will turn its head; the song shifts key, then resumes, but its location is barely more obvious.Flying nightjars constantly make another noise – a monosyllabic “gwic” call – that is so sharp, so emphatic that it seems almost to shine. Perhaps imagine the sound as an iridescent beetle, and as the bird moves so the glittering call shifts through the plantation shadows. If a nightjar’s churr is soothing, this call is maddening as you fail to fix the author while he passes.At last, you glimpse a silhouette and the thrill of nightjars finds full outlet. You’re struck most by the extraordinary length of its tail and body, but especially those slender wings, which yaw now almost in slow motion as it hangs or weaves through the trees. One detail comes to dominate, because a male’s outermost flight and tail feathers have intense white terminal spots and, while a flying bird merges with the background, those luminous dots inscribe zany lines of white into the darkness.There is one further sound to mention. If a pair combines in a brief aerial tangle, as they did tonight, both sexes can bring their wings together high overhead. The night air vibrates with their impact and it comes to the ear as a loud, clear clap. It is at once elemental and an outcome of exquisite control, and as you walk back into the increasing white noise of our kind, you realise you have encountered something precious that is indisputably ancient and mysterious.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryRural affairsAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grenfell cladding firm Arconic paid shareholders £23m more in compensation than to fire victims | Grenfell Tower fire | The Guardian
description: Report’s author said findings highlighted ‘near-total failure’ to hold corporations accountable over the disaster that killed 72 people
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Report’s author said findings highlighted ‘near-total failure’ to hold corporations accountable over the disaster that killed 72 people
Content: Arconic, which supplied flammable aluminium composite material used to clad Grenfell Tower, has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArconic, which supplied flammable aluminium composite material used to clad Grenfell Tower, has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesGrenfell Tower fireGrenfell cladding firm Arconic paid shareholders £23m more in compensation than to fire victimsReport’s author said findings highlighted ‘near-total failure’ to hold corporations accountable over the disaster that killed 72 peopleJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentTue 18 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe company behind Grenfell Tower’s flammable cladding gave more compensation to its shareholders than to victims of the disaster, an investigation has found.Arconic, which made and sold the cladding panels found to be the “primary cause” of the rapid spread of the Grenfell fire, paid $74m (£54.7m)) to its shareholders for economic loss they incurred after the blaze.In contrast, the company paid $43m (£31.8m) to the estates of the fire’s victims and survivors after a lengthy legal battle. Across both payouts, all but $2m was covered by Arconic’s insurers.The findings are part of a new report by thinktank Common Wealth and financial investigations group FIND, which calls for stronger corporate accountability laws inEnglandand Wales to ensure future misconduct does not go “unpunished and undeterred”.“Arconic successfully avoided consequential accountability for its role in the fire through a series of ordinary business practices,” the report said.Grenfell United, which represents the bereaved and survivors of the fire, said the investigation showed how “corporate structures and legal systems have allowed those responsible to move on while our community continues to live with the consequences”.“Grenfell was not just a tragedy – it was a preventable disaster. We hope these findings help drive the legal and political changes needed to ensure no company can evade responsibility in this way again,” they said.View image in fullscreenThe Grenfell inquiry accused firms that supplied cladding and other materials for the high-rise of ‘systematic dishonesty’ in its report.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesA total of 72 people, including 18 children, died as a result of the fire in the 24-storey Grenfell Tower in June 2017.Arconic sold Reynobond PE, the flammable aluminium composite material (ACM) used to clad the tower. Theinquiry into the blaze found the company “deliberately and dishonestly concealed from the market”the true danger of the product in the form in which it was used on Grenfell.Arconic hasrepeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and a criminal investigation by the Metropolitan police has yet to bring charges against any individuals or companies in relation to the fire.The report revealed how the Reynobond PE used on the tower made up less than 1% of annual Reynobond sales at the time, and said there was no evidence Arconic has tried to trace the rest of the product it has sold.It had been selling Reynobond globally for at least 20 years before the Grenfell fire, and previously said it had sold 12.75m square metres of it in total.The report urged Arconic to publicly reveal where the rest of the material had been sold, and said it should be debarred from public contracts in England until it does so.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCommon Wealth researcher and the report’s author, Leela Jadhav, said the findings “outline a near-total failure of legal mechanisms to hold corporations accountable”.It also called for stronger laws in England to punish corporate misconduct, saying the country lags far behind other countries in doing this.Its recommendations included making punitive damages available in England and Wales in cases where corporate illegality is implicated in death. Currently, these damages are awarded very rarely and only in narrowly defined circumstances.Courts should be given the power to direct a portion of shareholder settlement recoveries to victim funds where third-party harm is identified, it said, and insurance companies should conduct human rights and environmental due diligence to ensure they do not “facilitate and encourage” misconduct.The UK government has committed a maximum of £5.1bn to cladding removal, with £600m of public money put into an ACM Cladding Remediation Fund. The report said, “an order of punitive damages against Arconic could cover these expenses, at no public cost”.Arconic declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsGrenfell Tower fireConstruction industryHousingEnglandShareReuse this content

title: Burnham declares almost £350,000 in donations in months before becoming PM | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: MPs’ register of interests shows hospitality and trips worth more than £12,000 and contributions from longstanding Labour donors
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: MPs’ register of interests shows hospitality and trips worth more than £12,000 and contributions from longstanding Labour donors
Content: Burnham’s declarations include £20,000 from trade unions including Unison, the CWU and Fire Brigades Union.Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham’s declarations include £20,000 from trade unions including Unison, the CWU and Fire Brigades Union.Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamBurnham declares almost £350,000 in donations in months before becoming PMMPs’ register of interests shows hospitality and trips worth more than £12,000 and contributions from longstanding Labour donorsRowena MasonWhitehall editorTue 18 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonors toAndy Burnhamgave almost £350,000 over the months before he became Labour leader and prime minister, with major contributors including his former adviser Sacha Lord as well as billionaires David Sainsbury and Gary Lubner.The new MPs’ register of interests also shows Burnham declaring hospitality and trips worth more than £12,000 – many of them relating toGreater Manchesterin his former role as mayor but also including £1,500 of Glastonbury tickets in 2025, where he was speaking, and £500 of tickets to Ladies Day at Aintree this year.The register is the first in which Burnham has recorded his financial interests as an MP since he became prime minister. It also shows he recently set up a company called Office of Andy Burnham, which leaders often do to manage their financial affairs after leaving office, and that he owns a property in London with his wife, which is rented out.Other cabinet ministers to make new declarations include Louise Haigh, the chancellor of theDuchy of Lancaster, who accepted £11,000 from Sainsbury to pay for legal advice and £7,500 of legal services from Bindmans law firm.A source close to Haigh said: “The donations related to legal services provided during the declaration period in relation to misrepresentation in the media.”Haigh is believed to have taken legal advice around media coverage about her conviction for fraud in relation to a missing phone in 2024. She resigned as transport secretary when it became public last November but has since been brought back to run Burnham’s leadership campaign and as one of the most senior members of his cabinet.Burnham’s donations, which began in March this year, include £20,000 from trade unions including Unison, the CWU and Fire Brigades Union. But the biggest financial supporter was Sainsbury, a billionaire and long-termLabourdonor who gave more than £160,000, including paying for staff working on policy.He was also given the services of a staff member on secondment by Ernst & Young, and £35,000 from Lord, including staffing and contractor costs, travel, venue hire, digital platforms, social media support, message testing, polling and campaign setup.Lord, who was Burnham’s unpaid night-time economy adviser in Manchester, resigned from the role in January 2025 after the Arts Council England said that his company misled them in applying for a £400,000 Covid support grant, though Lord denies any wrongdoing. The donor was one of those present at No 10 at the time Burnham made his first speech as prime minister.Burnham was also given £50,000 by a company owned by media executive and Labour donor Charlie Parsons. A further £25,000 came from Lubner, the founder of Autoglass, £10,000 from Shalni Arora, the wife of billionaire Simon Arora, as well as £10,000 from David Blunkett, one of Burnham’s mentors and a former cabinet minister. ThinkLabour, the thinktank formerly known as Labour Together, gave more than £22,000 in staffing and IT equipment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShortly after entering Downing Street, Starmer faced criticism for the volume of free tickets to events he had received, including more than £100,000 in hospitality, as well as gifts of clothing and accommodation from Labour peer Waheed Alli. He later changed the rules brought in by the previous Conservative government to ensure that all hospitality taken by ministers is declared, and to create more transparency around the register.A Labour party spokesperson said: “It’s right that political campaigns are funded by the generous support of party donors, rather than via the public purse. All declarations have been made in line with parliamentary and Electoral Commission rules.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourParty fundingLouise HaighGreater ManchesterDuchy of LancasterTrade unionsShareReuse this content

title: One person dead and more than 200 ill in UK salmonella outbreak | Health | The Guardian
description: UKHSA rules out British produce as source of infections and says evidence points to consumption of imported eggs
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: UKHSA rules out British produce as source of infections and says evidence points to consumption of imported eggs
Content: Officials said whole-genome sequencing showed all cases so far were linked to a single strain of salmonella.Photograph: incamerastock/AlamyView image in fullscreenOfficials said whole-genome sequencing showed all cases so far were linked to a single strain of salmonella.Photograph: incamerastock/AlamyHealthOne person dead and more than 200 ill in UK salmonella outbreakUKHSA rules out British produce as source of infections and says evidence points to consumption of imported eggsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorTue 18 Aug 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne person has died and more than 200 others have fallen ill during a UK-wide outbreak of salmonella that health officials have linked to people eating imported eggs.The 207 people affected range in age from under one year to 90 years old,according to the UK Health Security Agency, which is leading an investigation into the outbreak.They appear to have consumed the contaminated eggs in cafes and restaurants, rather than at home.The UKHSA has ruled out UK-produced eggs or poultry as the source and said the available evidence pointed to eggs imported into Britain. It is working with other European countries, through their joint system of surveillance of threats to health, to identify how the outbreak began.The agency said it could not release any details of the person who died or circumstances of their death because it was the subject of a continuing investigation.It said at least 34 people were left so ill with salmonellosis, the illness caused bysalmonella, that they had to be treated in hospital, and two had a bloodstream infection.Officials have ascertained through whole-genome sequencing that all 207 cases are linked to a single strain of salmonella. The first case was identified on 11 August 2025, but most of them have been identified since the middle of last month.Most of the cases have been in England (199), six in Scotland and one each in Wales andNorthern Ireland. London has had 47 cases so far and the Yorkshire and the Humber region 38 cases.“This isn’t an isolated incident. This outbreak is closely related to one from 2025 that was also linked to imported eggs, with the identified strain genetically similar between the two years,” said Dr Safi Rehman, a research associate at King’s College London.UKHSA’s notice alerting the public to the outbreak, issued on Tuesday morning, said: “Extensive epidemiological and food chain investigations are ongoing to identify the source and origin of the contamination responsible for illness.”Interviews with 114 of those left ill have identified “five food businesses where two or more independent cases reported attending in the week prior to symptom onset. These food businesses link 24 cases in total.” The agency did not name the five businesses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMassive egg recall in US south and south-west due to salmonella outbreakRead moreIt added: “Food chain investigations to date have identified that these premises are supplied by eggs from multiple sources, including egg importers. Local investigations have also identified possible cross-contamination risk events within two of these settings. At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry.”Hannah Charles, the agency’s lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections, said: “We’re working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person to person. Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.“Symptoms of a salmonella infection include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out-of-hours service in the first instance.”She advised the public to take action to prevent the spread of salmonella. “Wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and, if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible.”Explore more on these topicsHealthFood safetyEnglandScotlandNorthern IrelandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Berry-Dee dropped by publisher after allegations of abuse made against him | Publishing | The Guardian
description: Bonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigation
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: Bonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigation
Content: His publisher said it was ‘shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations’ relating to Berry-Dee.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHis publisher said it was ‘shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations’ relating to Berry-Dee.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockPublishingChristopher Berry-Dee dropped by publisher after allegations of abuse made against himBonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigationElla CreamerTue 18 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe main publisher of the bestselling true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee has dropped the author after aGuardian investigationinto allegations of violence andsexual abuse against him, which he denies. Waterstones has also removed his books from sale.“We are shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations relating to Christopher Berry-Dee, and our thoughts are with those affected,” said the publisher Bonnier Books in a statement to the Guardian.“Bonnier Books UK will no longer publish Christopher Berry-Dee, we will not work with him on any future projects, and we are terminating all existing agreements”, it continued. “There are practical steps entailed in unwinding longstanding contracts, including those involving third parties, but we are working through them as quickly as we can. We will also be removing our existing stocks from the market.”An investigationpublished on Saturdaydetailed multiple allegations of abuse by Berry-Dee, including domestic violence and sexual assault of a 13-year-old student attending his art school. Berry-Dee refused to be interviewed for the piece, citing health issues, but denied the allegations: “I have not once committed any of the crimes you accuse me of.”Berry-Dee, 78, is the UK’s top-selling author of true crime. His books, including Talking With Serial Killers, draw on interviews with murderers and have sold nearly 1m copies.Berry-Dee has admitted lying to his subjects in order to gain access, telling them he intends “to write a book about the miscarriage of justice they are suffering”, he wrote in his 2023 book Talking With Psychopaths and Savages.Waterstones told the Guardian that Bonnier contacted the bookseller to say that it would no longer publish Berry-Dee’s books. “Following this advice, we have removed the titles from sale in our shops and online,” said a representative.Orion, an imprint of Hachette, published Inside the Darkest Minds by Berry-Dee last month, but did not respond when asked whether they will continue to publish it.Explore more on these topicsPublishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Second major fire at south London recycling centre in under three months | London | The Guardian
description: Fifteen fire engines tackling blaze at Landmann Way in Deptford involving 50 tonnes of household waste
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Fifteen fire engines tackling blaze at Landmann Way in Deptford involving 50 tonnes of household waste
Content: Fire seen at a waste facility in DeptfordLondonSecond major fire at south London recycling centre in under three monthsFifteen fire engines tackling blaze at Landmann Way in Deptford involving 50 tonnes of household wasteNadeem BadshahTue 18 Aug 2026 17.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 100 firefighters are dealing with a fire that has broken out at a waste facility inLondonfor the second time this summer.Fifteen fire engines are at the incident in Deptford, south-east London, which involves about 50 tonnes of stored household waste.People have been asked to avoid the area and keep their doors and windows closed where possible because of the large amount of smoke.In a video posted online, flames and smoke could be seen billowing above the surrounding buildings near a railway line.The London fire brigade (LFB) said the cause of the blaze has yet to be established.View image in fullscreenThe Landmann Way fire affected local train services.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PALFB added that it was first called about the incident at about 8pm and crews from East Greenwich, Old Kent Road, Deptford and surrounding fire stations were sent to the scene.It is understood firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in Junewhen a van and a car were destroyed and one man was treated on scene by London ambulance service.Station commander Duncan Rees said: “Approximately 100 firefighters are tackling a large fire at a recycling centre on an industrial estate on the border of Bermondsey and north Lewisham.“First calls were received at 19.58 and 15 fire appliances are now in attendance. Fire crews along with colleagues from partner blue light services are working hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control.“One of the brigade’s 32-metre turntable ladders and one 64-metre turntable ladder are being used as water towers to tackle the flames from above.”Rail services into London Bridge from New Cross are affected because the fire has blocked railway lines, National Rail said.Explore more on these topicsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: US sanctions international criminal court president and prosecutor | US news | The Guardian
description: Marco Rubio targets ICC’s Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Seye, who was investigating Israeli war crimes in Gaza
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Marco Rubio targets ICC’s Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Seye, who was investigating Israeli war crimes in Gaza
Content: Tomoko Akane makes a speech in Brussels, Belgium, on 19 March 2025.Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTomoko Akane makes a speech in Brussels, Belgium, on 19 March 2025.Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesUS newsUS sanctions international criminal court president and prosecutorMarco Rubio targets ICC’s Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Seye, who was investigating Israeli war crimes in GazaAndrew Rothin WashingtonTue 18 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has sanctioned the president of the international criminal court (ICC) and a prosecutor tasked with investigating crimes committed byIsraelduring itswar on Gaza.The new sanctions designations were unveiled byMarco Rubio, the US secretary of state, who called the Hague-based ICC a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate”, in a statement.Rubio announced that the US would sanction Tomoko Akane of Japan, the ICC president, and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, an ICC senior trial lawyer, because they had “directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”.The state department last month unveiled an effort to “dismantle the threat” posed by the ICC to US sovereignty.The ultimate goal was to “disable the ICC’s ability to operate, target American servicemen or officials, or otherwise threaten American sovereignty”, the department said in a statement.Netanyahu and Kushner talks make no breakthrough on stalled Gaza dealRead moreRubio has called on the 125 member countries of the ICC to withdraw from the body. Donald Trump has said that he istargetingthe ICC because of the threat it poses to Israel.The US had previously sanctionedKarim Khan, an ICC prosecutor, who had successfully sought arrest warrants for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and for former defense minister Yoav Gallant,over war crimes during the Gaza war. Trump in 2025sanctionedthe court, stating in an executive order that it had “engaged in illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel”.Rubio did not say specifically which efforts the two ICC officials had engaged in, but Israeli media have reported that Seye is also overseeing the investigation into Israeli funding for illegal settlements and the distribution of weapons to settlers in theWest Bank.Israeli officials warned local media in May that the ICC may seek five more arrest warrants for ministers and senior military officials involved in violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.The US has already designated at least 11 ICC officials for sanctions, stemming from cases that also include investigations into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan.Neither the US nor Israel are member states of the ICC or recognise its jurisdiction.Four human rights groupssuedTrump last week for targeting the ICC. In the lawsuit, they said that the sanctions prevent victims of war crimes from seeking justice.Explore more on these topicsUS newsInternational criminal courtMarco RubioBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelPalestineGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Death and alleged torture of man in detention sparks protests in Syria | Syria | The Guardian
description: Picture showing White Helmets volunteer unconscious and with bruises on his body went viral
Author: William Christou
Headline: Picture showing White Helmets volunteer unconscious and with bruises on his body went viral
Content: Mourners carry the coffin of Mohammad Ghamira for burial in the village of al-Haffah, in Latakia province, Syria on Monday.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenMourners carry the coffin of Mohammad Ghamira for burial in the village of al-Haffah, in Latakia province, Syria on Monday.Photograph: APSyriaDeath and alleged torture of man in detention sparks protests in SyriaPicture showing White Helmets volunteer unconscious and with bruises on his body went viralWilliam ChristouTue 18 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSyrians have protested over the death of a man who was arrested and allegedly beaten by security forces, sparking widespread anger at a practice thought to have ended with the fall of Bashar al-Assad.A crowd gathered in the city of Aleppo, demanding accountability for the security forces who are alleged to have carried out the torture, with participants holding signs and slogans such as: “Do not repeat the same oppression that we revolted against.” Protests were also planned to take place in front of Syria’s parliament in Damascus on Tuesday, as well.Mohammad Ghamira, a 29-year-old father of two and former volunteer in the White Helmets, had visited a police station in the coastal province of Latakia last week after an accusation of theft.Ghamira emerged from the station in a critical condition, and died in hospital on Sunday from “complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal haemorrhaging” that “resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained”, said Raed al-Saleh, the former head of the White Helmets and current Syrian minister of emergency and disaster management.A picture of Ghamira pre-detention, smiling and healthy, next to another picture of him unconscious in a hospital bed with bruises on his body, went viral, sparking outrage in Syria.Ghamira’s parents told the police station chief prior to their son’s detention that he had haemophilia, a disease which makes it hard to stop bleeding once started, and asked them not to beat him. Even with the warning, Ghamira was beaten while in custody, Issam Ghamira, the man’s uncle, told Syrian state media.The Syrian interior ministry promised accountability for Ghamira, forming a committee to investigate his death and detaining seven members of the interior ministry for questioning. The interior minister, Anas Khattab, vowed a “fair punishment” after the conclusion of the investigation.“I confirm that any violation or abuse by the elements of the ministry of interior will be dealt with firmly within the laws and procedures followed and any violator will receive his fair punishment,” Khattab said in a post on X.The interior minister spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba acknowledged issues in the ministry, but promised that justice would be served. Al-Baba said that the investigative committee met with family members on Tuesday and informed them of the progress of the investigation.Despite the promises of accountability, Syrians were incensed by the allegations of torture, enraged that the practice continued even after the 14-year revolution aimed at stopping such brutality. Al-Assad’s regime used mass detention and torture on a systematic scale to control its population, accelerating its brutality when protests broke out against the government in 2011.The current government, made up mostly of former members of the Islamist rebel groupHay’at Tahrir al-Sham(HTS), overthrew al-Assad in a lightning offensive in December 2024. It promised an end to the atrocities committed under the police state that al-Assad oversaw, dismantling the dense network of security agencies that oversaw the country.However, rights groups have alleged that torture continues to be used in Syrian detention centres, and that the policy of abuse is being rebuilt.Syrians for Truth and Justicedocumented14 cases of individuals being tortured or dying in custody from June 2025 to June 2026, and said that “the change in political authority has not yet been accompanied by the effective dismantling of the structures and practices that enable torture”.STJ collected testimonies that showed severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities by Syrian security forces across different agencies, often seemingly motivated by sectarian discrimination.The rights group pointed to a lack of oversight and accountability for militias and members of the security forces as an explanation for the persistence of torture in Syria, rather than a centralised policy of torture originating from security agencies themselves. It contrasted this with al-Assad’s regime, where torture was not due to gaps in law, but state policy itself.The report echoed the findings of the UN independent commission of inquiry in March, which documented torture and abuse in 30 official and makeshift detention facilities across Syria in 2025.Civil society groups called for protests and demanded accountability, pointing to the sacrifices of those who died under torture fighting for freedom in Syria.“So many sacrificed dearly for freedom and dignity, to close the dark chapter of their country’s history and to end these practices forever,” said Diab Serieh of the Association of Detainees and the Missing in Sednaya Prison. “Justice for [Ghamira], and for all those forcibly disappeared and under torture in detention, remains an unwavering demand that we will never abandon.”Explore more on these topicsSyriaHuman rightsTortureMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Mechanical fault suspected in helicopter crash that killed British newlyweds in Greece | Greece | The Guardian
description: Marie Ebert, Alexander Cromie and their pilot died when their aircraft crashed on island of Sifnos
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Marie Ebert, Alexander Cromie and their pilot died when their aircraft crashed on island of Sifnos
Content: Cromie, 31 and Ebert, 30, had chosen Sifnos to spend their honeymoon after recently marrying.Composite: XView image in fullscreenCromie, 31 and Ebert, 30, had chosen Sifnos to spend their honeymoon after recently marrying.Composite: XGreeceMechanical fault suspected in helicopter crash that killed British newlyweds in GreeceMarie Ebert, Alexander Cromie and their pilot died when their aircraft crashed on island of SifnosHelena Smithin AthensTue 18 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek police believe a mechanical fault may have caused a helicopter to crash moments before it was due to land on the island of Sifnos, killing a British couple on honeymoon and the pilot.Authorities were focusing on Tuesday on the “strange noise” the aircraft, a privately chartered Bell 206, is reported to have made before falling to the ground and exploding on impact.“We can confirm that two passengers, Marie Ebert and Alexander Cromie, died in the incident on Monday evening,” a police officer said.London-based Ebert and Cromie, aged 30 and 31 respectively, had selected Sifnos to spend their honeymoon after recently marrying.Officials in Syros, the Aegean’s administrative centre, identified the pilot as Giorgos Raikos, 53, saying he was a former air force officer and “extremely experienced”.One well-placed source said: “The focus of the inquiry is now on the helicopter and possible engine failure. What has happened is nothing short of a tragedy.”The deputy mayor of Sifnos, Manolis Fountolakis, told Greek TV: “People in the area have testified hearing the helicopter making a noise, a strange noise, probably a mechanical fault in the air and because the propeller was doing something strange.”CCTV footage is also being studied of the aircraft spiralling out of control as it approached the island’s helipad near the village of Exambela.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the site of the crash on Sifnos.Photograph: ReutersA spokesperson for the asset management company Blackstone, where Cromie worked as a vice-president in private wealth solutions, said in a statement issued to the Press Association: “We are shocked by the tragic passing of three people including our colleague Alex Cromie and his wife, Marie Ebert, who were celebrating their honeymoon.“Alex was beloved by everyone who knew and worked with him at Blackstone, and our thoughts and prayers are with his loved ones.”According to his LinkedIn profile, Cromie had worked at Blackstone for four years, first as an associate in private wealth solutions before being made a vice-president last January.A spokesperson for the management consultants Bain & Company, where, according to her LinkedIn page, Ebert was a senior specialist, said: “We are shocked to read reports of a tragic accident inGreeceregarding one of our colleagues and her husband.“Our thoughts and support are with the families involved at this very difficult time.”Further tests were expected to be conducted on all three bodies to determine the precise cause of death.The Greek transport ministry said the inquiry into the crash was being headed by the National Organisation for the Investigation of Air and Railway Accidents and Transport Safety.By Tuesday afternoon, Greece’s civil aviation authority had reportedly recalled all Bell 206 helicopters until further notice.Greece’s public broadcaster, ERT, quoted Antonis Zambelis, a local resident, as saying: “The helicopter crashed about 50 metres away from houses with people inside and about 50 metres from the landing spot next to the Panayia tis Vrysis monastery.”Thick plumes of smoke engulfed the crash site after the helicopter ignited in a fireball. Rescue workers who scrambled to douse the flames subsequently discovered the remains of all three victims.Greece’s ministry of infrastructure and transport was coordinating the inquiry on Tuesday as senior law enforcement officials converged on Sifnos.The island’s mayor, Maria Nadali, said: “We are shocked and are trying to manage, together with the right services, the consequences of this incident next to the helipad.”Hiring private helicopters has become ever more popular in Greece, with tourists increasingly chartering them to hop between islands in the Ionian and Aegean seas.Once considered remote, Sifnos is about 120 miles (195km) south-east of Athens and takes several hours to reach by ferry.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agent | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Amid race with Anthropic, firm plans to overhaul research and training and require more safety parameters after hack
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Amid race with Anthropic, firm plans to overhaul research and training and require more safety parameters after hack
Content: Sam Altman, the CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 29 July.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSam Altman, the CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 29 July.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpenAIOpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agentAmid race with Anthropic, firm plans to overhaul research and training and require more safety parameters after hackJohana Bhuiyanand agencyTue 18 Aug 2026 16.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAIon ⁠Tuesday said it had slowed down the ⁠pace of ⁠its ​AI development while it overhauled its ⁠research and training systems.The company’s researchers were ⁠caught unaware last month ​when an ‌AI agent ‌under testinghackedanother AI ‌firm, Hugging Face.The AI research lab behindChatGPTsaid its new measures included pausing its model testing for two ‌weeks and investing more in adding other AI ​systems to monitor the activities of AI agents in testing. Some of ⁠the company’s largest planned training runs ​remain ​on hold, ​the company said.The first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’Read moreThe company ​did ‌not reply ​to ​questions about when the slowdown began or when it planned to return to its normal pace of development. However, in an interview with tech blog Sources News, Mia Glaese, who leads safety atOpenAI, said: “We are very far from everything running back to normal.”The company is working to ensure the AI model is responsive to human oversight and will behave as intended, a process called alignment,Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, wrote in the post announcing the slower pace of development.“We now require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout all of training, building on research and evaluations already underway,” he wrote. “Keeping increasingly capable systems aligned is a challenge the whole field will need to address.”OpenAI is in a heated race with competitorAnthropic, both to develop the most advanced AI models and togopublicon the US stock market. Both companies have highlighted the pace at which the capabilities of their models are progressing, emphasizing both speed and danger.OpenAI, for its part, said the capabilities of its upcoming AI model Astra may be nearing what it calls the “critical cybersecurity threshold”, which prompted the decision to slow its development. “Our latest internal evaluations of Astra, one of our upcoming models, over the past few days indicate significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity,” the company said in anannouncementlast week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with stronger safeguardsRead moreThe decision to slow the development of its AI models also comes a week after Bernie Sanders, a Vermont senator, demanded the top AI firms in the country pause development of the AI models because the companies were losing control over the technology, he wrotein a letteraddressed to the firms’ CEOs.“Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development,” Sanders’ letter read.By then, OpenAI had announced that it was temporarily slowing the development of its latest model, Astra, in response to the model’s hack of the Hugging Face tech firm.The company says it now requires “the strictest level of security safeguards for workloads involving Astra”.“While some Astra training and evaluations meet those requirements, a significant number of workloads remain paused until they are fully migrated and enhanced to meet the new security bar,” the announcement reads.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)Sam AltmanAnthropicComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Philip Pullman and Maggie O’Farrell among authors urging Burnham to cut business rates on bookshops | Books | The Guardian
description: After pubs and clubs get rates relief, authors back open letter calling for similar support for bookshops, described as the ‘beating hearts’ of high streets
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: After pubs and clubs get rates relief, authors back open letter calling for similar support for bookshops, described as the ‘beating hearts’ of high streets
