Content: Customers browsing books outside the Brick Lane Bookshop in London.Photograph: Melanie Major/AlamyView image in fullscreenCustomers browsing books outside the Brick Lane Bookshop in London.Photograph: Melanie Major/AlamyBooksPhilip Pullman and Maggie O’Farrell among authors urging Burnham to cut business rates on bookshopsAfter pubs and clubs get rates relief, authors back open letter calling for similar support for bookshops, described as the ‘beating hearts’ of high streetsEmma LoffhagenTue 18 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaggie O’Farrell, Philip Pullman, Katherine Rundell and Elif Shafak are among the authors supporting a campaign by independent booksellers who have urged Andy Burnham to extendbusiness rates relieffor pubs, clubs and live music venues to bookshops, warning that rising bills could put some shops at risk of closure.A total of 234 independent booksellers have signed an open letter organised by theBooksellersAssociation, calling on the prime minister and the chancellor to give bookshops the same consideration as other businesses that play a significant, positive role in their communities.The campaign followsthe government’s announcement last monthof a 20% reduction in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April 2027.More than a dozen authors have told the Booksellers Association they support the letter, including children’s laureate Patrice Lawrence, Adam Kay, Lemn Sissay, Anthony Horowitz, Patrick Ness, Donna Ashworth and Rachel Joyce.Burnham alsorecently announcedplans to tackle the spread of vape shops, betting shops and “rogue operators” on high streets, giving local authorities the power to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres. He said such businesses had displaced “the shops, services and community spaces that people are crying out for”.The letter, sent on 13 August, states that bookshops were “deeply disappointed” to learn they would not be included in the additional relief. “The government has accepted that businesses which deliver significant community benefit deserve targeted support. Bookshops clearly meet that test.”“Business rates relief for bookshops would also provide a meaningful legacy for theNational Year of Reading,” it continued. “The government is rightly telling the country that reading matters. But as things stand, its legacy risks being contradictory: promoting reading on the one hand while implementing policies that reduce investment in bookshops and may contribute to their closure on the other.”“Independent bookshops are the beating hearts of our high streets and communities”, said O’Farrell, author of Hamnet. “They need all the support we can give them.”View image in fullscreenKatherine Rundell … ‘To lose bookshops would be to chip away at our culture.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianRundell said: “To lose [bookshops] from our high streets would be to chip away at our culture, and at our ability to access fresh thought and new ideas.”The Treasury has argued that bookshops already receive support through permanently lower business rates multipliersand a £4.3bn package intended to limit increases in bills.Analysis commissioned from economic consultancy Cebr found that independent bookshops in England that are not eligible for full small business rates relief face an average annual increase of £4,563 by 2029-30, with some bills expected to double when transitional relief ends.Across the sector, business rates receipts are projected to increase by 45% nominally.For the average independent bookshop, Cebr estimates this would require selling an extra 1,141 books a year to cover the additional cost.The impact is already being felt, according to separate Booksellers Association research, with 85% of independent booksellers saying they are less likely to invest in stock, staffing, events or their premises as a result of business rates changes.View image in fullscreenPhilip Pullman … ‘Almost the last beacons shining to remind us about personal discovery.’Photograph: Tom Nicholson/PinPep/PA“In the current encircling corporate darkness, independent booksellers are lighthouses,” Philip Pullman said. “They are almost the last beacons shining to remind us about private reading, personal discovery, and the life-saving joy of encountering minds and hearts that speak to us as one person to another.”Laura McCormack, the Booksellers Association’s head of policy and public affairs, said restricting high-street businesses deemed as negative was “only half the job”. “You can’t rebuild Britain’s high streets by tackling the wrong businesses while making it harder for the right ones to succeed,” she said.Explore more on these topicsBooksBooksellersBusiness ratesRetail industrySmall businessLocal governmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ikea to take on eBay and Vinted with UK online secondhand site  | Ikea | The Guardian
description: Platform set to launch later this year will enable loyalty card members to sell preloved Billy bookcases and Poäng chairs
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Platform set to launch later this year will enable loyalty card members to sell preloved Billy bookcases and Poäng chairs
Content: The Swedish company opened several stores selling preloved Ikea furniture and is now branching out into online secondhand marketplaces.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Swedish company opened several stores selling preloved Ikea furniture and is now branching out into online secondhand marketplaces.Photograph: ReutersIkeaIkea to take on eBay and Vinted with UK online secondhand sitePlatform set to launch later this year will enable loyalty card members to sell preloved Billy bookcases and Poäng chairsBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerTue 18 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIkea is taking oneBay, Facebook Marketplace and Vinted with its own secondhand selling site in the UK.The new platform, which will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-ownedIkeaitems locally, is due to launch in the next few months.The move by the world’s biggest furniture retailer follows its trials of online secondhand marketplaces in Spain and Norway, and comes five years after it began buying and selling used Ikea items in some of its UK stores.A spokesperson said: “Our goal is to make passing on beloved Ikea pieces as seamless as possible. We’re creating a trusted and vibrant space to make it quick and easy for our Ikea Family [loyalty scheme] members to trade directly with one another.”Further details of the UK online site will be announced in the coming months, the company said. On the Spanish version selling is made easier with pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions provided by Ikea. The retailer also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.Buyers in Spain – where a Poäng armchair is being sold for €56, about half the price of a new version – will have to pay a 5% “protection fee” from January next year to fund various costs related to the sale, in a similar system to thatoperated by Vinted.Britons are increasingly embracing secondhand buying, pushing up sales at Vinted, which began as a clothes resale site but is nowexpanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sitessuch as Vinterior.The US secondhand site eBay recentlybought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn. Preloved items now make up abouta 10th of global fashion sales.There is heavy competition for the preloved market as the trend moves into the mainstream, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling preloved items. The latter further boosted its position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat has added to pressure on charity retailers, such as British Heart Foundation, which hasclosed stores amid rising costs.Ikea’s move into secondhand items is partly motivated by its pledge to become “climate positive” by 2030, including an aim to make all products from renewable, recyclable and recycled materials.Explore more on these topicsIkeaRetail industryRecyclingWasteeBayInteriorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK pay growth slows as job vacancies hit five-year low | UK unemployment and employment statistics | The Guardian
description: Iran war prompts cost of living squeeze for workers as ONS reports unemployment rate stays at 4.9%
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Iran war prompts cost of living squeeze for workers as ONS reports unemployment rate stays at 4.9%
Content: UK private sector pay growth has continued to ease, an ONS official said.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenUK private sector pay growth has continued to ease, an ONS official said.Photograph: AlamyUK unemployment and employment statisticsUK pay growth slows as job vacancies hit five-year lowIran war prompts cost of living squeeze for workers as ONS reports unemployment rate stays at 4.9%Business live – latest updatesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentTue 18 Aug 2026 06.09 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 02.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWage growth in the UK slowed in June and vacancies hit a five-year low as workers came under pressure from a renewed cost of living squeeze amid the economic impact from the Iran war.Figures from theOffice for National Statisticsshow average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, fell to 4.1% in the three months to June, down from 4.4% in the three months to May.The pay slowdown could deter theBank of Englandfrom raising interest rates this year, some economists suggested.New UK cost of living crisis looms with soaring energy bills forecast to lift inflationRead moreLiz McKeown, the ONS director of economic statistics, said the data showed “some softening” in the jobs market despite a broadly unchanged picture overall, in a potential sign of stabilisation after a sharper slowdown earlier this year.“Regular wage growth has remained broadly stable in recent months. However, private sector pay growth has continued to ease, while public sector pay growth remains elevated due to the timing of the latest NHS pay awards,” she added.Pay growth excluding bonuses strengthened slightly from 3.4% to 3.5%. City economists had forecast the rate would remain unchanged. The number of workers on company payrolls fell by 13,000 in July, matching the decline in June after larger falls in previous months.Graphic showing UK unemployment since 2010However, earnings growth, excluding bonuses, in the private sector slowed to 2.8%, the weakest growth rate since October 2020. Pay growth in the public sector strengthened to 6.1%, reflecting the payment of NHS staff pay rises earlier in 2026 compared to 2025, which distorts the figure.Vacancies fell to a five-year low as small businesses warned they were facing a rise in employment costs. There were 707,000 in May to July, a drop of 6,000 compared with the previous three months and the lowest level since spring 2021.“Ongoing weakness in private sector hiring and wage growth suggests the bar is still relatively high for a rate hike in 2026, barring a severe and prolonged spike in energy prices,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.Modupe Adegbembo, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said there was little in the data to make the Bank of England more worried about labour-market-driven inflation pressure.“Whilst the adjustment still looks orderly rather than disorderly, we think the BoE will remain cautious around the state of the labour market,” Adegbembo added.Money market pricing shows City economists expect one increase in UK interest rates by the end of the year, which would lift the Bank rate from 3.75% to 4%.The headline rate of unemployment remained unchanged at 4.9%. City economists had forecast a drop to 4.8%.The snapshot comes ashouseholds face a fresh hit to living standardsas the fallout from the Middle East conflict rattles the world economy. Official figures due on Wednesday are expected to show that a rise in energy bills drove UK inflation close to 3% in July.Annual growth in earnings after taking account of inflation was 1.3% in the three months to June. However, workers could face a squeeze as rising inflation approaches the slowing rate of earnings growth.The figures highlight the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government to ease the financial pressure on households before a difficult autumn budget.The prime minister used his first week in office to announce a series of “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living, and he has promised to combat unemployment as young people bear the brunt from recent higher rates of joblessness.Ministers are awaiting a review into youth jobs from Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister, after the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet)surpassed a millionearlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.Before a final report this autumn, Milburn told the Guardian this week that he would call on the government to“turbocharge” the provision of internshipsfor young people with special educational needs.Earlier this month he told this newspaper he would recommend new requirements for English primary schools to take steps toidentify children at risk of leaving educationat 16 without finding a job.Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “It’s encouraging to see signs of progress in the latest figures, with employment on the up and a continued fall in unemployment rate.”He said the government had put in place measures to overhaul the benefits system and to support people to find work, including a youth jobs grant to encourage businesses to hire young people.“We will continue to reform welfare and employment support so that more people can live independently and restore opportunity across the country,” he added.Economists said the figures showed signs of a slowing jobs market that could strengthen the case for the Bank of England to hold back from raising interest rates.Threadneedle Street has signalled that a weaker backdrop in the labour market could help limit the capacity for stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched in the economy.Jake Finney, a senior economist at PwC UK, said: “On the face of it, the latest labour market report looks relatively benign. Unemployment, employment and inactivity remain broadly stable, while vacancies edged down but are essentially levelling off. The jobs market remains soft, but it isn’t collapsing.”Explore more on these topicsUK unemployment and employment statisticsEconomicsPayPublic sector payOffice for National StatisticsBank of EnglandInterest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Phyllida Law, prolific performer across stage and screen, dies aged 94 | Movies | The Guardian
description: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades
Content: Phyllida Law in 2013.Photograph: Pascal Saez/RexView image in fullscreenPhyllida Law in 2013.Photograph: Pascal Saez/RexMoviesPhyllida Law, prolific performer across stage and screen, dies aged 94As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decadesAndrew PulverTue 18 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhyllida Law, whose prolific acting career encompassed a wide range of stage, TV and film roles – a number of which were alongside her daughters, Emma and Sophie Thompson – has died aged 94. Her personal manager, Jacky Leggo, said in a statement that she “died supremely peacefully at home, surrounded by all her family”.Born in Glasgow in 1932, Law was accepted at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre school – initially intending to be a stage designer but then switching to acting. She appeared in a number of Bristol Old Vic productions in the 1950s, and it was there she met Eric Thompson, a fellow actor, whom she married in 1957.View image in fullscreenLaw alongside daughter Sophie Thompson in 1996’s Emma.Photograph: Matchmaker/Miramax/Kobal/ShutterstockLaw broke into TV in the late 50s, with numerous appearances on screen throughout the 60s in shows such as Dr Finlay’s Casebook, Dixon of Dock Green and The Troubleshooters. By the end of the 1970s she had appeared in significant stage roles, including replacing Carole Boyer in the original 1967 production of A Day in the Death of Joe Egg after it transferred to the Comedy theatre in London from the Citizens in Glasgow, and appearing alongside Alec Guinness in the first run of John Mortimer’s A Voyage Round My Father at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in 1971, and Alan Bennett’s Habeas Corpus at the Oxford Playhouse in 1973. She also joined the National Theatre, appearing in 1979 in Somerset Maugham’s For Services Rendered and JB Priestley’s When We Are Married, and was cast in the first London run of the English-language musical version of La Cage aux Folles.From the late 80s she achieved more prominence in film, appearing alongside daughter Emma in Peter’s Friends (directed by Thompson’s then husband Kenneth Branagh), Much Ado About Nothing (again with Thompson and Branagh), and the Gwyneth Paltrow-led adaptation of Jane Austen’s Emma alongside her other daughter Sophie. Law then appeared with Emma – playing mother and daughter – in The Winter Guest, Alan Rickman’s feature film directing debut, which won considerable acclaim.View image in fullscreenLaw and Emma Thompson in The Winter Guest.Photograph: Album/AlamyLaw continued to appear in high-prestige TV shows, including Waking the Dead, Rosemary & Thyme, Foyle’s War, Doc Martin and Agatha Christie’s Poirot, and had a recurring role in the Stephen Fry lawyer comedy drama Kingdom as Fry’s Aunt Auriel. Her final screen role was in the 2020 romance Then Came You, written by and starring Kathie Lee Gifford.Law was married to Thompson until his death in 1982, and is survived by their children, Emma and Sophie.Explore more on these topicsFilmTelevisionEmma ThompsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Laughing on the other side: the fringe shows turning painful breakups into comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Whether Elf Lyons’ high-concept Hollywood throwback, Kate Dehnert’s disorientating rave or Ele McKenzie’s Bob Dylan fantasy, heartbreak fuels fine humour at the festival
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Whether Elf Lyons’ high-concept Hollywood throwback, Kate Dehnert’s disorientating rave or Ele McKenzie’s Bob Dylan fantasy, heartbreak fuels fine humour at the festival
Content: Her work keeps getting richer … Elf Lyons.Photograph: Richard LakosView image in fullscreenHer work keeps getting richer … Elf Lyons.Photograph: Richard LakosEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLaughing on the other side: the fringe shows turning painful breakups into comedyWhether Elf Lyons’ high-concept Hollywood throwback, Kate Dehnert’s disorientating rave or Ele McKenzie’s Bob Dylan fantasy, heartbreak fuels fine humour at the festivalBrian LoganTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBreakups. We’ve all been through them. Sometimes they’re mutual, sometimes not. Sometimes agony, sometimes relief. And sometimes, they’re world-shattering bereavements that seem to end, or at least upend, everything. That’s the experience two comedy shows seek to express on this year’s fringe – an experience that can’t be captured by the usual conventions of the medium. Wry wisecracks into a microphone just won’t cut it. A whole new form is required.Perhaps formal innovation isn’t such a shock whenElf Lyonsis the innovator, as almost all of this dedicated nonconformist’s work has been entirely bespoke. But even for her, The Woman on the Edge is something different: shards of a disintegrating sense of self, grafted together to suggest the journey Lyons has been on since her relationship ended, shortly before her wedding day, early last year. The conceit is that the show is being performed by a Norma Desmond-alike alter ego. A brittle and wise-cracking refugee from vintage Hollywood, smoke plumes from her décolletage as she fills in for absent Elf while keeping at bay her husband, the clown Pagliacci, on the end of the phone.But that conceit soon devolves to others: audio clips of Lyons, her friends and family talking about her breakup and subsequent breakdown; scenes from an ill-advised romantic tryst in Thailand; an “opera” spliced together from remarks made to Lyons by self-absorbed men. There’s a subplot about the Apollo 13 mission, a private passion of Lyons’, which emerges as a metaphor for her search for fulfilment in love. All might look lost, but mission control could yet bring the crew home alive.View image in fullscreenFinding the right form … Kate Dehnert.Photograph: Emma HollandIt’s potent stuff, building to a fierce finale in which she claws back something defiant, celebratory even, from the wreckage of her love life. It’s often beautifully funny and idiosyncratic too, from an act whose work keeps getting richer. The surreal and aphoristic running jokes – the one about Pagliacci visiting the doctor; the one about the reflections her Hollywood alter ego sees in the mirror – are tart and emotionally charged. Her anecdote about a shared bath in Bangkok paints a vivid word-picture of underwhelming romance. A dumbshow at the end, that unites two of the show’s other strands (tango and snails), is captivatingly expressive of Lyons’ desolation.Kate Dehnert’s show Echo, award-nominated at Melbourne’s comedy festival, comes from a strikingly similar place. Dehnert’s relationship with an unnamed fellow comedian was a decade old when he left her for another woman. Her sense of herself, and of the life she’d anticipated, collapses. She returns home to Australia to rebuild her life. And none of this can be done justice by straightforward storytelling. So Dehnert goes for “1/3 play, 1/3 standup, 1/3 rave”, as the blurb has it; the show often sounds like a primal scream with repetitive beats.Lyons’ analogy of choice was Apollo 13; Dehnert’s is nuclear war, with her life reduced to a blasted post-apocalyptic landscape of confusion, depression and rage. She has to de-programme herself. She tries edging back towards coupledom – cue an unlovely dirty-talking skit with a man on a dating app. The show’s therapeutic journey towards “self-actualisation” is more conventional than Lyons’. Its several songs are sung tunelessly, which may be the point, but doesn’t make them great to listen to. But, as Dehnert navigates towards her own vindication at the end of the hour, there’s no denying Echo’s emotional punch, nor her achievement in finding an (insistent, suffocating) form to express the disorientation of a very bad breakup.View image in fullscreenTaking it in her stride … Ele McKenzie.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearIt’s quite the cognitive dissonance after those shows to then see Ele McKenzie’s debut, Bringing It All Back Home, which also addresses the fallout from a breakup. We look in vain here for nuclear war metaphors. Give or take a gag about how many Mini Milks it prompted her to eat, McKenzie takes the breakup in her stride, and focuses on the aftermath: a move back in to her parents’ house, and a reckoning with her arrested development as a 30-year-old trapped in her childhood home.Abby Govindan: Pushing 30 review – playful comic makes the case for marriage as a side questRead moreIt’s an eye-catching introduction to the work of a comic who recently starred in theBBC sitcom Funboys. McKenzie exploits for all its worth the mismatch between her gleefully juvenile sexual candour and the flat voice and sexless demeanour (she calls herself “the feral fourth Haim sister”) that back it up. The imagined May-to-September romance with Bob Dylan into which the show evolves is both blissfully silly and covertly expressive of her eagerness to bond with a dad who treats her less as daughter, more as colleague.Sometimes breakups feel as if they’ve ended everything – but as McKenzie’s show reminds us, when one door closes, others usually open. OK, so the life McKenzie encounters on the other side of this particular door (house-sharing with mum; intimate acts with a folk-rock icon) may not offer the likes of Dehnert and Lyons much consolation. But – like their own experiences, and in a radically different way – it makes for fine comedy.Elf Lyons is The Woman on the Edgeis at Pleasance Courtyard until 31 August.Kate Dehnert: EchoandEle McKenzie: Bringing It All Back Homeare at Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)RelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Match review – gory and slyly satirical catfishing horror for the age of Hinge | Movies | The Guardian
description: Online dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shocker
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Online dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shocker
Content: Against the wall … Humberly González in Match.Photograph: Marcos Cruz/Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenAgainst the wall … Humberly González in Match.Photograph: Marcos Cruz/Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewMatch review – gory and slyly satirical catfishing horror for the age of HingeOnline dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shockerLeslie FelperinTue 18 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaola (Humberly González) is a pretty young woman about to turn 30 who hasn’t found herself a steady boyfriend – so, like many people of her generation, she’s on all the dating apps. The algorithm finds her match in Henry, who looks clean cut and kind eyed – or, at least, that’s what he seems from a very short video conversation on the phone, which breaks up due to bad signal. Paola’s sister Maria (Shaeane Jimenez) is visiting town because her and Paola’s father (Peter Butler) is going in for an operation, and warns her more trusting sibling not to accept Henry’s invitation to come to dinner at his house, away from the public gaze.Of course, Paola should have listened to her sister. The good looking guy (played by Luke Volker) turns out to have been a catfishing lure, and therealHenry (Jacques Adriaanse) looks like what you’d get if a troll mated with a slime mould. Plus, it’s actually Henry’s deranged mother, Lucille (a fantastic Dianne Simpson) who’s been writing all those courtly messages to Paola – who is soon sedated with drugged wine and wakes up about to be raped, exactly the sort of scenario youractualmother warned you about.Fortunately, it’s not all grim worst-nightmare-ever stuff, thanks to a slyly witty script credited to Al Kaplan and Jon Kaplan, directed with impish verve by Danishka Esterhazy. There are some very funny scenes, including a great two-hander between Lucille and another possible victim, Natalie (Nikita Faber), who hasn’t been completely honest about her own presentation online. The last stretch has lashings of practical effect gore to keep the genre fans happy, but it’s the sour social satire that lingers in the imagination afterwards.Match is on digital platforms from 24 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersDatingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There was a certain hostility’: how Wet Hot American Summer went from miss to hit | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation
Content: ‘…this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh’ … the poster art for Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Everett Collection, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreen‘…this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh’ … the poster art for Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Everett Collection, Inc./AlamyComedy films‘There was a certain hostility’: how Wet Hot American Summer went from miss to hitCritics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciationMatthew Cantorin Los AngelesTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 2001, the film critic Roger Ebertwrote a scathing film reviewin song form, with lyrics set to the tune of a classic song about summer camp. “Hello muddah, hello fadduh/ Here I am at Wet Hot American Summah,” it began. The review proceeded to mock the film Wet Hot American Summer in rhyme.Wet Hot American Summer: a cult classic reborn on NetflixRead moreTwenty-five years later, the film’s director and co-writer, David Wain, joined several of its stars on the vast lawn of the Autry Museum in Los Angeles to sing the review to a crowd of thousands, many of them wearing Camp Firewood T-shirts and 80s-style sweat absorbers. The performance preceded an anniversary screening of what has become a cult classic.Ebert was one of many critics at the time who seemed baffled by the comedy, which follows the absurd adventures of a group of horny and/or lovelorn counselors desperate to make the most of their final day of camp in 1981. But if those early critics didn’t quite get it, plenty of viewers later did – enough to warrant two Netflix series, a place on variouslistsof thebest filmsof the century, and a return to theaters this month to mark its 25th anniversary.What changed over the years? “I would say that it’s just a slow-burn kind of movie,” Wain says. “I think there was a certain hostility among the first round of critics, being like, ‘Why was this even made?’” But the film’s quiet release ultimately served it well. Fans who discovered the movie in the ensuing years felt like “‘this is my thing. You need to know about it,’” Wain says. “There was a sense of ownership over it that I think made people connect to it in a deeper way.”Perhaps one reason the movie didn’t initially land is that its humor is difficult to define. It’s not a satire or a coming-of-age film or a straight camp-movie parody, though it does play on tropes like the training montage and the “anonymously evil” kids at a rival camp. But mostly, the camp serves as a setting that lends itself to an extremely high joke rate.Early critics might have gone in “with a certain expectation of what a comedy is supposed to be” and ended up unsure what to make of the movie, Wain says. Sometimes “the joke is that it’s so unfunny, or that there’s not a joke”. And much of the humor plumbs the depths of ridiculousness in a way that might have left early viewers dumbfounded – like when a group of nerds saves the camp from falling space junk, or when the counselors plan a reunion for 10 years in the future but can’t decide whether to meet at 9am or 9.30. Wain describes the humor as “joyfully nihilistic”. The jokes warp the boundaries of reality, but they work because they never lose touch with it. “The actual bedrock of it is: what was summer camp like for me in real life? What was it like to be that age in real life? And then draping all of these spoofy things around that,” Wain says. The goal for the performances is sincerity rather than silliness.Nor does the movie have a clear central plotline – while our hearts are with Coop (Michael Showalter), the well-meaning counselor who keeps losing out to Paul Rudd’s monstrous but very hot Andy in his pursuit of Katie (Marguerite Moreau), the film’s many storylines are given fairly equal weight. That gives breathing room to the alarmingly starry cast.It was Bradley Cooper’s first film, and among the first for Elizabeth Banks; it also stars Janeane Garofalo, as a camp director courting a local astrophysicist, played by David Hyde Pierce; Rudd as a counselor who’d rather let kids risk drowning than have to look up from a makeout session; Amy Poehler as a camp theater director who berates child cast members for not being Broadway-caliber; and Molly Shannon as an arts and crafts teacher who receives life coaching from a 10-year-old. Showalter, who co-wrote the movie, has gone on to direct films including The Big Sick, The Idea of You and The Eyes of Tammy Faye.View image in fullscreenMichael Showalter, Christopher Meloni and AD Miles in Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy“We wrote the whole thing with no actors in mind at all,” Wain says. The goal was to make a summer-camp movie inspired by their time as campers and counselors themselves. “We just vomited out back and forth to each other everything we could think of that had to do with each of our summer camp experiences,” Wain says. Many of those experiences made it into the movie, including an improbable incident in which a counselor, played by Ken Marino, is rushing back to camp to meet a crush and drives straight into a tree. Wain was that counselor. “I had just turned 16,” he says. After dropping kids off for an overnight trip, “I left late at night instead of early in the next morning because I was desperate to see this girl I had just met, and I smashed the van into a tree.”Filming, at a camp in Pennsylvania, was difficult. It rained almost every day, meaning the crew had to find constant workarounds for planned outdoor scenes. Some were moved inside; others were shot under partial cover; audio had to be re-recorded because the rain made it impossible to hear. But the whole experience was reminiscent of summer camp, Wain says. “We were all away from home, out of town, on location, the first time doing this for so many of us, and we all bonded,” Wain says. (The shoot was the subject of a film of its own,Hurricane of Fun: The Making of Wet Hot.)That bond has clearly held. Since Wet Hot, Wain’s films have included Role Models, written with Marino; They Came Together, written with Showalter; and this year,Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass. All of them have included fellow members of sketch comedy troupe the State and other cast members from Wet Hot American Summer. “We were doing [TV series] The State when we were very, very young, and we recognized at the time, when we were 18, that this was a special thing that we found each other,” Wain says. “We said out loud at the time: ‘Let’s not ruin this.’” They vowed to keep working together, and they’ve succeeded. “We continually recognize that it’s a gift to be able to do that.”View image in fullscreenMichael Showalter and David Wain in 2001.Photograph: Leslie Hassler/APThough Gail Daughtry, also written with Marino, got a theatrical release, studios have beenreluctant to back comediesin recent years. This year has seen an overallbox-office resurgence, but comedies remain few and far between. “There’s talk of the pendulum swinging back and comedies coming back, and I hope that’s true,” Wain says. “I just feel like going to a movie theater to see a comedy and laughing together is at least as important to me as going to a movie to see a big spectacle together.”Wain has spent the summer with those audiences, visiting cities including New York, Waterville, Maine (where the film is set) and San Francisco with his and Marino’s band,Middle Aged Dad Jam Band, and performing Theodore Shapiro and Craig Wedren’s music from the film.“I don’t love always looking backwards. I try to stay focused on what’s now and in the future as much as I can,” he says. But the tour has been “absolutely wonderful. People come up to me and say really beautiful things about how this movie has entertained them, or affected them, or been a bonding thing with them and their friends or their loved ones, or got them through hard times,” he says. “And the other thing about it, which makes me so happy, is this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh.“There’s no point really being made so much as just: let’s have an hour and a half where we’re not freaking out about the end of the Earth.”Wet Hot American Summer is out again now in select US cinemas and available to rent digitallyExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Waves Turn review – the exhausting, joyful, boring, wondrous realities of new motherhood | Movies | The Guardian
description: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments
Content: In the trenches … Waves Turn.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenIn the trenches … Waves Turn.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewWaves Turn review – the exhausting, joyful, boring, wondrous realities of new motherhoodJosephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching momentsCath ClarkeTue 18 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a piece of art depicting motherhood, Judith Rohrmoser’s self-portrait of breastfeeding sticks two fingers up at thetradition of the Madonna with child. In her painting, Rohrmoser’s baby feeds contentedly, chubby cheeked and sleepy under damp lashes. The artist is less serene, looking directly at us, headphones clamped over her ears, eyes filled with what might be a roar of grief, or possibly an overwhelming sense that everything has changed.Rohrmoser is one of five women who agreed to be filmed at their most vulnerable in the first year of motherhood for this Austrian documentary. It’s a gentle but truthful look at new motherhood, making the point that – ignore the Renaissance artists – having a tiny baby does not put you in perpetual state of bliss. The reality is exhaustion, joy, boredom, wonder and a rush of other feelings. Director Josephine Ahnelt shoots in 16mm, her camera up close, filming with the intimacy of a home video, cutting off heads to at one point zero in on what interests her: a mother snipping her baby’s tiny fingernails.The women share their experiences in voiceover. One mother says she didn’t experience the all-encompassing love she was told she’d feel when her baby was placed on her chest; instead, it happened little by little. Another talks about the judgmental comments she gets about bottle feeding her baby after struggling to breastfeed. One woman says she didn’t believe friends that her relationship would be changed by having a baby. Now she knows.There are some incredibly touching moments: mainly it’s the little things, the bouncing and jigging or massaging chunky little baby thighs, all done with love. And sometimes it’s the glazed over look of a soldier after a week in the trenches.Waves Turn is on True Story from 21 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsParents and parentingChildbirthAustriaFamilyWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gang of Youths are back: ‘Does it sound like a cynical gesture towards pop radio stardom?’ | Gang of Youths | The Guardian
description: Four years since their last album, the anthemic Australian band are back with a fresh sound and new music about finally being ‘overwhelmingly OK’
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Four years since their last album, the anthemic Australian band are back with a fresh sound and new music about finally being ‘overwhelmingly OK’
Content: ‘The best possible way to be is to not give a fuck’ … Gang of Youths members (L-R) Tom Hobden, Dave Le'aupepe and Jung Kim.Photograph: Remi Chauvin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The best possible way to be is to not give a fuck’ … Gang of Youths members (L-R) Tom Hobden, Dave Le'aupepe and Jung Kim.Photograph: Remi Chauvin/The GuardianGang of YouthsInterviewGang of Youths are back: ‘Does it sound like a cynical gesture towards pop radio stardom?’Sian CainFour years since their last album, the anthemic Australian band are back with a fresh sound and new music about finally being ‘overwhelmingly OK’Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 20.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen tickets for the firstGang of Youthsshows in Australia in four years went on sale last month, a one-off show in Thirroul sold out in 45 seconds; two shows at Sydney Opera House went in minutes. Though I have loved the band for years, I was surprised by how emotional it was to see them play on home soil again in Sydney. Dave Le’aupepe, who has a claim to being the country’s most charismatic frontman, seemed to sense the mood. “Thank you for loving me,” he told the audience. “I know it’s very difficult.”As I left the show, bewildered and tearful, I locked eyes with a stranger in the foyer who was also crying. Without saying a word, we both burst out laughing; feeling a bit silly, perhaps, but also a sense of wonder at our shared reaction. I later heard there were two marriage proposals in that audience; I wouldn’t be surprised if there were more.‘We want to get treated like normies’: Gang of Youths on fame, faith and family secretsRead moreI lastinterviewed Le’aupepein 2021, fresh out of lockdown in London, where Gang of Youths had decamped to en masse to escape their booming fame in Australia which Le’aupepe told me had “fucked me up really badly”. We were speaking ahead of the release of their last album, 2022’s angel in realtime, a grand, maximalist rock album about Le’aupepe’s dead father, his family’s hidden history and his Polynesian heritage. It was laden with emotion, as was Le’aupepe: he spoke with the hard fervour of a preacher, voicing all of his misgivings – about his voice, their past songs, their albums, their fame.But five years later, Le’aupepe looks noticeably relaxed and content; with that head of hair, there is something of a sleepy lion about him. He’s 34 now, and trying to be healthy. “No booze, no cigs. I fucking hate it,” he says cheerfully. He is also aware of an internal shift. “Last time we spoke, I was fraught because everything had so much fucking meaning – and it did, I guess,” he smiles. “The best possible way to be is to not give a fuck.”View image in fullscreenGang of Youths performing at Sydney Opera House on 8 August.Photograph: Jess GleesonWe’re speaking ahead of the release of their first song in four years, a silky three-minute single titled Things Take Time, out on Wednesday. “There’s heaven in the suburbs,” Le’aupepe croons on the track, which was a test on two fronts: could he, a famously wordy lyricist, write a song that “wasn’t really about anything”, and could he write a pop song? The result is Gang of Youths as you have never heard them before.“I need to know – does it sound like a cynical gesture towards pop radio stardom?” Le’aupepe asks. I don’t think so; it sounds like a happy man in a happy band. “Yeah, weirdly,” he says. “I’m not used to that.”While there are plenty of catchy Gang of Youths songs, Le’aupepe had never written a pop song and was curious about the architecture and mechanics of doing so. “I was drawn to the idea of actually writing songs for a change, instead of these fuckingmoodswith a bunch of fucking moody lyrics,” he laughs. “I’m at the stage of my life – I think we all are – where we want to make art, not a diary.“So taking all my ideas and lyrical concepts and metaphysical fucking curiosities and condensing that into a three-minute song – that was my Everest.”View image in fullscreen‘For the first time, I’m not worrying how this will be received’ … (L-R) Jung Kim, Dave Le’aupepe and Tom Hobden.Photograph: Remi Chauvin/The GuardianThings Take Time was inspired by an offhand joke from lead guitarist and keyboardist Jung Kim while they were sitting in one of their back yards: hey Dave, write a song about plants. “I was like, fuck off!” Le’aupepe says – but then he got to thinking about how they had settled in their respective homes, started families and how their blooming gardens were evidence that they’d finally put down roots. As Le’aupepe puts it, “the song is about things growing and dying, but also what happens if somebody’s just overwhelmingly OK”.Tom Hobden, who plays violin, guitar and keyboards in the band, calls Things Take Time “an exercise in restraint”.“It was a conscious decision not to be so grandiose and actually let Dave’s voice carry the song,” he says, “rather than ramming in a gazillion things.”“Look at his fucking smile!” says Le’aupepe.“Well, I am excited about it,” says Hobden. “It might sound stupid, but I think what’s going to strike people about this record is how much you actually get tosing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I do a lot of that talking garbage,” Le’aupepe adds – and while there are plenty of fans of that talking garbage, Le’aupepe has impressive pipes, though he doesn’t know it. “I have always been really fucking self-conscious in my voice. I still really struggle with it. But this was liberating.”Things Take Time was recorded in Hobden’s back yard studio in London. “Dave would be in there for hours and then come out and everyone would be wondering what he’s building in there,” Hobden says. “And then I’d sneak in, open the sessions, and see: take 389. Bloody hell.”“I cop all this shit for being a fucking perfectionist, but it’s not a joke. I really struggle with it,” Le’aupepe adds. “But for the first time, I’m not worrying how this will be received. Will people like it? Will we be able to do X, Y, Z? That’s not really part of the equation for me any more.”View image in fullscreen‘We just want zen these days’ … Tom Hobden, Jung Kim and Dave Le’aupepe.Photograph: Remi Chauvin/The GuardianLe’aupepe made a 300-track playlist for the band spanning their bedrock – Leonard Cohen, Tom Waits, Godspeed You! Black Emperor, Bruce Springsteen, Nick Cave, The Go-Betweens – and some surprises. “I made everyone listen to bloody Perry Como over and over again,” Le’aupepe says. “Yo La Tengo, Warren Zevon, Glen Campbell – Wichita Lineman is the greatest fucking song ever written. How do cunts come up with something so miraculous?”“We just want zen these days,” Kim adds. “We’re not as self-conscious about what our output is. Like, we played the Bloodhound Gang in the studio! It is liberating to not be overly shy about what you genuinely enjoy.”The band “went down a rabbit hole trying to find a sound that was simpler so that I could sing,” Le’aupepe says, and shed the baggage of what Gang Of Youths should sound like along the way. The result is “the most fun I’ve ever had doing a record,” he says. “We loved each other, and we loved it. Being in that studio felt fucking sacred.”This doesn’t seem to be a one off either; the band played three new songs at that equally sacred Opera House show. And as Le’aupepe told that ecstatic crowd: “You’ll have to come back and see us next year …”Things Take Time by Gang of Youths is out nowExplore more on these topicsGang of YouthsPop and rockAustralian musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCNOW/Bancroft review – McGill is a stylish soloist in Kahane’s likable clarinet concerto | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: With Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concert
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: With Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concert
Content: Silky smooth … clarinetist Anthony McGill with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales.Photograph: BBC/ Angus RaceView image in fullscreenSilky smooth … clarinetist Anthony McGill with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales.Photograph: BBC/ Angus RaceProms 2026ReviewBBCNOW/Bancroft review – McGill is a stylish soloist in Kahane’s likable clarinet concertoRoyal Albert Hall, LondonWith Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concertClive PagetTue 18 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn their different ways, both Stravinsky and Copland turned to the vernacular to lend authenticity and atmosphere to their ballet scores. Stravinsky incorporated folk tunes and popular song to depict the hurdy-gurdy players and wet nurses of St Petersburg’s bustling Shrovetide fair in Petrushka. For Billy the Kid, Copland used cowboy songs to paint a wild west settlement with its outlaws, saloons and gunfights. Fast-forward 80 years and Gabriel Kahane added a flavour of folk music, though without quoting anything specific, to spice up his clarinet concerto. Written for New York Philharmonic principal clarinet Anthony McGill, the work’s European premiere formed the centrepiece of a lively concert conducted with visible enthusiasm by Ryan Bancroft.The concerto opened with McGill slipping in seamlessly over shimmering tuned percussion and string glissandi. Elegant scalar passages led into a songful section with a jazz-meets-klezmer vibe. This is immensely likable music, with McGill a confident and stylish soloist. Orchestral textures featured pianos – both grand and muted upright – as well as celesta and percussion, the latter more often than not played unconventionally. The slow movement with its drawn-out lyrical lines found McGill cucumber cool, before eerie bowed vibraphone and a hair-raising cadenza launched a finale with a touch of an Irish jig about it. Kahane himself added a nice personal touch, taking to the stage to sing and play piano for McGill’s silky smooth encore.The Copland got off to an uneven start, the orchestra never quite capturing the mystery of the open prairie, though at full-throttle they certainly caught its majesty. In a neat move, Bancroft turned to the audience to play a mean tin whistle and introduce the frontier town. The Mexican dance, gun battle and celebratory polka were tight and spirited, even if there were occasional moments of slack ensemble.Petrushka suffered from a similarly rocky opening, not helped by Bancroft bringing down the baton while the audience was still applauding. Individual solos were characterfully pungent though not all were ideally secure. Clarinet, bassoon and piano stood out, with a hearty laugh for the flatulent rasp of the contrabassoon. Elsewhere, though, boisterous excitement sometimes came at the expense of nuance and balance.Available on BBC Sounds until 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBBC National Orchestra of WalesPromsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian Lessons by Charlotte Higgins review – when art and war collide | Art and design books | The Guardian
description: A vivid and hopeful study of how culture endures in the midst of extreme violence
Author: James Meek
Headline: A vivid and hopeful study of how culture endures in the midst of extreme violence
Content: Ukrainian artist Diana Berg at an exhibition of her work.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenUkrainian artist Diana Berg at an exhibition of her work.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianBook of the dayArt and design booksReviewUkrainian Lessons by Charlotte Higgins review – when art and war collideA vivid and hopeful study of how culture endures in the midst of extreme violenceJames MeekTue 18 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTowards the end of her subtly piercing book about art in wartime, Charlotte Higgins recounts an autumn visit to Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second city, in the north-east of the country, a short drive from the Russian border. In a tranquil park, she sees a man standing in a stream, making stones balance on top of each other in a teetering tower – “a metaphor of life in that city,” she writes, “that would have seemed too obvious for a novel”.Still, as a good novelist would, Higgins doesn’t seem to beg telling details from a place so much as have them leap to her open eye and ear. The cartoons a boy is watching that fall silent in a power cut, allowing the distant boom of explosions on the frontline to be heard. A cityscape tattooed on a young poet’s arm that cuts off suddenly where skin from his leg was grafted after he was torn up by shrapnel. Cataracts of larkspur, as Higgins describes them, in a field in the frontline Donbas region, “pouring down the hill, pooling at the bottom into a great lake of blooms … Larkspur thrives on ground where there has been recent disturbance.”This last leads Higgins on to a story her driver tells her about stopping to pee in a roadside ditch and looking down to see the face of a dead Russian soldier staring up at him. The image of the soldier becoming one with the land he was sent to conquer makes her think in turn of a viral video from the early days of the Russian invasion of 2022, in which an old Ukrainian woman thrusts a packet of sunflower seeds on a Russian soldier, urging him to put them in his pockets so that when he is killed, sunflowers will sprout from his body to adorn the Ukrainian soil.One of the artist heroes of Higgins’s book, Anna Zvyagintseva, designs a bodysuit impregnated with seeds as a piece calledSustainable Costume for an Invader. Another, Marharyta Polovinko, killed in action in 2025 while serving as a drone operator, made macabre pencil drawings about the war, latterly using her own blood as a medium. One of her pictures shows dogs eating a dead Russian soldier. The image, Higgins says is “gruesome, horrific”; she recalls Achilles’s taunt to Hector in The Iliad before he kills him that he will let his body become dog food. “In Polovinko’s hands you sense the image is less about such crude triumphalism and more about the idea of flesh transformed into something else.”These Ovidian metamorphoses lean into the ancient Greek strand of the book, where Higgins, a classicist as well as the Guardian’s chief culture writer, aligns Greek myth and the characters drawn by Homer and Aeschylus with the present-day choices and agonies of mortal Ukrainians. But such explicit transformations are subsidiary to her main matter, the metamorphoses of artists and art itself under conditions of war.double quotation markHiggins undergoes her own metamorphosis, from arts correspondent to something like a war correspondent interviewing artistsIn a city near the frontline she meets Yaroslav Pilunskiy, a cinematographer from the Kyiv-based film collective Babylon 13, now working drones for the army. Little remains for him of his art. Once in a while, when there’s a nice sunset, he flies a drone to a lake where explosions are guaranteed, just for the visuals, but otherwise he’s been transformed into a 21st-century drone soldier. On the eve of the invasion, he was in Rome, editing a film; by the time Higgins meets him, 19 months later, he can’t remember what it was. “Sometimes,” Higgins writes, “he felt he had imagined it all.”Higgins quotes Diana Berg, a cultural manager and activist twice forced to flee from eastern Ukrainian cities: “Until the war is over, the best conceptual artists in Ukraine are the army.” And the still bleaker words of the poet Halyna Kruk: “There is no place for poetry when you spend several days standing next to the collapsed basement of a high-rise building, hearing your children and grandchildren screaming under the rubble, and you cannot rescue them.” She regretted, she concluded, that poets could not take their verse to battle as literal weapons. “I’m sorry that poetry doesn’t kill.”Higgins undergoes her own metamorphosis, from arts correspondent to something like a war correspondent interviewing artists, as her curiosity takes her much closer to the actual fighting than she expected in the beginning. Russia’s promiscuous use of missiles and drones against Ukrainian cities, anyway, means that the whole of Ukraine is a frontline and, like most visitors to Kyiv, Higgins gets caught up in air raids. For much of the book the war is noises off stage, but the violence is so deep and wide that every so often a small parenthesis drops with force: the building where 50 people were killed, the conductor shot dead because he refused to take part in an occupation concert. Most devastatingly, one of the writers Higgins grows closest to is killed in a Russian missile attack.Higgins, present but not obtrusive in her account, says that her time in Ukraine “unanchored” her. “It altered and enlarged the way I saw things, as if I had been given different eyes.”Part of the change she imposes on herself is learning Ukrainian, at a time when Ukrainians are struggling with the fact that for many loyal anti-Putin Ukrainians, Russian is still their first language. The backlash against Russian culture in free Ukraine is fierce. Statues of Pushkin, once common enough, are now deemed signs of a hostile power marking its territory. Higgins quotes an essay by the writer and editor Sasha Dovzhyk: “Russian is my mother tongue and liberation means ripping it out of my throat.”Despite Berg and Kruk’s rageous words, Higgins finds that the artists, poets, diarists, novelists and film-makers she meets still find ways and reasons to create. Indeed, she writes, “the argument of this book is that the literature and art made by these people, some of whom have lost their lives, will shape the war’s memory”. It’s a strong claim, in a world where the meme makers and clip aggregators often seem to have usurped even the historian and the balladeer, let alone the writer and artist. But the impression left by Higgins’s vivid and hopeful book is one of a multitude of creative ripples spreading and overlapping through Ukrainians’ wartime consciousness. There is solace in art; here are ways to describe the incomprehensible; here is, if not your memory, at least my record.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘After the reading, the poets hold each other’: what happens when Ukraine’s largest literary festival comes under Russian attackRead more“For me, there is no sense in writing about war,” Artur Dron’, the poet and wounded soldier with the interrupted tattoo, tells Higgins. “But it’s very important to write about people. That’s my focus: not trenches or shelling, not rockets, bullets or guns. I went through it; I don’t want to write about it. The main thing is to write about how we can save our sense of love in the trenches.”Never, writes Higgins, has she seen people listening with such intensity to poetry as she did in a (literally) underground bar in Kharkiv in 2025. “The people in the audience were straining forward, caught up in the deeply felt present, of communal listening, and the sense of inchoate emotions being articulated. When the famous Kharkiv novelist, poet and now soldier Serhiy Zhadan read his work, I saw a woman in the audience mouthing the words along with him, because she knew his poems by heart.”Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). title: Sunrise by Téa Obreht review – secrets and myths in the American west  | Books | The Guardian
description: Set across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recorded
Author: Nina Allan
Headline: Set across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recorded
Content: Wyoming where Sunrise is set.Photograph: Takako Phillips/Getty Images/500pxView image in fullscreenWyoming where Sunrise is set.Photograph: Takako Phillips/Getty Images/500pxBooksReviewSunrise by Téa Obreht review – secrets and myths in the American westSet across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recordedNina AllanTue 18 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTéa Obreht’s novels teem with conflicting narratives, treacherous landscapes and speculative fictions. Her 2010 prizewinning debut,The Tiger’s Wife, examined themes of death, miracles and outsider status in the midst of a fictional Balkan war. Her fourth novel, Sunrise, returns to a western frontier haunted by ghosts and stalked by outlaws, a territory Obreht first explored in her second book,Inland.It is August 2024.Nina Terzic has just jumped – or was she pushed? – from a crash-landing Cessna into a lake somewhere in the mountains of Wyoming. She manages to swim to shore. There is no sign of her boyfriend Ben, who was in the plane with her, and her phone – though miraculously intact – has no signal. Nina, a postgraduate student, was supposed to be on holiday from her job as a live-in nanny in New York. We get the feeling that her relationship with Ben might have a darker underside.Nina quickly realises that she has happened upon a ghost town, one of the dozens of abandoned mining settlements scattered across the Old West. Exploring her surroundings further, she discovers the body of a woman hidden in a cellar. Beside the dead woman is a backpack containing a manuscript.The sequence that follows is a part of that manuscript. Its action takes place in 1902, in the mountain town of Sunrise – the ghost town as it was, before everyone left. A man named Anton Vargas has returned after a long absence. He carries with him an aura of celebrity – or is it notoriety? Only Fred Kipley, the town’s deputy, seems unsurprised to see him again. Kipley and Vargas were once involved in a shootout with local bandits. Their courageous actions saved lives and cast them as heroes; in the years since, their exploits have become the stuff of dime-store novels and wild west shows. But Vargas is not a well man, and he has business to settle in town before it is too late.double quotation markSunrise is an engrossing, original and thought-provoking novel, effortlessly readable and beautifully toldThe novel’s central section moves us a century forward to 2003. Sunrise is now a ghost town, the haunt of tourists. We meet Colin Yard, whose re-enactments of the Vargas story have become a valued source of income. Coll is greatly invested not only in Vargas’s story but in himself as the rightful guardian of that story. When he is contacted by a writer, Louise Hawley, asking if he will read the novel she has written about Vargas, Coll doesn’t pay her much attention. But Louise has her own deep-rooted connection with the place, and has discovered new information about Sunrise’s local hero that casts his story in a radically different light.Coll is furious at what he sees as her trespass: “We have this small thing, you know?… This tiny part of history that belongs to us. And I don’t want it to be fucked with or misinterpreted by someone who, frankly, doesn’t understand it or care about it.” Louise is adamant that the material she has unearthed deserves to be scrutinised. She argues that Coll himself has altered material facts to fit his re-enactments, that recorded history is by its nature partly fictitious. But for Coll, “his” Vargas is the only Vargas. How far will he be willing to go to protect his property?It is in this section that the novel’s themes and intertwined relationships come most persuasively to life. To Louise, Coll’s home town seems idyllic, the kind of place where neighbours are as good as family. But the situation is more fraught than surface impressions might suggest. Coll has recently had a disturbing altercation with the local bad boy, Bob Fournier. “Bob’s latest madness” is considered an outrage, yet no one has it in them to go up against him. Coll’s tacit condoning of Fournier’s actions has terrible consequences – not least for himself – but it is symptomatic also of a moral cowardice that will indirectly precipitate a greater calamity.Obreht’s portrayal of Colin Yard – his gradual, desperate slide from favoured son to villain of the piece – is a brilliant piece of theatre. Coll’s attempt to control the narrative is echoed in the bullying paternalism of John Daisy, the villain of Louise’s novel, a rich landowner and stockman whose “big house” casts its shadow over Sunrise back in 1902. Daisy is an avid collector of Native American artefacts and a supposed authority on Native traditions – too bad if his patronage does not extend to living people. Throughout all three of her interwoven timelines, Obreht raises similarly searching questions about courage and cowardice, idealism and pragmatism, and most of all about how history is recounted and who gets to own it.The novel does have its flaws. While the eventual revelations about Nina’s relationship with the ghastly Ben feel devastatingly real, it is difficult to ignore the loopholes in logic that characterise Nina’s portions of the narrative: how is she able to fall from a height on to water without getting injured? Having survived the crash unscathed, why does she waste time – and phone charge – trying to text her mother when she should be looking for a signal and calling 911? None of this detracts from the fact that Sunrise is an engrossing, original and thought-provoking novel, effortlessly readable and beautifully told. Given that most of what we come to know about Vargas is itself a series of fictions, it perhaps makes better sense to frame Nina’s miraculous survival as similarly mythic.Sunrise by Téa Obreht is published by W&N (£22).
