title: Dressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress design | Games | The Guardian
description: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Content: ‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesView image in fullscreen‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesSummer games previewsGamesDressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress designCo-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever madeJordan Erica WebberTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Jonathan Hau-Yoon wanted to make something as meaningful as the environmental strategy gameTerra Nil, he turned for inspiration to his longtime partner. Sabrina Becker had worn a dress she made herself to their very first date, and would have studied costume design abroad hadhypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome(a connective tissue disorder I also have) not put those plans on hold.The pair developed a concept around the creative decisions involved in dressmaking, like trying to fit pattern pieces on to available fabric while observing the grain line (the direction of the thread in woven fabric). Other decisions followed: a 3D model on which to place garment pieces, buttons and trims with which to decorate them, clients with commissions as creative prompts.View image in fullscreenNever run out of bobbin thread … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesHau-Yoon knew this ambitious project would benefit from the support of his employers at Free Lives. A bare-bones concept video got hundreds of thousands of views, and a prototype built with colleagues in three weeks had about 30,000 downloads, but he worried it wouldn’t be enough, that he might even have to leave a job he loved to pursue the game full-time. What convinced founder Evan Greenwood in the end was the passion of the player base. Many signed up foritch.ioaccounts just to play the prototype, and left paragraphs-long comments about how much it meant to them.And they had requests. “A surprising amount of people asked for ironing,” Becker laughs. Others wanted to be able to print out the patterns and use them in real life,Barbie Fashion Designerstyle, which isn’t possible here. “We don’t actually run a cloth simulation,” Hau-Yoon explains. Becker adds: “But you can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life. A lot of our players make whole paintings on the dresses, using the trims and buttons and things; they’re drawing Starry Night and the Sistine Chapel.”View image in fullscreen‘How elegant is elegant?’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesWhen I sew, I draft my own patterns to better fit my particular shape, so I wanted to know if Dressmaker includes this aspect. “We have a whole measurement system,” Becker says. “It is simplified, but it was really important to us to illustrate that if you’re coming in for a bespoke dress the dress should be made to fit you. So there’s this whole lattice deformer thing that allows our dress pieces to shift and scale proportionally.”Hau-Yoon says that programmer Ruan Rothmann calls Dressmaker “the most technically challenging game that he’s worked on”: “It really matters where seams are and that certain vertices align.” Other sewists can imagine what aspects have proved challenging: how the fabric stretches across a body, pattern distortion, creating gathers.Becker’s experience has been invaluable, and similarly her understanding of historical costume. Dressmaker isn’t era-specific, so as not to limit players, but it does have what she calls “a vintage feel”, looking as if it’s from “The sort of era where you would have actually gone to a dressmaker to have a dress made”. And when it came to the question of whether to branch off the story (from novelist Kerstin Hall), she knew that sewists would resent missing out: “I want to be able to make ALL of the dresses. If it’s branching and because of decisions you made you don’t get to make a wedding dress for a specific character, I would feel so gutted about that.”So what has she learned about the process of making games? “It’s all numbers and spreadsheets! At least the past two months of the work that I’ve been doing.” “It’s very difficult to capture how to score something when it’s just a vibe,” Hau-Yoon admits. “How elegant is elegant? What number describes elegance?”They hope players will appreciate their efforts, which include a whole-team sewing class arranged by Becker. “It was surprisingly Zen,” says Hau-Yoon. “Initially I was very slow and nervous, but that whirring of a sewing machine … it fades away into the background.” Players will soon be able to hear that whirr for themselves, as sound designer Jason Sutherland has painstakingly recorded Becker’s own weighty vintage Singer sewing machine, along with other related tools. “I’m obsessed with the scissors noise,” Becker smiles. “It’s so satisfying.”Dressmaker is coming to PC on 21 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Exit review – a circus squad who really drive each other up the wall | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The acrobats in this symphony of ins and outs build and break tension as they clamber over the set together
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The acrobats in this symphony of ins and outs build and break tension as they clamber over the set together
Content: Subtle changes … Exit.Photograph: Jona HarnischmacherView image in fullscreenSubtle changes … Exit.Photograph: Jona HarnischmacherEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewExit review – a circus squad who really drive each other up the wallZoo Southside, EdinburghThe acrobats in this symphony of ins and outs build and break tension as they clamber over the set togetherChris WiegandTue 18 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour performers enter the auditorium and walk among us but they’re sizing up the space not the audience. On stage is a scaffold structure with a cutaway design and a white facade featuring several doors, which soon frame a series of comings and goings. With this much slamming it’s no surprise that there’s an element of farce as the cast move in and out, become human dominoes and narrowly miss each other. No one has time to knock during the frantic arrivals. I’d recommend taking a side seat so you can appreciate the full effect.So far so frivolous in this family-friendly Belgian production, although there’s a cheeky hint at what might be happening behind those closed doors and whether swiping right is a factor among the increasing acrobatics. Choreographed by Piet Van Dycke, the show then knuckles down to more serious tricks, with the performers undertaking a series of costume changes that are so subtle you don’t notice them at first.View image in fullscreenElement of farce … Exit.Photograph: Jona HarnischmacherBastiaan van Vuuren’s initially twinkling score moves from accentuating light intrigue and comedy to building tension. Arjan Kruidhof and Arjen Schoneveld’s simple-seeming set opens up new possibilities when one wall becomes a giant teeterboard and one performer almost reaches the lighting rig.Taiwan Season: The Wall review – close encounters in a city that never sleepsRead moreThere’s a rotating cast and today’s quartet – Harrison Claxton, Luuk Brantjes, Christopher McAuley and Samuel Rhyner – have strength, skill and charisma, working harmoniously as a team. But the premise could become knottier yet and the production ultimately rests for too long in one register. I was reminded of the circus showSawdust Symphonyin this space two years ago and how it got richer by the minute. This fun symphony of swinging doors is more of an open-and-shut case – a bit of extra mystery wouldn’t go amiss.AtZoo Southside, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026CircusDanceTheatreEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: By a Thread review – soulful circus with a sprinkle of magic | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Emotional group dynamics and individual skills make Melbourne’s One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genre
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Emotional group dynamics and individual skills make Melbourne’s One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genre
Content: Now that’s a good idea … One Fell Swoop Circus: By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNow that’s a good idea … One Fell Swoop Circus: By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBy a Thread review – soulful circus with a sprinkle of magicAssembly Rooms, EdinburghEmotional group dynamics and individual skills make One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genreLyndsey WinshipTue 18 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou cannot move at the Edinburgh fringe for circus shows. There are so many people in this city who can climb a rope, hang upside down, swing on a trapeze – so how do you make a show special when plenty of other folks are hawking the same skills?Melbourne companyOne Fell Swoop Circushave worked out a way, sprinkling a bit of magic on their festival offering. It’s a show that wasoriginally made a decade ago, but had its Edinburgh debut last year and was such a hit that they have brought it back. Like many of the best shows, it’s really just one good idea, with all the juice thoroughly squeezed out of it across the course of an hour. That idea being: one giant rope, two pulleys, seven bodies, and everything they can do together.View image in fullscreenGroup hang … By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockLooped from the ceiling, the rope becomes a slackline to walk across, a trapeze to swing on, a vertical climb, a diagonal slide, and so much more. It’s all gently paced with a dreamy mood, but steadily engrossing, the soulful soundtrack slowly casting a spell. The skills are a given, but it becomes a great piece of theatre when the performers’ personalities start to emerge – the mechanics of the rope plus the dynamics of the group, that’s what is interesting.Plus there’s their individual skills, like Ellie Grow’s mind-blowing handstands. She’s more secure on two palms than most people are on two feet, which means she can turn what could be a quick trick into choreography, with rhythm, timing and wit. Then there’s a beautifully tender duet, multiple metres up in the air, that’s not really about acrobatics but human connection, hands and eyes meeting, warmth and friendship, all subtly done. The emotion feels real, and the tone is perfectly judged. Ropes aside, that’s what really elevates these acrobats.AtAssembly Rooms, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Then touringAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026CircusTheatreDanceEdinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Phoebe Bridgers review – high priestess of ambiguity turns grief Technicolor in intimate church show | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: Ahead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astounding
Author: Aimee Cliff
Headline: Ahead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astounding
Content: ‘I really did scrape the bottom of my guts’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in JulyPhotograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I really did scrape the bottom of my guts’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in JulyPhotograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesPhoebe BridgersReviewPhoebe Bridgers review – high priestess of ambiguity turns grief Technicolor in intimate church showUnion Chapel, LondonAhead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astoundingAimee CliffTue 18 Aug 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree days after the rapturous release of her third album,Lost Weekend, Phoebe Bridgers invites 900 people into her bedroom to hear her play some of its devastating songs live – or at least, that’s how it feels inside Union Chapel in north London on this Monday night. With Bridgers plopped on a throw-covered sofa, surrounded by lava lamps and with a TV showing the bouncing DVD logo screensaver, it becomes easy to forget the Victorian gothic architecture looming above our heads.This intimate scene is the indie superstar’s hugely anticipated first solo UK show since 2022, and the reverent awe in the church is palpable. Fans have obediently locked away their phones in magnetic pouches – as they will also have to on her arena run later this year – and fidget in the pews clutching CDs and T-shirts emblazoned with the artwork for her new record. You can hear a proverbial pin drop when Bridgers opens the show by belting her breakout song Motion Sickness solo with her guitar, her voice somersaulting around the domed ceiling. (After this, she is joined on stage by two bandmates, Nick White and Christian Lee Hutson.) But Bridgers, who hums with a slightly nervous energy, characteristically pierces through any solemnity by encouraging us to scream and sing along as the gig rolls on. After all, she quips: “God’s watching – fuckin’ freak.”The jokes and the screams feel like necessary pressure-relief valves, as Lost Weekend takes centre stage at this show. Focused primarily on the tangled knot of grief she feels for her father, who died in 2023, the album is a vividly cathartic body of work that, as Bridgers puts it: “I really did scrape from the bottom of my guts.” It is also the artist’s most musically adventurous outing yet, cloaked in a bewitching fog of crackling ambience reminiscent of Grouper, and surreal, robotic vocoder. But for this release show, she dismantles the songs to their parts, with just two guitars, keys, harmonica and the occasional addition of percussion and ghostly FX.Phoebe Bridgers: I Can’t Wait – videoIn this spectral, spare form, the songs are even more astounding. You can really hear the bristling, soft rage as Bridgers sings: “Sometimes I want you back / But not today,” on Still Standing, an unflinching portrait of her “complicated” relationship with her dad. (This song and others reference his physical abuse of Bridgers’ mother.) Likewise, the seething lyrics of The Governor’s Waltz, which appears to reflect on the breakdown of her engagement to Paul Mescal, seem to send a shiver through the congregation. Her words cut even deeper when near-whispered.‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriterRead moreBut it’s not all quiet worship. At points, stomping percussion rises to the rafters, Bridgers uses effects to contort and throw her voice, and Hutson plays some of the most ominous harmonica ever heard on their rendition of Kill Me. Then, of course, there is the album’s title track, which cracks open from a soft ballad into a triumphant clatter and swell of strings, electronic chatter and disembodied voices.In the Union Chapel, the song’s climax is highlighted with UV light, giving Bridgers’ blond bob and the images of planets hung behind her a creepy glow. At first, the effect is so incongruous to be almost funny – but then its uncanniness starts to make sense. Bridgers is often described in shorthand as a purveyor of “sad songs”, but what her latest release proves more than ever is that her writing contains vast emotional worlds. On Lost Weekend, she sketches grief as the sharpest edge of life: a time when your memories of the past feel so intense as to be Technicolor, and the present can feel like a distant fog; when emotions are both muted and turned up to 11. It makes sense that on the first UK live outing for these deliciously complex songs, there is humour and surrealism to be found even in the devastating dark.Explore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bigfoot Ripped My Dog in Half I Saw It review – Xhloe and Natasha create a monster hit | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treat
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: With physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treat
Content: Minimal props … Xhloe and Natasha in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMinimal props … Xhloe and Natasha in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBigfoot Ripped My Dog in Half I Saw It review – Xhloe and Natasha create a monster hitSummerhall, EdinburghWith physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treatChris WiegandTue 18 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a show every bit as breathless as its title, stoked by bursts of high-energy 90s chart hits and delivered just as slickly byXhloe and Natasha. Their physical precision is such that it’s almost as if these camo clowns with their rosy cheeks and tearstained eyes are executing a mission.The duo have previously portrayed confused cowboys (And Then the Rodeo Burned Down), spiralling housewives (What If They Ate the Baby?) and spit-promise scouts (A Letter to Lyndon B Johnson or God: Whoever Reads This First). Here the terrain is recognisable from those shows yet so much more expansive as they play numerous locals, from the corner shop to the highest office, in an Appalachian town. It gives more chance to showcase their vocal, as well as physical, agilities.View image in fullscreenLight touch … Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMostly they’re in character as a couple of teenagers who wind up in trouble until a scapegoat arrives in the unlikely form of Bigfoot. Soon other townspeople are saddling Sasquatch with assorted crimes. Like their previous shows it works on several levels, capturing a specific locale and era while remaining timeless and giving a state of the union address that is bang up to date. Misinformation, misdirection and flagrant cover-ups create a daisy chain of lies. The environment is treated like dirt. Division and suspicion are actively encouraged and enthusiastically embraced. Official statements from on top are meaninglessly empty. The Stop sign that looms in the background seems to call for nothing less than a complete reset for the US.I Made You a Mixtape review – frothy fringe fun as dorm mates party like it’s 1999Read moreIn a production co-directed by Tom Costello, the pair use minimal props and that sign is adorned with Bigfoot’s furry mitts, clawed shoes and a mask with its mouth agape – all detachable and wielded to schlocky effect. There is some of the duo’s signature off-kilter wordplay and bamboozling tactics. It is sometimes slightly too on the nose, and I missed the emotional hit of the friendship in their LBJ story. But what’s again almightily impressive, from a show punctuated with floor-trembling thuds, is the duo’s light touch in handling heavy subject matter.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August. title: ZZ Top drummer Frank Beard dies aged 77 | ZZ Top | The Guardian
description: Tributes paid to ‘great friend and collaborator’ who played with band for 56 years and died in hospice care in Texas
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Tributes paid to ‘great friend and collaborator’ who played with band for 56 years and died in hospice care in Texas
Content: Frank Beard of ZZ Top performs at Stiefel Theatre in Salina, Kansas.Photograph: Gary Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrank Beard of ZZ Top performs at Stiefel Theatre in Salina, Kansas.Photograph: Gary Miller/Getty ImagesZZ TopZZ Top drummer Frank Beard dies aged 77Tributes paid to ‘great friend and collaborator’ who played with band for 56 years and died in hospice care in TexasOwen MyersTue 18 Aug 2026 16.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheZZ Topdrummer Frank Beard has died at the age of 77.A spokesperson for the band confirmed that Beard died on 17 August in hospice care at his ranch in Richmond, Texas. His family were by his side.In a statement,ZZ Topsinger Billy Gibbons said: “Today, Elwood [Francis] and I lost a great friend and collaborator, and the world lost one of the most naturally innovative drummers and a great and true son of Texas.“His signature backbeat was key to keeping ZZ on top. The band of which he was part for six decades is going to keep on keeping on as he had wished.”Last week, the band cancelled a show at the Hollywood Bowl owing to Beard’s health. ZZ Top will also no longer play their Tuesday concert in Salt Lake City or Wednesday in Colorado Springs.Growing up in the small town of Frankston, Texas, Beard played in a number of local rock bands before joining ZZ Top in 1971. Although not a founding member, he came to be regarded as the band’s definitive drummer among fans thanks to his propulsive percussion on hits such as La Grange, Tush and Legs.As the band became rock heavyweights in the late 70s, Beard experienced drug addiction, leading to the band taking a hiatus. After the break, Beard got sober and toured with the band for decades.Beard faced other health problems over the years, including an emergency appendectomy, which caused him to miss some shows in 2002. Last year, he stepped away from the band due to undisclosed health issues.In 2021, ZZ Top bassist Dusty Hilldiedat the age of 72. After his death, Elwood Francis joined the band as bass player.In public, Beard consistently adopted a humble attitude towards his success. When ZZ Top were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004, he said: “All I have to say is that most of my life has been a pleasant surprise, and so is this. Thank you.”Explore more on these topicsZZ TopPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Wladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’ | US television | The Guardian
description: Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’
Content: Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week on 25 June 2013 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageView image in fullscreenWladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week on 25 June 2013 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageUS televisionWladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’Richard LuscombeTue 18 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHayden Panettiere’s daughter will be raised to remember her mother’s “immense talent” and “incredible career”, according toa tributeposted on social media on Tuesday by Wladimir Klitschko, the ex-lineal world heavyweight boxing champion and the late Hollywood actor’s former partner.Their daughter, Kaya, has been raised by the Ukrainian retired boxer since 2018, when Panettiere ceded full custody to concentrate on her battles with alcoholism, depression and substance abuse.Her death in Greenville, South Carolina, was reportedon Sunday, with no cause given.Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesRead more“Our family is going through a time of profound shock and grief,” Klitschko wrote in the Instagram post, which featured a photograph of himself and Panettiere smiling at a beach, with Kaya – whose face is obscured – perched on her mother’s shoulders.“The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon. Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.”The message also referenced the troubles that the Nashville and Heroes actor had experienced at a young age, following a succession of child stars who faced laterchallenges or tragedy.“She built an incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry,” Klitschko wrote of Panettiere. “Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives.“To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was.”Klitschko also sent his condolences to Panettiere’s grieving parents, friends and fans.“Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon,” boxing’s lineal heavyweight champion from 2009 to 2015 wrote. “I ask everyone to please respect our family’s feelings and privacy during this incredibly difficult time. For now, this is all I wish to say.“Rest easy, Hayden. May you find eternal peace.”In May, Panettiere expressed hope that she would one day be reunited with her daughter, who was born in 2014.“I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she toldpodcaster Jay Shettyin an emotional interview.“I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.”Hollywood continues to fail child stars and Hayden Panettiere is the latest casualty | Jesse HassengerRead moreKlitschko and Panettiere met at a book launch party in 2009, when the actor, then aged 20, was already a television star for her appearances as fictional high school cheerleader Claire Bennet in Heroes. After first splitting in 2011, they remained close friends and became engaged in 2013. Panettiere gave birth to Kaya a year later.The actor struggled with postpartum depression, and the couple split for good in 2018, with Kaya spending time with her father at residences in Florida and Europe, E! News reported at the time.Panettiere then had an on-again, off-again relationship with Brian Hickerson. TheAssociated Pressand NBC News on Tuesdayreportedthey had obtained a police report that said Hickerson and his brother, Zach, were at the scene inside the apartment complex where Panettiere died.The report said Hickerson showed police “a bag of medication” that Panettiere was taking at the time of her death, according to NBC.Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson was marred by domestic abuse allegations. He was arrested multiple times and reportedly jailed in 2021 after pleading no contest to domestic abuse charges.Explore more on these topicsUS televisionWladimir KlitschkoUS television industryTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchise | Games | The Guardian
description: Sonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Sonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’
Content: ‘At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity’ … a mural of Sonic the Hedgehog in Shoreditch, London.Photograph: SegaView image in fullscreen‘At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity’ … a mural of Sonic the Hedgehog in Shoreditch, London.Photograph: SegaGames‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseSonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’Keith StuartTue 18 Aug 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne day in the early 1990s, I came home from university for the weekend and discovered that my dad had bought himself a Sega Mega Drive, bundled with a copy ofSonic the Hedgehog2. I knew about Sega’s mascot of course. The launch of the original Sonic the Hedgehog game in 1991 was a landmark moment for the company, massively boosting the sales of its 16bit console in the west, ripping market share from the dominant Super Nintendo. While Mario was the family favourite, Sonic with his speed, attitude and brash visual energy encapsulated the edgy spirit of the early 1990s MTV culture. That weekend, Dad and I did little else but team up for daylong Sonic sessions, the game’s two-player mode letting us play cooperatively as we zoomed through those dense, beautiful play zones.Thirty-five years later, I am still a Sonic fan. There have been plenty of rough times (Sonic 06, Sonic and the Secret Rings, Sonic Free Riders – sorry, I can’t go on), but there have been plenty of good ones too. (Rush, Mania and Colors, and I have a soft spot for Sonic R, a racer developed by Traveller’s Tales, which went on to make the Lego games). Few people know this rollercoaster better than Takashi Iizuka, who worked on Sonic 3 as a designer and has been series producer for almost 20 years. When he joined Sega in 1992 he wanted to work for the company’s arcade division, but after playing the original Sonic – especially Sonic 2 – he was seduced.View image in fullscreenSpeed, attitude, and brash visual energy … Sonic the Hedgehog 2.Photograph: Sega“I do believe that Sonic the Hedgehog 2 is one of the best of the classic series, and the introduction of two-player gaming helped make it so special,” he says. “The team had been thinking about a two-player mode for Sonic the Hedgehog that we weren’t able to incorporate at the time, so achieving this in the sequel was vitally important. It was a challenge, because the development time for Sonic 2 was very tight; but Sega is always willing to try something new and take a risk, and it really paid off.”In 1993, Iizuka transferred to the Sega Technical Institute in California, the studio set up by industry veteran Mark Cerny (who would go on to design the PlayStation 4 and 5). Here he would begin the next phase of Sonic’s lifespan, working first on Sonic 3. “I knew almost nothing about countries outside Japan,” he says. “I still vividly remember being amazed by Sonic’s popularity when I arrived in the US. At the time, the TV animated series was airing, comic books were being published and the franchise was regularly covered in newspaper articles. It was in that moment that I truly grasped the reality that a game created in Japan had captured the hearts of players around the world.”Ivo Gerscovich, chief business and brand officer for Sonic the Hedgehog, sees this transmedia presence as vitally important. “What’s perhaps most telling of Sonic’s cultural staying power is what we’ve accomplished beyond gaming,” he says. “The Sonic the Hedgehog film franchise has been extraordinary, collectively grossing more than $1bn at the global box office and introducing Sonic to an entirely new generation of fans […] Partnerships like our ongoing collaboration with McLaren Racing speak to the breadth of audiences that Sonic can connect with.”I was too old to connect with the cartoons at the time, but when my sons were five and seven, they managed to find re-runs of the classic Sonic Underground cartoon on TV and were hooked – mostly by its crazed, over-dramatic pop punk theme tune. I took the opportunity to set up my dad’s Mega Drive so they could play Sonic 2 together. The fact that this happened 10 years after my dad’s death added a strange, sad poetry to the moment. It was my first real understanding of the fact that we pass our heroes down to our children, sometimes inadvertently, sometimes with forceful intention.View image in fullscreenFond memories … Sonic Adventure 2.Photograph: Sega/MobygamesIt’s difficult now to convey what an impact Sonic had on the industry in the 90s. The game’s idiosyncratic design, powered by Naoto Ohshima, Hirokazu Yasuhara and programming genius Yuji Naka, emphasised speed and impatience; Sonic was a semi-antagonistic presence who would fold his arms and tap his feet when the player wasn’t moving fast enough. It was Sonic 2sday on 24 November 1992, that perfected the concept of the global simultaneous video game launch – an idea repeated a year later with Mortal Monday for the console release of Mortal Kombat. Both Sonic and Mortal Kombat resonated with a teen audience brought up on Animaniacs, WWE and Green Day.Gerscovich agrees that retaining Sonic’s spiky and defiant persona has been vital. “At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity, which has always been bigger than any individual game or story,” he says. “Sonic has always represented freedom and an unmistakable attitude in the face of adversity that resonates across generations and that core DNA has remained consistent even as we’ve evolved the franchise.”In the late 90s, Iizuka took creative lead on what may be the most important title in the modernisation of the Sonic brand: the brilliant, flawed and ambitious Dreamcast open-world platformer Sonic Adventure. “Immediately following the completion of Nights into Dreams, ‘Sonic RPG’ began taking shape in my mind,” he recalls. “The concept was envisioned as a 3D action RPG in which players would traverse the world on foot, uncovering items and hidden passages along the way. While that vision ultimately never materialised, it laid the groundwork for what would become Sonic Adventure. While the transition to 3D was necessary, the biggest challenge was creating a system that would allow players to comfortably run around within a 3D space, as they did in the original Sonic games. I don’t think Sonic would have gone on to achieve the success it did if we hadn’t been able to bring Sonic’s 3D game to life back then.”His favourite part of the experience? Introducing the game’s dark antagonist Shadow the Hedgehog. “I love seeing fans connect to Shadow and his more emotional backstory,” he says. “He is essentially the opposite of Sonic.”View image in fullscreenLegacy juggling … Sonic Mania.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOver the past 20 years, Sonic developers have juggled the need to respect the legacy of the original games with exploring new trends and technologies – to varied effect. Iizuka loves Sonic Colors, Sonic Mania and Sonic Forces; Gerscovich namechecks Sonic Frontiers (“it introduced an open-zone gameplay experience that demonstrated Sonic’s ability to evolve and meet modern gamers where they are”). What I’ve loved is the sometimes experimental approach that Sega has taken, which harks back to the company’s defiant underdog status: Sonic Mania was created by a small team of independent developers, with wonderful results, while The Murder of Sonic the Hedgehog was a visual novel inspired by Agatha Christie and released in 2023 as an April Fools’ Day joke. I can’t really see Nintendo temporarily killing off Mario for a bit of a laugh.Sonic, I think, is the ultimate gamers’ mascot – at least he was for my generation. When I worked in games magazines in the 90s, he was such a natural cover star, with his bright colours and wry smile, throwing a thumbs up at the camera. He inspired the edgy feel of the dedicated Sega mags at the time – Sega Power, Mean Machines Sega, Sega Pro, and the design of the games – how twisty, demanding and uncompromising they were – provided clearer inspiration to modern indie developers than Super Mario, especially in the “masocore” genre of platformers.But I would say that, because I grew up with Sonic, I rooted for the games through fair and foul weather. Iizuka knows what I mean – I’ll leave the last words to him. “I’ve spent so much time with Sonic, and it has been incredible to see the franchise grow and expand,” he says. “Seeing Shadow arrive in movie theatres in Sonic the Hedgehog 3 was a full circle moment – I have such fond memories of working on Sonic Adventure 2 and Shadow’s introduction. I have been very lucky to continue working and creating for the franchise. I’m looking forward to the next 35 years!”Explore more on these topicsGamesSonic the HedgehogPlatform gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was abused as a child – and thought I had healed. Then I began drinking in lockdown | Rape and sexual assault | The Guardian
description: Decades after being sexually abused, the author and doctor Frank Spinelli believed he had moved on emotionally. But alcohol destroyed his sense of security. He describes how he confronted his shame
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Decades after being sexually abused, the author and doctor Frank Spinelli believed he had moved on emotionally. But alcohol destroyed his sense of security. He describes how he confronted his shame
Content: ‘All I saw was the end goal of bringing him to justice’ … Frank Spinelli.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘All I saw was the end goal of bringing him to justice’ … Frank Spinelli.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianRape and sexual assaultInterviewI was abused as a child – and thought I had healed. Then I began drinking in lockdownEmine SanerDecades after being sexually abused, the author and doctor Frank Spinelli believed he had moved on emotionally. But alcohol destroyed his sense of security. He describes how he confronted his shameTue 18 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot so long ago, Frank Spinelli seemed to have sorted out his life. He was happily married, working as a doctor and had a sideline writing medical thrillers. He thought he had dealt with the sexual abuse he had suffered as a child – not only had he helped bring the man who groomed and abused him to justice, but also he had written a memoir about it. “I felt that I had closure,” he says. “I had the good fortune of working with some amazing therapists and I believed I had done the work and moved past it and I was a healed person.”Little did he know that his recovery was fragile. The Covid pandemic took away his routine and structure: “All the external pillars that were tightly holding me together – the engagements at the office, the work trips.” Two years earlier, he and his husband had moved from Manhattan to a leafy suburb, from where he is speaking to me over a video call today. He was dealing with uncertainty and felt isolated. “We know one thing about shame: shame breeds in isolation.”Spinelli had never had a problem with alcohol before. In the lockdowns, though, he found himselfdrinking more and more. A glass of wine while cooking dinner turned into two; a bottle shared with his husband turned into another. Drinking was no longer something that mainly happened at the weekend, but had blurred into the week. Three months into lockdown, Spinelli’s husband realised it wasn’t doing him any good and decided to stop drinking, but Spinelli continued.“You make all these qualifying statements to yourself – you’re home, you’re not bothering anybody, I’m not driving,” he says. He convinced himself that if he drank in secret, it didn’t really count, so he started to take long dog walks, sipping from a water bottle filled with vodka; he hid empty bottles in the garage. When his husband confronted him about it, Spinelli promised to stop, but it lasted less than a week. He found better hiding spots: old bags in the wardrobe, empty cleaning-product bottles, the recycling bin.View image in fullscreenSpinelli and his dog at home in eastern New York.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianAt this time, a class-action lawsuit against the Boy Scouts of America was going through the courts. Spinelli was one of95,000 alleged survivors of sexual abusewithin the organisation. The man who had abused him from the age of 11, from 1978 to 1980, was his scoutmaster, William Fox. In September 2022,a $2.5bn (£2.2bn) compensation fund for victimswas established. In order to work out how much he would be entitled to, Spinelli was sent a 47-page questionnaire to fill out, in which he was asked to detail the abuse and its impact on him.He read this piece of brutal bureaucracy, relying on alcohol to get him through. It wasn’t the “dramatic rock bottom I’d expected from movies and recovery narratives”, he writes in his new book, The Shame Compass. “There was no car accident, no lost job, no intervention from concerned family members. I was alone in my home office, staring at a legal document that reduced my childhood sexual trauma to data points.” It felt like another violation, “documenting my own rape for a legal system that would assign it a dollar value”, he writes.The shame came flooding back – not just about the abuse, but also shame that he hadn’t got over it and shame that he was having to drink to cope with it. “You think you’re healed, you think you’ve moved on, and that is one of the myths,” he says. “The shame is still with you.”Spinelli on an expedition with the Boy Scouts of America.Photograph: Courtesy of Frank SpinelliSpinelli grew up in Staten Island, New York, the youngest of three children of Italian parents. “It was a very traditional background,” he says. His mother raised the children and sometimes worked in a supermarket; his father was a labourer. Neither had much education, but they expected big things of their children. “You really only get two choices: doctor or lawyer,” he says. Spinelli was already interested in science and wanted to become a doctor.He was a sensitive boy. “Joining the Boy Scouts was my parents’ way of perhaps toughening me up a little bit. Unfortunately, that’s where we were introduced to a man who would change all our lives,” he says. As a scout leader, Fox, who was also a police officer, was commanding and authoritative. Otherwise, “he was sort of jovial and there was a lot of camaraderie. And then the sexual abuse began.”In Spinelli’s previous book, his memoir Pee-Shy, “I wrote that the most insidious thing about child molestation is that it creates a desire in the child to want to please the molester, so I constantly was feeling: what am I doing wrong? How can I make him happy?” The psychological and physical bullying from other boys Fox had groomed was also extremely damaging. “There was this hierarchy that he established – if you got to ride in the front seat, you were one of Bill’s favourites that day. If not, you got to ride in the back. That is the type of psychological manipulation he employed as a tactic to keep you under his thumb.”A class photo of Spinelli, taken around the time of the abuse.Photograph: Courtesy of Frank SpinelliWhen Spinelli was 13, he told his parents about the abuse. “They went to the senior leaders and, in a sense, they were shamed into secrecy,” he says. “They were told: ‘You do not want this to get out – think of your son, think of your family,’ and I think they saw some truth in that. They agreed that Bill Fox could step down quietly, no charges pressed, and that would take care of matters. Now, unfortunately, we know many boys suffered after that fact.”Spinelli’s takeaway was: “This was how you handled matters – with secrecy.” He had begun to realise around this time that he was gay, another source of shame in his traditional Catholic community. He imagines his parents’ thought process: “A young boy who might be gay, or we’re not really sure, is involved in a sexual relationship with an adult man. While we know child molestation is not a consensual relationship, looking at it from the outside, they probably said: ‘Do we really want to shine a light on this? Think of the scrutiny.’” His parents also took advice from their priest, says Spinelli. “I think my parents thought they were protecting me. I was already being bullied at school; this would only add to it.”Spinelli struggled in his teenage years and dropped out of college. “This was not how I envisioned my life,” he says. “By accident, I came into contact with a therapist who happened to be an art therapist and she saved my life. I painted, she taught me to write, and I used that creative outlet to heal, to move beyond the trauma.” Other than his immediate family, she was the first person he told about the abuse. “I went into very specific details about what had happened and what made it so painful was to hear it out loud.” He was still blaming himself, thinking he was complicit. “But that’s what grooming is – making you believe that these actions are coming from you, when they’re being installed in your mind.”Spinelli says his parents were ‘shamed into secrecy’ when they alerted the Boy Scouts to the abuse perpetrated by Bill Fox(pictured).Photograph: Courtesy of Frank SpinelliSpinelli went back to college, then to medical school. He became a doctor, specialising in treating people living with HIV. The workload of being a doctor was a good distraction, although he was also being treated for anxiety and depression. “There was an undercurrent of unhappiness. Certainly, that was reflected in the relationships I had – perhaps dating people who weren’t always the nicest to me, or didn’t treat me as kindly as they should have.”In 2008, he published a book on men’s health. While he was promoting it, he got back in contact with two old friends from Staten Island. His childhood felt closer to him again. “That night, I had a dream about Bill Fox, me waiting by the screen door for his red truck to pull up.” Spinelli looked up Fox online – and what he found shocked him. “I discovered that the year after he stepped down [from the Boy Scouts], he talked a suicidal teenage boy off a ledge and adopted him.”Shortly afterwards, Fox was feted in TV appearances, won a “father of the year” award and published a book called The Cop and the Kid. He would go on to adopt about 15 boys – many, according to Spinelli, with special needs.Spinelli was astonished and appalled and knew he had to do something. “It was horrifying to me that we allowed this man to step down from the Boy Scouts of America and one year later he adopts a boy, but doesn’t stop there.” When Fox was finally arrested, in 2011, he still had some boys in his care, Spinelli says. “I found that story shocking, that this could have happened even after I came forward, and so I felt it was my obligation to finally see this to the end. What motivated me was a sense of blinding justice. All I saw was the end goal of bringing him to justice because that would be the only thing that would make sense.”View image in fullscreen‘I think my parents thought they were protecting me.’Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianSpinelli went to the police soon afterwards. Although his abuse was past the statute of limitations, he helped keep the pressure on the investigation, even wearing a wiretap in a phone call with Fox. Three young men, two of whom had been adopted by Fox as children, came forward. In August 2011, Fox pleaded no contest – by which he did not admit guilt, but accepted the conviction – and was sentenced to at least 35 years in prison. He died in prison not long afterwards.Spinelli’s memoir about the case was published in 2013. The act of writing everything down, along with securing Fox’s conviction, had felt like closure. And then came the pandemic and that questionnaire. “That’s when I thought: I really don’t have all of this managed. And that’s common: people who experience trauma will find that at different points in their lives it will re-emerge because something happens – life happens. It’s not as if you’re going to just be level for the rest of your life.” After completing the questionnaire, he woke up the next morning: “I looked myself in the mirror and I said: ‘This is not how the story ends.’”He turned his attention to the feelings of shame, which would become his Compass framework: confront, observe, map, process, accept and sustain, plus a final “S” for service, sharing your experience to help others. What if he could dismiss the inner voice that had told him he was “bad” all his life and instead see if shame was trying to tell him something important?“That inspired me to think about shame in a way that I hadn’t before. Shame is something we think is negative, but there’s also a way of looking at it where perhaps the shame is showing you that you are just out of alignment with your core values. My core values are kindness, compassion, loyalty.” His shame around drinking was reminding him not that he was a “broken” person, but that he had become someone who was lying to his husband and hurting him.In Spinelli’s framework, once he had confronted and observed his shame, he mapped the source of its inner voice – it was, unsurprisingly, his scout leader. Looking back over his life, he could see all the moments he was triggered by other authoritative men. “I had this wonderful professor, who was brilliant, but he would talk to me in a condescending tone and it would make me freeze,” he says. The voice reminded him of his scoutmaster. “But I’m not 11 years old. I’m an adult man. That’s how I utilise the framework to help get through those situations. It was important for me to go back to all those different times and to map out my reaction to that situation and what I could have done differently.”Learning to deal with his shame didn’t magically cure his alcohol dependency, but it helped, as did learning about the neuroscience of problem drinking: “It wasn’t necessarily a moral failing on my part. It was the fact that I had created these dopamine loops and the loop was encouraging me to drink more.”He is no longer ashamed of shame. “I feel those scars are battle wounds and I’m proud of them; they’ve developed who I am as a person. If we try to understand shame, we might be able to move through it, not run away from it.” Some days are still a struggle, but others are not. Daily practices, including journalling, help. “It goes back to being as honest as I can with my partner and my family. But understanding that, again, I’m not infallible – things are going to happen. I’m just more resilient.”The Shame Compass is published on 25 August (Level Tru, £13.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
