description: Two Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heat
Content: Max Rocha’s confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenMax Rocha’s confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodMax Rocha’s recipes for confit trout salad and grilled courgette with apricot, stracciatella and roasted almondsTwo Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heatMax RochaTue 18 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years after Café Cecilia opened, a handful of dishes have become permanent fixtures, returning to the menu time and again – and this confit trout salad is definitely one of them. During the recent heatwaves, we’ve naturally shifted towards dishes that are best served at room temperature or slightly warm, and both of these recipes reflect that approach. They’re designed to serve two, but can just as easily be scaled up for a larger group. And almost everything can be prepared in advance, making them ideal for entertaining at home.Confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook45 minServes2For the pickles1 tbsp sugar100ml white-wine vinegar1 tsp salt½ cucumber, finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)5 breakfast radishes,finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)For the trout2 trout fillets(about 150g each), skin onSalt and pepper300ml sunflower oil200ml olive oil3 sprigs thyme2 garlic cloves, peeledFor the salad6 tbsp good-quality olive oil2 tbsp dijon mustard2 tbsp white-wine vinegar1 bunch watercress(about 80g)Juice of ½ lemonExtra-virgin olive oil, to finish4 sprigs chervil, leaves picked4 sprigs dill, leaves pickedFirst, make the pickled cucumber by combining 100ml water with the sugar, vinegar and salt in a saucepan, then gradually increase the heat until the sugar dissolves. Pour this over the cucumber and radishes in a bowl, and set aside.Season the trout, then leave to sit at room temperature for 15 minutes.Meanwhile, place the sunflower oil, olive oil, thyme and garlic in a pan and heat to 50C (122F) (if you don’t have have a kitchen thermometer, the outside of the pan should feel warm to the touch). Pat the trout dry with kitchen paper, then lay the fish in the warm oil and keep it between 50-55C (120-130F) for 15-20 minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool a little, then peel off and discard the skin (this is easier to do while the fish is still warm) and leave to cool fully.Combine the olive oil, mustard and white-wine vinegar. Drain the pickles, then put in a bowl with the watercress and one and a half tablespoons of the vinaigrette (save the rest for other salads in the week). Mix and taste for seasoning, then add a squeeze of lemon juice, a few extra drops of olive oil and a pinch of sea salt and black pepper as required.Flake each trout fillet into four or five pieces, then divide half of the fish between two plates. Top with half the watercress and pickle salad, lay on the remaining trout, followed by the rest of the pickle mix. Top with the picked herbs, finish with a pinch of sea salt and serve.Grilled courgette, apricot, stracciatella and roast almondsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenMax Rocha’s grilled courgette, apricot, stracciatella and roast almonds.Prep10 minCook20 minServes21 green courgetteExtra-virgin olive oil1tsp balsamic vinegarZest of 1 lemon½ bunch basil, leaves picked1 garlic clove,peeled and thinly slicedSalt and black pepper2 ripe apricots200gstracciatellaFor the dressing45g whole roast almonds3tbsp olive oil1 tspred-wine vinegar1 tsp fresh rosemary leaves, choppedSlice the courgette lengthways into thin strips, brush with olive oil and grill in a hot griddle panfor about two minutes per side, until charred.Prepare the marinade by putting three tablespoons of olive oil, the balsamic vinegar, lemon zest, basil, garlic and some salt and pepper in a bowl. Fold in the courgettes until evenly coated.Pound the almonds in a mortar (or roughly chop them), then put in a bowl with the olive oil, vinegar, rosemary and some salt and pepper.Halve, stone and slice the apricots into thin half-moons. Spoon half the stracciatella on to each plate, followed by the courgettes. Finish with the apricots, dribble a tablespoon of the almond dressing over each portion and serve at once.Max Rocha is chef-owner ofCafé Cecilia, London E8Explore more on these topicsFoodFishSaladVegetablesMain courseFruitCheeserecipesShareReuse this content

title: The best vacuum cleaners in the UK for hard floors, carpet and pet hair – tested | Homes | The Guardian
description: From handheld to corded, self-emptying to stick models, these are our resident cleaner’s favourite vacuums for a spotless home
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: From handheld to corded, self-emptying to stick models, these are our resident cleaner’s favourite vacuums for a spotless home
Content: View image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHomesReviewThe best vacuum cleaners in the UK for hard floors, carpet and pet hair – testedFrom handheld to corded, self-emptying to stick models, these are our resident cleaner’s favourite vacuums for a spotless homeThe best cordless vacuum cleaners, testedHow to make your vacuum cleaner last longerAndy ShawTue 18 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBuying a vacuum cleaner isn’t as easy as you might think. With so many brands and models to choose from, it can be bewildering. Sticking with established brands isn’t necessarily a safe bet, with past performance being no guarantee that the latest models will be as good. Meanwhile, prices can be deceptive, with some affordable models now closing the gap on top-of-the-range brands when it comes to cleaning performance.You can’t know all this by browsing through a department store or online. The ideal thing to do would be to take a few models home to try them out – but good luck persuading anyone to let you do that. Thankfully, you won’t have to try because I’ve tested an array of models for you. I’ve measured each one’s ability to perform a range of real-world cleaning jobs, so you can discover the best vacuum cleaner for you.At a glanceBest corded vacuum cleaner overallSharkDetect XL Pet Pro LA791UKT£289 at AmazonBest cordless vacuum cleaner overallSharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKT£358 at AOBest budget corded vacuum cleanerHenryHome£199.99 at HenryBest cordless vacuum cleaner for pet hairVaxHomePro Pet-Design£139 at VeryWhy you should trust meThis isn’t the first time I’ve tested vacuum cleaners – over the past few years, I’ve reviewed them for various publications, which has given me a solid understanding of what makes a model good or bad. I’ve kept hold of a few of my favourite models for long-term testing, so I can easily make direct comparisons against those that are new on the block.My house is also perfectly set up for vacuuming challenges. It has a mix of carpet and hard floor, a ready supply of hair (pet from my own dog and a box of clippings I procured from a local groomer; human from the hairbrush and carpet surrounding the dressing tables of long-haired family members), and plenty of dusty flour and chunky cat litter for testing purposes.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach vacuum cleaner was tasked with clearing up flour, cat litter and pet hair.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianI tested 19 vacuums in total. Before I started any cleaning, I used a suction meter to test the suction power of every vacuum, usually by sealing it with tape over the closest suitable opening to the collection bin. I also tested the batteries of cordless vacuums, where I timed how long it took for the battery to run down on the most and least powerful settings.Then it was on to the nitty-gritty. I carefully weighed out quantities of flour, cat litter and pet hair, depositing them on carpet and hard floor to test each vacuum. I weighed each model’s collection bin before I started, then passed the vacuum over each type of mess using the standard floor head or most appropriate alternative. Each vacuum was passed over the spillage once, using a single forward and pull-back motion. Then, by weighing the collection bin again, I was able to establish how much of the dirt had been picked up.After the test, models were either returned to the appropriate manufacturers or – in the instance they didn’t want them back – donated to theBritish Heart Foundation.The best vacuum cleaners in 2026View image in fullscreenBunch of suckers: the vacuum cleaners we put to the test.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianBest corded vacuum cleaner overall:Shark Detect XL Pet Pro LA791UKTSharkDetect XL Pet Pro LA791UKTfrom£289£349.99 at SharkNinja£289 at AmazonWhat we lovePowerful, great performance, versatileWhat we don’t lovePricey if you won’t use all its featuresView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£349.99 at SharkNinja£289 at AmazonIf you want a vacuum that won’t run out of juice mid-clean, then the Shark LA791UKT is the best corded upright I’ve tested. It’s a modern-looking device with a sophisticated dual-roller floor head, a decent bin capacity of 2.5l, and no unnecessary features.Why we love itWhen it came to cleaning tests, this Shark literally cleaned up. Flour and pet hair disappeared into its collection bin, with no trace left behind. Admittedly, it didn’t pick up all the cat litter we put down on a single backward and forward pass, but unleashing the handle from the main unit lets you easily target larger chunks – and it finished the clean-up perfectly.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt comes with a useful selection of accessories for tackling upholstery and getting into nooks and crannies. Conveniently, you can lift the collection bin away from the floor head to help gain access to harder-to-reach areas, too.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive for a corded vacuum – the Henry Home is significantly cheaper.Type:corded uprightIncluded attachments:anti-hair wrap pet tool, combination duster, crevice toolWeight (measured):5.2kgSuction power (measured):17kPaNoise:80dBSize:31 x 43 x 116cm (WDH)Dust capacity:2.5lCord length:8mSharkDetect XL Pet Pro LA791UKTfrom£289£349.99 at SharkNinja£289 at AmazonWhat we lovePowerful, great performance, versatileWhat we don’t lovePricey if you won’t use all its featuresBest cordless vacuum cleaner overall:Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTSharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£358£358 at AO£399.99 at SharkNinjaWhat we loveExcellent performance and less manual emptyingWhat we don’t loveTakes up more storage space than a regular cordless stickView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£358 at AO£399.99 at SharkNinjaCordless vacuum cleaners are great for quick and efficient cleanups. However, they can be a pain to empty because of the dust cloud that billows out of bagless models and the relatively small size of their collection bins, which means more frequent emptying. The IP3251UKT takes some of this pain away by emptying itself into a larger, secondary collection bin on the stand.Why we love itThe IP3251UKT wins points for being exceptionally good at its job. During tests, its dual-roller floor head performed as well as that on the corded LA791UKT, reviewed above, but it fared better when picking up the larger cat litter particles, leaving nothing behind.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe self-emptying uses a bagless system that you just remove and tip into the bin, so there are no consumables to worry about. In addition, the base station also charges the device, so you can just slot the vacuum into its dock and forget about it. It isn’t as neat a solution as a wall mount, and it takes up more space, but the cleaner is always empty of dust and fully charged when you next need it.It’s a shame that …the capacity of the secondary collection bin in the base is only 2l, so it only takes three complete fills of the vacuum’s 0.7l bin before that needs emptying, too.Type:self-emptying cordless stickIncluded attachments:combination duster crevice tool, multi-surface tool, motorised hand toolWeight (measured):3.71kgSuction power (measured):28kPaNoise:86dBSize:26 x 47 x 118cm (WDH, including dock)Dust capacity:0.7l (vacuum), 2l (dock)Battery life (measured):43minsSharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£358£358 at AO£399.99 at SharkNinjaWhat we loveExcellent performance and less manual emptyingWhat we don’t loveTakes up more storage space than a regular cordless stickBest budget corded vacuum cleaner:Numatic Henry HomeHenryHome£199.99£199.99 at HenryWhat we loveMore cleaning attachments than the basic Henry modelWhat we don’t loveFloor heads don’t have all the features of sophisticated rivalsView image in fullscreen£199.99 at HenryThe Henry’s design has stood the test of time, finding favour with home users and professional cleaners since its introduction in the early 1980s. Not much has changed on the basic model, but I tested the Henry Home, exclusive to the Henry website, which comes with more floor accessories than are usually offered by other retailers.Why we love itAt the time of writing, the £199.99 Henry Home was only about £20 more than the standard Henry, available from the likes ofCurrysandArgos. That’s a good deal considering the extra equipment. For my carpet tests, I tried the AiroBrush, which is a brush roller that uses an internal air turbine to convert its own suction into the mechanical power needed to rotate the roller. It didn’t actually cope with pet hair or cat litter that well, becoming clogged by the former. Switching over to a simple funnel gathered the remainder. However, for vacuuming lighter everyday dirt on carpeted areas, the AiroBrush coped just fine.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe hard floor tool (basically a wide funnel with a stiff brush) did a cracking job on my hard floors, although I did find that it’s best held at an angle to ease the passage of larger particles and hair clumps.It’s a shame that …the AiroBrush doesn’t have an anti-tangle mechanism; hair quickly became wrapped around its roller.Type:corded barrelIncluded attachments:crevice tool, dusting tool, upholstery/mattress tool, AiroBrush, hard floor tool, multi-angle tool, flexi crevice toolWeight (measured):7.1kgSuction power (measured):18.5kPaNoise:72dBSize:32 x 34 x 35cm (WDH, cylinder unit only)Dust capacity:6lCord length:10mHenryHome£199.99£199.99 at HenryWhat we loveMore cleaning attachments than the basic Henry modelWhat we don’t loveFloor heads don’t have all the features of sophisticated rivalsBest cordless vacuum cleaner for pet hair:Vax HomePro Pet-DesignVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£139£139 at Very£139.99 at VaxWhat we loveGreat value for a feature-packed cordless stickWhat we don’t loveBetter on carpet than hard floorView image in fullscreen£139 at Very£139.99 at VaxCordless stick vacuums can be expensive, but they don’t have to be. The Vax HomePro Pet-Design isn’t the cheapest model out there, but it’s great value for money, combining decent cleaning skills with some handy features, including two attachments for pet hair.Why we love itAs you can see from my before-and-after picture below, the Vax did a brilliant job of collecting flour, cat litter and pet hair from carpet, and it was almost as good on hard floor, with only a few pieces of cat litter escaping its clutches – easy enough to gather on a subsequent pass.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt has two power settings, regular and boost, and lasted for 34 minutes in my battery rundown test on its standard setting. That makes it easy to operate, and I particularly like the way it can support itself when standing up, so you don’t have to find somewhere to prop it up when you need a break.It’s a shame that …it doesn’t come with a soft roller specifically for cleaning delicate hard floors.Type:cordless stickIncluded attachments:crevice tool, stair tool, pet hair remover, motorised pet toolWeight (measured):3.5kgSuction power (measured):19kPaNoise:86dBSize:22 x 25 x 116cm (WDH)Dust capacity:0.7lBattery life (measured):34minsVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£139£139 at Very£139.99 at VaxWhat we loveGreat value for a feature-packed cordless stickWhat we don’t loveBetter on carpet than hard floorThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Dirt leapt up the handheld funnel attachments’: the Numatic Henry Quick Pro.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro IA3241UKTSharkPowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro cordless vacuum IA3241UKTfrom£499.99£499.99 at SharkNinja£499.99 at CurrysWhy we love itAlways-ready self-emptying cordless vacuum for smaller homesWhy we don’t love itBattery power limits usefulness in larger housesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£499.99 at SharkNinja£499.99 at CurrysBest for:smaller homesThe Shark IA3241UKT is a slightly more compact and affordable version of the IP3251UKT, reviewed above. It still has the self-emptying base station but ditches Shark’s dual roller floor head, instead relying on a single brush bar with no soft roller. I was expecting worse performance on hard floors, but it did as well in my tests as its soft-rollered rivals.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhere it didn’t do so well was in battery life, failing to make it all the way around a thorough cleaning of a detached house without needing to be charged part way through. That makes it great for smaller houses and flats, but not so good for larger homes.It didn’t make the final cut because …the IP3251UKT lasted longer, so is better suited to homes of all sizes.Type:self-emptying cordless stick;included attachments:20cm duster-crevice tool, motorised pet tool;weight (measured):3.2kg;suction power (measured):24.5kPa;noise:75dB;size:26 x 37.5 x 114cm (WDH, including base station);dust capacity:0.47l (handheld), 2l (self-emptying base);battery life (measured):49mins 55secs (Eco mode with motorised floor head attached)Read our fullShark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro reviewSharkPowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro cordless vacuum IA3241UKTfrom£499.99£499.99 at SharkNinja£499.99 at CurrysWhy we love itAlways-ready self-emptying cordless vacuum for smaller homesWhy we don’t love itBattery power limits usefulness in larger housesMiele Guard L1 Comfort XLMieleGuard L1 Comfort XLfrom£419£419 at Miele£499 at John LewisWhat we loveA luxurious cylinder vacuum cleaner designed for ease of useWhat we don’t loveMore expensive than similar rivalsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£419 at Miele£499 at John LewisBest for:corded convenienceWhile the Henry Home offers an affordable corded cylinder experience, the Miele Guard L1 is a more luxurious rival. It’s crammed with features to make life easier, from the automatic cable retraction and accessory storage to the foot-controlled variable power settings. The model I tested came with two floor heads – a general-purpose one that relies on suction alone, but that can be switched between carpet and hard floor modes, and a second, larger floor head with a brush base that’s specifically for sweeping hard floor.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt performed very well in my tests, picking up at least 90% of every spillage in a single pass.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s expensive for a marginal performance improvement over the Henry Home.Type:corded barrel;included attachments:upholstery nozzle, crevice nozzle, dusting brush, parquet brush Twister XL;weight (measured):7kg;suction power (measured):21.5kPa;noise:60dB;size:50 x 29 x 24cm (WDH, cylinder unit only);dust capacity:3.5l;cable length:8.5mMieleGuard L1 Comfort XLfrom£419£419 at Miele£499 at John LewisWhat we loveA luxurious cylinder vacuum cleaner designed for ease of useWhat we don’t loveMore expensive than similar rivalsDyson Car+BoatDysonCar+Boatfrom£199.99£249.99 at Dyson£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveRelatively compact and excels at cleaning up small messesWhat we don’t lovePossibly not the best way to buy a Dyson V8View image in fullscreen£249.99 at Dyson£199.99 at AmazonBest for:handheld cleaningThe Dyson Car+Boat is essentially a reboxedDyson V8, although it drops the extension wand and two floor heads that come with the full model. That meant I couldn’t test it in quite the same way, since there’s no floor head to gather the mess. Instead, I got on my hands and knees and used the handheld attachments, which did a superb job of clearing up spillages.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …it’s worth checking prices on V8 models before you buy. At the time of writing, theV8 Absolute– with additional wand, two floor heads, a better upholstery tool and two more attachments – was available at Go Electrical for a similar price.Type:handheld;included attachments:crevice tool, combination tool, mini motorhead;weight (measured):1.9kg;suction power (measured):21kPa;noise:78dB;size:13 x 33 x 21cm (WDH);dust capacity:0.54l;battery life (measured):38minsDysonCar+Boatfrom£199.99£249.99 at Dyson£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveRelatively compact and excels at cleaning up small messesWhat we don’t lovePossibly not the best way to buy a Dyson V8Tower VL220 CycloneTowerVL220 Cyclonefrom£135.99£229.99 at Tower£135.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSelf-emptying base for lower price than the Shark rivalWhat we don’t loveNot as effective as Shark and replacement bags are expensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£229.99 at Tower£135.99 at AmazonBest for:budget self-emptyingThose looking for the self-emptying skills of the Shark IP3251UKT but with a more reasonable price should consider the Tower VL220 Cyclone. It’s a pared-back alternative in terms of features, but keeps the core concept of a base station with a secondary vacuum function that sucks the dirt out of the cordless stick’s collection bin and into a larger receptacle below. As with the Shark, the base station also serves as a charging dock, although this model uses bags to gather the dirt. That makes for a less messy emptying, but bags cost £9.99 each, only hold 2l at a time and need to be ordered through Tower’s customer service because they aren’t available on the website.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …it only comes with a fluffy roller floor head, so it isn’t great on carpet, plus the replacement bags are too expensive and a faff to buy.Type:self-emptying cordless stick;included attachments:2-in-1 crevice brush and nozzle tool;weight (measured):2.6kg;suction power (measured):28kPa;noise:73dB;size:35 x 24 x 131cm (WDH);dust capacity:2l (self-emptying base);battery life (measured):43minsTowerVL220 Cyclonefrom£135.99£229.99 at Tower£135.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSelf-emptying base for lower price than the Shark rivalWhat we don’t loveNot as effective as Shark and replacement bags are expensiveNumatic Henry Quick ProNumaticHenry Quick Profrom£399£399 at Currys£399.99 at ArgosWhat we loveClean and convenient emptyingWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags have plastic lidsView image in fullscreen£399 at Currys£399.99 at ArgosBest for:dust-free emptyingIn most of my cleaning tests, the Henry Quick Pro performed well. Its floor head isn’t the best at collecting cat litter from a hard floor, pushing it ahead instead of sucking it up, but it leapt up the handheld funnel attachments when I used those instead.ThisHenry uses bagsto collect the dirt, which eject neatly into the bin when they’re full. They also act as the filter, so there’s less general maintenance required, since they’re regularly replaced rather than needing cleaning.View image in fullscreenComposite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …thedisposable bagshave a plastic component to them, which isn’t ideal considering they’ll end up in landfill. Replacements cost about £1.30 each.Type:cordless stick;included attachments:crevice tool, 2-in-1 combi tool, mini motorised tool, flexi crevice tool, soft dusting brush, flexi hose;weight (measured):3.2kg;suction power (measured):10.75kPa;noise:68dB;size:24 x 27 x 122cm (WDH);dust capacity:1l;battery life (measured):1hr 11minsNumaticHenry Quick Profrom£399£399 at Currys£399.99 at ArgosWhat we loveClean and convenient emptyingWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags have plastic lidsWhat you need to knowCorded vs cordless vacuum cleanersThe first question you’ll need to ask yourself when buying a vacuum cleaner is whether you want a corded or a cordless model. Cordless sticks are the fashionable choice, with improvements in battery power and cleaning ability over the past decade bringing them in line with the performance of corded models.However, there are a few things to consider. While the batteries should last for about 40 minutes or more on their most economical setting, you won’t get anything like that if you need to run them at full power. If you have a larger home or persistent dirt problems (such as a pet that sheds a lot of hair), then a cordless might run out of power before you’ve finished cleaning. In these situations, a corded model makes more sense. As a side benefit, corded cleaners tend to have a larger capacity, so don’t need emptying as often.The downsides of a corded vacuum mostly concern the inconvenience of the cord. For example, you’ll need to keep switching plug sockets as you move around the house, as even the longest cables only reach around 10m. The cord will inevitably also get in the way as you clean. I tend to work with the cord slung over my shoulder as I vacuum, working away from the plug socket the machine is connected to, but this is all additional fuss that you don’t get from a cordless model.What should you look for in a vacuum cleaner?Whichever type of cleaner you choose, make sure that it has the right attachments. All vacuum cleaners should come with a floor head unless they’re specifically configured as handhelds, although the type you’ll need depends on whether you have mostly carpet or hard floor. Floor heads with brush rollers tend to work well at teasing dirt out of carpet, while fluffy rollers are excellent on hard floor. Suction-only floor heads can work well, but might not tease as much dirt out of thicker-pile carpets.If your floor seems to attract hair, then look for anti-tangle devices. When these work well they can dramatically reduce the amount of hair that becomes tangled around a floor head’s roller, which in my opinion is one of the least pleasant vacuum maintenance jobs that you’ll need to perform.Other attachments worth looking out for are the handheld options. I like to have a crevice tool, a soft dusting brush and an upholstery tool, with the latter preferably being motorised. Any further additions are a bonus.When it comes to emptying, bagless vacuums can get messy. If you’re looking for features such as Hepa filters to rid allergy-inducing particles, it’s also worth checking how they empty, as dust can just escape again unless you empty them outside. Vacuums with bags make emptying cleaner, but there’s an ongoing cost to replace them and it’s more rubbish headed for landfill.For more:The best cordless vacuum cleaners for a spotless homeThe best robot vacuums to keep your home clean and dust freeThe best steam cleaners and mops, testedHow to make your vacuum cleaner last longerShark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro reviewAndy Shaw is aconsumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return themThis article was originally published on 13 February 2026. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. title: Cool as a cucumber: recipes and tips to save you from cooking in a heatwave | Chefs | The Guardian
description: When ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook experts
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: When ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook experts
Content: Take heat out of the equation withThomasina Miers’ tomato toasts with smoky sesame harissa salsa.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Rachel Vere. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenTake heat out of the equation withThomasina Miers’ tomato toasts with smoky sesame harissa salsa.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Rachel Vere. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Kitchen aideChefsCool as a cucumber: recipes and tips to save you from cooking in a heatwaveWhen ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook expertsAnna BerrillTue 18 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s too hot to turn on the oven or stove. What can I make for dinner that’s still substantial?Mark, via emailThis sounds like a job for Lucy Carr-Ellison, ofTart London, who is fully functioning in a no-oven household. “We moved in last year and there’s an Aga, which was amazing in winter, but we can’t have it on in summer,” she says, so toast toppers have become a crucial category of cooking: “Try rubbing toasts with garlic, adding a bit of olive oil, some grated tomatoes, lots of salt and tinned anchovies.”Otherwise, Mark could do away with the toaster and get some focaccia, suggests Jamie Pickles, chef/co-owner ofStowandThe Trof, both in Manchester: “Mix picked brown crab meat with mayo, lemon juice and mustard, and spread that over the bread.” Next, combine the picked white meat with chopped chives and coriander, lemon juice, creme fraiche and black pepper. “Mix through some tinned sweetcorn, spread that over the brown crab mayo and finish with watercress.”No oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipesRead moreA kettle won’t add heat to your home, either. “I makea lotof rice noodle bowls,” says Alexandra Dudley, author ofCooking Made Simple, who keeps them in the fridge as the temperatures rise. “Soak the noodles in hot water while you make a dressing of peanut butter, miso, tahini, sesame oil, garlic and lime juice or rice-wine vinegar, then mix the two with cooked prawns from the supermarket and some smashed cucumbers.” Cool and crunchy cukes are also a go-to round at Pickles’, where they’re marinated for a “big punch of flavour” and served with salmon and rice: “Roughly chop a cucumber, throw it in a tub and add soy sauce, lemon juice, sesame oil, fish sauce and chilli crisp,” he says. “Put on the lid, seal, shake and put in the fridge to do its thing.” Some smoked salmon would be just the ticket alongside: pile it into bowls with cooked rice (“jasmine, ideally”), then finish with sesame seeds, chopped coriander, a touch of lime, plus the cucumbers, of course.When it’s all too hot to handle, it’s worth widening the parameters of pesto. “Switch out pine nuts for more affordable walnuts, and the same goes for the cheese,” says Pickles, who uses any firm cheese that takes his fancy. Blend the two with fresh herbs (“basil or flat-leaf parsley”), olive oil, a bit of garlic and lemon juice, plus ice to emulsify. Then get some courgettes: “Slice into strips using a peeler, dress with the pesto, then leave the courgettes to soak up all of that flavour.” Finish with torn mozzarella, freshly ground black pepper and pickled raisins – “they’ll bring a pop of life”.If all else fails, the assembly dinner is a classic move. “Learn to love your deli section,” campaigns Dudley, who more often than not has jars of artichokes, capers, olives and peppers to hand, ready to chop and chuck into a bowl with cooked lentils (“tinned or from a pouch”). Crumble over feta and there’s nothing better on a summer’s night. Or any night, really.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Student bank accounts: don’t be swayed by the freebies, freshers told | Student finance | The Guardian
description: Sign-up perks may capture the attention but should the focus be on the interest-free overdraft?
Author: Joe Pinner
Headline: Sign-up perks may capture the attention but should the focus be on the interest-free overdraft?
Content: Student bank accounts work like other current accounts but have an interest-free overdraft and sign-up offers designed to hook you as a customer for life.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudent bank accounts work like other current accounts but have an interest-free overdraft and sign-up offers designed to hook you as a customer for life.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesStudent financeStudent bank accounts: don’t be swayed by the freebies, freshers toldSign-up perks may capture the attention but should the focus be on the interest-free overdraft?The best student deals and discountsAn insider’s tips on student moneyJoe PinnerTue 18 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the scramble to sort out university accommodation, join freshers group chats and work out how a student loan payment is meant to stretch across a whole term, there is one big decision that is easy to put off but worth getting right: which student bank account to open.Student accounts work like any other current account but come with two extras that don’t apply to the general public: an interest-free overdraft, and a lot of perks designed to hook you in as a customer for life.However, while it is tempting to choose an account on the strength of the free cash, vouchers or other goodies, personal finance experts advise you not to be swayed by the extras.“An interest-free overdraft could provide greater value over the course of a degree than a one-off freebie,” says Caitlyn Eastell at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk.The ranking of the best student bank accounts for 2026-27 by the website Save the Student also places an emphasis on the size of the interest-free overdraft. “Maintenance loans now fall short of living costs by an average of £502 per month,” says Tom Allingham, the site’s student banking expert.Its top picks for this year are the NatWest/Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) student account, Nationwide FlexStudent and the Santander Edge student account.To help you make your own mind up, here’s what’s on offer.Santander Edge student current accountFreebies:a free four-year 16-25 Railcard, which is good for a third off most rail fares in Great Britain, as well as discounts on the tube when linked to an Oyster card. For students who travel home regularly, it is one of the more valuable perks on the market, potentially saving hundreds of pounds a year.Interest-free overdraft:£1,500 in years one to three, but up to £2,000 in year five (if relevant).View image in fullscreenThe Santander Edge account offers a free four-year 16-25 Railcard.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesAnything else?A prize draw: everyone who opens an account between 14 July and 16 October and makes a debit card purchase by the end of December is guaranteed at least £20, with one lucky student walking away with £100,000. Further prizes of £10,000, £1,000 and £100 are also on offer.NatWest/RBS student accountFreebies:£100 cash, plus a four-year Tastecard subscription, which gets you money off at thousands of restaurants and cafes across the UK. NatWest says the Tastecard is worth £79.99 a year, although at the time of writing it was on sale for £39.99.Interest-free overdraft:up to £2,000 from the second term of the first year (up to £500 available from day one), rising to up to £3,250 from year three onwards – one of the largest on the market.Anything else?RBS is running an identical offer to NatWest for students in Scotland.Nationwide FlexStudentFreebies:£100 cash plus £120 in Just Eat vouchers, paid as £10 a month for a year. To unlock the offer, students need to pay in £500 and make five debit card payments by 11 December.Interest-free overdraft:up to £1,000 in year one, up to £2,000 in year two and up to £3,000 in year three. (Your limit stays at £3,000 if your course is longer.)Anything else?You could get a “Fairer Share” payment: each year since 2023, Nationwide has paid £100 to eligible members with a qualifying current account and savings or mortgage. Also, there are no fees for using the debit card abroad.Lloyds/Bank of Scotland student accountFreebies:£100 to anyone who opens (or switches to) the account and pays in at least £500 by 30 October, plus up to £120 in Deliveroo vouchers – paid as £20 a month for six months to those making 20 or more debit card payments each month between November and April.View image in fullscreenLloyds and Bank of Scotland offer Deliveroo vouchers with the student account.Photograph: Frank Augstein/APInterest-free overdraft:up to £1,500 in years one to three, rising  to £2,000 for those studying on courses of four years or more.Anything else?Both let you earn up to 15% cashback on everyday spending with selected retailers. Lloyds is also offering a prize draw in which five students will each win £9,790 – equivalent of a year’s maximum tuition fees in England.HSBC Student bank accountFreebies:none at the time of writing.Interest-free overdraft:up to £1,000 from day one, then up to £2,000 in year two, and up to £3,000 in year three.Anything else?Access to HSBC’s 5% regular saver account, and to discounts via its home&Away offers programme.Barclays Student Additions accountFreebies:none at the time of writing.Interest-free overdraft:up to £500 from day one, rising to £1,000 in year one, and then up to £1,500 in year two and beyond.Anything else?Not much to shout about this year.TSB student bank accountFreebies:none at the time of writing, but the account pays a generous 5% (variable) interest on balances up to £500 – worth up to £25 a year.Interest-free overdraft:up to £500 during the first six months, then up to £1,000 from months seven to nine, then up to £1,500 from month 10 onwards.Anything else?Nothing of note.Whichever account you choose, remember that the overdraft is not free money forever: once you graduate, most accounts convert into a graduate account that gradually withdraws the interest-free borrowing over a year or two, after which unpaid balances start accruing interest like any other loan.Explore more on these topicsStudent financeBankingStudentsCurrent accountsHigher educationBanks and building societiesBorrowing & debtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Low carb’, ‘gluten-free’, with collagen or electrolytes: is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy? | Melissa Davey | The Guardian
description: Premixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers say
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Premixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers say
Content: Alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is actually no safe ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is actually no safe ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralHealth‘Low carb’, ‘gluten-free’, with collagen or electrolytes: is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy?Melissa DaveyPremixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers sayTue 18 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTSharePremixed alcoholic drinks are not known for their health benefits. But that hasn’t stopped a boom in products being marketed with “better for you” claims designed to appeal to younger, more health-conscious drinkers.Labels such as “low sugar”, “gluten-free” and “low carb” are being used in advertising to promote the products, and social media influencersspruik the productsunder the hashtag #healthydrinking.But what do these labels actually mean, and is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy?What is ‘low sugar’ or ‘low calorie’ alcohol?Food policy expert Prof Simone Pettigrew at the George Institute for GlobalHealthrecently ran a research focus group asking participants for their thoughts on a premixed alcoholic drink labelled as “low sugar” and “low carb”.She said that “as soon as you put low sugar, low carb, gluten free, any of these on a product, people assume it’s a relatively healthy product overall”.A recentpaper led by Pettigrewsaw researchers audit 534 ready-to-drink alcoholic products and found one in five did not display a mandatory ingredients list.On top of this, of the 424 products that did list ingredients, almost half contained industrial additives associated with ultra-processing, such as synthetic colours, sweeteners and flavour enhancers, placing them in the same category as chips and soft drinks.Rise in adulterated sexual enhancement supplements could mean users are getting stiffed | AntiviralRead moreDespite being ultra-processed, nearly half of those products carried what the researchers described as a “better for you” labels such as low/no sugar, low calorie, gluten free, low/no carb and other claims.Deputy chair of the Cancer Council’s nutrition, alcohol and physical activity committee, Julia Stafford, said marketing claims should not guide consumer behaviour, and that people should always read the full nutrition label, including ingredients.“The ingredient of most concern in an alcohol product is the alcohol,” she said. “It has nothing to do with the carb or sugar content.”Pettigrew agrees: “People just focus on that tiny little nutrient or ingredient,” she said.“But it’s not just the claim on the label that makes people assume that the whole product is healthy. We now see the sides of trams and massive billboards in train stations screaming low sugar, low calorie claims on alcohol ads. These ads are absolutely enormous. It’s not subtle messaging.”No ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumptionStafford said alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen – the highest risk category alongside tobacco and asbestos. It means there is actually no “healthy” level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Labels such as “low carb”, “natural” and “gluten-free” create a “health halo” around the product and remove the focus away from harmful ingredients, she said.Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (Fare) policy and research director, Dr Aimee Brownbill, said alcohol brands know that people are increasingly health conscious and interested in wellness. AFare surveypublished in 2025 found 44% of Australians want to stop or reduce drinking, with most citing health-related reasons.It means brandsneed to find waysto counteract alcohol being viewed as an unhealthy, harmful ingredient, she said, by using terms like “clean”, “natural” and “low sugar” to shift the focus.And it works, Brownbill said,citing researchfrom more than 2,000 Australian adults which found almost half of the participants indicated they were more likely to buy products that were marketed with such health claims.Younger people and those identifying as female had particularly positive attitudes towards the claims, especially around lower sugar and calories, the study found.Natural terminology ‘creeping in’ to advertisingPettigrew said alcohol brands are also promoting their products as containing collagen and electrolytes. “This natural kind of terminology and these healthy-sounding ingredients are creeping in to [alcohol] labels,” she said.“Consumers are very clear in saying they don’t want ultra-processed food … They probably don’t realise that ultra-processing is part of producing the alcohol they drink as well, particularly in this really youth-focused product category of premixed drinks.”She said people need to read the entire nutritional label to make decisions about food and beverage consumption, and to be aware healthy-sounding ingredients can’t counteract the impact of alcohol.“We do know that consumers are interested in the amount of sugar in products, but there are other ways of delivering that information without huge claims splattered across the front of the can that makes them assume that the whole product is healthy.”Melissa Davey is Guardian Australia’s medical editorAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or title: Transylvania beyond the spooky castles: a family adventure in Romania’s mountains | Romania holidays | The Guardian
description: Forget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitude
Author: Graeme Green
Headline: Forget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitude
Content: High in the mountains of Harghita County, Romania. All photographs: Graeme GreenView image in fullscreenHigh in the mountains of Harghita County, Romania. All photographs: Graeme GreenRomania holidaysTransylvania beyond the spooky castles: a family adventure in Romania’s mountainsForget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitudeGraeme GreenTue 18 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the sun disappears behind the high tree line, our campfire spits and crackles. Four plump trout are sizzling on a flame-heated slab of rock, a cooking technique used by people in the Gurghiu mountains, part of Transylvania’s Eastern Carpathians, for centuries. Apart from gentle birdsong, it’s the only sound up here, 1,550 metres above sea level and far from any town or village.“This area is very wild,” says Samir Teslovan, who drove us up through the densely forested peaks from his guesthouse in Toplița. “When I come here to the mountains, I charge my battery, charge my soul. I feel free, like the wind.”Romania mapSitting on the edge of a fragrant forest of spruce, fir, beech and pine, our view stretches over the valley to misty mountains receding in layers to the horizon. Samir points to a far-off peak in the east, a pyramid on a ragged ridge. “That’s Ukraine, maybe 200km,” he tells us. Then, pointing west: “That way, 400km, is Hungary.” The forest is still home to bears, wolves and lynx, but it’s the solitude that brings him here. “I prefer wild zones, where no one goes,” he says. “There are places here that nobody knows.”Across the vast forests and mountains of Harghita County in central Romania, there are many places that nobody knows. In fact, the whole region has flown under the radar of international travellers – 85% of visitors come from Romania itself, which feels bizarre when you discover the wonders here, as we did on a 12-day family road trip, staying at self-catering lodges and cabins along the way.double quotation markA holiday here costs a fraction of what it would in the Dolomites or the AlpsA holiday here costs a fraction of what it would in the Dolomites or the French or Swiss Alps. Even better, it’s remarkably uncrowded, which makes for a more authentic-feeling adventure.The region previously belonged to the Austro-Hungarian empire, butTransylvania, including Harghita,was awarded to Romania after the first world war.The local population remains largelyof Hungarian descent(about 85%), with most people identifying as Székelys (Szeklers), a distinct, Hungarian-speaking cultural group. And the Hungarian influence can be seen in the region’s food, from goulash tokürtőskalács(chimney cakes), and in the ornately carvedszékelykapu(wooden gates) outside houses.View image in fullscreenHarghita has one of the highest densities of bears in EuropeWe pick up a hire car in Brașov and drive north, in the opposite direction to Bran Castle and all the vampiric hoopla. Soon, we’re enjoying wide, open countryside, sharing the road with farmers on horse-drawn carts and passing churches with silvery spires and white storks nesting on top of electricity poles.Our first base is Sâncrăieni, staying inOrganicle Lodge,a lovely, quiet cabin with an upstairs spruce bedroom, spacious lounge and kitchen.While our four-year-old son races around the garden with the owners’ cats and French bulldog, we rest on our wooden deck, drinking Harghita beer, looking over a paddock, where a brown horse and white pony gambol and graze, and out towards the Harghita mountains. In the evenings, swifts flit about and white storks glide across pink skies.double quotation markWe spot a mother and cub ambling through the forest and sniffing the air by the roadside‘A muddy ride into Romania’s dreamy countryside’: cycling the Via TransilvanicaRead moreWe spend time at nearby Lacul Sfânta Ana (Saint Anne Lake), the only volcanic lake in Romania, wandering first throughMohoş Peat Bog, where the trees and curious plant life make it feel like stepping back into the ice age, then take a boat trip on the sparkling lake, surrounded on all sides by shades of forest green. In the evening, we head toMedveles Székelyföld observatory, where we watch four bears feeding on corn that’s laid out for them; Harghita hasone of the highest bear population densities in Europe. The best sighting of our trip, though, comes during our drive to the lake, when we spot a mother and cub ambling through the forest and sniffing the air by the roadside.Heading farther north, we spend a couple of days atVila Adela, near Lacu Roșu (Red Lake), an orange house decorated with red geraniums, with fairy houses, windmills, animal statues, see-saw and slide in the garden. Our bedroom looks out on to the majestic limestone massif Suhardul Mic.Later, we drive through Bicaz Gorge, gazing up at massive rock walls and structures, dominated byPiatra Altarului (Altar Rock), the summit marked with a metal cross. Stopping to climb the tower of medieval manor houseLázár Castleen route, we reach Toplița at the far north of the county, staying atCasa Samir, where Samir and his son David run wildlife photography and nature tours.View image in fullscreenReflected glory … lakeside in HarghitaAfter a steep and bumpy afternoon drive, we go hiking in the serene Gurghiu mountains. Golden sunlight winks through the trees as David points out the tracks of wild animals as we walk to where his father has parked and started a campfire. Along with trout, Samir serves a homemade salty sheep’s cheese, calledburduf, and lamb sausage, both from his farm, and a bottle ofpalinka, a warming plum brandy. “I’ve been coming here all my life,” he tells us. “My grandfather and great-grandfather came here. I listen to the silence and the sounds of the forest, the birds and wild animals.”Looping back around through the county, we make one final stop atTurul Guesthouse, a row of neat, two-storey, wooden lodges with hot tubs and a big trampoline. We wander among detailed models of Transylvanian castles, palaces, and churches, including Bran Castle, atMini Transylvania Parkand large-scale, moving models of ants, butterflies and the like at neighbouringInsect Park.One morning, we hike up to the top of Harghita Mădăraș, at 1,801m (5,909ft) the highest peak in the Harghita mountains. Thunder rumbles and rain drenches us, as we reach the gold, white and blue Székely flag, the reportedly magnificent views blocked out by cloud that gives a sombre, funereal atmosphere to the cairns, flags, crosses and other memorials clustered around the summit.We watch more bears at a tucked-awayforest hideoutside the Băile Homorod resort, including two mighty females who look as if they might clash over the feeding area, and spend one of our last afternoons at Zetea lake, where we take out a kayak. “It’s really a beautiful experience to be on the water,” Előd Tímár, co-owner of KayaKing, tells us. “Bears sometimes come to drink on the shore.”Paddling south towards a forested peninsula,we’re surrounded on all sides by swaying trees.We pause in the vast expanse of open water and put down the paddles to float and drift for a while, and there it is again: a glorious, battery-charging feeling of peace, nature and being free, like the wind.The trip was provided byVisit Harghita. Graeme stayed atOrganicle Lodge(from £75 a night),Vila Adela(£50),Casa Samir(£43B&B)which offers mountain adventures from £94 per person, andTurul Guesthouse(£87).Bear-watching atMedveles Székelyföld£35pp and atBăile Homorod£25pp.KayakingwithKayaKingfrom £6.50 per hourExplore more on these topicsRomania holidaysWildlife holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: should you always quarantine new plants to avoid pests spreading? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: Any new addition to your collection can contain stowaways, so you’d be wise to deploy a little patience – but how long is long enough?
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Any new addition to your collection can contain stowaways, so you’d be wise to deploy a little patience – but how long is long enough?
Content: Treat any pests while the plant is isolated.Photograph: Issarawat Tattong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTreat any pests while the plant is isolated.Photograph: Issarawat Tattong/Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: should you always quarantine new plants to avoid pests spreading?Any new addition to your collection can contain stowaways, so you’d be wise to deploy a little patience – but how long is long enough?Gynelle LeonTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 05.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemThere is nothing quite like the joy of bringing home a new plant. You find the perfect spot, nestle it in among your others, and stand back to admire the new arrival. What you cannot see are its passengers: a few spider mites tucked under a leaf, mealybug eggs in a joint, or fungus gnat larvae in the compost. A fortnight later, plants that were perfectly healthy are speckled, sticky or swarming, and you have no idea how it happened.The hackQuarantining means keeping any new plant separated from the rest of your collection for a few weeks before letting it join the others. The logic is simple: if something is going to emerge, you want it to do so in isolation, where it can be dealt with before it spreads to the whole crew.The methodPlace your new plant in a different room from the rest of your collection for two or three weeks. Every few days, check for webbing, sticky residue, tiny moving specks, or gnats rising from the compost. Treat any pests while the plant is isolated, and only move it in with the others once you are confident it is clean.Houseplant hacks: do plant care kits actually work?Read moreThe testI have been quarantining new plants for several years now, and it works. New arrivals have come in with the odd stowaway, but because they were isolated, whatever they brought stayed contained to that one pot rather than becoming everyone’s problem.TheverdictNearly every serious infestation I have seen, my own included, traces back to a new plant being introduced straight into your home collection. Quarantining is not a sign of paranoia; it’s the best way to protect your plants, and it costs nothing but a little patience.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Creators of chase compilations reject any moral qualms and say they show ‘death is waiting’ for those who join war
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Creators of chase compilations reject any moral qualms and say they show ‘death is waiting’ for those who join war
Content: A Ukrainian military editor known by his call sign Catman edits footage taken by a Ukrainian kamikaze drone.Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Ukrainian military editor known by his call sign Catman edits footage taken by a Ukrainian kamikaze drone.Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The GuardianUkraine‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last momentsCreators of chase compilations reject any moral qualms and say they show ‘death is waiting’ for those who join warLuke Hardingin KyivTue 18 Aug 2026 07.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo many observers they will appear dehumanising and offensive. To many Ukrainians, however, they are a brutal reminder of the fate that awaits Russian soldiers who take part in Vladimir Putin’s invasion, as well as a potent propaganda weapon.Over the past year and a half, videos of kamikaze drones chasing Russian service personnel to their deaths have become a distinctive genre on social media. They are the brainchild ofRobert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces and founder of“Magyar’s Birds”, named after his call sign.Brovdi’s 414th aviation strike brigade has pioneered the use of battlefield video, much of it recorded by first-person-view drones. The death videos are known asyoblyks, a portmanteau that combines the root of the Ukrainian for “fuck” with an affectionate diminutive form. The closest English translation is probably “fuckling”.An excerpt of footage from a drone following a Russian soldier into woodlandEarly each morning, a military editor known by his call sign Catman sifts through battlefield clips recorded the previous day, selecting some for a two-minute compilation and adding pulsing or mystical music. A longer online reel is titled “Yoblyks of the Week”.Defending his work, Catman said the videos played an important role in demoralising ordinary Russians and revealing the true cost of the Kremlin’s unprovoked war. “My goal is to show Russians that if they mobilise inUkrainethey will be killed, that it’s a one-way ticket and death is waiting for them,” he said.He acknowledged that the clips were deliberately arranged to mock the victims, who are sometimes seen throwing sticks at the drones to try to knock them off course, or falling over as they run. Though the moment of death is not shown, the last frame is a closeup of a soldier’s face.“We have a phrase: laughter kills fear. Our main task is to laugh at these enemies and to depict them as helpless. This boosts the morale of our forces,” he said. “It’s impossible for me to feel sorry for them. It’s war, after all, not a movie.”View image in fullscreenCatman sitting in front of his computer: ‘My goal is to show Russians that if they mobilise in Ukraine they will be killed.’Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The GuardianTypically, the Russian soldiers are killed while walking or travelling by motorbike to the frontline. Some are unaware they are at risk from drones, Catman said, and appear to have been tricked by their commanders. “Their training is short. A lot die just two weeks after enlisting,” he said.He described most of the soldiers as “banal donkey men” ordered to carry provisions or fuel to exposed Russian positions. Others drag communication cables. Since February, when Elon Musk shut down his satellite internet service Starlink in Russia, officers in the rear have struggled to contact frontline units.Another member of Magyar’s Birds said there was compelling evidence the Russians were routinely misled about dangers. “You can see from the videos a lot of them are not even hiding,” he said. “They use their radio sets. A large number are fooled by the lie that everything will be OK, that they are going to their positions and are totally safe.”The brigade has an archive of about 3,600 videos. Only two feature women, both wearing combat uniform and carrying assault rifles. “There is no difference for me. They are all enemies,” Catman said.The videos play an important part in verifying Russian losses, which are running at more than 30,000 soldiers a month killed or injured, according to Kyiv.An excerpt of footage from a drone following a Russian soldier into a houseBrovdi said he had no qualms about publishing material that many in the west might find distasteful and morally dubious. “God forbid they should ever experience pain. Because those of us in Ukraine who have experienced real physical pain from war would never agree with that perspective,” he said.In daily posts, Brovdi uses language that some might find gratuitous, for instance describing Russians as “worms” pecked by “birds”.He said: “When the war started, everything changed. There was a desire to humiliate the enemy as much as possible, not with typical words but exotic ones. It was only natural that military technical folklore and coinages such as ‘yoblyk’ found their way into my speech. They existed before AI.”View image in fullscreenRobert ‘Magyar’ Brovdi, the commander of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces.Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The GuardianThe videos have sparked several trolling subgenres. Some Russian women post photos of themselves saying farewell to their husbands as they leave to take part in what Putin calls a “special military operation”. Ukrainians identify the men and subsequently reply with drone footage showing their deaths.According to Catman, theyoblykshave a wide audience, including inside Russia. “There is very little information there about soldiers who go missing. Some people search and take screenshots. Mothers or wives then post messages saying something bad has happened to their loved ones,” he said.Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mountRead morePro-war Russian bloggers post images on Telegram channels of Ukrainian soldiers dying in battle. Other videos show thekilling of unarmed Ukrainian prisoners of war– a crime. The Russian internet includesAI-generated fakesthat purport to show Ukrainian military personnel criticising their army leadership.Anatolii Loza, a Ukrainian volunteer who was captured and imprisoned by Russia and recently swapped, said he saw nothing wrong withyoblyks. “International law doesn’t apply to killing combatants on the field of battle,” he said. “The Russians come to shoot our soldiers and civilians. They are wearing uniform. They deserve their fate.”Loza’s wife, Olena, said attitudes inside Ukraine hardened after spring 2022, when Russian forces killed hundreds of civilians in the cities of Bucha and Mariupol, leaving their bodies on the streets. Ofyoblyks, she said: “I don’t find these videos informative. I’m already furious with Russia.”At the HQ of Magyar’s Birds, Catman said black humour was essential during wartime. “It’s important for our own people to say we are not just surviving. We need to show we are flourishing and hitting back hard against the enemy.”Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, by Luke Harding, is published on 27 August by Guardian Faber.
