title: ‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchise | Games | The Guardian
description: Sonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Sonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’
Content: ‘At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity’ … a mural of Sonic the Hedgehog in Shoreditch, London.Photograph: SegaView image in fullscreen‘At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity’ … a mural of Sonic the Hedgehog in Shoreditch, London.Photograph: SegaGames‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseSonic’s creators explain how the speedy scamp has kept on running through generations as an enduring avatar of ‘attitude in the face of adversity’Keith StuartTue 18 Aug 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne day in the early 1990s, I came home from university for the weekend and discovered that my dad had bought himself a Sega Mega Drive, bundled with a copy ofSonic the Hedgehog2. I knew about Sega’s mascot of course. The launch of the original Sonic the Hedgehog game in 1991 was a landmark moment for the company, massively boosting the sales of its 16bit console in the west, ripping market share from the dominant Super Nintendo. While Mario was the family favourite, Sonic with his speed, attitude and brash visual energy encapsulated the edgy spirit of the early 1990s MTV culture. That weekend, Dad and I did little else but team up for daylong Sonic sessions, the game’s two-player mode letting us play cooperatively as we zoomed through those dense, beautiful play zones.Thirty-five years later, I am still a Sonic fan. There have been plenty of rough times (Sonic 06, Sonic and the Secret Rings, Sonic Free Riders – sorry, I can’t go on), but there have been plenty of good ones too. (Rush, Mania and Colors, and I have a soft spot for Sonic R, a racer developed by Traveller’s Tales, which went on to make the Lego games). Few people know this rollercoaster better than Takashi Iizuka, who worked on Sonic 3 as a designer and has been series producer for almost 20 years. When he joined Sega in 1992 he wanted to work for the company’s arcade division, but after playing the original Sonic – especially Sonic 2 – he was seduced.View image in fullscreenSpeed, attitude, and brash visual energy … Sonic the Hedgehog 2.Photograph: Sega“I do believe that Sonic the Hedgehog 2 is one of the best of the classic series, and the introduction of two-player gaming helped make it so special,” he says. “The team had been thinking about a two-player mode for Sonic the Hedgehog that we weren’t able to incorporate at the time, so achieving this in the sequel was vitally important. It was a challenge, because the development time for Sonic 2 was very tight; but Sega is always willing to try something new and take a risk, and it really paid off.”In 1993, Iizuka transferred to the Sega Technical Institute in California, the studio set up by industry veteran Mark Cerny (who would go on to design the PlayStation 4 and 5). Here he would begin the next phase of Sonic’s lifespan, working first on Sonic 3. “I knew almost nothing about countries outside Japan,” he says. “I still vividly remember being amazed by Sonic’s popularity when I arrived in the US. At the time, the TV animated series was airing, comic books were being published and the franchise was regularly covered in newspaper articles. It was in that moment that I truly grasped the reality that a game created in Japan had captured the hearts of players around the world.”Ivo Gerscovich, chief business and brand officer for Sonic the Hedgehog, sees this transmedia presence as vitally important. “What’s perhaps most telling of Sonic’s cultural staying power is what we’ve accomplished beyond gaming,” he says. “The Sonic the Hedgehog film franchise has been extraordinary, collectively grossing more than $1bn at the global box office and introducing Sonic to an entirely new generation of fans […] Partnerships like our ongoing collaboration with McLaren Racing speak to the breadth of audiences that Sonic can connect with.”I was too old to connect with the cartoons at the time, but when my sons were five and seven, they managed to find re-runs of the classic Sonic Underground cartoon on TV and were hooked – mostly by its crazed, over-dramatic pop punk theme tune. I took the opportunity to set up my dad’s Mega Drive so they could play Sonic 2 together. The fact that this happened 10 years after my dad’s death added a strange, sad poetry to the moment. It was my first real understanding of the fact that we pass our heroes down to our children, sometimes inadvertently, sometimes with forceful intention.View image in fullscreenFond memories … Sonic Adventure 2.Photograph: Sega/MobygamesIt’s difficult now to convey what an impact Sonic had on the industry in the 90s. The game’s idiosyncratic design, powered by Naoto Ohshima, Hirokazu Yasuhara and programming genius Yuji Naka, emphasised speed and impatience; Sonic was a semi-antagonistic presence who would fold his arms and tap his feet when the player wasn’t moving fast enough. It was Sonic 2sday on 24 November 1992, that perfected the concept of the global simultaneous video game launch – an idea repeated a year later with Mortal Monday for the console release of Mortal Kombat. Both Sonic and Mortal Kombat resonated with a teen audience brought up on Animaniacs, WWE and Green Day.Gerscovich agrees that retaining Sonic’s spiky and defiant persona has been vital. “At the heart of it is his strong personality-driven identity, which has always been bigger than any individual game or story,” he says. “Sonic has always represented freedom and an unmistakable attitude in the face of adversity that resonates across generations and that core DNA has remained consistent even as we’ve evolved the franchise.”In the late 90s, Iizuka took creative lead on what may be the most important title in the modernisation of the Sonic brand: the brilliant, flawed and ambitious Dreamcast open-world platformer Sonic Adventure. “Immediately following the completion of Nights into Dreams, ‘Sonic RPG’ began taking shape in my mind,” he recalls. “The concept was envisioned as a 3D action RPG in which players would traverse the world on foot, uncovering items and hidden passages along the way. While that vision ultimately never materialised, it laid the groundwork for what would become Sonic Adventure. While the transition to 3D was necessary, the biggest challenge was creating a system that would allow players to comfortably run around within a 3D space, as they did in the original Sonic games. I don’t think Sonic would have gone on to achieve the success it did if we hadn’t been able to bring Sonic’s 3D game to life back then.”His favourite part of the experience? Introducing the game’s dark antagonist Shadow the Hedgehog. “I love seeing fans connect to Shadow and his more emotional backstory,” he says. “He is essentially the opposite of Sonic.”View image in fullscreenLegacy juggling … Sonic Mania.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOver the past 20 years, Sonic developers have juggled the need to respect the legacy of the original games with exploring new trends and technologies – to varied effect. Iizuka loves Sonic Colors, Sonic Mania and Sonic Forces; Gerscovich namechecks Sonic Frontiers (“it introduced an open-zone gameplay experience that demonstrated Sonic’s ability to evolve and meet modern gamers where they are”). What I’ve loved is the sometimes experimental approach that Sega has taken, which harks back to the company’s defiant underdog status: Sonic Mania was created by a small team of independent developers, with wonderful results, while The Murder of Sonic the Hedgehog was a visual novel inspired by Agatha Christie and released in 2023 as an April Fools’ Day joke. I can’t really see Nintendo temporarily killing off Mario for a bit of a laugh.Sonic, I think, is the ultimate gamers’ mascot – at least he was for my generation. When I worked in games magazines in the 90s, he was such a natural cover star, with his bright colours and wry smile, throwing a thumbs up at the camera. He inspired the edgy feel of the dedicated Sega mags at the time – Sega Power, Mean Machines Sega, Sega Pro, and the design of the games – how twisty, demanding and uncompromising they were – provided clearer inspiration to modern indie developers than Super Mario, especially in the “masocore” genre of platformers.But I would say that, because I grew up with Sonic, I rooted for the games through fair and foul weather. Iizuka knows what I mean – I’ll leave the last words to him. “I’ve spent so much time with Sonic, and it has been incredible to see the franchise grow and expand,” he says. “Seeing Shadow arrive in movie theatres in Sonic the Hedgehog 3 was a full circle moment – I have such fond memories of working on Sonic Adventure 2 and Shadow’s introduction. I have been very lucky to continue working and creating for the franchise. I’m looking forward to the next 35 years!”Explore more on these topicsGamesSonic the HedgehogPlatform gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress design | Games | The Guardian
description: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Content: ‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesView image in fullscreen‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesSummer games previewsGamesDressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress designCo-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever madeJordan Erica WebberTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Jonathan Hau-Yoon wanted to make something as meaningful as the environmental strategy gameTerra Nil, he turned for inspiration to his longtime partner. Sabrina Becker had worn a dress she made herself to their very first date, and would have studied costume design abroad hadhypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome(a connective tissue disorder I also have) not put those plans on hold.The pair developed a concept around the creative decisions involved in dressmaking, like trying to fit pattern pieces on to available fabric while observing the grain line (the direction of the thread in woven fabric). Other decisions followed: a 3D model on which to place garment pieces, buttons and trims with which to decorate them, clients with commissions as creative prompts.View image in fullscreenNever run out of bobbin thread … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesHau-Yoon knew this ambitious project would benefit from the support of his employers at Free Lives. A bare-bones concept video got hundreds of thousands of views, and a prototype built with colleagues in three weeks had about 30,000 downloads, but he worried it wouldn’t be enough, that he might even have to leave a job he loved to pursue the game full-time. What convinced founder Evan Greenwood in the end was the passion of the player base. Many signed up foritch.ioaccounts just to play the prototype, and left paragraphs-long comments about how much it meant to them.And they had requests. “A surprising amount of people asked for ironing,” Becker laughs. Others wanted to be able to print out the patterns and use them in real life,Barbie Fashion Designerstyle, which isn’t possible here. “We don’t actually run a cloth simulation,” Hau-Yoon explains. Becker adds: “But you can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life. A lot of our players make whole paintings on the dresses, using the trims and buttons and things; they’re drawing Starry Night and the Sistine Chapel.”View image in fullscreen‘How elegant is elegant?’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesWhen I sew, I draft my own patterns to better fit my particular shape, so I wanted to know if Dressmaker includes this aspect. “We have a whole measurement system,” Becker says. “It is simplified, but it was really important to us to illustrate that if you’re coming in for a bespoke dress the dress should be made to fit you. So there’s this whole lattice deformer thing that allows our dress pieces to shift and scale proportionally.”Hau-Yoon says that programmer Ruan Rothmann calls Dressmaker “the most technically challenging game that he’s worked on”: “It really matters where seams are and that certain vertices align.” Other sewists can imagine what aspects have proved challenging: how the fabric stretches across a body, pattern distortion, creating gathers.Becker’s experience has been invaluable, and similarly her understanding of historical costume. Dressmaker isn’t era-specific, so as not to limit players, but it does have what she calls “a vintage feel”, looking as if it’s from “The sort of era where you would have actually gone to a dressmaker to have a dress made”. And when it came to the question of whether to branch off the story (from novelist Kerstin Hall), she knew that sewists would resent missing out: “I want to be able to make ALL of the dresses. If it’s branching and because of decisions you made you don’t get to make a wedding dress for a specific character, I would feel so gutted about that.”So what has she learned about the process of making games? “It’s all numbers and spreadsheets! At least the past two months of the work that I’ve been doing.” “It’s very difficult to capture how to score something when it’s just a vibe,” Hau-Yoon admits. “How elegant is elegant? What number describes elegance?”They hope players will appreciate their efforts, which include a whole-team sewing class arranged by Becker. “It was surprisingly Zen,” says Hau-Yoon. “Initially I was very slow and nervous, but that whirring of a sewing machine … it fades away into the background.” Players will soon be able to hear that whirr for themselves, as sound designer Jason Sutherland has painstakingly recorded Becker’s own weighty vintage Singer sewing machine, along with other related tools. “I’m obsessed with the scissors noise,” Becker smiles. “It’s so satisfying.”Dressmaker is coming to PC on 21 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Introducing Ulez was my hardest decision as mayor of London – but now we know its astonishing impact | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Critics said I was attacking motorists. It’s more important for me that the city’s children are no longer breathing dangerous levels of pollution, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Critics said I was attacking motorists. It’s more important for me that the city’s children are no longer breathing dangerous levels of pollution, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: London’s ultra-low emission zone was introduced in 2019.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenLondon’s ultra-low emission zone was introduced in 2019.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAOpinionAir pollutionIntroducing Ulez was my hardest decision as mayor of London – but now we know its astonishing impactSadiq KhanCritics said I was attacking motorists. It’s more important for me that the city’s children are no longer breathing dangerous levels of pollutionUlez led to better lung size and function among London children, study findsTue 18 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTShareWhen I introduced London’sclean air zone– the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – more than seven years ago, no city had ever attempted anything quite like it. At the time, the scheme in central London provoked fierce opposition. When I decided to expand it – first in 2021, to inner London, and then again in 2023 to the whole city, making it the biggest clean-air zone in the world – my detractors were louder still. I had, they claimed, declared war on drivers in blind pursuit of a policy that may not even work. All the mainstream political parties, including my own, were opposed. In recent years, though, those critics have gone quiet.There is now a mountain of evidence to show that the Ulez has slashed air pollution andimproved air qualityacross London, and research published by Imperial College London earlier this year showed that this is already saving lives. Between 2019 (when I first introduced the Ulez) and 2024, estimated deaths associated with air pollution in the capital fell by around 40%. But a new,independent studypublished by Queen Mary University of London today goes further still, showing how – by helping to clean up the capital’s air – the Ulez is improving the lungs and lives of London’s children.Young children are the first to feel the impact of air pollution. They breathe faster than adults, and more often through their mouths, allowing more pollution to pass into their bodies. Their heads are lower to the ground, too, meaning they’re closer to vehicle exhausts pumping out poisonous chemicals. And, because they’re still growing, long-term exposure to air pollution can do lasting damage to their development, leading to problems such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung cancer when they’re older.One of the first places I visited when I was elected mayor 10 years ago was the Sir John Cass’s Foundation primary school in Aldgate, now known as The Aldgate school. On the school’s roof, I joined children who were growing a garden. As they proudly showed me what they’d planted, the kids told me about how much they loved spending time outdoors. But, speaking to their teachers, it was obvious that they were worried about the air the children were breathing. The school was next to one of inner London’s busiest roads and, while an air-quality monitor had been installed in the playground, they were powerless to stop toxic fumes from the traffic passing by. As a father of two daughters myself, I remember trying to imagine how those children’s parents must have felt, knowing that every day their kids were being exposed to a danger that they couldn’t control.I’ve never forgotten that day. Because, for me, meeting those kids confirmed what the fight for cleaner air was really about: not punishing motorists or making money, but protecting the lives of London’s most vulnerable people.The Ulez has already had an astonishing impact on London’s air. According to research done by King’s College London,without additional action, it would take almost two centuries to get levels of one of themost toxic chemicalsin our air – nitrogen dioxide (NO2) – within legal limits. But, last year,we announced that we’d done italready – 184 years earlier than predicted. Now, we’re beginning to see what our success means for London’s children.The independent study published by scientists at Queen Mary today is one of the most comprehensive of its kind. In it, researchers tracked the lung growth of more than 3,400 children in Luton and central London, beginning in 2019 and concluding five years later. The results are remarkable.Before we introduced the Ulez, London’s filthy air meant that children in the capital had significantly poorer lung function than children in Luton. But, across the five-year period when the Ulez was in force, children’s exposure to NO2fell twice as fast in London as it did in Luton. And, when scientists measured lung function again at the end of the study, young Londoners’ lungs had caught up. This shows that cutting air pollution doesn’t just help Londoners being born today – it can help children whose lungs have already been stunted by toxic air to recover, proving that it’s never too late to act. Over the course of the research, the proportion of children in London with clinically impaired lung function fell from 14% to 9%.Introducing and expanding the Ulez involved some incredibly difficult decisions. I never took them lightly, but I knew that – as mayor – I could not stand by while Londoners young and old lost their lives to a problem it was within my power to solve. For years, politicians and pundits opposed to the Ulez have cynically sought to turn questions of public health into a crude culture war. Today, though, it’s clear that we’re winning the battle against toxic air in the capital – and it’s London’s children who are reaping the rewards.Two months ago, I returned to the roof garden of The Aldgate school. It was just over 10 years since my first visit and, getting ready to garden with a group of smiling children, I felt a strange sense of deja vu. This time, though, something was different. Back in 2016, the air-quality monitor in the playground showed that levels of nitrogen dioxide in the air were exceeding legal limits. But, when they were measured again last year, they’d fallen by 48%. As a result, the kids I met didn’t have to think twice about what a game of football outside may mean for their health, and their parents didn’t have to worry about whether walking to school may stunt the growth of their lungs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionToday, you’ll find stories like this in schools across the capital: kids who are breathing easier and parents who are sleeping better because they no longer have to worry about the damage being done by toxic air. The Ulez has been the toughest fight of my political life, but I have no regrets. Though there’s more to be done, it’s clear that cleaning up the capital’s air has changed young Londoners’ lives for the better – and nothing could matter more than that.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promise | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Today we begin our drive to get everyone in for Christmas. And it will be for local communities up and down the land to decide how best to do it, says prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Today we begin our drive to get everyone in for Christmas. And it will be for local communities up and down the land to decide how best to do it, says prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: ‘We’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionHomelessnessI won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promiseAndy BurnhamToday we begin our drive to get everyone in for Christmas. And it will be for local communities up and down the land to decide how best to do itBurnham launches ‘national drive’ to get rough sleepers off streets by ChristmasTue 18 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.37 EDTShareI’ve always thought you can tell something about a country by what it learns to walk past. And, somewhere along the way, we’ve got used to seeing people sleeping rough on our streets.We see people bedded down in doorways and sat outside stations, carrying their lives in rucksacks and with sleeping bags on their backs. And I think most people have the same reaction: this isn’t right; it shouldn’t be happening here. But we’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.That’s not on the public. It’s on us as politicians. For decades, Westminster has treated rough sleeping like a problem to step around rather than solve. It’s a philosophy that took hold in the 1980s and came back full force in the era of austerity: this idea that rough sleeping is just a fact of life rather than something government has a responsibility to end.I’ve never accepted that. Britain is thefifth largest economy in the world. We’ve built the NHS, developed life-saving vaccines and invented the world wide web. But it’s somehow beyond us to get our own people off the streets? I don’t believe it for a minute. Wedid it during the pandemic. We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again.That’s why thefirst thing I announcedwhen I became prime minister was a commitment to end rough sleeping. Not to manage it, not to reduce it – but to end it. And today, we’re taking the first step in getting it done.We’re putting £442m behind a national drive in England to get everyone in for Christmas. I don’t want Whitehall trying to dictate how every penny of that is spent. The people who know what will work in Newcastle, Liverpool or Plymouthare the people who live there and see the problem first-hand every day. I’ll expect every person to be offered a route off the streets, but beyond that it will be up to local leaders to decide what type of support their community needs most.But I also know from my time in Manchester that public money alone won’t solve this. Ending rough sleeping has to be something we all take responsibility for. That means councils, charities, businesses, faith groups and local communities all pulling together. And, even more importantly, it means all of us asking what we can do to help.So alongside the money we’re putting in, I’m asking leaders across society to get behind this national drive. Because if we all play our part – if we all put care of people at the heart of what we do – we can bring some of that hope back to our communities. No matter who they are or what they’ve been through, every person sleeping rough deserves a chance to get back on their feet – and, together, that’s exactly what we’ll give them.I don’t pretend this is a permanent fix – far from it. It’s not enough just to help people when they fall on hard times. It’s our job to catch people long before they hit the pavement, and that means dealing with the multitude of reasons why someone might be sleeping rough in the first place.That’s why we’re reforming education so every young person, whatever their talents, has a route to a good job. It’s why we’re reindustrialising our towns and cities to make sure we get good growth in every postcode. It’s why we’ve committed to the biggest housebuilding programmesince the second world war. And it’s why we’ll keep transferring power back to the local people who are closest to the problems they face and are best placed to solve them.But today is about making that crucial first step. It’s about giving people a safe place to sleep tonight, and hope that tomorrow might be different. And, fundamentally, it’s about answering that defining question: what kind of country do we want Britain to be?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBecause, of course, I want us to be the fastest-growing economy in Europe. I want to see new businesses in our cities, investment in our towns, and homes in every community that desperately needs them. I want people to look around and feel that this country is finally moving forward again.But all of that growth has to mean something. And if people are still sleeping beneath the cranes building that new Britain, I’ll never kid myself that our job’s done.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Low carb’, ‘gluten-free’, with collagen or electrolytes: is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy? | Melissa Davey | The Guardian
description: Premixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers say
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Premixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers say
Content: Alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is actually no safe ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is actually no safe ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralHealth‘Low carb’, ‘gluten-free’, with collagen or electrolytes: is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy?Melissa DaveyPremixed drinks are ultra-processed products but their marketing claims create a ‘health halo’ that takes the focus away from the harms of alcohol, researchers sayTue 18 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTSharePremixed alcoholic drinks are not known for their health benefits. But that hasn’t stopped a boom in products being marketed with “better for you” claims designed to appeal to younger, more health-conscious drinkers.Labels such as “low sugar”, “gluten-free” and “low carb” are being used in advertising to promote the products, and social media influencersspruik the productsunder the hashtag #healthydrinking.But what do these labels actually mean, and is it really possible for alcohol to be healthy?What is ‘low sugar’ or ‘low calorie’ alcohol?Food policy expert Prof Simone Pettigrew at the George Institute for GlobalHealthrecently ran a research focus group asking participants for their thoughts on a premixed alcoholic drink labelled as “low sugar” and “low carb”.She said that “as soon as you put low sugar, low carb, gluten free, any of these on a product, people assume it’s a relatively healthy product overall”.A recentpaper led by Pettigrewsaw researchers audit 534 ready-to-drink alcoholic products and found one in five did not display a mandatory ingredients list.On top of this, of the 424 products that did list ingredients, almost half contained industrial additives associated with ultra-processing, such as synthetic colours, sweeteners and flavour enhancers, placing them in the same category as chips and soft drinks.Rise in adulterated sexual enhancement supplements could mean users are getting stiffed | AntiviralRead moreDespite being ultra-processed, nearly half of those products carried what the researchers described as a “better for you” labels such as low/no sugar, low calorie, gluten free, low/no carb and other claims.Deputy chair of the Cancer Council’s nutrition, alcohol and physical activity committee, Julia Stafford, said marketing claims should not guide consumer behaviour, and that people should always read the full nutrition label, including ingredients.“The ingredient of most concern in an alcohol product is the alcohol,” she said. “It has nothing to do with the carb or sugar content.”Pettigrew agrees: “People just focus on that tiny little nutrient or ingredient,” she said.“But it’s not just the claim on the label that makes people assume that the whole product is healthy. We now see the sides of trams and massive billboards in train stations screaming low sugar, low calorie claims on alcohol ads. These ads are absolutely enormous. It’s not subtle messaging.”No ‘healthy’ level of alcohol consumptionStafford said alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen – the highest risk category alongside tobacco and asbestos. It means there is actually no “healthy” level of alcohol consumption when it comes to cancer risk.Labels such as “low carb”, “natural” and “gluten-free” create a “health halo” around the product and remove the focus away from harmful ingredients, she said.Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (Fare) policy and research director, Dr Aimee Brownbill, said alcohol brands know that people are increasingly health conscious and interested in wellness. AFare surveypublished in 2025 found 44% of Australians want to stop or reduce drinking, with most citing health-related reasons.It means brandsneed to find waysto counteract alcohol being viewed as an unhealthy, harmful ingredient, she said, by using terms like “clean”, “natural” and “low sugar” to shift the focus.And it works, Brownbill said,citing researchfrom more than 2,000 Australian adults which found almost half of the participants indicated they were more likely to buy products that were marketed with such health claims.Younger people and those identifying as female had particularly positive attitudes towards the claims, especially around lower sugar and calories, the study found.Natural terminology ‘creeping in’ to advertisingPettigrew said alcohol brands are also promoting their products as containing collagen and electrolytes. “This natural kind of terminology and these healthy-sounding ingredients are creeping in to [alcohol] labels,” she said.“Consumers are very clear in saying they don’t want ultra-processed food … They probably don’t realise that ultra-processing is part of producing the alcohol they drink as well, particularly in this really youth-focused product category of premixed drinks.”She said people need to read the entire nutritional label to make decisions about food and beverage consumption, and to be aware healthy-sounding ingredients can’t counteract the impact of alcohol.“We do know that consumers are interested in the amount of sugar in products, but there are other ways of delivering that information without huge claims splattered across the front of the can that makes them assume that the whole product is healthy.”Melissa Davey is Guardian Australia’s medical editorAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or title: Why is Sweden deporting Britons faster than any other EU country post-Brexit?  | David Milstead | The Guardian
description: The official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another story, says David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner
Author: David Milstead
Headline: The official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another story, says David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner
Content: Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years, has been told to leave the country.Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardianView image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, a retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years, has been told to leave the country.Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardianOpinionSwedenWhy is Sweden deporting Britons faster than any other EU country post-Brexit?David MilsteadThe official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another storyTue 18 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTShareThere is anger about the case ofJoyce Thomas, a 78-year-old retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years. Her husband died there; her son, grandchildren and home are there. Yet she has been told to leave because her post-Brexit residence application was late. Her case is appalling and predictable – but far from isolated.The Guardian has also reported on the plight ofHorace Mason, 74, who faces being deported after a court ruling, despite having lived in Sweden for 25 years. This is sad but not surprising.When Sweden set out its plans in 2020, we at theBrits in Swedencampaign warned in an official submission that the application scheme could strip vulnerable people of their rights if they missed the deadline. We urged a flexible and generous approach, and later raised concerns about outreach and refusals with the UK government and European Commission. We have watched Britons fall off that cliff edge since 2021; only occasionally does a case reach the media.The new scheme gave British residents safeguards under free-movement law – including assistance, reasonable grounds for lateness and proportionality – that were untested.View image in fullscreenKenny Solomons with his wife, Tess. Solomons’ application to remain in Sweden was rejected.Photograph: Kenny SolomonsWe were not alone. The Swedish Bar Association said the new rules must be applied generously to both evidence and deadlines, to which the government insisted that the authorities already had sufficient flexibility.The truth of the situationis now clear, for the statistics only point in one direction. Almost4,000 of 14,200 applications in Sweden have been refused. The UK Foreign Office calculates a 27.5% refusal rate – three times that of any other member state and far above the EU average of 3–4%. Eurostat records 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave Sweden since 2021, about a third of the EU total.Reporting differences complicate detailed comparisons, but the statistics show a red flag consistent with lived experience.Kathleen Poolehad advanced Alzheimer’s when Sweden tried to remove her in 2023.Nichola Stanlickarrived aged seven, 40 years ago, and applied on time, yet was refused withdrawal agreement protection and given a national permit expiring in 2027.Kenny Solomons, the husband of a Swedish singer, was forced to leave and would have to qualify under national law to return as a resident.Data on genuine missed-deadline applications remains opaque. Earlier figures mixed them with legitimate later applicants, including people joining family members and those seeking permanent status. After we raised this with Whitehall, the UK challenged the data andSwedenno longer show it in EU reports. Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late.TheBrexittreaty called for an awareness campaign, but unlike Denmark and the Netherlands, the Swedish government chose not to contact registered Britons individually. Some people who enquired to Swedish authorities were told they need do nothing; official information did not always say that this meant “not yet”. Older people and those without computers were easily missed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSweden also tried to deport Kathleen Poole, seen here in a dementia care home with her son Wayne and daughter-in-law Angelica.Photograph: Angelica PooleThe then director general of the SwedishMigrationAgency stated that he believed contacting registered Britons individually would not have made a difference. This is difficult to reconcile with the evidence base.The problem is not confined to those who submitted late applications. Sweden sometimes refused withdrawal agreement status but granted temporary national permits. That merely kicks the can down the road. As those permits expire, some people cannot meet newer permanent-residence requirements, or no longer have the family circumstances on which their permits depended.So why Sweden, and why now? The answer is that Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically. A Swedish faith in neutral rules and independent agencies can also mistake procedural uniformity for justice when radically different human circumstances are reduced to data points.Britons in the EU are caught in a political perfect storm. EU citizens in Britain have a constituency and dedicated monitoring authority, whereas Britons are divided among 27 systems. Brexit created the problem, but did not require Sweden to conduct inadequate outreach, obscure statistics or stretch proportionality.We are stuck in a very difficult middle: Brexiters resist admitting that Brexit created these problems, while some remainers resist criticising an EU member state. Both, in their relative positions, abandon the people the agreement protects.In the Whitehall satire Yes, Prime Minister, the official response to a foreign problem progresses from “nothing is going to happen”, to “maybe we should do something about it, but there’s nothing wecando”, and finally to “maybe there was something we could have done, but it’s too late now”. The UK government and commission must intervene before reaching that final stage. Sweden should pause disputed removals, publish reliable cohort statistics and submit the scheme to independent review before more lives are irreversibly uprooted.David Milstead is a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner, working through theBrits in SwedengroupExplore more on these topicsSwedenOpinionBrexitMigrationEuropean UnionEuropeForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Packing light is for cowards. Pack heavy | Max Olesker | The Guardian
description: Trip-prepping shouldn’t be a grim exercise in minimising your milligrams. Take day outfits, night outfits, gymwear, swimwear – and prepare for an adventure, says writer and comedian Max Olesker
Author: Max Olesker
Headline: Trip-prepping shouldn’t be a grim exercise in minimising your milligrams. Take day outfits, night outfits, gymwear, swimwear – and prepare for an adventure, says writer and comedian Max Olesker
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onEdinburgh festival 2026The hill I will die on: Packing light is for cowards. Pack heavyMax OleskerTrip-prepping shouldn’t be a grim exercise in minimising your milligrams. Take day outfits, night outfits, gymwear, swimwear – and prepare for an adventureTue 18 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTShareIf you’re on the hunt for a streamlined way to travel internationally while only packing a toothbrush, an iPad, a single white T-shirt made of technical fabric and a lukewarm sachet of Huel, then keep scrolling. I simply couldn’t care less.Packing for travel shouldn’t be a grim logistical exercise in minimising the milligrams of mass one must transport. It should be a prelude to an adventure – and an adventure in itself!(Suit)case in point, I have recently embarked on a journey to the Edinburgh fringe, where – after many years as a double-act comedian – I am performing myfirst ever solo theatre show. Thus, I have packed whatIdeem the essentials – which is to say, for every possible eventuality.Dressing up. Dressing down. A dressing gown (and pyjamas and slippers, naturally). Gymwear, swimwear. Day outfits, night outfits, show outfits. A series of mysterious items for vocal rest (Dr Nelson’s legendary inhaler). Books! More books! Face masks (why not?).I’ve no interest in dull consumerism – but thereisa joy in choice; a power in seeing what the universe has to hurl at you that day, and reaching into your luggage to meet the moment.As an extension of my extravagant travel philosophy, my verysuitcaseis preposterous. Some years ago, at a sample sale, I acquired a vast Globe-Trotter. It was for many years the most expensive item I owned, and I have never regretted a purchase less. It’s beautiful, practical and every scuff and torn sticker is transportive.Via careful planning, numerous packing cubes and a straining-at-the-edges suit carrier, I loaded up my Globe-Trotter to the brim. I packed, exactly, everything I could possibly need.And then I packed another full suitcase. Just in case.Max Olesker is a writer and comedian. His showMax Olesker: Making the Cutis playing at the Edinburgh fringe, until 30 August 2026Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026The hill I will die onEdinburgh festivalTheatreFestivalscommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The PM’s net zero pragmatism may please some voters, but as parts of the country go up in flames, it’s an increasingly hard sell, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The PM’s net zero pragmatism may please some voters, but as parts of the country go up in flames, it’s an increasingly hard sell, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: A protest outside the Treasury in Westminster on Monday, against new drilling at the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest outside the Treasury in Westminster on Monday, against new drilling at the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionEnvironment policyBurnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big riskGaby HinsliffThe PM’s net zero pragmatism may please some voters, but as parts of the country go up in flames, it’s an increasingly hard sellTue 18 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTShareWhen the siren sounded on Friday night, my first thought was fire.Weeks of unrelenting sun in the normally soggy Peak District, where I was visiting my mum, have bleached green valleys a dangerously dry, crispy blond. One of her neighbours had earlier pointed out an ominous cloud of smoke on the horizon, coming from one of the wildfires raging all summer on the moor. When that harsh, discordant shriek blared from every mobile phone in the house, I was half-braced for an evacuation order, not what turned out to be a faintly melodramaticwarning to the nationto lay off the barbecues. A false alarm, of sorts, but one that felt uneasily like a wake-up call.Scientists can warn until they’re blue in the face about the consequences of what we’re doing to the planet, but nothing beats the visceral shock of idly scrolling on your phone and seeing panicky footage of flames leaping over suburban British fences, or terrified horses being turned loose from fields where the hedges are starting to catch light. A friend just back from the south of France, somewhere far enough from the raging wildfires there to be considered safe, was spooked by ash raining from the sky as she ate lunch in the garden: it felt like the beginning of an apocalypse, she said, or the opening scenes of a disaster movie. Something has shifted even in people who were once blase about the climate crisis, and judging by last week’s sudden flurry of government activity – aCobra meetingon fighting wildfires called after hefty pressure from the Greens, extrasupport for drought-stricken farmers, and finallythat emergency alertlighting up everyone’s phones – Andy Burnham has clocked the dangers of not being seen to respond.Yet there’s something jarring about a new prime minister spending the hottest summer on record talking up the prospect ofnew drilling for oil and gasin the North Sea, or consulting on easing net zero targets for carmakers. He was rightly quick to visit people affectedby a wildfire near the West Midlands town of Stourbridge, but has been noticeably slower to respond publiclyto warningsfrom the town’s Labour MP, Cat Eccles, that this is not the time to start extracting yet more fossil fuels. So far, his is more a strategy for picking up the pieces of damage already done than for gripping the root causes.View image in fullscreenNetwork Rail workers inspecting the track near homes destroyed by the Stourbridge wildfire, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesJust how serious is Burnham about the climate crisis? It’s very early days, but a pattern is emerging that may be familiar to some in Greater Manchester, remembering the then mayor’s swift rethink of attempts to impose an unpopularclean air zoneon drivers. He is not complacent about the threat to the planet – but where green policies clash with his mission to create jobs and rebuild the social fabric, Burnham and his deputy, Louise Haigh, both seem instinctively protective of the latter. This prime minister isn’t swayed by expensive fossil fuel lobbyists, but he is sensitive to unions defending the interests of oil rig workers in Aberdeen, or car manufacturers who have been warning for years that Britain’s rigidzero emission vehicle (Zev) mandatecould push them into closing factories across what is left of the country’s industrial heartlands. Under the mandate, carmakers are fined if they don’t hit constantly rising targets to sell more electric cars as a percentage of total sales. If people feeling the pinch refuse to buy enough expensive new electric cars, and governments decline to subsidise them, the cheapest way of avoiding massive fines is to mothball product lines for petrol and diesel cars, to stop drivers buying too many of them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury | John HarrisRead moreNobody in this government needs reminding of how a big employer closing its gates in places where jobs are scarce can rip the heart out of a community, nor how the far right feeds off that sense of hopelessness. Britain isn’t the only country considering watering down targets that few in the car industry now expect to be met. Nor, I suspect, will Burnham’s be the only government staring down the barrel of higher gas bills this autumn – caused by Donald Trump’s disastrous war on Iran – and worrying about how this new cost of living crisis might be exploited by rightwing parties blaming it on supposedly“woke” net zero policiesthey aredesperate to revoke.There are compelling reasons, in short, for Burnham to pitch himself as a net zero pragmatist – the word ministers keep falling back on when asked about the looming and increasingly fraught decision on drilling in theRosebank and Jackdawoil and gasfields. (And yes, even that act of apparent climate vandalism has friends in surprising places, with the eco-entrepreneurs Dale Vince and Greg Jacksonboth arguing that, if we need oil and gas from somewhere, getting it from our own back yard is a cleaner option that might also help reduce the backlash against net zero.)But if the Labour party wanted naked pragmatism, frankly it could have stuck with Keir Starmer. It looks toAndy Burnhamfor something more: the courage to face up to difficult questions but also the political skills to sell difficult answers, and the emotional intelligence to manage the fallout. As this unnaturally hot summer fades into what may be an equally unnaturally wet autumn, we’ll soon know whether he can actually deliver.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEnvironment policyOpinionAndy BurnhamWildfiresExtreme heatFossil fuelscommentShareReuse this content

title: What legacy do we leave behind when we die? As Sam Neill taught me, it’s more about sweetness than ego | Clarke Gayford | The Guardian
description: As men we’re often taught to chase lives defined by vanity and hollow expressions. But genuine decency lasts far longer than any name on a building
Author: Clarke Gayford
Headline: As men we’re often taught to chase lives defined by vanity and hollow expressions. But genuine decency lasts far longer than any name on a building
Content: ‘It was in the outpouring of words for Sir Sam Neill after his death that we got a better glimpse of the person behind the actor, and a wonderful mosaic of a life properly lived,’ writes Clarke Gayford.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It was in the outpouring of words for Sir Sam Neill after his death that we got a better glimpse of the person behind the actor, and a wonderful mosaic of a life properly lived,’ writes Clarke Gayford.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/The GuardianOpinionGenderWhat legacy do we leave behind when we die? As Sam Neill taught me, it’s more about sweetness than egoClarke GayfordAs men we’re often taught to chase lives defined by vanity and hollow expressions. But genuine decency lasts far longer than any name on a buildingTue 18 Aug 2026 00.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 03.13 EDTShareOccasionally, in our lives, there are markers that arrive with enough strength to hop us off the treadmill just long enough to remind ourselves that everyone’s race has a finish line, and none of us are getting out of this jolly for free.One of these blots is often when someone we know passes away.I always find the saddest part of a funeral the idea that the deceased will never hear the nice words being shared around the room in that moment. Our online world has enhanced this grieving process with posthumous accolades flowing from friends and strangers alike, creating yet more space for others to add comment as well. These modern outpourings help shape a fuller picture of the person we’ve just lost and what that person meant to others.The recent death of the New Zealand acting legendSam Neillis one such marker for so many of us. It was in the outpouring of words for Sir Sam after his death that we got a better glimpse of the person behind the actor, and a wonderful mosaic of a life properly lived.double quotation markIn New Zealand’s Māori culture, there is a saying that ‘the kumara (sweet potato) never speaks of its own sweetness’We heard from the range of people he positively affected, via the causes he championed loudly and, in many cases, quietly and personally. The people, the wildlife, the nature and the campaigns he spoke up for were all put into kind words by others about Sam. It was such a wonderful lesson in human legacy.In New Zealand’s Māori culture, there is a saying that “the kumara (sweet potato) never speaks of its own sweetness”, an adage Sam lived by. Those who read and listened to the many tributes for him all got to collectively enjoy this hidden sweetness, learning how he had selflessly affected those in his orbit and beyond. That’s not a legacy of ego, but a legacy of presence and genuine human decency.Some men (and it’s nearly always men) spend their life striving for a tainted version of legacy. It presents in the extremes of authoritarianism, with insatiable desires to have names on buildings, excessive money in banks or statues in streets. Men, who may be trying to soothe the gnawing hole left by the lack of attention from their own dads, who were perhaps absent as they too chased straw deity legacies of their own.In my years of spearfishing, I’ve never encountered more sharks than now. But I know where I stand in the underwater pecking order | Clarke GayfordRead moreSpending your life trying to create a plinth for remembrance in death is an odd concept to all but those who think we get to somehow watch this soapbox existence from afar.It’s not like Julius Caesar’s life improved because he was remembered by name long after his death. Perhaps if he’d been a bit more present with Brutus at the time, he might have got to enjoy more of it.It’s certain most of us will never have a month named after us like Caesar, but – as Sam has demonstrated – it’s possible to have a richer legacy simply by contributing in meaningful ways to those around us.In facing the diagnosis of his illness, Sam said, “I’m not in any way frightened of dying … but I would be annoyed. I’d be annoyed because there are things I still want to do.”Sam’s life ended too soon for him, and for us, but the beautiful thing about a legacy of positive activity like this is that the spread and reach of its flow will keep moving through all those who benefited. It would be impossible for the world not to be a better place if we could all find a way to live a bit more like Sam.Clarke Gayford is a New Zealand TV host now living in Australia. He won two Emmy awards for the filmPrime Minister, and hosted the award-winning series Fish of the DayExplore more on these topicsGenderOpinionSam NeillcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringe | Theatre | The Guardian
description: How do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to Edinburgh
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: How do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to Edinburgh
Content: About-to-fall-apart energy … Megan Tomei in SpinQueen™.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAbout-to-fall-apart energy … Megan Tomei in SpinQueen™.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianTheatre‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringeHow do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to EdinburghKate WyverTue 18 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlood and sweat drip to the floor. Tears are on their way. In a small room in Edinburgh, Megan Tomei is cleat-clipped into a stationary bike, yelling above the music as she leads a high-intensity spin class gone wrong. “We take the thing you’re running from,” Tomei shouts, pink lights bouncing off her gleaming shoulders, “and turn it into fuel!” This is SpinQueen™, one of a handful of shows at this year’s fringe demanding epic endurance from their performers through the use of jazzed-up gym equipment. Employing various bikes and a treadmill to authentically illustrate the struggle for success, the pain of failure, and the escape from reality, a profoundly fit group of actors are pushing themselves to their physical limits.Across the city, Connor Delves’s calves are worth watching. The workout from his cycling-obsessed play,Cadel: Lungs on Legs, is so powerful that people have come up to him after, wanting to touch them. “To make sure they’re real,” says Delves, who cycles a whopping 27km per show. Does he mind this attention? He shrugs. “If they’re OK with getting their hands sweaty, go for it.”double quotation markYou’re watching it cost me something. You’re watching this body really workDelves grew up in his parents’ bike shop in Perth, Western Australia. His mum was a triathlete, his dad an international mountain-biker. “It’s always been acting and sport for me,” he says. When he was replaced by a bigger name in a transferring show, he decided to make a production in which he was irreplaceable. “I’d never seen a play that showed endurance sport at its best,” he says, “where the sport is an actual effort.”In 2016, Baby Reindeer’s Richard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award forMonkey See Monkey Do, an exposing show about toxic masculinity and sexual assault, performed on a treadmill. Two decades before, performance artist Kim Noble pounded away on a treadmill while the other half of theirdouble act, Stuart Silver, played chess against the audience. Over lockdown, Katie Mitchell created eco-theatre showA Play for the Living in a Time of Extinction, with cyclists generating the show’s lights and sound. But few shows that involve this kind of equipment are about sport, where the exercise is in the story as well as in the doing.View image in fullscreenHero’s arc … Connor Delves in Cadel: Lungs on Legs.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianWith Cadel, this is what Delves set out to do. The result is a sincere, leg-burning ode toCadel Evans, the first Aussie to win the Tour de France. Delves performs on a series of the real bikes that Evans used to win the 2011 race, clamped in place. The operation is a family affair: Delves’s father is the show’s mechanic. Head down, Delves’s teardrop-shaped helmet is steady as his legs whir round for the sprint stages. Remarkably riding the same mountain gradients as they do in the Tour, Delves is adept at explaining clearly to the uninitiated how the race works. It’s evident just how tough it is: every stage, every day, every kilometre. “It means you’ve got to think about nutrition,” Delves says of his show. “About sleep.” He quit drinking to train for it. “It means treating acting like being an athlete.”While Evans’s story is the hero’s arc, The Distance is about the also-rans. “I’m interested in what happens to the legions of sportspeople who are very, very good, but not good enough to make a living from it,” says Ben Norris, the show’s writer and performer, and vocally recognisable as farmer’s son Ben in The Archers. “For every one who wins the Olympics,” he says, “there are at least eight who lose the final. Then 100 or 200 who were in the heats. Then tens of thousands who are very good but don’t get there.” So, he asks, what happens then? “Who are you when the thing to which your identity has been shackled is no longer viable?”double quotation markI’ve had to start behaving like I’m an elite athlete againNorris plays Chris, a young boy realising his potential as a cross-country runner and dreaming of competing in the Olympics. The Distance is inspired by Norris’s time as a teenage international long-distance runner, but he worked hard to extricate it from himself. When he was mentored by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, she told him: “Be less concerned with being likable.” During each show, he runs roughly 8km on a “geriatric, old, foldable treadmill” that he’s wheeled all over the country. “One time, a local MP helped me on to the train with it,” he says. In Edinburgh, on Summerhall’s main stage, the treadmill is surrounded by a scaffolding pole, which Norris nimbly clambers over as Chris’s success rises and rises – and then begins to fall.Norris starts running as the audience file into the room. Soon, his clothes are drenched. As he strips down, we see the effort this is taking; his chest heaving, his body glistening. The sweat and ragged breath are important, he explains. “You’re watching it cost something. You’re watching this body really work.” That cost is already making itself evident. Norris pulled his calf in March, then again in April. “I’ve had to start behaving like I’m an elite athlete again, in terms of the rigour of my training and recovery,” he says. “I’m not 18 any more. Everything takes longer on an older body.”To be fit enough for the show, he has been cross-training, doing strength and conditioning, and phoning friends while on the treadmill to practise speaking at the same time as running at a furious speed. Throughout the fringe, he’s forcing himself to rest. “I’ve done a musical at the fringe and that requires a different kind of discipline. This will be like that, but on steroids.” He frowns. “Although crucially,” he says, “not on steroids.” His one request for accommodation: could he please have a bath?View image in fullscreen‘I’m not 18 any more!’ … Ben Norris in The Distance.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicI want to get a sense of the effort demanded by these shows, so when I talk to Tomei, the creator and performer of SpinQueen™, before the fringe, I suggest we do it on exercise bikes. My thighs soon regret it. “Oh God,” says Tomei, halfway through our chat. “I’m sweating so much.” She is in New York, calling from the spin studio at which she works. I quickly realise how hard it is to speak and ride at the same time.In SpinQueen™, Tomei plays a heightened, emotionally cracked version of herself as our manic spin instructor, spewing out “toxic positivity” as Tomei calls it, her character obsessed with thinness, optimisation and escape from the quiet that lets thoughts seep in. “Keep pushing, keep starving!” she calls in the show with a too-wide grin. In real life, Tomei is similarly peppy, but without the desperate about-to-fall-apart energy of her character. But that version of herself isn’t a world away, she says; the story’s climax borrows from a traumatic experience she had with an ex. When our narrator won’t allow herself to stop cycling, Tomei says: “It’s a physical representation of her emotional state.”View image in fullscreenRunning to survive … Richard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award for Monkey See Monkey Do in 2016.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSweat is blurring my vision now. “Oh God, no, same,” Tomei tries to reassure me. Every show, she cycles 16km, wanting people to feel the pain her character goes through, emotionally and physically. Tomei started taking spin classes with her dad in high school, and began teaching it as a way to earn money alongside acting. But after running the New York marathon, she got injured. “I had to slow down for the first time in my life,” she says. “I struggled with it, and it made me think of all the standards we hold ourselves to, because of what we think makes us better or successful. It made me think: ‘Why are we killing ourselves trying to reach this standard that can’t be met?’”What happens if these performers fall or twist an ankle during the fringe? “The same thing as in the Tour de France,” Delves says frankly. “I think that’s part of the allure of this. There’s no understudy.” With her massage gun packed, Tomei is more conscious of the emotional health she needs to maintain across the festival. “Every performance, I’m reliving what happened to me,” she says. “It’s a high-intensity emotional workout too.”Even when their characters near the dreamed-of success in these shows, failure is only a breath away. One fall, one second behind in a race, one last chance. These plays capture the itch of pushing just that tiny bit harder, as well as the dangers of running on empty. “There’s a little ambition monster within you,” Norris says, “that will wonder if you should just quit everything else and give this one last big go.” You can keep batting it down, he says, but the monster is persistent. “LA Olympics 2028?” Norris muses, only just joking. “Is it too late?”SpinQueen™is atJade StudioatGreenside @ George Street, until 29 August.The Distance,Main Hall at Summerhall, until 31 August.Cadel: Lungs on Legs,Auditorium at Gilded Balloon at the Museum, until 30 August; thenRiverside Studios, London, 13 October-15 NovemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsTheatreEdinburgh festival 2026FitnessEdinburgh festivalTraining programmesFringe theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Even its loos are on the outside’: hi-tech, inside-out marvel the Lloyd’s building is partying with the public | Architecture | The Guardian
description: It has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the inside
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: It has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the inside
Content: ‘There was whooping in the office’ … the Lloyd's building, designed by Richard Rogers.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘There was whooping in the office’ … the Lloyd's building, designed by Richard Rogers.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Rex/ShutterstockArchitecture‘Even its loos are on the outside’: hi-tech, inside-out marvel the Lloyd’s building is partying with the publicIt has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the insideAlice FisherTue 18 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his 2012 book A New Kind of Bleak, the criticOwen Hatherleycalled it “monstrous, compelling” and utterly messed-up. Back in the 1980s, a then Prince Charles suggested it had been inspired by a North Sea oil rig. But none of this stopped it from becoming, in 2011, the youngest ever building to be given Grade I-listed status in the UK.And now, as part of its 40th anniversary celebrations, the Lloyd’s building will open to the public for the first time since 2014 for one day only during London’s Open House festival. The iconic building in the heart of the financial district was designed by architectRichard Rogersto house the global insurance marketplace. Its futuristic facade has been a celebrated part of the City of London skyline since it opened in 1986, but the interior is rarely seen by the public. Visitor galleries with a view of the trading floor have long been shut for security reasons.double quotation markThe Adam Room was sliced into 1,500 pieces and moved to Lloyd’s HQOpen House festival is organised by the charity Open City, which aims to make architecture more accessible by inviting government offices, private properties and heritage buildings to let the public in. Free tickets for the Lloyd’s building are released tomorrow for the one day the building is open, on 19 September. The tour will include the underwriting room and the Adam Room as well as examining how the building was designed. “There was whooping in the office when the Lloyd’s building came in,” says festival director Celia Mead, “because we know our visitors really, really want to get inside this landmark institution.”View image in fullscreenCompared with the Parthenon … Lloyd’s main trading floor, with its mahogany ‘temple’ holding the Lutine Bell, rung at moments of disaster.Photograph: Jason Alden/LloydsLloyd’s is a key example of British hi-tech architecture. This late modernist style evolved in the 1970s and celebrates industrial engineering and prefabricated materials. Lloyd’s is famous for its exposed concrete frame and the six external steel towers that house its staircases, lifts, pipes and ducts. The building’s 12 glass lifts were the first of their kind in the UK, and each tower is permanently topped with steel cranes - partly for maintenance but also to make the building look like a gothic cathedral.“It’s a masterpiece of radical, inside-out architecture,” says Mead, “representing London’s confidence and swagger.” From the street, she says, “it catches the attention and you wonder, ‘What could it be like inside?’” Mead has experienced the building first-hand: “My mum was an economics teacher and I joined one of her school trips to Lloyd’s 38 years ago. I remember then thinking it was huge.”With all the infrastructure removed from the inside, the Lloyd’s building has capacity for a double-height space for the trading floor and a galleried atrium that reaches to the steel and glass barrel-vaulted roof, 14 floors above. Historian Reyner Banham compared the atrium to the Parthenon when he presented Rogers with the Royal Institute of British Architects’ gold medal in 1985.The building also includes historical artefacts from Lloyd’s of London’s 338-year history. The Adam Room, originally designed in 1763 for Bowood House in Wiltshire by neoclassical architect Robert Adam, was sliced into 1,500 pieces in 1958 and moved to Lloyd’s HQ. The old library from Lloyds’ former home in the Cooper building on Leadenhall Street – designed by Sir Edwin Cooper in 1928 – was similarly salvaged. There is also a 1958 war memorial stained glass by artist Hugh Easton while, on the main trading floor, the Lutine Bell sits, hung within a mahogany, pillared temple. The bell, rescued from the wreck of HMS Lutine, has been used since 1858 to alert insurance underwriters to a maritime disaster. It’s still used to acknowledge ceremonial occasions such as Remembrance Sunday.View image in fullscreenPieced together …the 18th-century Adam Room within the Lloyds building at One Lime Street.Photograph: Northern Exposure/AlamyThe Lloyd’s building’s place in British culture is nuanced. It appeared in 1986,the same year the City was deregulated, and came to symbolise that gear change to a voracious capitalist financial market shaped by international powers. The design’s references to industrialism and religion married to futurism invite ruminations about ideas of power in British history.Architecturally, though, its reputation has endured. Not everyone is as damning as King Charles. Historian Geraint Franklin, of Historic England, who last year featured the building on the cover of his book High-Tech Britain, says it was designed to adapt and evolve. “Lloyd’s is flexible. Its services, lifts and even loos are mounted on the outside, freeing up the workplace inside. In recent years, the glazing has been renovated, carefully recutting the original ‘sparkle glass’.” This refers to textured glass panes that refract light so the building glitters in the sun.“The main trading areas have been recently refurbished,” adds Franklin. “On paper, the plan is rational and diagrammatic, but it’s a dynamic, romantic exterior. Lloyd’s was never intended to be taken in at a single glance but to be encountered in snatched views from the streets. It’s obsessively detailed – with stainless steel, glass and white concrete making up a sharp City palette, highlighted by careful lighting.”Mead is just pleased that more people will get to experience this. “In our programme of over 730 buildings, Lloyd’s is perhaps the greatest statement building. It’s heavyweight, look-at-me and counterintuitive. We’re all about the social impact that access brings – it gives people a sense of belonging to the city. Can’t wait to hear what they say about Lloyd’s.”Tickets to Lloyd’s are free but must be booked in advance atopenhouse.org.uk. Booking opens at noontomorrow. London Open House festival runs 12-20 September.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureCity of LondonOpen HouseHeritageDesignLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We are defying the laws of physics!’ How pole dancing exploded into the Edinburgh fringe | Dance | The Guardian
description: With abs like Olympians and skin like hide, pole dancers are besieging the festival. We meet four high-flying, high-octane acts tackling everything from New York’s underbelly to neurodiversity
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: With abs like Olympians and skin like hide, pole dancers are besieging the festival. We meet four high-flying, high-octane acts tackling everything from New York’s underbelly to neurodiversity
Content: ‘I’m literally hanging on by a couple of skin cells!’ … Donna Carnow and Gina Alm in Dusk/Night/Dawn.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m literally hanging on by a couple of skin cells!’ … Donna Carnow and Gina Alm in Dusk/Night/Dawn.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDance‘We are defying the laws of physics!’ How pole dancing exploded into the Edinburgh fringeWith abs like Olympians and skin like hide, pole dancers are besieging the festival. We meet four high-flying, high-octane acts tackling everything from New York’s underbelly to neurodiversityLyndsey WinshipTue 18 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you tell someone in Edinburgh you’re going to see a pole dancing show, they might direct you towards the so-called Pubic Triangle, where the city’s strip clubs are. But pole dance is actually a big part of the festival this year, popping up in sweaty, dazzling shows right across the fringe. Not only do these acts show off amazing physical feats, they also tell stories that range from one woman’s HIV diagnosis, to the relationship between a neurodivergent mother and son.Since the boom of the 1990s, when Zoe Ball famously had a pole in her living room, pole has been taught at dance studios, has become a competition sport – there’s a campaign to get it into the Olympics – and made its way from cabaret stages to theatres. It’s an impressive and fiendishly difficult art.double quotation markYou have calluses in weird places – the backs of my knees feel like a lizardGina Alm saw a video of a pole dancer on YouTube when she was 15 and immediately knew she wanted to do it. “I was very moved,” she says. “I asked my parents for a pole for my 16th birthday.” And she got it, a pink aluminium one. What was the appeal? “It’s a visually stunning thing,” she says, “but also, I’m a lifelong athlete and the exertion, the exhaustion and the physical quest of it, is really appealing. You can do things that appear to defy physics. It’s magnetic to watch and I saw a lot of potential in it, immediately, as an art form.”View image in fullscreen‘Travelling through the underbelly of night’ … Carnow, left, and Alm on terra firma.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianYvonne Smink came to pole dance having been a climber, and transferred her grip, strength and balance to this new discipline (she’s since won multiple Dutch championship titles). She says for her it’s a kind of movement therapy. “I can just shut off my thinking and move with the music. It’s like time stops.” Smink calls herself a dinosaur, having been in the industry a long time. “When I started, there were no theatre pieces using pole dance. That just didn’t exist. It came from the strip clubs. Now it’s like a whole revolution happening. It’s exciting for me to see.”“I think pole really contains multitudes,” says Alm. “People can appreciate how sexy it is, how athletic it is. It can be an art piece or a piece of dance theatre.” In Edinburgh, Alm is performing Dusk/Night/Dawn alongside US national pole art champion Donna Carnow, whose background is in contemporary dance. The pair both work on the New York cabaret scene and their show is a dreamlike journey through the world they inhabit. “Travelling through the underbelly of night into the dawn,” says Carnow. It’s a show about the act of entertainment, and the grind of a dancer’s life: “Our lives and our labour.” The pair recall finding themselves on all sorts of stages, at all hours of the night. “Risking our lives for $250,” says Alm, “under the craziest circumstances.”They perform on a hanging pole that swings 5m above the stage, although in other shows Carnow has performed 15m up. “It’s been such a joy,” she says, “but it’s a lot for your nervous system, ‘Wow, I’m literally hanging on by a couple of skin cells!’” Watching Carnow perform, she is superhero-strong – her abs even get a gasp when she first reveals them – but it’s her moves that are most impressive, spinning up the pole in a red sequinned bikini and killer heels, glittering as she turns. It’s mesmerising. She pretzels her limbs into knots around the pole, at speed, suspended seemingly by just the arch of a foot, a hip, an elbow.As well as the hanging pole, there’s the static pole and the spinning pole. They’re made out of shiny, slippery chrome, and you need bare skin to get any traction (that’s why pole dancers are so scantily clad), but you can get poles coated in silicone, for more grip.
