Like a guitarist’s fingers on steel strings, your skin has to toughen up. “You have calluses in weird places, but it’s crazy what your body can get used to,” says Carnow. “The backs of my knees feel like a lizard,” says Alm, “but I need that to hang on there.”Yvonne Smink, over video call, shows me her battle scars. “Can you see that discolouration?” she says pointing to her wrist. “And I have thicker skin on the inside of my right thigh, and also more hair.” The hair growth is apparently a response to the friction. “A lot of women have this. Some shave it off but I’m like, ‘It’s natural, it’s just how it is.’”View image in fullscreen‘I caught the rubber and blew out my bicep’ … Tell Me by Sadiq Ali Company.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFor Smink’s Edinburgh show, Poles, she has a specially created piece of apparatus, a frame made of multiple poles: vertical, horizontal and diagonal. “It’s like a spider,” she says. Poles was created with director Guilherme Miotto. “It blew my mind,” he says of her first performance. “Yvonne has such a deep commitment – it’s almost a spiritual experience.”Poles is about Smink’s relationship with the pole, based on what Miotto calls “instinctive performance”, which makes room for improvisation and exploration within the framework of the show. “I’ve done pole dance for 15 years now,” says Smink. “I show up every day to the pole dance studio and the pole is always the same. But every time I do it, something new happens. The performance is about instinctive discoveries. It is somehow really magical.”double quotation markIf people clap mid-show, I’ve done it wrongSadiq Ali describes himself as a “pole-trained circus go-go boy and dancer”. The Scot started out in circus and trained on Chinese pole, a traditional circus apparatus coated in rubber – you can scamper up it like climbing a tree. For that one, you need to be fully clothed or we’re talking serious friction burns. He thrusts his arm at me and displays a blurry red mark. “I caught this on the rubber and blew out my bicep.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s like time stops’ … Yvonne Smink in Poles.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAli forged a busy career in cabaret and also dances in clubs – he did a season in Ibiza last year. But he wanted to move towards something deeper and more narrative. His first theatre piece, The Chosen Haram, about a queer Muslim couple, got glowing reviews. His latest piece, Tell Me, is about a woman’s response to being diagnosed with HIV.“Why is pole a good way of telling any story?” Ali muses. “It doesn’t seem a natural fit to storytelling,” he admits. “But there’s something about the physicality of the body overriding the need for intellectual narrative.” In other words, the audience get a visceral experience of the story. In Tell Me, pole work exists inside the world of the show, not as a separate trick. “Drops and descents, things like that, are exciting when they’re used sparingly, and can enhance story without spectacle. If people stop and clap mid-show,” he adds, “I’ve done it wrong.”View image in fullscreen‘People have very strong opinions about pole’ … Tamsin Shasha as a struggling mother in Forgive Me.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAs a choreographer, the pole literally adds another dimension. “It’s a continuation of the stage in a different direction,” says Ali, something Tamsin Shasha also brings up when we discuss her fringe show, Forgive Me; she talks about swimming up the pole to a world that’s beyond the ceiling, or the pole representing a place of imagination separate to the stage.Shasha has a background in restaging ancient Greek dramas and in circus, while her last show was about the Japanese art of bondage,shibari. “I’m interested in using my body, and in unconventional ways of telling stories,” she says. “I want to tell a story that’s really compelling. Last year I got a diagnosis ofADHDand the possibility of spinning on the pole and telling that story really appealed to me.” Shasha’s son had had an autism diagnosis a few years before, and Forgive Me examines their sometimes discordant relationship.Shasha’s pole is visible behind her in her Brighton living room. She turns 60 this year and loves being “on the air” as she puts it. “I love the grace of it. And I love that it’s a workout for your whole body.” She also loves her pole community in Brighton and doesn’t shy away from pole’s roots in the sex industry: “It’s an opportunity to get on these big heels,” she laughs, pulling out a pair of giant platforms with what must be 8in heels.She still gets a few comments and raised eyebrows. “People have very strong opinions about pole,” she says. “When you say you do pole there’s still that, ‘Oh! You do that?’” Ali gets a different kind of comment when people see the level of strength it takes to suspend his bodyweight in the air. “Men see my show and say, ‘Oh, you do callisthenics, bruh!’ And I’m like, ‘It’s pole dance, guys.’”Dusk/Night/Dawnis at Assembly Roxy until 30 August.Forgive MeandTell Meare at Summerhall until 31 August.Polesis at Assembly @ Dance Base, 18-30 August.Explore more on these topicsDanceEdinburgh festival 2026CabaretFringe theatreEdinburgh festivalTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Berry-Dee dropped by publisher after allegations of abuse made against him | Publishing | The Guardian
description: Bonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigation
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: Bonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigation
Content: His publisher said it was ‘shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations’ relating to Berry-Dee.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHis publisher said it was ‘shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations’ relating to Berry-Dee.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockPublishingChristopher Berry-Dee dropped by publisher after allegations of abuse made against himBonnier Books will no longer publish UK’s top-selling true crime author following Guardian investigationElla CreamerTue 18 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe main publisher of the bestselling true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee has dropped the author after aGuardian investigationinto allegations of violence andsexual abuse against him, which he denies. Waterstones has also removed his books from sale.“We are shocked and appalled by the very serious allegations relating to Christopher Berry-Dee, and our thoughts are with those affected,” said the publisher Bonnier Books in a statement to the Guardian.“Bonnier Books UK will no longer publish Christopher Berry-Dee, we will not work with him on any future projects, and we are terminating all existing agreements”, it continued. “There are practical steps entailed in unwinding longstanding contracts, including those involving third parties, but we are working through them as quickly as we can. We will also be removing our existing stocks from the market.”An investigationpublished on Saturdaydetailed multiple allegations of abuse by Berry-Dee, including domestic violence and sexual assault of a 13-year-old student attending his art school. Berry-Dee refused to be interviewed for the piece, citing health issues, but denied the allegations: “I have not once committed any of the crimes you accuse me of.”Berry-Dee, 78, is the UK’s top-selling author of true crime. His books, including Talking With Serial Killers, draw on interviews with murderers and have sold nearly 1m copies.Berry-Dee has admitted lying to his subjects in order to gain access, telling them he intends “to write a book about the miscarriage of justice they are suffering”, he wrote in his 2023 book Talking With Psychopaths and Savages.Waterstones told the Guardian that Bonnier contacted the bookseller to say that it would no longer publish Berry-Dee’s books. “Following this advice, we have removed the titles from sale in our shops and online,” said a representative.Orion, an imprint of Hachette, published Inside the Darkest Minds by Berry-Dee last month, but did not respond when asked whether they will continue to publish it.Explore more on these topicsPublishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Great ADHD Myth? review – the most controversial show of the year is here | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Dr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend many
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Dr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend many
Content: Having his ‘fun-ness’ taken away? … Mason on The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsView image in fullscreenHaving his ‘fun-ness’ taken away? … Mason on The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Great ADHD Myth? review – the most controversial show of the year is hereDr Max Pemberton isn’t uncompassionate or especially radical, but he assembles a team of medics whose stance on the condition is clear from the off. This is a documentary that will incense and offend manyLucy ManganTue 18 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePresenter Max Pemberton, a psychiatrist in the NHS, Daily Mail columnist and author, and the experts he has assembled, waste no time in setting out their stall in The Great ADHD Myth?. This is a documentary that will incense and offend some of its viewers, and its scepticism regarding ADHD is clear from the outset. “It’s certainly not a medical condition as far as I’m concerned,” says the former president of the Royal College of General Practitioners, Dr Iona Heath. “We’re going to look back and think: did we actually put a chemical cosh on an entire developing generation of brains?” says a neurophysiological psychologist. “The industry around ADHD is about making money at the cost of the misery of others,” says a former president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists.These represent the three main questions raised by Pemberton. The first is whether ADHD is a neuro-developmental disorder – ie do those diagnosed with the condition have different brains from those without – or whether it is a way of suppressing natural tendencies (especially those of children) and inducing behaviours that society deems acceptable. The second is how doctors should approach treatment, which most often involves amphetamines. “These are controlled drugs,” says consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Sami Timimi. “There’s good reason why we warn the rest of the population [about them].” The third question is – who benefits from the increase in diagnoses we have seen in the past decade or so? How has ADHD moved from a relatively unknown condition 10 years ago to affecting about 2.5 million people in the UK today (including a 200% increase in people being referred for diagnosis in the past five years)?Pemberton interviews cognitive neuroscientist Prof Katya Rubia, who has 30 years of experience working with brain imaging. She says that there is no convincing data that “ADHD brains” are any different from “normal” brains. Others go through the list of diagnostic criteria, which include things such as finding it difficult to wait your turn, squirming in your seat and being unable to play quietly. The broadness with which the criteria are drawn means that, according to Dr Heath: “If you want the diagnosis, you will be able to get it.”View image in fullscreen‘Wastes no time in setting out his stall’ … Max Pemberton in The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsPemberton himself undergoes a £1,200 private assessment and comes away with a diagnosis of “combined” ADHD (impulsivity, hyperactivity, inattentiveness) and a prescription for medication. He takes a dose to see what it’s like and reports feeling blunted, not wanting to chat as he usually does (“The fact you’re here is quite irritating actually,” he tells the crew) and feeling as if he could happily sit quietly alone. It’s a stunt, but, I suppose – much as I would love him to stick with the science and do a deeper dive on the data – an inevitable one.The main stunt, however, is following 10-year-old Mason as he comes off the ADHD meds he has been on for two years (“They take my fun-ness away”) for a six-week period to see if a programme of yoga, outdoor activities, no screen time and less processed food and sugar can help instead. It can. Mason, says his mother, Shauna, is funnier, happier, more of a character, more himself. But he is more trouble at school. His teacher says that seeing “his true, honest self” is more important than him being easier to teach. His mother decides to keep him off the drugs.We live in a time when to question any prevailing orthodoxy will, in many cases, be met with an emotional outpouring. Casting any form of doubt on ADHD will absolutely not be the exception. But Pemberton answers his questions convincingly. And the redresses proposed – try changing diet, screen and activity levels first, making school curricula more flexible, and making drugs the last resort – seem neither radical nor uncompassionate. They seem, if primum non nocere (“first do no harm”) is your goal rather than profit (there is little money to be made in encouraging parents to take their children to the park), to be quite the opposite.The Great ADHD Myth? is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Phyllida Law, prolific performer across stage and screen, dies aged 94 | Movies | The Guardian
description: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades
Content: Phyllida Law in 2013.Photograph: Pascal Saez/RexView image in fullscreenPhyllida Law in 2013.Photograph: Pascal Saez/RexMoviesPhyllida Law, prolific performer across stage and screen, dies aged 94As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decadesAndrew PulverTue 18 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhyllida Law, whose prolific acting career encompassed a wide range of stage, TV and film roles – a number of which were alongside her daughters, Emma and Sophie Thompson – has died aged 94. Her personal manager, Jacky Leggo, said in a statement that she “died supremely peacefully at home, surrounded by all her family”.Born in Glasgow in 1932, Law was accepted at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre school – initially intending to be a stage designer but then switching to acting. She appeared in a number of Bristol Old Vic productions in the 1950s, and it was there she met Eric Thompson, a fellow actor, whom she married in 1957.View image in fullscreenLaw alongside daughter Sophie Thompson in 1996’s Emma.Photograph: Matchmaker/Miramax/Kobal/ShutterstockLaw broke into TV in the late 50s, with numerous appearances on screen throughout the 60s in shows such as Dr Finlay’s Casebook, Dixon of Dock Green and The Troubleshooters. By the end of the 1970s she had appeared in significant stage roles, including replacing Carole Boyer in the original 1967 production of A Day in the Death of Joe Egg after it transferred to the Comedy theatre in London from the Citizens in Glasgow, and appearing alongside Alec Guinness in the first run of John Mortimer’s A Voyage Round My Father at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in 1971, and Alan Bennett’s Habeas Corpus at the Oxford Playhouse in 1973. She also joined the National Theatre, appearing in 1979 in Somerset Maugham’s For Services Rendered and JB Priestley’s When We Are Married, and was cast in the first London run of the English-language musical version of La Cage aux Folles.From the late 80s she achieved more prominence in film, appearing alongside daughter Emma in Peter’s Friends (directed by Thompson’s then husband Kenneth Branagh), Much Ado About Nothing (again with Thompson and Branagh), and the Gwyneth Paltrow-led adaptation of Jane Austen’s Emma alongside her other daughter Sophie. Law then appeared with Emma – playing mother and daughter – in The Winter Guest, Alan Rickman’s feature film directing debut, which won considerable acclaim.View image in fullscreenLaw and Emma Thompson in The Winter Guest.Photograph: Album/AlamyLaw continued to appear in high-prestige TV shows, including Waking the Dead, Rosemary & Thyme, Foyle’s War, Doc Martin and Agatha Christie’s Poirot, and had a recurring role in the Stephen Fry lawyer comedy drama Kingdom as Fry’s Aunt Auriel. Her final screen role was in the 2020 romance Then Came You, written by and starring Kathie Lee Gifford.Law was married to Thompson until his death in 1982, and is survived by their children, Emma and Sophie.Explore more on these topicsFilmTelevisionEmma ThompsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brain-breaking sex, bad boys in leather and queer glory: why TV vampires are so intoxicating | Television | The Guardian
description: The Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced blood
Author: Kayleigh Dray
Headline: The Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced blood
Content: Sam Reid as the eponymous glam rocker in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudView image in fullscreenSam Reid as the eponymous glam rocker in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudTelevisionBrain-breaking sex, bad boys in leather and queer glory: why TV vampires are so intoxicatingThe Vampire Lestat has seduced fans around the world with his eye-popping antics. But this obsession with hot vamps goes way beyond forbidden love, bare chests and a taste for LSD-laced bloodKayleigh DrayTue 18 Aug 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want TV audiences to forgive a fictional man for absolutely anything, just sharpen his fangs and stick him in velvet. Case in point? The horny musical drama The Vampire Lestat, which became a cult hit in the US earlier this year. The show has now arrived in the UK and Sam Reid’s searing performance as Lestat has fans on their knees.The Vampire Lestat review – a mega-fun glam-rock musical … with bloodsuckingRead moreThe first two seasons, which went by the title Interview With the Vampire, were about the “interview” in which Louis (Jacob Anderson) tells a journalist about his toxic relationship with Lestat. Now, the focus has shifted to Lestat – hence the new title and new narrator – as the golden-locked prince of darkness swaps centuries of secrecy for glam-rock stardom.View image in fullscreenToxic love … Jacob Anderson as Louis de Pointe du Lac in The Vampire Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC All Rights Reserved/Sophie GiraudReid turned to bootlegs of David Bowie’s 1974 Cracked Actor tour for inspiration on the “showmanship, magic and mystery” needed to hypnotise an arena, with the result that Lestat now embodies a magnificent “dandy of the underworld” energy. He writhes, growls and grinds on stage as he plays the fiddle and belts out ridiculously campy songs. He wears glittery eyeshadow, his hair is in ribboned pigtails. He appears to have lost his shirt permanently and bares his scarred chest to adoring fans, while singing “Don’t wanna learn another TikTok dance/Wanna stay in bed, eating black liquorice” and “You can’t fuck away the loneliness / It’ll wait til you’re done / Til you come / Like a vampire”. Off-stage he is in a sexual relationship with his mother, gets high off LSD-laced blood and comes out with phrases such as: “I carry with me an immortal erection.”View image in fullscreenBreakthrough role … Alexander Skarsgård in True Blood.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIt’s not the first time a vampire has sucked in audiences. Eric Northman’s full-frontal glory as he lounges on an ice peak reading a book in True Blood was Alexander Skarsgård’s breakthrough role, while Lady Gaga’s The Countess in season five of American Horror Story proved that bloodlust is the ultimate couture accessory. Endlessly seductive vamps show up, too, in The Vampire Diaries, Supernatural and the entire cast ofWhat We Do in the Shadows, who are somehow ridiculously hot despite being total buffoons (Matt Berry has ruined normal men for me). Claes Bang in the BBC’s otherwise chaotic Dracula wasundeniably easy on the eye, and even Jeff’s fleeting stint as a vampire in Community’s Horror Fiction in Seven Spooky Steps episode sees Annie swoon over her tame bloodsucker, breathlessly sighing, “Look how much I’ve changed you!” when he begins quoting literature at her.View image in fullscreenHigh vamp … Lady Gaga as the Countess in American Horror Story: Hotel.Photograph: Suzanne Tenner/APWhy we are so hooked? Vampires embody absolute freedom, power, immortality, beauty and often forbidden love. They can also tap directly into our shadow selves, serving as the ultimate canvas for the toxic romantic tropes we secretly indulge in on screen. (Think about it: pop culture has long conditioned us to desire the romcom hero who relentlessly pursues a female lead despite being told no until he wears her down, such as Joe Fox (Tom Hanks) in You’ve Got Mail orJoe Goldberg (Penn Badgeley) in You.) When it comes to vampires as romantic figures, we’re leaning heavily into the ultimate “I can fix him” trope. What is more intoxicating than a dangerous immortal who wipes out entire towns, yet kneels at your feet?Just look at Spike inBuffy the Vampire Slayer– the ultimate leather-bound bad boy who is quite literally “changed” by the love of a good slayer. On the flipside, you have Angel, whose curse dictates that one night of mindblowing sex with Buffy literally breaks his brain, shatters his morality and turns him back into a psychopathic monster.View image in fullscreenMindblowing … Sarah Michelle Gellar as Buffy and David Boreanaz as Angel in Buffy the Vampire Slayer.Photograph: 1997 Twentieth Century Fox Film CorporationAnd there’s even more beneath the surface level of camp leather jackets, bad-boy redemptions and jawlines that could cut glass. In her 2024 book, Vampires: A Handbook of History & Lore of the Undead, Agnes Hollyhock explores how gothic fiction used the vampire to subvert Victorian moral panic. In a society that strictly forbade non-normative intimacy, the vampiric bite symbolised forbidden desire in the form of a total surrender of control, an exchange of bodily fluid and a rejection of polite society.Disrupting heteronormative expectations, vampires exist entirely outside the linear mortal timeline. They don’t participate in conventional family units or rigid gendered expectations. Their power relies on aura and seduction rather than traditional gender roles.Lestat embodies all of this in his flamboyant, powerful and unapologetically queer glory, which is why we can’t stop thinking about his unhinged romance with Louis (that passionate kiss-turned-skull-smashing-murder in season two lives rent-free in fans’ heads). It’s why he’s become a poster-vamp for sexual freedom. And why we can apparently all get on board with his sordid affair with Gabriella (Jennifer Ehle), the lover he turned into a vampire, who also happens to be his mother.View image in fullscreenSexy buffoon … Matt Berry as Laszlo in What We Do in the Shadows.Photograph: Russ MartinIs it the danger? The immortal good looks? The need to be set free from societal constraints? The TV vampire is irresistible. No wonder so many of us are queueing up for a bite from Lestat.The Vampire Lestat is on iPlayer now in the UK, on SBS and SBS on Demand in Australia and on AMC+ in the US.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionHorror (TV)Anne RicefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Phoebe Bridgers review – high priestess of ambiguity turns grief Technicolor in intimate church show | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: Ahead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astounding
Author: Aimee Cliff
Headline: Ahead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astounding
Content: ‘I really did scrape the bottom of my guts’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in JulyPhotograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I really did scrape the bottom of my guts’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in JulyPhotograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesPhoebe BridgersReviewPhoebe Bridgers review – high priestess of ambiguity turns grief Technicolor in intimate church showUnion Chapel, LondonAhead of playing arenas this winter, Bridgers gives her third album, Lost Weekend, a stripped-back UK debut that makes its bewitching songs sound even more astoundingAimee CliffTue 18 Aug 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree days after the rapturous release of her third album,Lost Weekend, Phoebe Bridgers invites 900 people into her bedroom to hear her play some of its devastating songs live – or at least, that’s how it feels inside Union Chapel in north London on this Monday night. With Bridgers plopped on a throw-covered sofa, surrounded by lava lamps and with a TV showing the bouncing DVD logo screensaver, it becomes easy to forget the Victorian gothic architecture looming above our heads.This intimate scene is the indie superstar’s hugely anticipated first solo UK show since 2022, and the reverent awe in the church is palpable. Fans have obediently locked away their phones in magnetic pouches – as they will also have to on her arena run later this year – and fidget in the pews clutching CDs and T-shirts emblazoned with the artwork for her new record. You can hear a proverbial pin drop when Bridgers opens the show by belting her breakout song Motion Sickness solo with her guitar, her voice somersaulting around the domed ceiling. (After this, she is joined on stage by two bandmates, Nick White and Christian Lee Hutson.) But Bridgers, who hums with a slightly nervous energy, characteristically pierces through any solemnity by encouraging us to scream and sing along as the gig rolls on. After all, she quips: “God’s watching – fuckin’ freak.”The jokes and the screams feel like necessary pressure-relief valves, as Lost Weekend takes centre stage at this show. Focused primarily on the tangled knot of grief she feels for her father, who died in 2023, the album is a vividly cathartic body of work that, as Bridgers puts it: “I really did scrape from the bottom of my guts.” It is also the artist’s most musically adventurous outing yet, cloaked in a bewitching fog of crackling ambience reminiscent of Grouper, and surreal, robotic vocoder. But for this release show, she dismantles the songs to their parts, with just two guitars, keys, harmonica and the occasional addition of percussion and ghostly FX.Phoebe Bridgers: I Can’t Wait – videoIn this spectral, spare form, the songs are even more astounding. You can really hear the bristling, soft rage as Bridgers sings: “Sometimes I want you back / But not today,” on Still Standing, an unflinching portrait of her “complicated” relationship with her dad. (This song and others reference his physical abuse of Bridgers’ mother.) Likewise, the seething lyrics of The Governor’s Waltz, which appears to reflect on the breakdown of her engagement to Paul Mescal, seem to send a shiver through the congregation. Her words cut even deeper when near-whispered.‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriterRead moreBut it’s not all quiet worship. At points, stomping percussion rises to the rafters, Bridgers uses effects to contort and throw her voice, and Hutson plays some of the most ominous harmonica ever heard on their rendition of Kill Me. Then, of course, there is the album’s title track, which cracks open from a soft ballad into a triumphant clatter and swell of strings, electronic chatter and disembodied voices.In the Union Chapel, the song’s climax is highlighted with UV light, giving Bridgers’ blond bob and the images of planets hung behind her a creepy glow. At first, the effect is so incongruous to be almost funny – but then its uncanniness starts to make sense. Bridgers is often described in shorthand as a purveyor of “sad songs”, but what her latest release proves more than ever is that her writing contains vast emotional worlds. On Lost Weekend, she sketches grief as the sharpest edge of life: a time when your memories of the past feel so intense as to be Technicolor, and the present can feel like a distant fog; when emotions are both muted and turned up to 11. It makes sense that on the first UK live outing for these deliciously complex songs, there is humour and surrealism to be found even in the devastating dark.Explore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: By a Thread review – soulful circus with a sprinkle of magic | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Emotional group dynamics and individual skills make Melbourne’s One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genre
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Emotional group dynamics and individual skills make Melbourne’s One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genre
Content: Now that’s a good idea … One Fell Swoop Circus: By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNow that’s a good idea … One Fell Swoop Circus: By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBy a Thread review – soulful circus with a sprinkle of magicAssembly Rooms, EdinburghEmotional group dynamics and individual skills make One Fell Swoop stand out in the crowded circus genreLyndsey WinshipTue 18 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou cannot move at the Edinburgh fringe for circus shows. There are so many people in this city who can climb a rope, hang upside down, swing on a trapeze – so how do you make a show special when plenty of other folks are hawking the same skills?Melbourne companyOne Fell Swoop Circushave worked out a way, sprinkling a bit of magic on their festival offering. It’s a show that wasoriginally made a decade ago, but had its Edinburgh debut last year and was such a hit that they have brought it back. Like many of the best shows, it’s really just one good idea, with all the juice thoroughly squeezed out of it across the course of an hour. That idea being: one giant rope, two pulleys, seven bodies, and everything they can do together.View image in fullscreenGroup hang … By a Thread.Photograph: Jane Hobson/ShutterstockLooped from the ceiling, the rope becomes a slackline to walk across, a trapeze to swing on, a vertical climb, a diagonal slide, and so much more. It’s all gently paced with a dreamy mood, but steadily engrossing, the soulful soundtrack slowly casting a spell. The skills are a given, but it becomes a great piece of theatre when the performers’ personalities start to emerge – the mechanics of the rope plus the dynamics of the group, that’s what is interesting.Plus there’s their individual skills, like Ellie Grow’s mind-blowing handstands. She’s more secure on two palms than most people are on two feet, which means she can turn what could be a quick trick into choreography, with rhythm, timing and wit. Then there’s a beautifully tender duet, multiple metres up in the air, that’s not really about acrobatics but human connection, hands and eyes meeting, warmth and friendship, all subtly done. The emotion feels real, and the tone is perfectly judged. Ropes aside, that’s what really elevates these acrobats.AtAssembly Rooms, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Then touringAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026CircusTheatreDanceEdinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bigfoot Ripped My Dog in Half I Saw It review – Xhloe and Natasha create a monster hit | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treat
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: With physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treat
Content: Minimal props … Xhloe and Natasha in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMinimal props … Xhloe and Natasha in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBigfoot Ripped My Dog in Half I Saw It review – Xhloe and Natasha create a monster hitSummerhall, EdinburghWith physical and vocal agility, the tricksy clown duo trigger an avalanche of misinformation in this feverish treatChris WiegandTue 18 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a show every bit as breathless as its title, stoked by bursts of high-energy 90s chart hits and delivered just as slickly byXhloe and Natasha. Their physical precision is such that it’s almost as if these camo clowns with their rosy cheeks and tearstained eyes are executing a mission.The duo have previously portrayed confused cowboys (And Then the Rodeo Burned Down), spiralling housewives (What If They Ate the Baby?) and spit-promise scouts (A Letter to Lyndon B Johnson or God: Whoever Reads This First). Here the terrain is recognisable from those shows yet so much more expansive as they play numerous locals, from the corner shop to the highest office, in an Appalachian town. It gives more chance to showcase their vocal, as well as physical, agilities.View image in fullscreenLight touch … Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMostly they’re in character as a couple of teenagers who wind up in trouble until a scapegoat arrives in the unlikely form of Bigfoot. Soon other townspeople are saddling Sasquatch with assorted crimes. Like their previous shows it works on several levels, capturing a specific locale and era while remaining timeless and giving a state of the union address that is bang up to date. Misinformation, misdirection and flagrant cover-ups create a daisy chain of lies. The environment is treated like dirt. Division and suspicion are actively encouraged and enthusiastically embraced. Official statements from on top are meaninglessly empty. The Stop sign that looms in the background seems to call for nothing less than a complete reset for the US.I Made You a Mixtape review – frothy fringe fun as dorm mates party like it’s 1999Read moreIn a production co-directed by Tom Costello, the pair use minimal props and that sign is adorned with Bigfoot’s furry mitts, clawed shoes and a mask with its mouth agape – all detachable and wielded to schlocky effect. There is some of the duo’s signature off-kilter wordplay and bamboozling tactics. It is sometimes slightly too on the nose, and I missed the emotional hit of the friendship in their LBJ story. But what’s again almightily impressive, from a show punctuated with floor-trembling thuds, is the duo’s light touch in handling heavy subject matter.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 7–26 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Robot helpers and flying houses: Edinburgh fringe tips for families | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From wacky versions of The ABC Song to Quentin Blake’s eccentric Mrs Armitage, these five shows offer fun for young audiences
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: From wacky versions of The ABC Song to Quentin Blake’s eccentric Mrs Armitage, these five shows offer fun for young audiences
Content: Gleeful abandon … Bleep Bleep.Photograph: Remke SpijkersView image in fullscreenGleeful abandon … Bleep Bleep.Photograph: Remke SpijkersEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewRobot helpers and flying houses: Edinburgh fringe tips for familiesFrom wacky versions of The ABC Song to Quentin Blake’s eccentric Mrs Armitage, these five shows offer fun for young audiencesMark FisherTue 18 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBleep Bleep!Underbelly until 31 AugustImagineDiane Morgan’s Ann Droidfor the over fives crowd. A man takes delivery of a lifesize robot helper, only to find this eager-to-please android takes his tasks too seriously. Creating props out of hastily sketched illustrations, he takes a drill to the wall to hang up a picture and hoovers the stage (and some of the audience) with gleeful abandon. His attempts to sing his new owner to sleep only keep him awake.All the while, in this lighthearted production by Dender Cartoontheater from the Netherlands, Thanos Fotiadis builds a quirky soundtrack from guitar loops, vocal ticks and assorted percussion instruments. Even if the show loses some discipline as the robot’s owner makes his escape via submarine and space rocket, it continues to delight the young audience.Don’t Wait for Me …French Institute in Scotland until 23 AugustView image in fullscreenHome truths … Vera Rozanova in Don’t Wait For Me.Photograph: David LippeYou know that thing when you wake up and your house has disappeared? This is the debacle facing the little puppet child at the heart of this delightful show, which has the added novelty of being bilingual.Aimed at the over fours, Vera Rozanova’s high-precision production takes us on a night-time adventure in which houses take flight like birds leaving their nests. To track down your own house is a challenge: they can be too small, or too easy to get trapped inside of; they may even transform into a galleon on which to sail the high seas.Switching by the line from French to English, Rozanova is thinking about displacement, finding yourself in strange lands and learning that home is where the heart is. It looks and sounds gorgeous.FloatPleasance at EICC until 23 AugustView image in fullscreenSublime …  Float by Starcatchers.Photograph: Ben WingerNot just what a baby needs, Float is also what every parent needs. Aimed at those under 12 months, Kerry Cleland’s show for Starcatchers is a sublime aquatic-themed experience, staged for three hours at a time, allowing you to come and go.But why would you want to leave? Taking place around a translucent barrel of water, with the audience snuggling down on beanbags, Float is hypnotic and dreamlike. It shifts imperceptibly from the plip-plop of vocal improvisation to the gentle movement of dancers, catching the light in their silvery costumes and creating a breeze with the sail-like flaps at the top of Alison Brown’s set.There is a swirling solo in the barrel itself and, when the audience gets sleepy, warm blankets for everyone. Quite the most beguiling show on the fringe.The LettermanGilded Balloon Teviot until 31 AugustView image in fullscreenGentle comedy … The Letterman.Photograph: Barroz ProductionsIn this silent introduction to the alphabet, Bryce Flint-Somerville does things with his eyes that other performers could not do without lengthy verbal exposition. With the hangdog look of a naughty schoolboy, he is left unsupervised and makes the most of his freedom. Wordlessly, he makes his intentions clear, instructing the audience to join in with his pranks.In a gentle comedy for the over fives, he sits on a forbidden chair before sharpening someone else’s pencil and turning it into a balloon-popping weapon. Meanwhile, the towering set of boxes showing every letter of the alphabet except one is taking on a life of its own. He tries hard to keep the letters from falling and even harder to keep them in order while we sing truncated versions of The ABC Song. It is silly and, possibly, even educational.Quentin Blake’s Mrs Armitage on WheelsAssembly George Square until 30 AugustView image in fullscreenWholesome fun … Quentin Blake’s Mrs Armitage on Wheels.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicFans ofQuentin Blake’s Box of Treasures, the BBC’s adaptation of the illustrator’s charming books, will be well at home in a quaintly old-fashioned landscape of Victoria sponges, letterboxes and hedgehogs. Here, the eccentric inventor Mrs Armitage makes repeated attempts to visit her cousin two villages down. Forever distracted, she never quite gets there.In Samantha Lane’s version with Esk, we also get jolly songs about making the “ordinary extraordinary”, well sung by Lottie Johnson in the title role, supported by puppeteers Christopher Dobson and Duncan Taylor (taking control of Breakspear, the enthusiastic dog). It is bright, mainstream entertainment played inside and outside an inventive wooden shed designed by Ryan Dawson Laight. If it loses some of the ironic wit of the original, it offers wholesome fun all the same.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalChildrenTheatreChildren's theatreQuentin BlakePuppetryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Temi Wilkey: Lover Girl review – wildly intimate comedy goes to infinity and beyond | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Both outrageous and tender, this stellar follow-up to Main Character Energy gives new meaning to the idea of body language
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Both outrageous and tender, this stellar follow-up to Main Character Energy gives new meaning to the idea of body language
Content: This one’s from the heart … Temi Wilkey in Lover Girl.Photograph: Jonny RuffView image in fullscreenThis one’s from the heart … Temi Wilkey in Lover Girl.Photograph: Jonny RuffEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTemi Wilkey: Lover Girl review – wildly intimate comedy goes to infinity and beyondPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghBoth outrageous and tender, this stellar follow-up to Main Character Energy gives new meaning to body languageChris WiegandTue 18 Aug 2026 02.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 02.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemi Wilkey serenades us, asks if we fancy her and wonders if the love of her life could be here right now. The G spot? Call it the T spot, says Temi, before popping the question: “Do you want to come inside my Infinity Pussy?”It’s seductive stuff and, naturally, the room agrees to take things to the next level. Cue a conversation between Wilkey and, with a soundscape to make you blush and a quick change into a ruffled reddish peignoir, her forthright vagina.View image in fullscreenTheatrical ritual … Temi Wilkey in Lover Girl.Photograph: Jonny RuffThis sets up a spiky duologue initially akin to how Elouise Eftos, also juggling roles, is emboldened and mocked by the goddess of love in her equally fun fringe hourAphrodite. Wilkey, more briefly, touches on Greek mythology too. Both shows speak from the heart – directly, in Wilkey’s case, as she gently cradles herself to act out the role of that organ, not blithely pumping away but aching and in need of healing.Is it character comedy if you’re portraying your own nether regions? For Wilkey that’s not (just) a route to rude laughs but a bid to understand how she fits together as a person. The show follows her journey to self-love – which is also the key relationship inElf Lyons’s memorable breakup show this year.Directed by Ragevan Vasan, with a glam stage design akin to her 2024 debutMain Character Energy, Wilkey’s Lover Girl is in the theatre not comedy section of the festival. She isalso a playwrightand its stirring final minutes combine free-flowing performance poetry with intimate ritual. Not that she is short on one-liners, including how British culture is frozen in time for her Nigerian family (“less gen X, more Gen Austen”), while she squeezes a lot of juice fromRon DeSantis’s “don’t say gay” edict for Florida. It’s not the only bit where the gags arrive from all angles.The storytelling comes with bursts of dance and she sings snippets of lyrics (including from Tevin Campbell’s Can We Talk) to locate autobiographical scenes yet expand them into a recognisable shared experience. Music is also used to distinguish between her notions of straight and queer sex as she brings wild physicality first to a bluntly staccato accompaniment and then to multitudinous free jazz.It’s a stellar sophomore fringe hour, still full of main character energy but slowly building in communal hope as she calls for social change. Standup may not get much more inward-looking thanthatearly offer to the audience but Wilkey clearly cares deeply about what’s happening in the outside world too.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)TheatreComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’ | US television | The Guardian
description: Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’
Content: Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week on 25 June 2013 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageView image in fullscreenWladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week on 25 June 2013 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageUS televisionWladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’Richard LuscombeTue 18 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHayden Panettiere’s daughter will be raised to remember her mother’s “immense talent” and “incredible career”, according toa tributeposted on social media on Tuesday by Wladimir Klitschko, the ex-lineal world heavyweight boxing champion and the late Hollywood actor’s former partner.Their daughter, Kaya, has been raised by the Ukrainian retired boxer since 2018, when Panettiere ceded full custody to concentrate on her battles with alcoholism, depression and substance abuse.Her death in Greenville, South Carolina, was reportedon Sunday, with no cause given.Hayden Panettiere – a life in picturesRead more“Our family is going through a time of profound shock and grief,” Klitschko wrote in the Instagram post, which featured a photograph of himself and Panettiere smiling at a beach, with Kaya – whose face is obscured – perched on her mother’s shoulders.“The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon. Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.”The message also referenced the troubles that the Nashville and Heroes actor had experienced at a young age, following a succession of child stars who faced laterchallenges or tragedy.“She built an incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry,” Klitschko wrote of Panettiere. “Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives.“To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was.”Klitschko also sent his condolences to Panettiere’s grieving parents, friends and fans.“Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon,” boxing’s lineal heavyweight champion from 2009 to 2015 wrote. “I ask everyone to please respect our family’s feelings and privacy during this incredibly difficult time. For now, this is all I wish to say.“Rest easy, Hayden. May you find eternal peace.”In May, Panettiere expressed hope that she would one day be reunited with her daughter, who was born in 2014.“I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she toldpodcaster Jay Shettyin an emotional interview.“I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.”Hollywood continues to fail child stars and Hayden Panettiere is the latest casualty | Jesse HassengerRead moreKlitschko and Panettiere met at a book launch party in 2009, when the actor, then aged 20, was already a television star for her appearances as fictional high school cheerleader Claire Bennet in Heroes. After first splitting in 2011, they remained close friends and became engaged in 2013. Panettiere gave birth to Kaya a year later.The actor struggled with postpartum depression, and the couple split for good in 2018, with Kaya spending time with her father at residences in Florida and Europe, E! News reported at the time.Panettiere then had an on-again, off-again relationship with Brian Hickerson. TheAssociated Pressand NBC News on Tuesdayreportedthey had obtained a police report that said Hickerson and his brother, Zach, were at the scene inside the apartment complex where Panettiere died.The report said Hickerson showed police “a bag of medication” that Panettiere was taking at the time of her death, according to NBC.Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson was marred by domestic abuse allegations. He was arrested multiple times and reportedly jailed in 2021 after pleading no contest to domestic abuse charges.Explore more on these topicsUS televisionWladimir KlitschkoUS television industryTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The truth about Diana’: Charles Spencer to publish book about late sister | Diana, Princess of Wales | The Guardian
description: Earl says he wanted to ‘write down my own thoughts and memories’ with 30th anniversary of Diana’s death ‘on the skyline’
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: Earl says he wanted to ‘write down my own thoughts and memories’ with 30th anniversary of Diana’s death ‘on the skyline’
Content: Diana and Charles Spencer at a ball in London in 1985. Spencer said his sister had been ‘a one-off, dynamic character, full of love’.Photograph: Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDiana and Charles Spencer at a ball in London in 1985. Spencer said his sister had been ‘a one-off, dynamic character, full of love’.Photograph: Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty ImagesDiana, Princess of Wales‘The truth about Diana’: Charles Spencer to publish book about late sisterEarl says he wanted to ‘write down my own thoughts and memories’ with 30th anniversary of Diana’s death ‘on the skyline’Ella CreamerTue 18 Aug 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharles Spencer is to publish a book about his sister Diana in September.In the book – titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – Spencer recounts the story of Diana’s life and the week of her death. It marks “the first time that Earl Spencer has spoken openly and at length about his sister”, according to the book’s publisher, the Penguin imprint Michael Joseph. The book will be released on 22 September in the UK.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Penguin“With the 30th anniversary of Diana’s tragic death on the skyline, I’ve been inundated yet again with requests for interviews about my sister,” said Spencer. “This has convinced me to write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time.”“The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral. As with my eulogy, I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.”Spencer delivered his sister’s eulogy at Westminster Abbey in September 1997, after her death on 31 August.Daniel Bunyard, publishing director at Penguin Michael Joseph, said the book contained “many revelations that will draw considerable attention”, but was also “a fitting tribute to the beloved woman who was Princess Diana”.Spencer said: “I hope this book will be of interest to the many who still cherish the memory of Diana when she was alive.“I would be delighted if those too young to remember her in her heyday feel, after reading this, that they ‘get’ who she really was: a one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.”Explore more on these topicsDiana, Princess of WalesMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Kanye West to become biggest western act to play in Russia since start of Ukraine war | Kanye West | The Guardian
description: Artist also known as Ye, who has attracted controversy in recent years over antisemitic outbursts, to perform two shows in October
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Artist also known as Ye, who has attracted controversy in recent years over antisemitic outbursts, to perform two shows in October
Content: Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, has become an increasingly controversial figure in recent years.Photograph: Scott Dudelson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYe, formerly known as Kanye West, has become an increasingly controversial figure in recent years.Photograph: Scott Dudelson/Getty ImagesKanye WestKanye West to become biggest western act to play in Russia since start of Ukraine warArtist also known as Ye, who has attracted controversy in recent years over antisemitic outbursts, to perform two shows in OctoberPjotr SauerTue 18 Aug 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYe, the rapper formerly known asKanye West, will perform two shows in St Petersburg this October, becoming the most well-known western star to play in Russia since its invasion of Ukraine four years ago.The artist has attracted controversy in recent years, with his antisemitic outbursts and expressions of sympathy towards nazism increasingly overshadowing his music and making some countries and venues uneasy about hosting his tour.He is set to perform on 10 and 11 October at St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena.Russian fans rushed to secure tickets after the shows were announced on Monday. Nearly all of the most expensive tickets, costing upwards of $1,850, were snapped up within hours, according to the concerts’ website. By the evening, the cheapest tickets, priced at about $105, had also sold out.Yehad been rumoured to be planning a performance in Russia for some time. Speculation intensified in 2024, when he travelled to Moscow to attend the birthday celebrations of Gosha Rubchinskiy, the Russian fashion designer and longtime collaborator with the rapper.As well asa series of antisemitic remarks, Ye has drawn outrage through his embrace of Nazi imagery, even selling T-shirts bearing swastikas and releasing a song titled Heil Hitler.View image in fullscreenYe performs at Riyadh Air Metropolitano stadium in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Mercedes Ortuno/EPAHe has since tried to rehabilitate his image,taking out a full-page advert in the Wall Street Journalapologising for his antisemitic behaviour and discussing his struggles with mental health. “I am not a Nazi or an antisemite,” he wrote. “I love Jewish people.”But the apology has done little to quell the backlash. Yehas faced resistance to performing in several European countries, with planned concerts inthe UK, France andItaly cancelledand calls elsewhere for him to be barred from performing.He has found a more receptive audience elsewhere. A record-breaking concert in Istanbul drew 118,000 fans, while 70,000 came to watch him in Tbilisi. Earlier this month, he also performed a sold-out show in Almaty, Kazakhstan.His St Petersburg dates are also likely to draw pushback within Russia, where conservative activists have increasingly sought to sever the country’s ties with western cultural influence, and where expressions of support for nazism can carry lengthy prison sentences.The politician Nikolay Novichkov has already called for an investigation into Ye’s past remarks praising Hitler, including his 2022 claim that there were “good things” about the Nazi leader. Novichkov also told the Russian outlet Ostorozhno Novosti that the concerts should be cancelled unless the singer publicly expresses “moral support for Russia and the special military operation”.Ye’s visit could nevertheless offer a propaganda coup, bolstering the Kremlin’s efforts to show that Russia remains connected to the outside world despite sweeping sanctions and calls for cultural boycotts.A trickle of western artists have performed in Russia in recent years, including Lil Pump, Flo Rida, and Jason Derulo.Explore more on these topicsKanye WestRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCNOW/Bancroft review – McGill is a stylish soloist in Kahane’s likable clarinet concerto | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: With Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concert
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: With Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concert
Content: Silky smooth … clarinetist Anthony McGill with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales.Photograph: BBC/ Angus RaceView image in fullscreenSilky smooth … clarinetist Anthony McGill with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales.Photograph: BBC/ Angus RaceProms 2026ReviewBBCNOW/Bancroft review – McGill is a stylish soloist in Kahane’s likable clarinet concertoRoyal Albert Hall, LondonWith Stravinsky and Copland also on the programme, this was a lively if uneven concertClive PagetTue 18 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn their different ways, both Stravinsky and Copland turned to the vernacular to lend authenticity and atmosphere to their ballet scores. Stravinsky incorporated folk tunes and popular song to depict the hurdy-gurdy players and wet nurses of St Petersburg’s bustling Shrovetide fair in Petrushka. For Billy the Kid, Copland used cowboy songs to paint a wild west settlement with its outlaws, saloons and gunfights. Fast-forward 80 years and Gabriel Kahane added a flavour of folk music, though without quoting anything specific, to spice up his clarinet concerto. Written for New York Philharmonic principal clarinet Anthony McGill, the work’s European premiere formed the centrepiece of a lively concert conducted with visible enthusiasm by Ryan Bancroft.The concerto opened with McGill slipping in seamlessly over shimmering tuned percussion and string glissandi. Elegant scalar passages led into a songful section with a jazz-meets-klezmer vibe. This is immensely likable music, with McGill a confident and stylish soloist. Orchestral textures featured pianos – both grand and muted upright – as well as celesta and percussion, the latter more often than not played unconventionally. The slow movement with its drawn-out lyrical lines found McGill cucumber cool, before eerie bowed vibraphone and a hair-raising cadenza launched a finale with a touch of an Irish jig about it. Kahane himself added a nice personal touch, taking to the stage to sing and play piano for McGill’s silky smooth encore.The Copland got off to an uneven start, the orchestra never quite capturing the mystery of the open prairie, though at full-throttle they certainly caught its majesty. In a neat move, Bancroft turned to the audience to play a mean tin whistle and introduce the frontier town. The Mexican dance, gun battle and celebratory polka were tight and spirited, even if there were occasional moments of slack ensemble.Petrushka suffered from a similarly rocky opening, not helped by Bancroft bringing down the baton while the audience was still applauding. Individual solos were characterfully pungent though not all were ideally secure. Clarinet, bassoon and piano stood out, with a hearty laugh for the flatulent rasp of the contrabassoon. Elsewhere, though, boisterous excitement sometimes came at the expense of nuance and balance.Available on BBC Sounds until 12 October. title: TV tonight: a devastating drama about the mass removal of Canada’s Indigenous children  | Television | The Guardian
description: A young woman sacrifices everything to find the siblings she lost in the sixties. Plus: Ricky Gervais jumps aboard the Magical Sitcom Tour. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A young woman sacrifices everything to find the siblings she lost in the sixties. Plus: Ricky Gervais jumps aboard the Magical Sitcom Tour. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Heartache … Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.View image in fullscreenHeartache … Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: a devastating drama about the mass removal of Canada’s Indigenous childrenA young woman sacrifices everything to find the siblings she lost in the 1960s. Plus: Ricky Gervais jumps aboard the Magical Sitcom Tour. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Hannah VerdierandPhil HarrisonTue 18 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLittle Bird9pm, Sky AtlanticA devastating drama aboutthe “Sixties Scoop”– when Canadian authorities enabled a mass removal of Indigenous children from their families and put them into the welfare system. Twentysomething Esther Rosenblum is investigating how she came to be adopted as a five-year-old in Montreal and is looking for her estranged siblings. Flashbacks to 15 years earlier show what happened after the night they were taken from their parents.Hollie RichardsonRace Against the Tide7.30pm, BBC TwoThe Bake Off-ification of TV continues apace, with this super-gentle sand-sculpting contest based on a Canadian series. Iain Stirling hosts, as pairs of pros and amateurs team up to craft impressive beach-based artworks. But who will be the ace of spades, and who will be all washed up?Hannah J DaviesThe Great ADHD Myth?8pm, Channel 4This provocatively titled show has already received a backlash from attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) charities. “It’s certainly not a medical condition as far as I’m concerned,” says one GP, alongside others ready to question the disorder. NHS psychiatrist and writer Max Pemberton investigates and meets a young boy hoping to stop taking ADHD medication.HRCelebrity MasterChef9pm, BBC OneLove Island’s Shakira Khan, Olympic weightlifter Emily Campbell, ex-boybander Jay McGuiness, comedian Joe Pasquale and presenter Jason Mohammad try their luck in the kitchen. Whose trademark technique is “dash dash, sprinkle sprinkle”, and who’s asking for yet another plaster as they make a Frankenstein-inspired dish?Hannah VerdierJoe & David’s Magical Sitcom Tour9pm, U&GoldView image in fullscreenHyena laugh … David Earl, Ricky Gervais and Joe Wilkinson.Photograph: U&GoldThe patchiness of Ricky Gervais’s subsequent career doesn’t detract from the lightning-in-a-bottle brilliance of his and Stephen Merchant’s first creation The Office. The final of these sitcom journeys sees Joe Wilkinson and David Earl meet cast members, endure Gervais’s hyena laugh and cheerfully traipse around the filming venues (most of which have been knocked down).Phil HarrisonThe Vampire Lestat: Interview with the Vampire11.05pm, BBC Two“That’s right, I’m finally going to talk about … the queen.” The troubled vampire Lestat (Sam Reid) goes to great lengths to make new music (see: scorching himself in daylight to reach a perfectly pained pitch). More flashbacks explain why he’s so obsessed with music – and his time with the terrifying Queen Akasha.HRLive sportSuper League Rugby:Hull KR v Warrington7.30pm, Sky Sports Main Event.At Craven Park Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightReality TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sunrise by Téa Obreht review – secrets and myths in the American west  | Books | The Guardian
description: Set across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recorded
Author: Nina Allan
Headline: Set across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recorded
Content: Wyoming where Sunrise is set.Photograph: Takako Phillips/Getty Images/500pxView image in fullscreenWyoming where Sunrise is set.Photograph: Takako Phillips/Getty Images/500pxBooksReviewSunrise by Téa Obreht review – secrets and myths in the American westSet across three interwoven timelines, this absorbing tale of an abandoned mining town explores courage, cowardice and how history is recordedNina AllanTue 18 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTéa Obreht’s novels teem with conflicting narratives, treacherous landscapes and speculative fictions. Her 2010 prizewinning debut,The Tiger’s Wife, examined themes of death, miracles and outsider status in the midst of a fictional Balkan war. Her fourth novel, Sunrise, returns to a western frontier haunted by ghosts and stalked by outlaws, a territory Obreht first explored in her second book,Inland.It is August 2024.Nina Terzic has just jumped – or was she pushed? – from a crash-landing Cessna into a lake somewhere in the mountains of Wyoming. She manages to swim to shore. There is no sign of her boyfriend Ben, who was in the plane with her, and her phone – though miraculously intact – has no signal. Nina, a postgraduate student, was supposed to be on holiday from her job as a live-in nanny in New York. We get the feeling that her relationship with Ben might have a darker underside.Nina quickly realises that she has happened upon a ghost town, one of the dozens of abandoned mining settlements scattered across the Old West. Exploring her surroundings further, she discovers the body of a woman hidden in a cellar. Beside the dead woman is a backpack containing a manuscript.The sequence that follows is a part of that manuscript. Its action takes place in 1902, in the mountain town of Sunrise – the ghost town as it was, before everyone left. A man named Anton Vargas has returned after a long absence. He carries with him an aura of celebrity – or is it notoriety? Only Fred Kipley, the town’s deputy, seems unsurprised to see him again. Kipley and Vargas were once involved in a shootout with local bandits. Their courageous actions saved lives and cast them as heroes; in the years since, their exploits have become the stuff of dime-store novels and wild west shows. But Vargas is not a well man, and he has business to settle in town before it is too late.double quotation markSunrise is an engrossing, original and thought-provoking novel, effortlessly readable and beautifully toldThe novel’s central section moves us a century forward to 2003. Sunrise is now a ghost town, the haunt of tourists. We meet Colin Yard, whose re-enactments of the Vargas story have become a valued source of income. Coll is greatly invested not only in Vargas’s story but in himself as the rightful guardian of that story. When he is contacted by a writer, Louise Hawley, asking if he will read the novel she has written about Vargas, Coll doesn’t pay her much attention. But Louise has her own deep-rooted connection with the place, and has discovered new information about Sunrise’s local hero that casts his story in a radically different light.Coll is furious at what he sees as her trespass: “We have this small thing, you know?… This tiny part of history that belongs to us. And I don’t want it to be fucked with or misinterpreted by someone who, frankly, doesn’t understand it or care about it.” Louise is adamant that the material she has unearthed deserves to be scrutinised. She argues that Coll himself has altered material facts to fit his re-enactments, that recorded history is by its nature partly fictitious. But for Coll, “his” Vargas is the only Vargas. How far will he be willing to go to protect his property?It is in this section that the novel’s themes and intertwined relationships come most persuasively to life. To Louise, Coll’s home town seems idyllic, the kind of place where neighbours are as good as family. But the situation is more fraught than surface impressions might suggest. Coll has recently had a disturbing altercation with the local bad boy, Bob Fournier. “Bob’s latest madness” is considered an outrage, yet no one has it in them to go up against him. Coll’s tacit condoning of Fournier’s actions has terrible consequences – not least for himself – but it is symptomatic also of a moral cowardice that will indirectly precipitate a greater calamity.Obreht’s portrayal of Colin Yard – his gradual, desperate slide from favoured son to villain of the piece – is a brilliant piece of theatre. Coll’s attempt to control the narrative is echoed in the bullying paternalism of John Daisy, the villain of Louise’s novel, a rich landowner and stockman whose “big house” casts its shadow over Sunrise back in 1902. Daisy is an avid collector of Native American artefacts and a supposed authority on Native traditions – too bad if his patronage does not extend to living people. Throughout all three of her interwoven timelines, Obreht raises similarly searching questions about courage and cowardice, idealism and pragmatism, and most of all about how history is recounted and who gets to own it.The novel does have its flaws. While the eventual revelations about Nina’s relationship with the ghastly Ben feel devastatingly real, it is difficult to ignore the loopholes in logic that characterise Nina’s portions of the narrative: how is she able to fall from a height on to water without getting injured? Having survived the crash unscathed, why does she waste time – and phone charge – trying to text her mother when she should be looking for a signal and calling 911? None of this detracts from the fact that Sunrise is an engrossing, original and thought-provoking novel, effortlessly readable and beautifully told. Given that most of what we come to know about Vargas is itself a series of fictions, it perhaps makes better sense to frame Nina’s miraculous survival as similarly mythic.Sunrise by Téa Obreht is published by W&N (£22).
