title: ‘There was a certain hostility’: how Wet Hot American Summer went from miss to hit | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation
Content: ‘…this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh’ … the poster art for Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Everett Collection, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreen‘…this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh’ … the poster art for Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Everett Collection, Inc./AlamyComedy films‘There was a certain hostility’: how Wet Hot American Summer went from miss to hitCritics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciationMatthew Cantorin Los AngelesTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 2001, the film critic Roger Ebertwrote a scathing film reviewin song form, with lyrics set to the tune of a classic song about summer camp. “Hello muddah, hello fadduh/ Here I am at Wet Hot American Summah,” it began. The review proceeded to mock the film Wet Hot American Summer in rhyme.Wet Hot American Summer: a cult classic reborn on NetflixRead moreTwenty-five years later, the film’s director and co-writer, David Wain, joined several of its stars on the vast lawn of the Autry Museum in Los Angeles to sing the review to a crowd of thousands, many of them wearing Camp Firewood T-shirts and 80s-style sweat absorbers. The performance preceded an anniversary screening of what has become a cult classic.Ebert was one of many critics at the time who seemed baffled by the comedy, which follows the absurd adventures of a group of horny and/or lovelorn counselors desperate to make the most of their final day of camp in 1981. But if those early critics didn’t quite get it, plenty of viewers later did – enough to warrant two Netflix series, a place on variouslistsof thebest filmsof the century, and a return to theaters this month to mark its 25th anniversary.What changed over the years? “I would say that it’s just a slow-burn kind of movie,” Wain says. “I think there was a certain hostility among the first round of critics, being like, ‘Why was this even made?’” But the film’s quiet release ultimately served it well. Fans who discovered the movie in the ensuing years felt like “‘this is my thing. You need to know about it,’” Wain says. “There was a sense of ownership over it that I think made people connect to it in a deeper way.”Perhaps one reason the movie didn’t initially land is that its humor is difficult to define. It’s not a satire or a coming-of-age film or a straight camp-movie parody, though it does play on tropes like the training montage and the “anonymously evil” kids at a rival camp. But mostly, the camp serves as a setting that lends itself to an extremely high joke rate.Early critics might have gone in “with a certain expectation of what a comedy is supposed to be” and ended up unsure what to make of the movie, Wain says. Sometimes “the joke is that it’s so unfunny, or that there’s not a joke”. And much of the humor plumbs the depths of ridiculousness in a way that might have left early viewers dumbfounded – like when a group of nerds saves the camp from falling space junk, or when the counselors plan a reunion for 10 years in the future but can’t decide whether to meet at 9am or 9.30. Wain describes the humor as “joyfully nihilistic”. The jokes warp the boundaries of reality, but they work because they never lose touch with it. “The actual bedrock of it is: what was summer camp like for me in real life? What was it like to be that age in real life? And then draping all of these spoofy things around that,” Wain says. The goal for the performances is sincerity rather than silliness.Nor does the movie have a clear central plotline – while our hearts are with Coop (Michael Showalter), the well-meaning counselor who keeps losing out to Paul Rudd’s monstrous but very hot Andy in his pursuit of Katie (Marguerite Moreau), the film’s many storylines are given fairly equal weight. That gives breathing room to the alarmingly starry cast.It was Bradley Cooper’s first film, and among the first for Elizabeth Banks; it also stars Janeane Garofalo, as a camp director courting a local astrophysicist, played by David Hyde Pierce; Rudd as a counselor who’d rather let kids risk drowning than have to look up from a makeout session; Amy Poehler as a camp theater director who berates child cast members for not being Broadway-caliber; and Molly Shannon as an arts and crafts teacher who receives life coaching from a 10-year-old. Showalter, who co-wrote the movie, has gone on to direct films including The Big Sick, The Idea of You and The Eyes of Tammy Faye.View image in fullscreenMichael Showalter, Christopher Meloni and AD Miles in Wet Hot American Summer.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy“We wrote the whole thing with no actors in mind at all,” Wain says. The goal was to make a summer-camp movie inspired by their time as campers and counselors themselves. “We just vomited out back and forth to each other everything we could think of that had to do with each of our summer camp experiences,” Wain says. Many of those experiences made it into the movie, including an improbable incident in which a counselor, played by Ken Marino, is rushing back to camp to meet a crush and drives straight into a tree. Wain was that counselor. “I had just turned 16,” he says. After dropping kids off for an overnight trip, “I left late at night instead of early in the next morning because I was desperate to see this girl I had just met, and I smashed the van into a tree.”Filming, at a camp in Pennsylvania, was difficult. It rained almost every day, meaning the crew had to find constant workarounds for planned outdoor scenes. Some were moved inside; others were shot under partial cover; audio had to be re-recorded because the rain made it impossible to hear. But the whole experience was reminiscent of summer camp, Wain says. “We were all away from home, out of town, on location, the first time doing this for so many of us, and we all bonded,” Wain says. (The shoot was the subject of a film of its own,Hurricane of Fun: The Making of Wet Hot.)That bond has clearly held. Since Wet Hot, Wain’s films have included Role Models, written with Marino; They Came Together, written with Showalter; and this year,Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass. All of them have included fellow members of sketch comedy troupe the State and other cast members from Wet Hot American Summer. “We were doing [TV series] The State when we were very, very young, and we recognized at the time, when we were 18, that this was a special thing that we found each other,” Wain says. “We said out loud at the time: ‘Let’s not ruin this.’” They vowed to keep working together, and they’ve succeeded. “We continually recognize that it’s a gift to be able to do that.”View image in fullscreenMichael Showalter and David Wain in 2001.Photograph: Leslie Hassler/APThough Gail Daughtry, also written with Marino, got a theatrical release, studios have beenreluctant to back comediesin recent years. This year has seen an overallbox-office resurgence, but comedies remain few and far between. “There’s talk of the pendulum swinging back and comedies coming back, and I hope that’s true,” Wain says. “I just feel like going to a movie theater to see a comedy and laughing together is at least as important to me as going to a movie to see a big spectacle together.”Wain has spent the summer with those audiences, visiting cities including New York, Waterville, Maine (where the film is set) and San Francisco with his and Marino’s band,Middle Aged Dad Jam Band, and performing Theodore Shapiro and Craig Wedren’s music from the film.“I don’t love always looking backwards. I try to stay focused on what’s now and in the future as much as I can,” he says. But the tour has been “absolutely wonderful. People come up to me and say really beautiful things about how this movie has entertained them, or affected them, or been a bonding thing with them and their friends or their loved ones, or got them through hard times,” he says. “And the other thing about it, which makes me so happy, is this is a movie that is by design not trying to achieve anything except to make you laugh.“There’s no point really being made so much as just: let’s have an hour and a half where we’re not freaking out about the end of the Earth.”Wet Hot American Summer is out again now in select US cinemas and available to rent digitallyExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Match review – gory and slyly satirical catfishing horror for the age of Hinge | Movies | The Guardian
description: Online dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shocker
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Online dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shocker
Content: Against the wall … Humberly González in Match.Photograph: Marcos Cruz/Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenAgainst the wall … Humberly González in Match.Photograph: Marcos Cruz/Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewMatch review – gory and slyly satirical catfishing horror for the age of HingeOnline dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shockerLeslie FelperinTue 18 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaola (Humberly González) is a pretty young woman about to turn 30 who hasn’t found herself a steady boyfriend – so, like many people of her generation, she’s on all the dating apps. The algorithm finds her match in Henry, who looks clean cut and kind eyed – or, at least, that’s what he seems from a very short video conversation on the phone, which breaks up due to bad signal. Paola’s sister Maria (Shaeane Jimenez) is visiting town because her and Paola’s father (Peter Butler) is going in for an operation, and warns her more trusting sibling not to accept Henry’s invitation to come to dinner at his house, away from the public gaze.Of course, Paola should have listened to her sister. The good looking guy (played by Luke Volker) turns out to have been a catfishing lure, and therealHenry (Jacques Adriaanse) looks like what you’d get if a troll mated with a slime mould. Plus, it’s actually Henry’s deranged mother, Lucille (a fantastic Dianne Simpson) who’s been writing all those courtly messages to Paola – who is soon sedated with drugged wine and wakes up about to be raped, exactly the sort of scenario youractualmother warned you about.Fortunately, it’s not all grim worst-nightmare-ever stuff, thanks to a slyly witty script credited to Al Kaplan and Jon Kaplan, directed with impish verve by Danishka Esterhazy. There are some very funny scenes, including a great two-hander between Lucille and another possible victim, Natalie (Nikita Faber), who hasn’t been completely honest about her own presentation online. The last stretch has lashings of practical effect gore to keep the genre fans happy, but it’s the sour social satire that lingers in the imagination afterwards.Match is on digital platforms from 24 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersDatingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Waves Turn review – the exhausting, joyful, boring, wondrous realities of new motherhood | Movies | The Guardian
description: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments
Content: In the trenches … Waves Turn.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenIn the trenches … Waves Turn.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewWaves Turn review – the exhausting, joyful, boring, wondrous realities of new motherhoodJosephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching momentsCath ClarkeTue 18 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a piece of art depicting motherhood, Judith Rohrmoser’s self-portrait of breastfeeding sticks two fingers up at thetradition of the Madonna with child. In her painting, Rohrmoser’s baby feeds contentedly, chubby cheeked and sleepy under damp lashes. The artist is less serene, looking directly at us, headphones clamped over her ears, eyes filled with what might be a roar of grief, or possibly an overwhelming sense that everything has changed.Rohrmoser is one of five women who agreed to be filmed at their most vulnerable in the first year of motherhood for this Austrian documentary. It’s a gentle but truthful look at new motherhood, making the point that – ignore the Renaissance artists – having a tiny baby does not put you in perpetual state of bliss. The reality is exhaustion, joy, boredom, wonder and a rush of other feelings. Director Josephine Ahnelt shoots in 16mm, her camera up close, filming with the intimacy of a home video, cutting off heads to at one point zero in on what interests her: a mother snipping her baby’s tiny fingernails.The women share their experiences in voiceover. One mother says she didn’t experience the all-encompassing love she was told she’d feel when her baby was placed on her chest; instead, it happened little by little. Another talks about the judgmental comments she gets about bottle feeding her baby after struggling to breastfeed. One woman says she didn’t believe friends that her relationship would be changed by having a baby. Now she knows.There are some incredibly touching moments: mainly it’s the little things, the bouncing and jigging or massaging chunky little baby thighs, all done with love. And sometimes it’s the glazed over look of a soldier after a week in the trenches.Waves Turn is on True Story from 21 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsParents and parentingChildbirthAustriaFamilyWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress design | Games | The Guardian
description: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Co-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever made
Content: ‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesView image in fullscreen‘You can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/Free LivesSummer games previewsGamesDressmaker – a canvas for the creativity of dream dress designCo-created by a developer and his sewing-obsessed partner, this design game is ‘the most technically challenging’ its lead programmer has ever madeJordan Erica WebberTue 18 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Jonathan Hau-Yoon wanted to make something as meaningful as the environmental strategy gameTerra Nil, he turned for inspiration to his longtime partner. Sabrina Becker had worn a dress she made herself to their very first date, and would have studied costume design abroad hadhypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome(a connective tissue disorder I also have) not put those plans on hold.The pair developed a concept around the creative decisions involved in dressmaking, like trying to fit pattern pieces on to available fabric while observing the grain line (the direction of the thread in woven fabric). Other decisions followed: a 3D model on which to place garment pieces, buttons and trims with which to decorate them, clients with commissions as creative prompts.View image in fullscreenNever run out of bobbin thread … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesHau-Yoon knew this ambitious project would benefit from the support of his employers at Free Lives. A bare-bones concept video got hundreds of thousands of views, and a prototype built with colleagues in three weeks had about 30,000 downloads, but he worried it wouldn’t be enough, that he might even have to leave a job he loved to pursue the game full-time. What convinced founder Evan Greenwood in the end was the passion of the player base. Many signed up foritch.ioaccounts just to play the prototype, and left paragraphs-long comments about how much it meant to them.And they had requests. “A surprising amount of people asked for ironing,” Becker laughs. Others wanted to be able to print out the patterns and use them in real life,Barbie Fashion Designerstyle, which isn’t possible here. “We don’t actually run a cloth simulation,” Hau-Yoon explains. Becker adds: “But you can get incredibly creative in a way that you couldn’t in real life. A lot of our players make whole paintings on the dresses, using the trims and buttons and things; they’re drawing Starry Night and the Sistine Chapel.”View image in fullscreen‘How elegant is elegant?’ … Dressmaker.Illustration: Cozy Lives/ Free LivesWhen I sew, I draft my own patterns to better fit my particular shape, so I wanted to know if Dressmaker includes this aspect. “We have a whole measurement system,” Becker says. “It is simplified, but it was really important to us to illustrate that if you’re coming in for a bespoke dress the dress should be made to fit you. So there’s this whole lattice deformer thing that allows our dress pieces to shift and scale proportionally.”Hau-Yoon says that programmer Ruan Rothmann calls Dressmaker “the most technically challenging game that he’s worked on”: “It really matters where seams are and that certain vertices align.” Other sewists can imagine what aspects have proved challenging: how the fabric stretches across a body, pattern distortion, creating gathers.Becker’s experience has been invaluable, and similarly her understanding of historical costume. Dressmaker isn’t era-specific, so as not to limit players, but it does have what she calls “a vintage feel”, looking as if it’s from “The sort of era where you would have actually gone to a dressmaker to have a dress made”. And when it came to the question of whether to branch off the story (from novelist Kerstin Hall), she knew that sewists would resent missing out: “I want to be able to make ALL of the dresses. If it’s branching and because of decisions you made you don’t get to make a wedding dress for a specific character, I would feel so gutted about that.”So what has she learned about the process of making games? “It’s all numbers and spreadsheets! At least the past two months of the work that I’ve been doing.” “It’s very difficult to capture how to score something when it’s just a vibe,” Hau-Yoon admits. “How elegant is elegant? What number describes elegance?”They hope players will appreciate their efforts, which include a whole-team sewing class arranged by Becker. “It was surprisingly Zen,” says Hau-Yoon. “Initially I was very slow and nervous, but that whirring of a sewing machine … it fades away into the background.” Players will soon be able to hear that whirr for themselves, as sound designer Jason Sutherland has painstakingly recorded Becker’s own weighty vintage Singer sewing machine, along with other related tools. “I’m obsessed with the scissors noise,” Becker smiles. “It’s so satisfying.”Dressmaker is coming to PC on 21 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vans, ghosts, sofas and a kiss from Katy Perry: artist France-Lise McGurn and her paint-everything ethos | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Tackling grief, time, parties and spaceflight, the Scottish artist uses film stills, magazine ads, family photos and even her own furniture to create a show you can settle into and figure out
Author: Eliza Goodpasture
Headline: Tackling grief, time, parties and spaceflight, the Scottish artist uses film stills, magazine ads, family photos and even her own furniture to create a show you can settle into and figure out
Content: ‘Get in my paintings and figure them out with me’ … Fun Fun, 2026, France-Lise McGurn.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist, Massimo De Carlo, London and The Modern Institute, GlasgowView image in fullscreen‘Get in my paintings and figure them out with me’ … Fun Fun, 2026, France-Lise McGurn.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist, Massimo De Carlo, London and The Modern Institute, GlasgowArt and designVans, ghosts, sofas and a kiss from Katy Perry: artist France-Lise McGurn and her paint-everything ethosTackling grief, time, parties and spaceflight, the Scottish artist uses film stills, magazine ads, family photos and even her own furniture to create a show you can settle into and figure outEliza GoodpastureTue 18 Aug 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ilove parties,” says France-Lise McGurn, “but they’re complicated, and there’s a time when you leave.” Her new show at Dundee Contemporary Arts, called The Charm Offensive, carries her dynamic, vital paintings into a new era – and on an unprecedented huge scale. Grappling with grief, the passing of time, and the paradoxes and slippery truths of modern womanhood, the work chases the desire to be present, balancing the fun of the party with the melancholy of leaving it.McGurn was born and raised in Glasgow and studied painting in Dundee, so this show is something of a homecoming. As a student, she lived three doors down from DCA. Although she knows nostalgia can be a “dirty word” among artists, McGurn says that “a melancholic grappling with the past is part of painting”. She has always worked from extensive source material, but for this show, she has allowed that archive of images to be visible to viewers.Film stills, magazine ads, family photos, and other ephemera that inspire her find their way on to the canvas for the first time. Working with a studio in Glasgow, she has the images blown up and printed on canvases, resulting in a lo-fi, retro aesthetic. Sometimes, the images are entirely obscured by paint, existing as ghosts beneath another composition. In other works, McGurn adds very little paint to the canvas, allowing the printed image to dominate.View image in fullscreen‘Grappling with the past is part of painting’ … Blow Your House Down, 2026, by France-Lise McGurn.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist, Massimo De Carlo, London and The Modern Institute, GlasgowIn one large work, Motor,an image of the van her family drove throughout her childhood is printed on the canvas. On top of it, McGurn has painted silhouettes of her young daughter and her mother, the artistRita McGurn, who died in 2015. It becomes a circular portrait of time passing, of intergenerational inheritance and legacy. As McGurn and I talk, her mother seems almost to be in the studio with us: her influence on her daughter is so evident.“She had this radical feminist idea that you don’t wait for the studio,” McGurn says. “Painting can happen around real life – and it had to.” McGurn hasn’t taken this as literally as her mother, who painted most of the inside of their family home: we sit among the more usual detritus of a working artist’s studio in east London. But the ethos of using what you have and figuring it out as you go along is fundamental to McGurn.In that vein, the DCA show also includesstufffor the first time: McGurn has transported the paint-covered sofa from her studio, hoping that visitors will feel inclined to settle into it and spend time in the space. There are painted wallets and other ephemera, partly there to revel in the luxury of having such a huge gallery space to fill with anything and everything – but also there to reaffirm her mother’s maxim that anything can be painted on. There is a spatial element, too. “I want people to come in,” she says, “and stay and spend time there and feel like it’s for them.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTouchdown … a work based on the photo of Katy Perry kissing the earth after spaceflight that went viral.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist, Massimo De Carlo, London and The Modern Institute, GlasgowSexy, dynamic female figures have always characterised McGurn’s work. She often features her own body as a reference. “It’s my body,” she says with a laugh, “and I’ll use it.” But by the time the figures reach the canvas, they have become what McGurn calls glyphs: abstracted, classical symbols of the female figure rather than portraits of an individual. She bristles at any easy reading of them as purely hedonistic and fun. “I think there is a much harder, more subversive relationship women have to their bodies now,” she says.One of the printed, archival images she includes in this show depicts Katy Perry kissing the Earth after returning from space – a photo that went viral, possibly for its absurdity. “This is an image of a woman coming down and kissing the Earth that, by going into space, she has done something to harm,” McGurn says. There is a knife-edge balance in McGurn’s work between tongue-in-cheek irreverence and deadly serious critique, which makes her paintings feel full of real-life contradictions and anomalies.Her perky pastel colour palette is often read for its surface, too. “Like, ‘Oh, how feminine!’’’ she laughs. It seems to be such a dead-end, one-liner reading: if work is feminine, that’s all it is. McGurn is as interested in that reality as she is in turning it on its head. For her, the palette she has developed comes from the materiality of her paints and the textures they produce on the canvas. Her aesthetic raises questions about the line between decoration and depth, surface and meaning, looking and being looked at.In fact, McGurn’s paintings are far more than that: they’re invitations. “Get in this painting and figure it out with me,” she says. The many paradoxes of modern life that dog us all seem to come to rest on McGurn’s canvases, tangled up but somehow in balance. Like her, the paintings exude a generous, deeply human warmth.The Charm Offensive is at Dundee Contemporary Artsfrom 22 August–15 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtExhibitionsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How architect Paul Revere Williams fought racism and changed the face of Los Angeles | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Creating homes for Frank Sinatra, Cary Grant and Lucille Ball made Williams a star. A trio of new exhibitions shows he belongs among the 20th century’s greats
Author: Paula Mejía
Headline: Creating homes for Frank Sinatra, Cary Grant and Lucille Ball made Williams a star. A trio of new exhibitions shows he belongs among the 20th century’s greats
Content: Paul R Williams standing with two men at Compton Imperial Housing Project site in 1952.Photograph: Getty Research Institute/University of Southern California School of Architecture ©Merge StudiosView image in fullscreenPaul R Williams standing with two men at Compton Imperial Housing Project site in 1952.Photograph: Getty Research Institute/University of Southern California School of Architecture ©Merge StudiosArchitectureHow architect Paul Revere Williams fought racism and changed the face of Los AngelesCreating homes for Frank Sinatra, Cary Grant and Lucille Ball made Williams a star. A trio of new exhibitions shows he belongs among the 20th century’s greatsPaula MejíaTue 18 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen you fly into theLos Angelesairport LAX, a spindly space-age contraption is the first thing that greets your eyes outside the window. Built in the early 1960s, the Theme Building – which once attracted travelers to its in-house restaurant, designed by Walt Disney Imagineering, towering above airfields – was built by a supergroup of architects whose structures helped define the city’s midcentury aesthetic: William Pereira, Welton Becket, Charles Luckman and Paul Revere Williams.‘A frightening piece to perform’: can Yoko Ono’s Cut Piece still shock?Read moreOf these architects, Williams, the first licensed Black architect in California, arguably shaped the contours of Los Angeles most deeply. In the six decades before his death in 1980, Williams completed an estimated 3,000 structures ranging from single-family residences, commercial buildings, affordable housing projects, the Los Angeles county courthouse, a reimagining of the now-razed Ambassador hotel and opulent homes for celebrities includingFrank Sinatra,Barbara StanwyckandLucille Balland Desi Arnaz. Perhaps most iconic of all is the Beverly Hills hotel; Williams led its renovation, and its recognizable curlicued sign is scrawled in Williams’s own handwriting.Without him, LA’s crown jewel of Case Study homes (a program that commissioned architects to study and build well-designed, single-family homes in an attempt to help shore up housing during the post-second world war boom), Stahl House, might have never been funded. “It was a torrid pace,” says Milton S F Curry, professor and senior associate dean, Cornell University. “I don’t know that many of the starchitects today would have that many projects.”View image in fullscreenPaul R Williams, Williams Apartment Building  perspective drawing, 1958.Photograph: Getty Research Institute/University of Southern California School of Architecture ©Della M Williams TrustDespite his prolific output and outsized role in sculpting Los Angeles, Williams’s name has, until recently, been a footnote within architecture. Beyond the distinction of being one of the first Black architects licensed in the US, Williams was known for the breadth of projects he took on, as well as the meticulousness and skill he imbued into these varied buildings. “The work is worthy of entering into the canon of major architects [such as]:Frank Lloyd Wright, Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier, Thom Mayne, Frank Gehry,” says Curry. “They deserve to be in [Williams’s] company, I’ll put it that way.”Williams is the subject of a forthcoming exhibition spread across three institutions in Los Angeles, with each show – the first of which opens on 18 August at the USC Fisher Museum of Art – focusing on a distinct facet of Williams’s life, career trajectory and societal impact. The Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s exhibition tracks the overarching scope of Williams’s work; the Getty Research Institute’s entry will tackle how Williams helped construct core components of Black Los Angeles; andUSC Fisherwill showcase many of his archival drawings in conversation with pieces by contemporary artists and architects. USC’s inclusion bears another significance: Williams is an alumnus of the school.View image in fullscreenThe Theme Building at Los Angeles international airport, in 1955, built by a team of artists including Williams.Photograph: Authenticated News/Getty ImagesBorn in 1894, Williams knew he wanted to pursue architecture by the time he was in high school. As Williams later described in the 1937 essay he wrote for The American Magazine,I Am a Negro, one of his teachers dismissed his aspirations in the field “with as much astonishment as he would have displayed had I proposed a rocket flight to Mars. ‘Who ever heard of a Negro being an architect?’ he demanded, with justice.” Williams added: “It was apparent that my personal ability weighed less in his estimation than the burden of my color. His advice – if such blank discouragement can be termed advice – was an invitation to thought.”Early in his career, Williams first became a draftsperson, then applied for and won a series of grants that didn’t disclose his race. Around the time Williams entered the field, Los Angeles’s population surged; housing construction charged ahead at a steady clip to meet demand. Williams, who began his own office, was hired to build homes in a burgeoning development, and, later, by a bevy of wealthy Angelenos, includingCary Grant, for their stately homes. Williams was known as someone who could deliver on his clients’ specifications and quirks without sacrificing quality: Sinatra, for instance, wanted the architect to build him a bachelor pad that had a button that could roll his bed out from the bedroom on to the patio. Williams’s talents extended far beyond those projects, yet a stubborn myth has long persisted that he only built single-family mansions to the stars. What truly distinguishes Williams as an architect is his attention to craftsmanship.View image in fullscreenPaul R Williams, proposed minimal cost dwelling for Excelsonite Inc, on 25 September 1959.Photograph: Getty Research Institute/University of Southern California School of Architecture ©Della M Williams TrustWhen Curry first saw the trove of Williams’s architectural drawings, which are featured in the retrospective, he was stunned by their detail. “The craft and the quality of the work is extraordinary,” says Curry, who helped curate the USC exhibition and, when he was the dean of the university’s school of architecture years back, acquired Williams’s archives there. “Clearly he had a deep knowledge of construction, constructability and material power.” In an unusual turn for architects at the time, Williams worked across multiple genres simultaneously and bore a penchant for distinctive eclecticism. (He also came to be known for his striking take on spiral staircases). “It’s a dimension of him and the work that deserves to be brought into focus,” says Curry. “And becomes a part of the total story and the arc of his career.”From Felix the Cat to MTV: MoMA explores a century of animationRead moreAdditionally, Williams helped build one of the first public housing projects in the US, Langston Terrace Dwellings; advocated for multifamily housing projects; and tinkered with aluminum prototypes considered experimental at the time. He also worked to deliver affordable housing to an emerging Black middle class, and to Black GIs, during a time of racist redlining policies.The trio of Williams shows constitute the first major retrospective of any Black architect. To Curry, it’s indicative of “how far behind we are in understanding, recognizing, analyzing, theorizing about the legacy of Black people’s contributions to the built environment in this country, in a time where we’re facing efforts to extinguish Black cultural production”. While reintroducing Williams to the public, the exhibition aims to make his archives accessible so that scholarly research might yield as-yet-unrealized dimensions to his work – such as his inventive use of color and the furniture he designed. “Whenever you open up archives, unexpected things happen,” says Curry. “Stories and narratives emerge that you didn’t know about.”Paul R Williams: An Architect Considered is at USC Fisher Museum ofArtin Los Angeles until 13 March 2027Explore more on these topicsArchitectureArtLos AngelesExhibitionsMuseumsCaliforniaWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Transylvania beyond the spooky castles: a family adventure in Romania’s mountains | Romania holidays | The Guardian
description: Forget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitude
Author: Graeme Green
Headline: Forget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitude
Content: High in the mountains of Harghita County, Romania. All photographs: Graeme GreenView image in fullscreenHigh in the mountains of Harghita County, Romania. All photographs: Graeme GreenRomania holidaysTransylvania beyond the spooky castles: a family adventure in Romania’s mountainsForget the vampire tales – the Eastern Carpathians deliver dramatic peaks, roaming bears and deep solitudeGraeme GreenTue 18 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the sun disappears behind the high tree line, our campfire spits and crackles. Four plump trout are sizzling on a flame-heated slab of rock, a cooking technique used by people in the Gurghiu mountains, part of Transylvania’s Eastern Carpathians, for centuries. Apart from gentle birdsong, it’s the only sound up here, 1,550 metres above sea level and far from any town or village.“This area is very wild,” says Samir Teslovan, who drove us up through the densely forested peaks from his guesthouse in Toplița. “When I come here to the mountains, I charge my battery, charge my soul. I feel free, like the wind.”Romania mapSitting on the edge of a fragrant forest of spruce, fir, beech and pine, our view stretches over the valley to misty mountains receding in layers to the horizon. Samir points to a far-off peak in the east, a pyramid on a ragged ridge. “That’s Ukraine, maybe 200km,” he tells us. Then, pointing west: “That way, 400km, is Hungary.” The forest is still home to bears, wolves and lynx, but it’s the solitude that brings him here. “I prefer wild zones, where no one goes,” he says. “There are places here that nobody knows.”Across the vast forests and mountains of Harghita County in central Romania, there are many places that nobody knows. In fact, the whole region has flown under the radar of international travellers – 85% of visitors come from Romania itself, which feels bizarre when you discover the wonders here, as we did on a 12-day family road trip, staying at self-catering lodges and cabins along the way.double quotation markA holiday here costs a fraction of what it would in the Dolomites or the AlpsA holiday here costs a fraction of what it would in the Dolomites or the French or Swiss Alps. Even better, it’s remarkably uncrowded, which makes for a more authentic-feeling adventure.The region previously belonged to the Austro-Hungarian empire, butTransylvania, including Harghita,was awarded to Romania after the first world war.The local population remains largelyof Hungarian descent(about 85%), with most people identifying as Székelys (Szeklers), a distinct, Hungarian-speaking cultural group. And the Hungarian influence can be seen in the region’s food, from goulash tokürtőskalács(chimney cakes), and in the ornately carvedszékelykapu(wooden gates) outside houses.View image in fullscreenHarghita has one of the highest densities of bears in EuropeWe pick up a hire car in Brașov and drive north, in the opposite direction to Bran Castle and all the vampiric hoopla. Soon, we’re enjoying wide, open countryside, sharing the road with farmers on horse-drawn carts and passing churches with silvery spires and white storks nesting on top of electricity poles.Our first base is Sâncrăieni, staying inOrganicle Lodge,a lovely, quiet cabin with an upstairs spruce bedroom, spacious lounge and kitchen.While our four-year-old son races around the garden with the owners’ cats and French bulldog, we rest on our wooden deck, drinking Harghita beer, looking over a paddock, where a brown horse and white pony gambol and graze, and out towards the Harghita mountains. In the evenings, swifts flit about and white storks glide across pink skies.double quotation markWe spot a mother and cub ambling through the forest and sniffing the air by the roadside‘A muddy ride into Romania’s dreamy countryside’: cycling the Via TransilvanicaRead moreWe spend time at nearby Lacul Sfânta Ana (Saint Anne Lake), the only volcanic lake in Romania, wandering first throughMohoş Peat Bog, where the trees and curious plant life make it feel like stepping back into the ice age, then take a boat trip on the sparkling lake, surrounded on all sides by shades of forest green. In the evening, we head toMedveles Székelyföld observatory, where we watch four bears feeding on corn that’s laid out for them; Harghita hasone of the highest bear population densities in Europe. The best sighting of our trip, though, comes during our drive to the lake, when we spot a mother and cub ambling through the forest and sniffing the air by the roadside.Heading farther north, we spend a couple of days atVila Adela, near Lacu Roșu (Red Lake), an orange house decorated with red geraniums, with fairy houses, windmills, animal statues, see-saw and slide in the garden. Our bedroom looks out on to the majestic limestone massif Suhardul Mic.Later, we drive through Bicaz Gorge, gazing up at massive rock walls and structures, dominated byPiatra Altarului (Altar Rock), the summit marked with a metal cross. Stopping to climb the tower of medieval manor houseLázár Castleen route, we reach Toplița at the far north of the county, staying atCasa Samir, where Samir and his son David run wildlife photography and nature tours.View image in fullscreenReflected glory … lakeside in HarghitaAfter a steep and bumpy afternoon drive, we go hiking in the serene Gurghiu mountains. Golden sunlight winks through the trees as David points out the tracks of wild animals as we walk to where his father has parked and started a campfire. Along with trout, Samir serves a homemade salty sheep’s cheese, calledburduf, and lamb sausage, both from his farm, and a bottle ofpalinka, a warming plum brandy. “I’ve been coming here all my life,” he tells us. “My grandfather and great-grandfather came here. I listen to the silence and the sounds of the forest, the birds and wild animals.”Looping back around through the county, we make one final stop atTurul Guesthouse, a row of neat, two-storey, wooden lodges with hot tubs and a big trampoline. We wander among detailed models of Transylvanian castles, palaces, and churches, including Bran Castle, atMini Transylvania Parkand large-scale, moving models of ants, butterflies and the like at neighbouringInsect Park.One morning, we hike up to the top of Harghita Mădăraș, at 1,801m (5,909ft) the highest peak in the Harghita mountains. Thunder rumbles and rain drenches us, as we reach the gold, white and blue Székely flag, the reportedly magnificent views blocked out by cloud that gives a sombre, funereal atmosphere to the cairns, flags, crosses and other memorials clustered around the summit.We watch more bears at a tucked-awayforest hideoutside the Băile Homorod resort, including two mighty females who look as if they might clash over the feeding area, and spend one of our last afternoons at Zetea lake, where we take out a kayak. “It’s really a beautiful experience to be on the water,” Előd Tímár, co-owner of KayaKing, tells us. “Bears sometimes come to drink on the shore.”Paddling south towards a forested peninsula,we’re surrounded on all sides by swaying trees.We pause in the vast expanse of open water and put down the paddles to float and drift for a while, and there it is again: a glorious, battery-charging feeling of peace, nature and being free, like the wind.The trip was provided byVisit Harghita. Graeme stayed atOrganicle Lodge(from £75 a night),Vila Adela(£50),Casa Samir(£43B&B)which offers mountain adventures from £94 per person, andTurul Guesthouse(£87).Bear-watching atMedveles Székelyföld£35pp and atBăile Homorod£25pp.KayakingwithKayaKingfrom £6.50 per hourExplore more on these topicsRomania holidaysWildlife holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cool as a cucumber: recipes and tips to save you from cooking in a heatwave | Chefs | The Guardian
description: When ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook experts
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: When ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook experts
Content: Take heat out of the equation withThomasina Miers’ tomato toasts with smoky sesame harissa salsa.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Rachel Vere. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenTake heat out of the equation withThomasina Miers’ tomato toasts with smoky sesame harissa salsa.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Rachel Vere. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Kitchen aideChefsCool as a cucumber: recipes and tips to save you from cooking in a heatwaveWhen ovens and stovetops just won’t do, turn to loaded toasts, open sandwiches, cold noodles and smashed cucumbers, say our no-cook expertsAnna BerrillTue 18 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s too hot to turn on the oven or stove. What can I make for dinner that’s still substantial?Mark, via emailThis sounds like a job for Lucy Carr-Ellison, ofTart London, who is fully functioning in a no-oven household. “We moved in last year and there’s an Aga, which was amazing in winter, but we can’t have it on in summer,” she says, so toast toppers have become a crucial category of cooking: “Try rubbing toasts with garlic, adding a bit of olive oil, some grated tomatoes, lots of salt and tinned anchovies.”Otherwise, Mark could do away with the toaster and get some focaccia, suggests Jamie Pickles, chef/co-owner ofStowandThe Trof, both in Manchester: “Mix picked brown crab meat with mayo, lemon juice and mustard, and spread that over the bread.” Next, combine the picked white meat with chopped chives and coriander, lemon juice, creme fraiche and black pepper. “Mix through some tinned sweetcorn, spread that over the brown crab mayo and finish with watercress.”No oven required: Alexina Anatole’s quick and easy no-heat recipesRead moreA kettle won’t add heat to your home, either. “I makea lotof rice noodle bowls,” says Alexandra Dudley, author ofCooking Made Simple, who keeps them in the fridge as the temperatures rise. “Soak the noodles in hot water while you make a dressing of peanut butter, miso, tahini, sesame oil, garlic and lime juice or rice-wine vinegar, then mix the two with cooked prawns from the supermarket and some smashed cucumbers.” Cool and crunchy cukes are also a go-to round at Pickles’, where they’re marinated for a “big punch of flavour” and served with salmon and rice: “Roughly chop a cucumber, throw it in a tub and add soy sauce, lemon juice, sesame oil, fish sauce and chilli crisp,” he says. “Put on the lid, seal, shake and put in the fridge to do its thing.” Some smoked salmon would be just the ticket alongside: pile it into bowls with cooked rice (“jasmine, ideally”), then finish with sesame seeds, chopped coriander, a touch of lime, plus the cucumbers, of course.When it’s all too hot to handle, it’s worth widening the parameters of pesto. “Switch out pine nuts for more affordable walnuts, and the same goes for the cheese,” says Pickles, who uses any firm cheese that takes his fancy. Blend the two with fresh herbs (“basil or flat-leaf parsley”), olive oil, a bit of garlic and lemon juice, plus ice to emulsify. Then get some courgettes: “Slice into strips using a peeler, dress with the pesto, then leave the courgettes to soak up all of that flavour.” Finish with torn mozzarella, freshly ground black pepper and pickled raisins – “they’ll bring a pop of life”.If all else fails, the assembly dinner is a classic move. “Learn to love your deli section,” campaigns Dudley, who more often than not has jars of artichokes, capers, olives and peppers to hand, ready to chop and chuck into a bowl with cooked lentils (“tinned or from a pouch”). Crumble over feta and there’s nothing better on a summer’s night. Or any night, really.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Max Rocha’s recipes for confit trout salad and grilled courgette with apricot, stracciatella and roasted almonds | Food | The Guardian
description: Two Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heat
Content: Max Rocha’s confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenMax Rocha’s confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodMax Rocha’s recipes for confit trout salad and grilled courgette with apricot, stracciatella and roasted almondsTwo Café Cecilia stalwarts that are just the thing for the summer heatMax RochaTue 18 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years after Café Cecilia opened, a handful of dishes have become permanent fixtures, returning to the menu time and again – and this confit trout salad is definitely one of them. During the recent heatwaves, we’ve naturally shifted towards dishes that are best served at room temperature or slightly warm, and both of these recipes reflect that approach. They’re designed to serve two, but can just as easily be scaled up for a larger group. And almost everything can be prepared in advance, making them ideal for entertaining at home.Confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook45 minServes2For the pickles1 tbsp sugar100ml white-wine vinegar1 tsp salt½ cucumber, finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)5 breakfast radishes,finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)For the trout2 trout fillets(about 150g each), skin onSalt and pepper300ml sunflower oil200ml olive oil3 sprigs thyme2 garlic cloves, peeledFor the salad6 tbsp good-quality olive oil2 tbsp dijon mustard2 tbsp white-wine vinegar1 bunch watercress(about 80g)Juice of ½ lemonExtra-virgin olive oil, to finish4 sprigs chervil, leaves picked4 sprigs dill, leaves pickedFirst, make the pickled cucumber by combining 100ml water with the sugar, vinegar and salt in a saucepan, then gradually increase the heat until the sugar dissolves. Pour this over the cucumber and radishes in a bowl, and set aside.Season the trout, then leave to sit at room temperature for 15 minutes.Meanwhile, place the sunflower oil, olive oil, thyme and garlic in a pan and heat to 50C (122F) (if you don’t have have a kitchen thermometer, the outside of the pan should feel warm to the touch). Pat the trout dry with kitchen paper, then lay the fish in the warm oil and keep it between 50-55C (120-130F) for 15-20 minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool a little, then peel off and discard the skin (this is easier to do while the fish is still warm) and leave to cool fully.Combine the olive oil, mustard and white-wine vinegar. Drain the pickles, then put in a bowl with the watercress and one and a half tablespoons of the vinaigrette (save the rest for other salads in the week). Mix and taste for seasoning, then add a squeeze of lemon juice, a few extra drops of olive oil and a pinch of sea salt and black pepper as required.Flake each trout fillet into four or five pieces, then divide half of the fish between two plates. Top with half the watercress and pickle salad, lay on the remaining trout, followed by the rest of the pickle mix. Top with the picked herbs, finish with a pinch of sea salt and serve.Grilled courgette, apricot, stracciatella and roast almondsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenMax Rocha’s grilled courgette, apricot, stracciatella and roast almonds.Prep10 minCook20 minServes21 green courgetteExtra-virgin olive oil1tsp balsamic vinegarZest of 1 lemon½ bunch basil, leaves picked1 garlic clove,peeled and thinly slicedSalt and black pepper2 ripe apricots200gstracciatellaFor the dressing45g whole roast almonds3tbsp olive oil1 tspred-wine vinegar1 tsp fresh rosemary leaves, choppedSlice the courgette lengthways into thin strips, brush with olive oil and grill in a hot griddle panfor about two minutes per side, until charred.Prepare the marinade by putting three tablespoons of olive oil, the balsamic vinegar, lemon zest, basil, garlic and some salt and pepper in a bowl. Fold in the courgettes until evenly coated.Pound the almonds in a mortar (or roughly chop them), then put in a bowl with the olive oil, vinegar, rosemary and some salt and pepper.Halve, stone and slice the apricots into thin half-moons. Spoon half the stracciatella on to each plate, followed by the courgettes. Finish with the apricots, dribble a tablespoon of the almond dressing over each portion and serve at once.Max Rocha is chef-owner ofCafé Cecilia, London E8Explore more on these topicsFoodFishSaladVegetablesMain courseFruitCheeserecipesShareReuse this content
